Hearing this, the guardians of the kingdom of Arles surrendered the kingdom to the king, on the condition or agreement that he would return the kingdom to the king of the Romans, or make peace with him, at a suitable time. The king of France, having received the kingdom, then joined his daughter to him in marriage.

units.la: Audiens rex Angliæ, quòd rex Franciæ regnum Arelatense regi Romanorum subtraxisset atque filiæ tradidisset: mandauit regi Romanorum Adolfo, quòd si vellet eum iuuare, quò ciuitatem quam sibi rex Franciæ subtraxerat, recuperaret: vellet eum, vt Arelatense regnum recuperaret, cum propria persona, cum hominibus, cum pecunia fideliter adiuuare. Audiens hæc rex Romanorum, gauisus Angliæ regi mandauit, quòd eum vellet fideliter adiuuare. Insuper mandauit, quòd homines multos habere posset, si eis victualia ministraret. Tunc Rex Anglię misit regi Romanorum xxx millia Marcarum (vt retulit qui vidit) vt hominibus armatis necessaria ministraret. Acta sunt haec anno Domini M. cc. xcv i.
units.tr: When the king of England heard that the king of France had withdrawn the kingdom of Arles from the king of the Romans, Adolf, and had handed it over to his daughter, he sent word to the king of the Romans that if he would like to help him, so that he might recover the town which the king of France had taken from him, he would wish him to help him faithfully, in person, with men and money, to recover the kingdom of Arles. Hearing this, the king of the Romans, rejoicing, sent word to the king of England that he would gladly help him faithfully. He added that he could have many men if they were supplied with provisions. Then the king of England sent the king of the Romans thirty thousand marks (as one who saw it reported), so that he could supply the armed men with what they needed. These things were done in the year of the Lord 1295.

units.la: Eo tempore rex Franciæ comitem Brabantiæ & cæteros adiutores regis Anglię, pro viribus impugnauit, & magna suis intulit inimicis. Venerunt́ q; nudi bubunes, & agros bene seminatos euerterunt, & semina destruxerunt, & eos propter eorum multitudinem nullus poterat impedire.
units.tr: At that time the king of France attacked, as far as he could, the count of Brabant and the other allies of the king of England, and inflicted great harm on his enemies. They came naked, like peasants, and overturned well-sown fields and destroyed the seed, and no one could stop them because of their numbers.

units.la: Auditis his rex Angliæ transfretauit, & ad partes nostras, id est, in Brabantiam ad adiuuandum suos adiutores, in die decollat. S. Ioannis baptistæ, cum quingentis nauibus magnis, & sex millibus militum noscitur peruenisse. Tulit & pecuniam multis hominibus copiosam. Tulit enim secum septem millia librarum singulis diebus, quinq; annis exercitui ministrandam.
units.tr: Hearing of this, the king of England crossed the sea, and it is known that he arrived in our regions, that is, in Brabant, to help his allies, on the feast of the Beheading of St John the Baptist, with five hundred great ships and six thousand soldiers. He also brought a copious sum of money for many men. For he carried with him seven thousand pounds to be paid out to the army every day for five years.

units.la: Cumq; rex Romanorum pecuniam regis Angliæ accepisset, misit de Alsatia in ciuitatem milites probos, qui Gallicorum insultus pro posse impedirent. Cumque septimanis aliquot fideliter laborassent, & impetum Gallorum fideliter impedissent: ciues eos odisse coeperunt, quia filias & vxores carnaliter dilexerunt. Ciues de communi consilio regi Franciæ mandauerunt, quòd si vellet eos de inimicis suis, id est, hospitibus, quos rex Romanorum in ciuitatem suam obtuitionem collocauerat, liberare, interficere vellent eos, eisq; interfectis ciuitatem suam in ipsius tradere potestatem. Rex Franciæ respondit: Facite quod dicitis, & vestram voluntatem in omnibus adimplebo. Tunc ciues dixerunt: Domine, tali die milites vestros ad nostram ciuitatem dirigatis, & nos hospites nostros ad vos exire faciemus, & ipsis captiuatis vel interfectis, ad nostram ciuitatem veniatis, & eam in potestatem vestram dabimus. Ciues vt praeordinauerunt, per omnia compleuerunt.
units.tr: When the king of the Romans had received the money of the king of England, he sent from Alsace into the city proven soldiers, who were to resist the attacks of the French as far as they could. And after they had faithfully laboured for some weeks and had faithfully held back the assault of the French, the citizens began to hate them, because they loved their daughters and wives carnally. By common counsel the citizens sent word to the king of France that if he wished to free them from their enemies, that is, from the guests whom the king of the Romans had placed in their city for protection, they would be willing to kill them, and once they were killed, to hand their city over to his power. The king of France replied: "Do what you say, and I will fulfil your wishes in everything." Then the citizens said: "Lord, send your soldiers to our city on such and such a day, and we will bring our guests out to you, and once they have been captured or killed, come to our city, and we will give it into your power." The citizens carried out everything exactly as they had planned.

units.la: In hac interfectione occisus est Dominus Theobaldus, miles iuuenis, virtuosus, filius filiæ Comitis Phirretarum, & filius Conradi Wernheri de Hadstat, cum aliis gloriosis.
units.tr: In this slaughter Lord Theobald was killed, a young knight, virtuous, son of the daughter of the Count of Pfirt and son of Conrad Werner of Hadstat, together with other distinguished men.

units.la: Post haec Franciæ ciuitati nouos praepositos atq; magistratus praefecit, eisq; dicebat: Omnes maiores huius ciuitatis, mihi non sua dederunt, & Dominum suum spoliauerunt, morte digni sunt: mihi quoq; cras idem facient. Vnde perfidos capiatis, res q; eorum confiscetis, eos q; de medio tollatis, & ciuitatem funditus euertatis, & regis voluntatem subito compleuerunt.
units.tr: After this he set new prefects and magistrates over the city of France and said to them: "All the greater men of this city have not given me what was mine, and they have despoiled their lord; they deserve death, and tomorrow they will do the same to me. Therefore seize the treacherous, confiscate their goods, remove them from the midst, and overthrow the city utterly." They quickly carried out the king's will.

units.la: Rex Romanorum volens adiuuare regem Anglorum, in Alsatiam perrexit, D. Theobaldum Comitem Phirretarum aduocatum terræ constituit, & ad inferiores partes descendere festinabat. Cum autem in Selecistat peruenisset, dicebatur ei, quòd episcopus Argentinensis insidias sibi posuisset, & quòd regem Franciæ iuuare vellet: per partes episcopi descendere non audebat, sed se in Brisacum transtulit, & in naui cum paucis descendit, in Germisheim peruenit, & sic de manibus episcopi se defendit.
units.tr: The King of the Romans, wishing to help the King of the English, went into Alsace, appointed Lord Theobald, Count of Pfirt, advocate of the land, and hastened to go down to the lower parts. When he had come to Selestat, he was told that the bishop of Strasbourg had laid an ambush for him and that he wished to help the King of France. He did not dare to go down through the bishop's lands, but transferred himself to Breisach, went down by ship with a few men, reached Germersheim, and so defended himself from the bishop's hands.

units.la: His gestis, mandauit rex comiti Phirretarum aduocato terræ, vt regem Franciæ fideliter impugnaret, quia & ipse in inferioribus partibus eum vellet impugnare, quod & fideliter adimpleuit. Congregauit enim exercitum magnum, perrexit ad Gallos, & eos atrociter infestauit. Cognati sui venerunt, eumque supplicciter rogauerunt, vt eos à suis proprietatibus non deleret, insuper quinque millia librarum Tullensium porrexerunt. Ipse eorum precibus acquieuit, & ad propria redijt festinanter.
units.tr: After these events, the king ordered the Count of Pfirt, advocate of the land, to attack the King of France faithfully, since the king himself wished to attack him in the lower parts; this he also carried out faithfully. For he gathered a great army, marched against the French, and savagely harassed them. His kinsmen came and earnestly begged him not to destroy them in their properties, and moreover offered five thousand pounds of Toul. He yielded to their prayers and returned hastily to his own lands.

units.la: Rex Romanorum cum de Alsatia peruenisset ad terram inferiorem, congregauit exercitum, vt cū rege Angliæ terrā regis Franciæ pro viribus demoliretur. Audiens hęc Papa, compassus hominibus, timęs eorum occisione, misit duos Legatos & Magistrum .
units.tr: When the King of the Romans had come from Alsace to the lower land, he gathered an army, so that with the King of England he might pull down the land of the King of France with all his strength. Hearing this, the Pope, moved with compassion for the people and fearing their slaughter, sent two legates and a master.

units.la: Traditores etiam hostis insidiis. Comes in Phirretarum prafectus Alsatia Caesareus. Adolfus Ca far Gallos infestat. Pax inter reges Bonifacius facit Pontificis auctoritate conciliata. ordinis fratrum Prædicatorum, & Magistrum ordinis Minorum, ad Reges suprà memoratos, vt inter eos ad tempus facerent pacem, vel simpliciter concordarent. Cardinales cum duobus Magistris Ordinum litem regum, quibusdam nobilibus commiserunt, vt ipsi infra annum compositionem amicabilem inuenirent, quam Papa postea confirmauit.
units.tr: Traitors also by the ambush of the enemy. The Count of Pfirt, prefect of Alsace for Caesar. Adolf Caesar harasses the French. Peace between the kings, brought about by the authority of Boniface the Pope. Of the order of the Preaching friars, and the Master of the order of the Minors, sent to the kings mentioned above, that they should make peace between them for a time, or simply reconcile. The cardinals, with two masters of the orders, committed the dispute of the kings to certain nobles, that they themselves should find an amicable settlement within a year, which the Pope afterwards confirmed.

units.la: Præfecti Imperialis Alsatiæ res gestæ.
units.tr: The deeds of the imperial prefect of Alsace.

units.la: ANNO M. CC. XCVII, Comes Friburgensis cepit ante festum sancti Martini plus quàm XL colonos imperij fraudulenter, diuites & honestos. Ex his fame quosdam perire sine omni gratia faciebat. Ex hoc aduocatus Alsatiæ comes Phirretarum, ciuitatibus Imperij mandauit, quatenus ad ipsum prope Brisacum peruenirent, imperij pauperes vindicare, & res comitis Friburgensis pro viribus deuastare. Qui circa festum Martini plures villas fortes, quas exercitus nullus vnquam inuaserat, intrauerunt, & fodinas argenti destruxerunt, & cultores eorum coegerunt. Ad Friburgenses venerunt, sed eos laedere noluerunt, quòd cum ipsis pacem habere fideliter promiserunt.
units.tr: In the year 1297, before the feast of St Martin, the Count of Freiburg seized more than forty farmers of the empire, wealthy and respectable men, by fraud. Some of these he caused to die of hunger without any mercy. On account of this the advocate of Alsace, the Count of Pfirt, ordered the cities of the empire to come to him near Breisach, to vindicate the empire's poor and to lay waste the Count of Freiburg's property as far as they could. Around the feast of Martin they entered several strong villages which no army had ever attacked, destroyed the silver mines, and forced their workers to leave. They came to the men of Freiburg but did not wish to harm them, because they had faithfully promised to keep the peace with them.

units.la: Anno M. CC. XCVIII, circa purificationem pauperes quinq; mercatores Argentinenses Hagenoiam transfuerunt, quos ciues ceperunt, & Argentinensibus reddere noluerunt. De consilio autem episcopi Conradi de Liechtenberg Haginoiam obsidere firmiter proponebant. Deliberatione super hoc facta, misit episcopus Argentinensis Columbarienfibus literas, continentes, quòd ciues Argentinenses Haginoiam obsidere proponerent: propterea quòd ciues eorum coepissent, & eos reddere noluissent. Ego verò quia fidelitatem eis seruare promisi, non eos audeo relinquere in hac parte, nec propter hoc volo imperialem inuadere potestatem. Columbarienses episcopo mandauerunt: Amici vestri fuimus, semper sumus, & esse volumus, in nullo vos laedere cupientes. Si autem Dominus noster vos laedere, & nos in adiutorium suum vocare voluerit, ipsum adiuuabimus diligenter, vestram super hoc indignationem minimè formidantes.
units.tr: In the year 1298, about the Purification, five poor merchants of Strasbourg crossed over to Haguenau; the citizens of Haguenau seized them and refused to return them to Strasbourg. On the advice of Bishop Conrad of Lichtenberg, the Strasbourgers firmly resolved to besiege Haguenau. After deliberating on this, the bishop of Strasbourg sent a letter to the Colmarians stating that the citizens of Strasbourg intended to besiege Haguenau, because the citizens of Haguenau had begun it and refused to give back their men. "But since I have promised to keep faith with them, I dare not abandon them in this matter, nor do I wish, on account of this, to invade imperial power." The Colmarians replied to the bishop: "We have been your friends, we always are, and we wish to remain so, desiring in no way to harm you. But if our lord wishes to harm you and calls us to his aid, we will help him diligently, not at all fearing your indignation on this account."

units.la: Ciues Argentinenses v Idus Februarij, vt obsiderent Haginoiam, communiter exiuerunt, & prima nocte in via media pernoctabant. Sequenti die cum hominum multitudine peruenerunt. Cùm igitur ciuitatem paucis diebus obsedissent, & duo per ignem suburbia deleuissent, & aliquot homines occidissent: tunc quidam de Hagenoia multitudinem ciuium Argentinensium intrauerunt, & quosdam vulnerauerunt, aliquos occiderunt, & ad propria redierunt.
units.tr: The citizens of Strasbourg set out together on the fifth day before the Ides of February, to besiege Haguenau, and spent the first night on the middle of the road. The next day they arrived with a multitude of men. When they had besieged the city for a few days, and had destroyed two suburbs by fire and killed some men, then certain men of Haguenau attacked the multitude of Strasbourg citizens, wounded some, killed some, and returned to their homes.

units.la: Audiens haec comes Phirretarum, Imperij ciuitates conuocauit, & villas cum vallibus Argentinensis episcopi cum multis millibus deuastauit. Vallem Sultzmattin igni tradidit. Festo Valentini etiam Burggrauius castrum suum in eius tradidit potestatem. Coemiterium in Gebliswire destruxit, & vinum ex vasis effudit, & coemiteria Morsuilre & Chilishofen destruxit. Ciues verò in Eginsheim suburbium suum proprium exusserunt. Suburbium rubeum Rubiacense deleuit, & villam Suntheim, & domum dominorum Teutonicorum, scilicet hospitium aduocati Imperij, bubones incenderunt, & à suis defendere non valebant. Post haec ad Sanctam Crucem perrexerunt, syluam praeciderunt, & castrum cum multitudine hominum obsiderunt. Post Triburium turrim ligneam altam fecerunt, & ad fossatum cum violentia pertraxerunt, videntes interiores, quòd castrum defendere non valerent, castrum cum quibusdam conditionibus voluntariè tradiderunt. Post haec episcopus Argentinensis intellexit in Rodisheim ortam seditionem, venit cum hominibus ad vnam portam, & vna partium tradidit sibi ciuitatem.
units.tr: Hearing this, the Count of Pfirt summoned the cities of the empire and, with many thousands, laid waste the villages and valleys of the bishop of Strasbourg. He gave the valley of Sulzmatt to the fire. On the feast of Valentine, the burgrave also surrendered his castle into his power. He destroyed the cemetery at Gebweiler, poured out the wine from the casks, and destroyed the cemeteries of Morschwiller and Kilchhofen. The citizens burned their own suburb at Egisheim. He destroyed the red suburb of Rouffach, and the village of Sundheim, and the house of the Teutonic lords, namely the lodging of the imperial advocate; the oxen they set on fire, and could not defend them from their own people. After this they went to Heiligenkreuz, cut down the forest, and besieged the castle with a multitude of men. Behind Dreibrunnen they built a high wooden tower and dragged it with force to the ditch; the men inside, seeing that they could not defend the castle, voluntarily surrendered it on certain conditions. After this the bishop of Strasbourg learned that a sedition had arisen in Rosheim; he came with men to one gate, and one part of the city handed the town over to him.

units.la: De reprobatione Adolfi Cæsaris, & electione Alberti Habspurgensis ducis Austriæ in regem Romanorum.
units.tr: On the deposition of Adolf Caesar and the election of Albert, Duke of Austria of Habsburg, as King of the Romans.

units.la: QVIDAM ex principibus electorum Regis, scilicet, archiepiscopus Maguntinus, dux Saxoniæ, & dux de Brandeburc, videntes quòd Adolfus rex Romanorum nollet nõllet regnum secundum eorum regere voluntatem, taliter sibi mutuo loquebantur. Adolfus rex pauper est in rebus pariter & amicis: stultus est: regnum sub eo breviter deficiet, in diuitiis & honore. Tunc vnus eorum dixit: Necesse est eius solutio procuretur. Alter dixit: mittamus Duci Austriæ defectus regis, rogantes, vt ad curiam nuntios mittat, literas nostras cum defectibus regis secum deferat, eius absolutionem promoueat diligenter. Dicatur etiam Duci, quod vt rex noster efficiatur, omnes in eum pariter consentimus. Tertius dixit: Sanum hoc consilium subitò compleatur. Principes hi duci Austriæ voluntatem suam subitò transmiserunt. Dux Austriæ literis his ac nuntijs visis, gauisus est valde.
units.tr: Some of the princes-electors of the king, namely the Archbishop of Mainz, the Duke of Saxony and the Margrave of Brandenburg, seeing that King Adolf would not rule the kingdom according to their wishes, spoke to one another in this way: "King Adolf is poor both in resources and in friends; he is foolish. Under him the kingdom will soon fail, both in wealth and in honour." Then one of them said: "His removal must be arranged." Another said: "Let us send the Duke of Austria the king's shortcomings, asking him to send envoys to the court, carrying our letter with the king's failings, and to press diligently for his deposition. Let the Duke also be told that we all agree together to make him our king." A third said: "Let this sound plan be carried out at once." The princes at once sent their wishes to the Duke of Austria. When the Duke saw this letter and these messengers, he rejoiced greatly.

units.la: Post hæc misit dux Austriæ cognato suo domino comiti de Hegirloch literas ac nuntios, mandans sibi, quatenus ad ipsum veniret festinanter. Comes Albertus cognatus Ducis voluntatem eius voluntarius adimpleuit. Comes Albertus cùm ad ducis præsentiam peruenisset, dicebat: Ecce domine, adsum, quid placet vobis, faciam? Qui dixit: Cognate ecce xv i millia marcarum pecuniam suscipias, Romam velociter pergas, & literas principum electorum regis, quas pro regis electione Papæ transmittunt, vt sigillentur, promoueas diligenter. Is Romam adijt, iussaq; complevit: Papæ Cardinalibusq; causam pro qua venerat, recitauit. Qui (vt dixit) literas quasdam tradiderunt; & ad propria pergere permiserunt. Tenorem literarum omnis homo simpliciter ignorauit. Hæ literæ Papæ, supradictis electoribus regis subitò transmittuntur.
units.tr: After this the Duke of Austria sent letters and messengers to his kinsman, Count of Hegirloch, ordering him to come to him quickly. Count Albert, the Duke's kinsman, willingly carried out his wishes. When Count Albert had come into the Duke's presence, he said: "Behold, my lord, I am here. What pleases you? What shall I do?" The Duke said: "Kinsman, take here fifteen thousand marks of money, go quickly to Rome, and diligently see to it that the letters which the princes-electors of the king are sending to the Pope concerning the election of the king are sealed." He went to Rome and did as he was told. He set out to the Pope and the cardinals the matter for which he had come. They (as he said) handed over certain letters and allowed him to return home. Nobody at all knew the contents of the letters. These letters were at once sent on to the aforementioned electors of the king.

units.la: Principes his visis literis Papæ, conuenerunt, & colloquium seu Curiam in festo sanctorum Philippi & Iacobi pro regni negotijs edixerunt, & regem Adolfum, & ducem specialiter vocauerunt.
units.tr: When the princes had seen the Pope's letters, they met, and on the feast of Saints Philip and James they called an assembly or diet concerning the affairs of the kingdom, and summoned King Adolf and the Duke by name.

units.la: Audiens hæc Adolfus rex, nuntios misit ad Curiam, vt literas ducis Austriæ seu principum electorum regis irritas facerent aut delerent. Cùm nuntij regis ad Curiam peruenissent, & Papæ regis negotia reuelassent, taliter respondit: Neque dux Austriæ neque principes ad petitiones quas porrexerunt à me literas poterant impetrare. Si autem literas aliquas obtinuerunt, hoc per me non fecerunt: quia hoc dicme penitus ignorare, & verbis meis credatis, dicatisq; securè Regi, vt veniat ad me, & ipsum in Cæsarem consecrabo. Auditis his, nuntij regis ad propria redierunt.
units.tr: When King Adolf heard this, he sent envoys to the court to annul or destroy the letters of the Duke of Austria and of the princes-electors of the king. When the king's envoys reached the court and had disclosed the king's affairs to the Pope, he replied as follows: "Neither the Duke of Austria nor the princes were able to obtain letters from me in response to the petitions they put forward. But if they have obtained any letters, they have not done so through me, for I know nothing of this at all. Believe my words, and tell the king confidently that he should come to me, and I will consecrate him as Caesar." Having heard this, the king's envoys returned home.

units.la: Comes Albertus de Haigerloch, cognatus ducis Austriæ, cùm literas obtentis in Curia Duci demonstrasset, & eisdem postea principibus, electoribus regis tradidisset, ciuitatibus quæ sunt in Sueuia damna multipliciter inferebat. Quod cùm per tempus sustinuissent, & defendere minimè potuissent, conuenerunt & coniurauerunt, fidelitatem sibi mutuam promittentes. Post hæc simul egressi, castellum quoddam pariter obsederunt, violenter obtinuerunt, & totaliter destruxerunt. Post hæc ciuitates audaces effectæ, res Comitis viriliter impugnabant, expugnatisque quatuor castellis, funditus euerterunt, & cum de rebus proprijs fugere coëgerunt.
units.tr: Count Albert of Haigerloch, the Duke of Austria's kinsman, after he had shown the letters obtained at the court to the Duke, and afterwards handed them to the same princes, the electors of the king, inflicted damage in many ways on the cities in Swabia. When they had endured this for a time and were quite unable to defend themselves, they met together and swore an oath, pledging mutual loyalty. After this they went out together, besieged a certain castle jointly, took it by force and utterly destroyed it. After this the cities, grown bold, attacked the Count's property manfully, and having taken four castles, overthrew them to the ground, and forced him to flee from his own estates.

units.la: Dux Austriæ vocatus, cum infinita multitudine Vngarorum & Cumanorum venit, qui omnes pugnare cum sagittis & arcubus consueuerant. Habuit secum Australes, qui armis ferreis vtebantur. Igitur rex Adolfus contra ducem Austriæ cum magna multitudine venientem, in occursum currit, cum hominum armata multitudine copiosa. Armati reputabantur qui galeas ferreas in capitibus habebant, & qui Wambasia, id est, tunicam spissam ex lino & stuppa vel veteribus pannis confectam, & desuper camisiam ferream, id est vestem ex circulis ferreis contextam, per quæ nulla sagitta arcus poterat hominem vulnerare. Ex his armatis centum, inermes mille lædi potuerunt. Habebat & multos qui habebant dextrarios, id est, equos magnos, qui inter equos communes quasi Bucephalus Alexandri inter alios eminebant. Hi equi cooperti fuerunt coopertarijs ferreis, id est, veste ex circulis ferreis connexa. Assessores dextrariorum habebant loricas ferreas, habebant & caligas, manipulos ferreos, & in capitibus galeas ferreas splendidas & ornatas, & alia multa, quæ me tæduit enarrare.
units.tr: The Duke of Austria, summoned, came with an endless multitude of Hungarians and Cumans, who were all accustomed to fight with arrows and bows. He had with him the Austrians, who used iron weapons. So King Adolf ran to meet the Duke of Austria, who was coming with a great multitude, with a large armed host of men. Those were regarded as armed who had iron helmets on their heads, and who wore a wambasium, that is, a thick tunic made of linen and tow or old rags, and over it a mail shirt, that is, a garment woven of iron rings, through which no arrow from a bow could wound a man. Of these armed men, a hundred could injure a thousand unarmed. He also had many who had dextrarii, that is, large horses, which stood out among common horses as Bucephalus did among the horses of Alexander. These horses were covered with iron caparisons, that is, garments of linked iron rings. Their riders had iron breastplates, also leg armour and iron gauntlets, and on their heads splendid and decorated iron helmets, and many other things which would weary me to describe.

units.la: Exercitus Regis inuadere Ducis exercitum voluntariè voluisset, si locorum opportunitas affuisset. Dux fugiendo ab Vlma, vsq; Waldishut regis exercitum dereliquit, & Rex eum persequi desistebat.
units.tr: The king's army would have willingly attacked the Duke's army, had the opportunity of the ground allowed it. The Duke, fleeing from Ulm as far as Waldshut, left the king's army behind, and the king ceased to pursue him.

units.la: Post hæc significauit dux Austriæ Principibus electoribus, qui colloquium condixerant festo Philippi & Iacobi prope Franckinfurt, quòd ad id propter impetum regis Romanorum non posset commodè peruenire. Quapropter rogauit, vt hoc in alteram transferrent. In hoc subitò consenserunt, quia & tribus vicibus transtulerunt.
units.tr: After this the Duke of Austria notified the princes-electors, who had agreed to a meeting on the feast of Philip and James near Frankfurt, that because of the attack of the King of the Romans he could not conveniently come to it. He therefore asked that they transfer it to another time. They agreed to this at once, and indeed they postponed it three times.

units.la: Exeunte duce Austriæ terram suam, venit ad eum dux Bauariæ, eiq; amicabiliter dixit: Socer meus petiuit à me, quatenus eum in necessitatibus cum suis fideliter adiuuarem. Ego verò, vt me decuit, exaudiui. Rogo igitur quatenus me in hoc casu habeatis excusatum. Dux dixit: Frater mi, adiutores habeo multos, unde fac sicut tibi videbitur expedire. Audiens hæc Comes Albertus cognatus ducum, dixit consanguineo: Scias cognate, quia socerum, me contradicente, non poteris visitare. Si verò socerum tuum visitaueris, tibi valide contradicam. Dux Bauariæ plus quàm ccc milites habens, ad socerum suum Adolfum regem Romanorum versus Alsatiam declinauit. Occurrit autem ei cognatus suus, Comes Albertus de Hegirloch, cum militibus multis, & Ducem cognatum suum capere nitebatur? Milites verò ducis eum fideliter defenderunt. Post longam concertationem, comes Albertus læsus de dextrario cecidit. Videntes rustici suum dominum cecidisse: ad ipsum conuenerunt, multos dextrarios confoderunt, vt dominum suum à mortis periculo liberarent. Milites videntes se dextrarios amisisse, subitò conuenerunt, rusticos gladijs inuaserunt, & penè ccc occiderunt, plurimos vulnerauerunt: reliqui perterriti, duce Bauariæ pergere, quò voluit, liberè permiserunt. Comes verò Albertus de Hegirloch obijt cum cæteris interfectis.
units.tr: As the Duke of Austria was leaving his land, the Duke of Bavaria came to him and said in a friendly way: "My father-in-law has asked me to help him faithfully in his difficulties with his men. I, as was fitting, have granted his request. I therefore ask that you excuse me in this matter." The Duke said: "My brother, I have many helpers, so do what seems to you advisable." Hearing this, Count Albert, the dukes' kinsman, said to his cousin: "Know, cousin, that you will not be able to visit your father-in-law while I oppose it. But if you do visit your father-in-law, I will strongly oppose you." The Duke of Bavaria, having more than three hundred knights, turned aside towards Alsace to visit his father-in-law, King Adolf of the Romans. But his kinsman, Count Albert of Hegirloch, met him with many knights, and tried to seize his cousin the Duke. The Duke's knights, however, defended him faithfully. After a long fight, Count Albert, unhorsed and wounded, fell. The peasants, seeing their lord fallen, gathered round him and stabbed many of the horses, so as to free their lord from the danger of death. The knights, seeing that they had lost their horses, suddenly gathered, attacked the peasants with swords, and killed almost three hundred, wounding very many; the rest, terrified, freely allowed the Duke of Bavaria to go wherever he wished. Count Albert of Hegirloch died with the others who were slain.

units.la: Cùm dux Austriæ in Baldiehut oppidum peruenisset, rex Adolfus declinauit in Alsatiam, volens duci viam præcludere descendenti. Dux audiens regem Adolsum in Alsatiam descendisse, in Friburgum & ipse subitò declinauit. Ciues autem Friburgenses ipsum intrare ciuitatem cum armatis hominibus renuerunt. Adolfus rex intelligens, ducem Friburgum peruenisse, castellum Kencingen petrexit, Duci descendenti viam obstructurus. Dux intelligens in Kencingen se regem transtulisse: descendit & ipse, ac sua tentoria prope regis tentoria collocauit. Exercitus sibi mutuo loquebantur, sed ad se peruenire, propter aquæ transitum, non valebant. Regis exercitus penuriam panis interdum patiebatur, quia ciuitas Brisacensis & Columbariensis pinsere panem sufficientem exercitui non valebat.
units.tr: When the Duke of Austria had reached the town of Waldshut, King Adolf turned aside into Alsace, wishing to block the Duke's way as he came down. The Duke, hearing that King Adolf had come down into Alsace, himself suddenly turned aside to Freiburg. But the citizens of Freiburg refused to let him enter the city with armed men. King Adolf, learning that the Duke had reached Freiburg, made for the castle of Kenzingen, intending to block the Duke's way as he descended. The Duke, learning that the king had moved to Kenzingen, also came down and pitched his tents near the king's tents. The armies spoke with one another, but because of the crossing of the water they could not reach each other. The king's army sometimes suffered a lack of bread, because the citizens of Breisach and Colmar could not bake enough bread for the army.

units.la: Hiltebrandus dapifer de Wappingheim, vir iuuenis, fortis, nobilis ac diues de exercitu Regis, fratrem visitans in treugis de exercitu ducis, occiditur faudulenter, circa Kalendas Maij: per Predicatores in Columbariam ducitur, & apud eosdem solenniter sepelitur. Dominus de Berchheim, & dominus de Haginecks, ducatores bigarum sedecim, quæ exercitui necessaria portabant, ab inimicis superuenientibus capiuntur.
units.tr: Hiltebrand, steward of Wappingheim, a young, brave, noble and wealthy man of the king's army, while visiting his brother in the truce from the Duke's army, was treacherously killed around the Kalends of May. He was taken to Colmar by the Preaching friars and solemnly buried among them. Sir of Berchheim and Sir of Haginecks, drivers of sixteen wagons which were carrying necessities for the army, were captured by enemies who came upon them.

units.la: Cum rex Adolfus cum grandi exercitu penè diebus quatuordecim prope Kencingen quieuisset, nihilq; esset notabile perpetratum: emit à domino de Wsinberch castellum Kencingen, obligans ei vallem S. Gregorij, cum castro Blitsberg, vt posset habere liberum aditum ad ducis exercitum veniendi. Audiens dux, treugas ratione componendi petijt, & vnius diei inducias impetrauit. Dux circa principium noctis illius, cum militibus suis versus Rinaugiam declinauit, & ipsos alij silenter & velociter sequebantur. Circa diem castra pauperes succenderunt, & post suos dominos velociter abierunt. Ducis tabernaculis succensis, quidam ex militibus regis, ducis pauperes persequi voluissent, sed alij dissuaserunt, quia in treugis & pacis tempore recesserant. Insuper dicebant: Hac nocte ducis milites quieuerunt, & nos cum ad eos lassi & dispersi venerimus, sine labore capient vniuersos. Post hæc in Argentinam dux peruenit.
units.tr: When King Adolf, with a great army, had rested for almost fourteen days near Kenzingen, and nothing noteworthy had been done, he bought the castle of Kenzingen from the lord of Wsinberch, pledging to him the valley of Saint Gregory with the castle of Blitsberg, so that he might have free access for coming to the Duke's army. The Duke, hearing this, sought a truce for the purpose of negotiating, and obtained a truce of one day. Around the beginning of that night the Duke, with his knights, turned aside towards Rheinau, and others silently and swiftly followed them. Around daybreak the poor set fire to the camp and quickly left after their lords. When the Duke's tents had been set on fire, some of the king's knights wished to pursue the Duke's poor, but others dissuaded them, because they had withdrawn during the truce and a time of peace. Moreover they said: "The Duke's knights have rested this night, and when we come to them weary and scattered, they will take us all without effort." After this the Duke reached Strasbourg.

units.la: Vigilia natiuitatis Ioannis Baptistæ, cycli Lunaris VII, tres electores regis Romanorum, Moguntinus, Brandeburgensis & Saxo, Moguntiæ conuenerunt, campanas compulsauerunt, populū conuocauerūt, quædam quæ fecerant, quaedã facienda fideliter retulerunt. Ascenderunt igitur in ecclesiam, facies suas vertetes ad altare, manus suas eleuauerunt, per Deum viuentē iurauerunt: quod cũ ante sex annos regnū Rege caruerit Romanorum, nos electores tres, ex parte nostra, & ex parte reliquorum Electorum, qui in nos eligendi vota sua transtulerunt, iure ac canonice Adolsum de Nassowe, tunc non cognoscentes meliorem, in regem elegimus Romanorum. Post electionem suam Adolfus rex sapienter se tenuit, electoribus atq; prudentibus acquiescit. Post breve tempus sapientum consilia spreuit, iuuenum consilijs acquiescit, & regenda minimè terminauit: diuitias per se non habuit, nec amicos, qui eum vellent fideliter iuuare. Electores videntes hos defectus regis, & plus quàm viginti alios: papæ significauerunt, rogantes, quatenus ipsum nobis dare auctoritatem absoluendi, & alium confirmandi vellet. (Id obtinuerant, vt à pluribus dicebatur: nuncij vero Adolfi regis dixerunt, quòd his Papa simpliciter contradixerit.) Auctoritate igitur nobis commissa, Adolfum regem insufficientem inuenientes, absoluimus eum à regiminis dignitate, & dominum Albertum ducem Austriæ, in dominum & regem eligimus Romanorum, & potestate nobis tradita similiter confirmamus, & Te Deum laudamus solenniter cantauerunt. Cumque Dux præsens non adesset, extra ciuitatem ad tabernacula perrexerunt, & ibi pannum pretiosum supra equum proiecerunt, regemq; desuper sedere præceperunt, & Te Deum laudamus cum magna lætitia cantauerunt.
units.tr: On the vigil of the Nativity of John the Baptist, in the seventh year of the lunar cycle, the three electors of the King of the Romans, Mainz, Brandenburg and Saxony, met at Mainz. They had the bells rung, summoned the people, and faithfully reported what they had done and what remained to be done. They went up into the church, turned their faces to the altar, raised their hands, and swore by the living God: that six years earlier, when the kingdom of the Romans had been without a king, we three electors, on our own behalf and on behalf of the other electors who had transferred their votes to us, had lawfully and canonically elected Adolf of Nassau as King of the Romans, not then knowing a better man. After his election Adolf conducted himself wisely for a while, and he deferred to the electors and to prudent men. After a short time, however, he scorned the counsel of the wise, gave ear to the advice of young men, and did not bring the business of government to an end; he had no wealth of his own, nor friends who would faithfully help him. The electors, seeing these defects in the king, and more than twenty others, sent word to the Pope, asking that he would grant us authority to depose him and to confirm another. (It was thought by many that this had been obtained; but the messengers of King Adolf said that the Pope had flatly refused it.) Therefore, with the authority committed to us, finding Adolf an unfit king, we deposed him from the dignity of rule, and we elected Duke Albert of Austria as lord and King of the Romans, and by the power given to us we similarly confirmed him; and they solemnly sang the Te Deum laudamus. And since the duke was not present, they went out of the city to the tents, and there they threw a precious cloth over a horse, and ordered the king to sit upon it, and they sang the Te Deum laudamus with great joy.

units.la: Ciuitatum ciues hunc regem deriserunt, & ei nullatenus parere voluerunt, eiq; vendere necessaria renuerunt: regem Adolfum pro rege tenuerunt, & ei necessaria præbuerunt, fidemq; ad ipsius obitum vsq; tenuerunt. Post mortem Adolfi regis, ciuitates Albertum ducem Austriæ electum regem à principibus, subitò pro suo domino receperunt, & in omnibus paruerunt.
units.tr: The citizens of the cities mocked this king and were in no way willing to obey him; they refused to sell him necessities. They held King Adolf to be king and supplied him with necessities, and they kept faith with him until his death. After the death of King Adolf, the cities suddenly received Duke Albert of Austria, chosen king by the princes, as their lord, and obeyed him in all things.

units.la: Dux Argentinæ exercitum suum pro magna parte proprijs pauerat expensis, ibiq; septimanis circiter quinq; quieuerat: quia neq; ad dextram neq; ad sinistram commodè poterat declinare. Post hæc cum paucis ad archiepiscopum Moguntinum descenderat, & exercitus eius eum, sicut potuit, sequebatur. Audiens rex, Ducem cum paucis Moguntiam peruenisse, Rubeacensem reliquit obsidionem, in Brisaco Rhenum transiuit, & ad inferiores partes venire, quanto plus potuit, festinauit.
units.tr: The Duke of Argentina had largely paid for his army out of his own pocket, and had rested there for about five weeks, because he could not conveniently turn either to the right or to the left. After this he had gone down with a few men to the Archbishop of Mainz, and his army followed him as well as it could. The king, hearing that the duke had come to Mainz with a few men, left the siege of Rubeacum, crossed the Rhine at Breisach, and hastened to the lower regions as fast as he could.

units.la: Cùm Albertus dux Austriæ de Argentina recessisset, duxit secum triginta naues bonis quibusq; oneratas, quas ibi si non obtinuisset, in inferioribus partibus obtinere minimè potuisset. Ciuitates enim sibi necessaria vendere noluerunt. Obsedit autem dux Alcinache castellum, illiq; se sub conditione tradiderunt, vt si infra octo dies non liberarentur, vt in potestatem Ducis liberè transferrentur. Rex hæc intelligens, descendit, vt obsessos restituueret pristinæ libertati. Tanta autem fuit in Ducis exercitu caristia, quòd panis vix valens denarium, pro sex denarijs vendebatur. Rex prope Alcinache tua tentoria collocauit. Tantæ autem potentiæ ac multitudinis exercitus regis extitit, vt Ducis exercitum facile vicisset, si eum sui dolosi (vt dicebatur) consiliarij permisissent.
units.tr: When Duke Albert of Austria had withdrawn from Argentina, he took with him thirty ships laden with goods of every kind, which, had he not secured them there, he could by no means have secured in the lower regions, for the cities refused to sell him necessities. The duke besieged the castle of Alcinach, and its garrison surrendered on condition that, if they were not relieved within eight days, they would be freely handed over into the duke's power. The king, learning of this, came down to restore the besieged to their former liberty. There was such a famine in the duke's army that bread, scarcely worth a penny, was sold for six pence. The king pitched his tents near Alcinach. The king's army was so powerful and so numerous that it could easily have defeated the duke's army, had his counsellors, who were said to be treacherous, not allowed it.

units.la: Octaua sancti Ioannis baptistæ, archiepiscopus Moguntinus & dux Austriæ in penuria fuerunt, quia ciuitates imperij eis necessaria vendere noluerunt. Tunc ad inuicem dixerunt: aliquantulum fugiamus, vt inimicos vincere valeamus. Tunc archiepiscopus suos armare se fecit ad dimidium miliare, ibiq; Ducis exercitum expectare. Dux verò suis dicebat: Præparate vos ad pugnandum atque ad recedendum. Cumq; se præparassent, recesserunt atq; tabernacula succenderunt. Dux processit à loco, quo tentoria fixerat, ad dimidium miliare, volens ibi cum exercitu regis dimicare. Videns exercitus regis castra Ducis succensa: consiliarij subitò venerunt, Ducis gesta, secundum quod apparuerunt, fideliter retulerunt, dicentes: Dominus archiepiscopus cum suo comitatu hodie mane de Ducis exercitu recedebat: nunc dux, sicut fecit in Kencingen, idem quoque facere disponit, & animam suam atq; suorum cogitat à mortis periculo liberare.
units.tr: On the octave of St John the Baptist, the Archbishop of Mainz and the Duke of Austria were in want, because the cities of the empire refused to sell them necessities. Then they said to one another: "Let us withdraw a little, so that we may be able to defeat our enemies." Then the archbishop had his men arm themselves half a mile off, and there await the duke's army. The duke, however, said to his men: "Prepare yourselves both for fighting and for withdrawing." When they had made ready, they withdrew and set fire to the tents. The duke advanced half a mile from the place where he had pitched his tents, wishing to fight there with the king's army. The king's army, seeing the duke's camp burning, suddenly sent word, and the counsellors faithfully reported what the duke had done, as far as it appeared, saying: "The lord archbishop with his company withdrew from the duke's army this morning; now the duke, just as he did at Kenzingen, intends to do the same, and is thinking of saving his own life and that of his men from the danger of death."

units.la: Rex credens consiliarijs infidelibus, tanquam fidelibus acquieuit, suis arma sumi præcepit, fugientes persequi fideliter adhortatur. Rex cum paucis primus paratus ad prælium, Ducem persequitur confidenter. Dux videns regem cum paucis venientem, securus de victoria, dicebat: Exercitus meus in tres partes diuidatur, & Regis exercitus ad medium mei venire, sine obstaculo permittatur. Cùm autem in nostra peruenerit, à nostris circumdetur, & rex in primis capiatur, vel velociter occidatur, equi inimicorum lanceis perfodiantur, assessores eorum sine læsione corporum capiantur. Sicut Dux suis dixit faciendum, sic omnia fideliter persecerunt.
units.tr: The king, believing the faithless counsellors as if they were loyal, ordered his men to take up arms and urged them faithfully to pursue the fleeing enemy. The king, first and ready for battle with a few men, confidently pursued the duke. The duke, seeing the king coming with a few men and confident of victory, said: "Let my army be divided into three parts, and let the king's army be allowed to come into the middle of mine without hindrance. When it has come in among ours, it shall be surrounded by our men, and the king shall be seized first or quickly killed; the horses of the enemy shall be pierced with lances, and their riders taken without injury to their bodies." Just as the duke told his men to do, so they carried out everything faithfully.

units.la: Ad bellum Dux cum signo peregrino processit, proprium verò suum pluribus committebat. Rex verò cum signo proprio dimicauit, malens sub signo proprio capi vel occidi, quàm inimicis tradere sanguinem innocentum. Cùm Rex cum suis ad Ducis exercitum peruenisset, & Ducis exercitum in tres partes diuisum, & ad prælium dum non fugiendum considerasset, dixit eum sequentibus cum dolore: Væ: amici nostri, imò potiùs inimici manibus inimicorum nostrorum sine misericordia nos tradiderunt. Si enim fugiamus, omnes perditi sumus: si verò pugnauerimus, quis rei euentus euenìat, penitus ignoramus. Tunc dixit filio suo: Recede à me, quia inimici mei non me viuere patientur. Tunc filius dixit: Pater, quocunq; perrexeris, ero tecum, in mortem pariter & ad vitam. Rex cum signis regijs atq; vexillo regis, cum militibus melioribus quos secũ habuit, ad vexillum Ducis sine pugna & obstaculo peruenerunt. Occurrit primò regi ferens insignia Ducis, quem ferociter aggreditur, & velociter interfecit. Occurrit & alter Regi, qui per interfectionem regis magnam pecuniam deseruisset: hic gladio Regem petens, in ipsum irruit vehementer. Cum hoc Rex diutius dimicat, tandem verò ipsum vulnerauit: qui de equo cecidit, & equorum pedibus conculcatur. Post hæc regem plures pariter inuaserunt, à quibus omnibus, vt homo desperatus, viriliter se defendebat. Tandem equus regis in anterioribus pedibus vulneratur: tum rex & equus pariter ceciderunt. Post hæc rex percutitur atq; vulneratur, & sic in Domino requieuit. Dux tuis præcepit, quòd præter regem nullus hominum læderetur, sed tantùm equi mortis supplicio traderentur: quod fuerunt fideliter exequuti. Interfecti fuerunt duo millia, triginta quinq;, vt quidam retulerunt. Alij dixerunt, quòd equorum interfectorum fuerint tria millia computata. Ex hominibus occisi fuerunt centum, & non amplius computati. Excoriati fuerunt ipso die omnes equi, vt plurimi retulerunt.
units.tr: The duke advanced to battle under a foreign standard, but entrusted his own to many. The king fought under his own standard, preferring to be taken or killed under his own banner rather than to hand over innocent blood to his enemies. When the king with his men had come to the duke's army, and saw that the duke's army had been divided into three parts, and that there was no escape but to fight, he said to those following him, in grief: "Alas, our friends, or rather our enemies, have delivered us without mercy into the hands of our enemies. For if we flee, we are all lost; if we fight, we know quite well not what the outcome of the matter will be." Then he said to his son: "Withdraw from me, for my enemies will not suffer me to live." Then the son said: "Father, wherever you go, I will be with you, equally in death and in life." The king, with the royal insignia and the royal banner, and with the best soldiers he had with him, came without battle or hindrance to the duke's standard. First he met the one bearing the duke's insignia, whom he fiercely attacked and quickly killed. Another came against the king, who had hoped for a great sum of money from the king's death; he, seeking the king with a sword, rushed fiercely upon him. The king fought with him for a long time, but at last he wounded him, and he fell from his horse and was trampled under the horses' feet. After this many attacked the king together, against all of whom he defended himself manfully, like a desperate man. At last the king's horse was wounded in its forelegs; then the king and the horse fell together. After this the king was struck and wounded, and so he rested in the Lord. The duke ordered that no one be harmed except the king, but that only the horses be put to death; and this his men faithfully carried out. Two thousand and thirty-five were killed, as some reported; others said that the number of horses killed was counted as three thousand. Of men, one hundred were killed, and no more were counted. All the horses were flayed that same day, as most reported.

units.la: De nonnullis ab Alberto Cæsare gestis.
units.tr: On certain deeds of Emperor Albert.

units.la: ANNO M. CC. XCVIII, rex Romanorum Albertus, in octaua Martini, in Nuremberg Curiam solennem celebrauit, ibiq; regina more debito coronatur, & penè omnes Electores præsentes exiterunt. Ibi dignitas cuiuslibet domini coram Rege solenniter recitatur, & quilibet dominorum Regi in officio suo, sicut debuit, ministrauit. Rex verò Bohemus cum pretiosissima veste & equo, qui ad mille marcas æstimabatur, sedens, in cypho aureo sibi porrexit. Audiens rex Albertus, quòd pater suus Rudolfus rex in die anniuersaria sua, vt eius haberetur memoria, minimè contulisset: contulit eis L librarum redditus, vt in altari, quod in ecclesia eorum construxerat, quotidie Missam dicerent aut cantarent.
units.tr: In the year 1298, King Albert of the Romans held a solemn court at Nuremberg on the octave of St Martin's Day, and there the queen was crowned in the customary manner. Nearly all the electors were present. There the rank of each lord was solemnly read out in the king's presence, and each of the lords served the king in his office as he ought. The Bohemian king, seated and wearing a most precious robe, with a horse valued at a thousand marks, handed him a golden cup. King Albert heard that his father Rudolf had not, on the anniversary of his death, made any provision to keep his memory alive, so he granted them an income of fifty pounds, so that they might say or sing Mass every day at the altar which he had built in their church.

units.la: Anno M. CCC, Comes de Holandia, vir iuuenis & fortis, habens in matrimonio sibi coniunctam iuvenculam nobilem & facundam, ad mensam pariter sederunt hilares & iocundi. Hi toxico perierunt pariter innocentes. Horum Comitatum vsurpauit Comes Hanogogiæ velociter & potenter. Hæc audiens Albertus rex Romanorum, mandauit comiti Hanogogiæ, quòd has res contra iustitiam possedisset, & eas dari sibi liberè, postulabat. Comes hæc facere simpliciter recusabat. His rex Albertus auditis, exercitum cõgregauit, & Comitem obsidere velociter cogitauit. Cùm rex prope Coloniam cum exercitu peruenisset: quidam cum interficere voluerunt. Hæc quidam ex consanguineis regis intelligentes, statim miserunt ei nuntium: Nisi ad nos ante prandium veneris, in prandio morieris. Hæc rex cùm audisset, ascendit dextrarium & fugit velociter ad cognatos. Pauci autem ex suis, quos rex vocauit, velociter sequebantur. Postquam ad suos peruenit, fuerunt insidiæ patefactæ.
units.tr: In the year 1300, the Count of Holland, a young and brave man, sat down at table together with his young wife, a noble and eloquent woman joined to him in marriage, both cheerful and merry. Both died together of poison, though innocent. The Count of Hainault swiftly and forcefully seized their county. King Albert of the Romans, hearing this, ordered the Count of Hainault that he had possessed these things against justice, and demanded that they be handed over to him freely. The count flatly refused to do so. When King Albert heard this, he gathered an army and resolved to besiege the count at once. When the king had arrived with his army near Cologne, some men wanted to kill him. Some of the king's relatives, learning of this, immediately sent him a message: "Unless you come to us before dinner, you will die at dinner." When the king heard this, he mounted his warhorse and fled swiftly to his kinsmen. Only a few of his own men, whom the king had summoned, followed him quickly. After he reached his people, the ambush was exposed.

units.la: His sic gestis, vocauit rex suos, eisq; dicebat: Ad terram meam redire dispono & quò cò peruenìam, mihi consulite. Qui dixerunt: cum multitudine militum potestis terram vestrorum inimicorum velociter pertransire. Rex militibus dicebat: Præparate parate ergo vos, me ad meos cum potentia perducendum. Qui dixerunt: Domine, deficiunt nobis expensæ, & ideo vobiscum pergere non valemus. Rex dicebat: dabo vobis mille quingentas marcas, vt me ad propria perducatis. Milites dixerūt: voluntariè faciemus. Ascenderunt milites dextrarios suos, & regem ad suos cum lætitia perduxerunt: quò cum peruenisset, dedit militibus pecuniam quam promisit.
units.tr: When these things had been done, the king summoned his men and said to them: "I intend to return to my land; advise me how I may get there." They replied: "With a large body of soldiers you can cross your enemies' land quickly." The king said to the soldiers: "Prepare yourselves, then, to lead me back to my people with a strong force." They said: "Lord, we are short of money, and so we cannot go with you." The king said: "I will give you fifteen hundred marks to lead me to my own lands." The soldiers answered: "We will do it willingly." They mounted their warhorses and joyfully led the king back to his people. When he arrived there, he gave the soldiers the money he had promised.

units.la: Cum regi visum fuisset, quòd Rhenū potenter teneret, & se confirmatū crederet: mandauit archiepiscopo Moguntino, archiepiscopo Coloniensi, atq; cæteris accipientibus telonium supra Rhenum, ne incurrerent in indignationem regiæ maiestatis. Episcopi regi responderunt: telonia nostra longo tempore debitè accepimus, & antecessores nostri longo tempore receperunt, & eos reges Romanorum minime turbarunt. Vnde & nos hæc telonia nolumus voluntariè resignare. Rex his auditis, significauit Papæ, quòd domini archiepiscopi supra Rhenū fluuium per telonium iniustas exactiones facerent, & totam terram grauiter perturbarent. Episcopos papa corrigere tardauit. Rex tamen quomodo eos suis corrigeret, cogitauit, & de consilio suorum eos diffidauit. Non post multum temporis Rex in Moguntia coram quibusdam Principibus super futuris grauaminibus solenniter appellauit.
units.tr: When it seemed to the king that he held the Rhine firmly, and believed himself secure, he ordered the archbishop of Mainz, the archbishop of Cologne, and the others who collected tolls on the Rhine not to incur the displeasure of the royal majesty. The bishops replied to the king: "We have rightly received our tolls for a long time; our predecessors received them for a long time too, and the kings of the Romans never disturbed them. Therefore we are unwilling to surrender these tolls of our own accord." When the king heard this, he informed the Pope that the lord archbishops along the Rhine were making unjust exactions through their tolls and were gravely disturbing the whole land. The Pope was slow to correct the bishops. Yet the king considered how he might correct them himself, and with the advice of his men he declared them his enemies. Not long afterwards, the king solemnly lodged an appeal at Mainz, in the presence of some princes, concerning the burdens that were to come.

units.la: Eodem tempore filij sororis Regis & ducis Bauariæ, scilicet Rudolfus & Otto, litigabant inter se pro dominio, & seniorem iuniorem de paternis possessionibus expulit violenter. Tunc iunior se contulit ad Regem Romanorum, senior verò confœderatus se archiepiscopo Moguntino. Iunior rogauit regem Roman. vt eum secundum iusticiam promoueret. Dixit ei Rex: accipe tuos amicos, egoque mittam tibi de meis hominibus, & fratris obsideas ciuitatem: atq; hanc Regis voluntatem iunior adimpleuit. Cumque dux Otto ciuitatem diebus pluribus obsedisset, nec dominus archiepiscopus liberare eam potuisset: venit rex Romanorum, ciuitatem potenter obsedit, & obtinuit violenter. Cumque Dux multas munitiones perdidisset, & liberare eam minime valuisset, tunc regi res & corpus simpliciter conferebat. Rex verò inter fratres, vt placuit, diuidebat. Existens autem in obsidione rex, res domini archiepiscopi Moguntini potenter inuasit, & dicebatur multas ciuitates & villas in cinerem redegisse.
units.tr: At the same time, the sons of the king's sister and of the Duke of Bavaria, namely Rudolf and Otto, were quarrelling with each other over the lordship, and the elder violently drove the younger out of their paternal possessions. Then the younger went to the King of the Romans, while the elder allied himself with the archbishop of Mainz. The younger asked the King of the Romans to advance him in accordance with justice. The king said to him: "Take your friends, and I will send you some of my own men, and you shall besiege your brother's city." The younger carried out the king's wish. And when Duke Otto had besieged the city for many days, and the lord archbishop had been unable to free it, the King of the Romans came, besieged the city with force, and took it by violence. When the duke had lost many of his fortifications and could not relieve the city, he simply surrendered his property and his person to the king. The king divided the lands between the brothers as he saw fit. While the king was engaged in the siege, he also violently invaded the goods of the lord archbishop of Mainz, and it was said that he had reduced many towns and villages to ashes.

units.la: Post hæc acceptis illorum Ducum hominibus, ad ciuitatem quæ dicitur Bingin, cum lætitia se transferebant. Quam cum obsedissent, misit eis rex Franciæ Gallicos multos, qui ciuitatem viriliter impugnabant: tamen inter omnes nationes Alsatæ laudabilius faciebant. Erat hæc ciuitas munita valde: habebat enim ex vna parte aquam, id est Rhenum, per quem naues magnæ sine periculo non poterant pertransire. Habebat ex altera parte aquam magnam, quæ sine nauibus, sine periculo non poterat pertransiri. In tertia parte sui habuit castrum forte, in Lapide situm, quod non poterat subfodi nec expugnari, sine laboribus maximis & expensis. In quarta parte habebat fossam profundam, murum fortem & altum, portam & terram quæ non poterat faciliter expugnari. Habebat homines fortes, quinq; Comites & electos eorum, qui exercitati fuerant in prælijs, & alios quingentos, qui si in campo plano fuissent, & circa se sepem habuissent, ab infinita hominū multitudine sese diutius defendissent. Rex habebat homines nimios, ita vt antiqui patres dicerent: nunquam vidisse eos talem & tantam militiam congregatam. Seruorum autem pauperum, qui dicuntur bubij, tanta fuit multitudo, quòd regi dicebant: Domine, date nobis res in ciuitate, & vobis eam trademus sine læsione ac detrimento in vestram potestatem. Rex hoc renuit facere, vt res inimicorum suorum ad libitum deuastaret.
units.tr: After this, having taken on the men of those dukes, they set out joyfully for the town called Bingen. When they had besieged it, the king of France sent them many Frenchmen, who fought the city fiercely; yet among all the nations of Alsace these men acquitted themselves more commendably. This city was very strongly fortified. On one side it had water, namely the Rhine, which large ships could not cross without danger. On another side it had a great expanse of water, which could not be crossed without boats and without danger. On the third side it had a strong castle, set upon a rock, which could not be undermined or taken without very great labour and expense. On the fourth side it had a deep ditch, a strong and high wall, a gate, and an earthwork that could not easily be stormed. It had brave men: five counts and their chosen followers, who had been trained in battle, and another five hundred who, had they been on open ground with a hedge about them, could have held out far longer against the countless multitude of men. The king had an excessive number of men, so that the old fathers said they had never seen such a great army assembled. The multitude of poor servants, called bubij, was so great that they said to the king: "Lord, give us the goods in the city, and we will hand the city over to you, undamaged and without loss, under your power." The king refused to do this, since he wished to lay waste his enemies' goods as he pleased.

units.la: Expugnauit rex hanc ciuitatem per duo vasa concaua, quæ faciebant artifices sapientes: Vnum vas Cattus vocabatur, aliud Cancer. Erant hæc vasa longa, quadrata, demissa, ex omni parte laterum clausa. Versus terram nullum munimen habebat, sed versus cælum de tabulis fortibus & spissis tectum, machinarum lapides minime metuebat. Per duo vasa hæc fuit ciuitas faciliter expugnata. Cattus leue vas erat, & faciliter trahebatur. Cum hoc vas ad ciuitatem fuisset perductum, *signa quædam pro pedibus sibi fecerunt, vt ad murum per fossatum possent faciliter peruenire. Cum ad murum peruenissent, iuuenes de ciuitate egressi Catto pedes succiderunt, & in fossatum cadere coegerunt. De hoc rex fuit non modicum perturbatus.
units.tr: The king took this city by means of two hollow engines, which skilful craftsmen had made. One engine was called the Cat, the other the Crab. These engines were long and square, low-slung, and closed on every side. They had no protection facing the ground, but facing the sky they were roofed with strong, thick planks, so they did not fear stones hurled from siege engines. By these two engines the city was easily taken. The Cat was a light engine and was easily dragged along. When it had been brought up to the city, they made certain supports for its feet, so that it could easily reach the wall across the ditch. When it reached the wall, young men came out of the city and cut through the Cat's feet, forcing it to fall into the ditch. The king was not a little dismayed by this.

units.la: Post hæc Cancrum ad ciuitatem perduxerunt. Fuit cancer instrumentum magnum, forte, pariter & ponderosum. In eo erat trabs magna, pariter longa, in vna parte grossa, in altera parte parua. In grossiori parte siue in capite, fuit ferro forti circumdata, & in fronte ipsius Cancri fortissimè colligata. Trabs hæc super quædam instrumenta iacuit, quòd faciliter moueretur. Hic Cancer cum ad murum peruenisset, octo in circulos qui in trabe erat, funes immisissent, ex paucis ictibus pro magna parte cadere coegerunt. Vno etiam ictu turrim tetigerunt, & in tantum laeserunt, quòd ruinam fortissimè minabatur. Hospites videntes murum cecidisse, timuerunt: proin omnes machinas & instrumenta quæ fecerant ad defendendum ciuitatem, velociter deseruerunt, & in castrum se cum festinantia receperût. Post hæc ciues se cum paucis conditionibus tradiderunt, quod & circa principium libenter fecissent, si eis hospites permisissent. Cum obsessa ciuitas fuisset, Scultetus hospitibus dixerat: Vos domini, quid oportet nos facere? Melius esset vt res & corpora possideamus, quàm vt cum nostris omnibus pariter pereamus. Tunc hospites pariter irruerant & cum miserabiliter occiderant.
units.tr: After this they brought the Crab up to the city. The Crab was a large, strong and at the same time heavy machine. In it was a great beam, also long, thick at one end and thin at the other. The thicker part, or head, was bound with strong iron and very firmly fixed to the front of the Crab. This beam lay upon certain frames so that it could be moved easily. When the Crab reached the wall, they let ropes down into the rings that were on the beam, and with a few blows they caused a large part of the wall to fall. With one blow they also struck the tower and damaged it so badly that it threatened to collapse entirely. The garrison, seeing that the wall had fallen, were afraid; therefore they quickly abandoned all the machines and devices they had made for defending the city, and hastily withdrew into the castle. After this, the citizens surrendered on a few conditions, which they would gladly have accepted at the beginning, had the foreign troops allowed it. When the city was besieged, the Schultheiss said to the foreign troops: "Gentlemen, what must we do? It would be better for us to keep our goods and our lives than to perish together with all our people." Then the foreign troops suddenly rushed in together and cruelly killed them.

units.la: Fuerunt equi phalerati seu dextrarii seu militum, præter aliorum hominum M.M C C. in hoc exercitu numerati. Hominum tanta fuit multitudo, quòd non poterant computari. Obsessa est hæc ciuitas Bingin ex parte Rheni, quia totus Rhenus repletus nauibus erat, & via patuit transeuntibus. Fuit & obsessa ex parte altera, qui etiam eos grauiter infestabant. Ex parte terræ fuerunt obsessi per Cattum atq; Cancrum, quia solus Cancer quingentos homines occupabat.
units.tr: There were horses caparisoned, both war-horses and those of the knights, counted in this army besides the other men, two thousand five hundred. The multitude of men was so great that they could not be counted. This city of Bingen was besieged on the side of the Rhine, because the whole Rhine was filled with ships, and the way lay open to those passing through. It was also besieged on the other side, and those men too attacked them severely. On the land side they were besieged by Cattus and Cancer, because Cancer alone held five hundred men.

units.la: Anno M. C C C. 11, rex misit solennes nuntios ad Papam, scilicet episcopum Tullensem atque suum Cancellarium, cum magnis expensis, qui ante festum sancti Ioannis baptistæ cum literis clausis redierunt, quæ statim lectæ non sunt, quia rex cum suis legere timuerunt.
units.tr: In the year 1311 the king sent solemn envoys to the Pope, namely the bishop of Toul and his chancellor, at great expense; they returned before the feast of St. John the Baptist with sealed letters, which were not read at once, because the king and his men were afraid to read them.

units.la: Circa festum Mariæ Magdalenæ, Albertus rex cum hominibus Austriæ, Bauariæ, Vngariæ, Bohemiæ & superioris Rheni hominibus Coloniam perrexit, & res triu archiepiscoporum, & aliorum episcoporum suorum aduersariorum ad libitum devastauit. Dixit enim se Holandiam atq; Flandriam breuiter peruenturū. Inimici regis plurimùm vexati, cum rege composuerunt, & homines cum nauibus Rhenum ascendere ac descendere liberè permiserunt.
units.tr: Around the feast of Mary Magdalene, King Albert went to Cologne with men of Austria, Bavaria, Hungary, Bohemia and the men of Upper Rhine, and laid waste at will the goods of the three archbishops and of his other episcopal adversaries. For he said that he would shortly reach Holland and Flanders. The king's enemies, much harassed, came to terms with the king, and he freely allowed men with ships to go up and down the Rhine.

units.la: Nuntij regis Alberti, quos superiore anno ad Papam Romam miserat, nempe duo milites & tertius miles clericus, in iure plurimùm versatus, circa Purificationem redierunt, & ad Reginæ præsentiam peruenerunt. Regina verò vnum ex eis, Monachum militem, festinanter ad regem transmisit, rogans suppliciter, quatenus subitò dignaretur ad eius præsentiam venire. Hoc rex subitò adimpleuit.
units.tr: The messengers of King Albert, whom he had sent to the Pope at Rome the previous year, namely two knights and a third, a clerk well versed in law, returned about the Purification and came into the presence of the Queen. The Queen then hastily sent one of them, a monk and knight, to the king, begging him earnestly that he would deign to come to her presence at once. The king at once complied.

units.la: Venerunt nuntij regis Romanorum infra octauam Ioannis baptistæ Columbariam, dicentes, quod Papa in consistorio coram pluribus millibus hominum dixisset, quòd rex Romanorum esset verus, & in gratia sua: & quando veniret, sicut rex teneretur, vellet eum consecrare in Cæsarem.
units.tr: The messengers of the King of the Romans came to Columbaria within the octave of John the Baptist, saying that the Pope had said in consistory, before several thousand people, that the King of the Romans was the true king and in his favour, and that when he came, as a king should be, he would be willing to consecrate him as Emperor.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: FINIS.

units.la: CONRADI VECERII, RE- GII SECRETARII, DE REBVS GESTIS IMPERATORIS HENRICI VII, LIBELLVS.
units.tr: CONRAD VECERIUS, SECRETARY TO THE KING, A LITTLE BOOK ON THE DEEDS OF THE EMPEROR HENRY VII.

units.la: ISTORIAM quisquis aggreditur scribere, eam maximè virtutem tacitè polliceri videtur, vti fide nitatur assertio: pusillumque interest, munus ne commemorandi res gestas, integritatis suæ conscius, vltrò quis suscipiat; an publicandorum potestatem actorum Cæsaris permissu nancisceatur. Atq; eò magis, quòd hunc quum seligit Princeps, non illud agit, vt bonum gra- uemq; velut efficere (quis enim præter immortalem Deum cuiquâ probita- tem conferat?) sed quo veracem videri iniunctione mandati testetur. At historicus vt primum res memorandas commendare posteritati decreuerit: primùm omnium de moribus suis ipse videtur iudicium facere, seq; eum promittere, qui & fideliter & accuratè cogitata prompturus sit. Has res ego mecum etiam atq; etiam reputans, quanquam non ignorabam propensiorem illico fore lectorem ad carpenda quàm comprobanda: speraret tamen cæpisseri posse, vt quum singularem regem describendi causa assumptum cognouisset, institutum nostrum boni consuleret. Namque & res digne videbantur, quæ referrentur in literas, & extabat qui ante nos id fecisset nemo, quod equidem nouerim. Tum necessitudo patriæ me vel maximè impulit, nõ ea quidem, vt Principis nostri facta plus æquo prædicarem: sed quæ apud varias sparsim gentes & barbaras linguas, & per partes legi comperieram, in corpus libri cuiusquam Latini possem redigere, omni interim soli natalis affectione seposita: alioquin nec veterum cuiusquam acceptanda esset industria: qui quum regum res maximis voluminibus posteritati traderent, eorum ipsorum tamen quos perscribebant & clientes & populares habebantur: adeò quæ ex officio gerimus, ab iis quæ forte priuatim fiunt, distinguuntur. Nunc ad inceptum redeo.
units.tr: Whoever undertakes to write a history seems tacitly to promise above all else that his account will rest on trustworthy evidence. It makes little difference whether someone, conscious of his own integrity, takes up the task of recording deeds of his own accord, or obtains the power to publish the acts of an emperor by his permission. All the more so, because when a prince chooses a man for this, he is not aiming to make him good and serious (for who but the immortal God can bestow goodness on anyone?), but only to have the writer's truthfulness attested by the commission he gives. The historian, as soon as he resolves to commend the memorable deeds to posterity, first of all seems to pass judgment on his own character, and to promise that he will set out what he has thought through faithfully and carefully. Weighing these matters again and again, I knew that a reader would be more inclined at once to carp at things than to approve them. Still, I hoped that when he learned I had taken up the task to describe an outstanding king, he would be willing to accept my undertaking kindly. For the deeds seemed worthy of being committed to writing, and so far as I know no one before me has done it. Then my duty to my homeland pressed me most of all. I do not mean that I wanted to praise our prince's deeds beyond what is right, but I wished to gather into one Latin book what I had found scattered among various peoples and barbarous tongues, and read only in parts, setting aside all affection for my native soil. Otherwise the diligence of no ancient writer would be worth accepting: although they handed down the deeds of kings to posterity in very large volumes, those very kings whom they described were nonetheless regarded as their own clients and fellow citizens. So far are the things we do in our public office distinguished from those that happen to be done privately. Now I return to my undertaking.

units.la: VT maiores imperatori Henrico, aut omnino parentes fuerint, quanuis curiosa vestigatione cognoscere non potui: sed & vxor illi quæ cuiasque fuerit, itidem prope in ambiguo est. Ipse, quod constat, Luceburgiæ comitatum hæreditate obtinuit. Romam profectus, & Baldvino fratri Treuirensis ecclesiæ archiepiscopatum confecit, & summis antistitibus ac bono cuique, sapientiæ & comitatis ingens argumentum edidit. Fuit autem olim Luceburgia Treuirorum portio, idque vt credam, propinquitate locorum adducor. Hanc postmodum Henricus Romano admotam imperio, Ducariæ dignitatis insignib. exornauit. Situs eius ab Arduennæ sylvæ termino, quatenus hodie appellationem obtinet, ad Mosellam fluuium, cuius amnis, Burdegalensis Ausonius carmine satis prolixè meminit, finitimarum ditionum his limitibus cingitur: Gallico, Lotaringo, Metensi, Treuirico, Iuliaceno, Leodio. Oppida non amplius nouem: maior quondam numerus. Sed eum & pia (vt aiunt) Henrici liberalitas, tribus municipijs Sareburgo, Vitelliaco &c. Treuirorum maximo templo donatis, & Gallica bella coartarunt. Gens potiore ex parte Germanica: regione tamen Galliam spectante, eius quoque nationis moribus linguaque vtens. Hæc de Henrici origine patriaque, tametsi pauxilla, tenuitatem confesso premittere placuit.
units.tr: It is not possible for me to discover, even by the most careful investigation, who the emperor Henry's ancestors or parents were; and it is almost equally uncertain whose daughter his wife was. What is known is that he obtained the county of Luxembourg by inheritance. After going to Rome, he also secured the archbishopric of the church of Trier for his brother Baldwin, and he showed great wisdom and courtesy to the highest prelates and to every good man. Luxembourg was formerly part of the territory of Trier, and I am led to believe this by the closeness of the places. Afterwards Henry, once he had been raised to the imperial office, adorned it with the insignia of the dignity of a duchy. Its extent, from the border of the Ardennes forest, as far as it is now called by that name, to the river Moselle, of which Ausonius of Bordeaux speaks at some length in his poem, is enclosed by these boundaries of the neighbouring lands: French, Lorrainer, Metz, Trier, Jülich, Liège. It has no more than nine towns; once the number was larger. But the pious generosity of Henry (as they say), who gave three market towns, Sarrebourg, Vitry and others, to the great church of Trier, and the French wars, have reduced it. Its people are for the most part German, though because the region faces France they also use the customs and language of that nation. I have thought it right to set these things about Henry's origin and homeland before my account, although they are few and slight, as a confession of my own limitation.

units.la: Quanquam non me praeterit, circumferri iampridem libellum vernacula lingua conscriptum, de fœminæ Melyssinæ præstigijs, octauo quoque die pubetenus in anguem commutari solitæ, quam inter maiores Septimi nostri connumerate nituntur. Eum vt nec approbare, ita nec refellere animus est. Cur enim nõ veneficia fieri posse concesserim, dum si tradantur vt veneficia. Quis enim non illa fascina legens obstupescat, neque tamen protinus tanquam confecta repudiet? Scylla venit, mediaque tenus descenderat aluo, Cum sua fœdari latrantibus inguina monstris Aspicit: ac primò non credens corporis illaa Esse sui partes refugit ______ Et Cerbereos rictus pro partibus invenit illis.
units.tr: Yet I am not unaware that a little book written in the vernacular has been circulating for some time, about the sorceries of a woman named Melusine, who was accustomed to turn into a serpent from the waist down every eighth day, and whom they strive to count among the ancestors of our Seventh Henry. I have no wish either to approve or to refute it. For why should I not concede that sorceries can happen, provided they are handed down as sorceries? Who, reading those tales, would not be astonished, and yet would not at once reject them as made up? "Scylla came, and had already come down to her middle in the belly, when she saw her groin defiled by barking monsters, and at first, not believing that those parts were her own body, she shrank back ______ and found in place of those parts the snarling jaws of Cerberus."

units.la: Sed à fabulante Poeta eos versus exaratos obijcies? Historiam accipe. Hac se carminibus promittit soluere mentes Quas velit, aut aliis duras immittere curas, Sistere aquam fluuijs, & vertere sidera retrò: Nocturnosq; ciet manes: mugire videbis Sub pedibus terram, & descendere montibus ornos.
units.tr: But you will object that these verses were written by a poet who tells fables? Hear the story. She promises that with these songs she can loosen the minds she wishes, or send hard cares into others, stop rivers in their course and turn the stars backwards; she calls up the ghosts of the night; you will see the earth bellow under your feet and the ash trees come down from the mountains.

units.la: Alius quoque eiusdem professionis scriptor, hunc in modum cecinit: Mens hausti nulla saniepolluta veneni, Incantata perit.
units.tr: Another writer of the same profession also sang in this way: "A mind, polluted by no infection of the poison it has drunk, perishes enchanted."

units.la: Liber & testimonium, quanquam non admodum diffinitum, vnius è nostris fapientibus afferre in medium.Hæc vel falsa sunt, inquit diuus pater Augustinus, veltam inusitata, vt merito non credantur. Firmissimè tamen tenendum est, omnipotentem Deum omnia posse facere quæ voluerit, siue iudicando siue præstando: nec daemones aliquid operari secundum naturæ suæ potentiam (quia & ipsa angelica creatura est, licet propior sit vitio, maligna) nisi quod ille permiserit, cuius iudicia occulta sunt multa, iniusta nulla. Nec sanè daemones natura creant, si aliquid tale faciunt, sed specie tenus, quæ à Deo vera sunt creata, commutant, &c. Quid? an non consonantia, de ortu maximorum quondam Principum aliorum, traduntur? Alexandrum nempe Macedonem, complexu Olympiæ matris draconisque, genitum, ideoque appellatum fuisse Hammonem? Scipionem Africanum & diuum Augustum eiusdem superstitionis interuentu conceptos? Quin & in oceani Gallici insula quadam, nouè Gallicenas illas fuisse, tradunt auctores, cum alijs artibus praeditas, tum vertendi se in quas formas liberet. Quibus ex locis ortam fuisse Melysinam, non est absurda coniectatio. Sed de his alias. Certè praenobiles tum in Gallijs, tum apud inferiores Germanos scio familias, & patriæ nostræ deferentes praenomen, & in galeato imaginum apice (cuius stemmatis diligentissima ac minimè perfunctoria cura fuit veteribus) id monstrū, cuppæ balneatoriæ insidens. Sed & turrim ingentem medio ciuitatis nostræ sitam, paulò supra ætatem nostram bona ex parte prolapsam vetustate compereri, in qua vanitatè illam fuisse peractam, fama per manus traditur. Postremò Carolum felicissimum seculi nostri Principem nondum pubescentem, quum de nuptiarum foedere cum Renata, Ludouici Gallorum regis filia ineundo, tractaretur (quanquam illi larga potestas erat è subiectis aliis gentibus titulum assumendi) totis tamen tabulis haud alia quàm Lucenburgiæ appellatione fuisse denotatum, non in minima gloria posuerim, vsque adeò, vt nisi aliis vitijs supradictum opusculum laboraret, quippe in quo parum verisimilia referuntur, interdum aduersa, nonnunquam dissonantia, non difficile fidem mihi facerèt. Enimuerò quò commodiùs ad ipsius Henrici res nostra feratur oratio, & rectum visum est & necessarium pauca prius de statu temporum illorum supra repetere.
units.tr: I will also bring forward, though not very precisely defined, the testimony of one of our wise men. "These things," says the blessed father Augustine, "are either false or so unusual that they are rightly not believed.
