Yet it must be held most firmly that almighty God can do all that he wills, whether by judging or by bestowing; and that demons do nothing according to the power of their own nature (since they too are angelic creatures, although they are nearer to vice, being malignant), except what he has permitted, whose judgments are many and hidden, none unjust. Nor indeed do the demons create anything by nature when they do such things, but they change the appearance of things which were truly created by God," and so on. What then? Are not similar things handed down about the birth of other very great princes of old? Is it not said that Alexander the Macedonian was begotten in the embrace of his mother Olympias and a dragon, and for that reason was called the son of Ammon? That Scipio Africanus and the deified Augustus were conceived through the intervention of the same superstition? Moreover, the authors tell that on a certain island in the Gallic ocean there were those new kinds of Gallic women, endowed with other arts, and with the power to change themselves into whatever shapes they pleased. It is not an absurd conjecture that Melusine arose from those regions. But of these matters at another time. I certainly know of very noble families both in France and among the lower Germans which bear the name of our homeland, and on the crest of whose helmets (a genealogy to which the ancients gave the most careful and by no means perfunctory attention) sits that monster, perched on a bathing tub. Moreover, it is passed down by word of mouth that a huge tower in the middle of our city, which has for the most part collapsed through age a little before our own time, was the place where that vanity was carried out. Lastly, I would not think it of little importance that when Charles, the most fortunate prince of our age, was not yet grown up and marriage terms with Renée, daughter of Louis, king of the French, were being discussed (although he had ample power to take the title from the other peoples subject to him), he was nevertheless designated in all the documents by no other name than Luxembourg. I would say this were it not that the above-mentioned little work labours under other faults, since in it things are reported that are scarcely credible, sometimes contrary, sometimes inconsistent, and so it would not be hard to make me doubt it. But since it is both fitting and necessary for my account to proceed more conveniently to the affairs of Henry himself, I thought it right and needful to go briefly back over the state of those times beforehand.

units.la: Anno à Christo saluatore genito, M.CCCII, Francorum rex Philippus, cognomento pulcher, graue aduersum pontificem maximum Bonifacium octauum conceperat odium, tum Gibellinæ factionis studiosiorem existimans, tum quod fidem temerè praevaricatum contenderet. Promisisse enim sibi paucis ante annis, cum alia quaedam, tum de summa Romani imperij potestate ab Germanis ad Gallos transcenda, atq; adeò Carolum fratrem diserte fuisse in conuentis nominatum, cui id decus primum assignaretur. Hæc videlicet pollicita nunc cecidisse ad nihilum, Alberto Austrino Teutonico principe palam nuper decretis eius comprobato.
units.tr: In the year 1302 after the birth of Christ the Saviour, Philip, king of the Franks, surnamed the Fair, had conceived a grave hatred against the pontiff maximus Boniface VIII, partly because he judged him too partial to the Ghibelline faction, and partly because he maintained that he had broken faith rashly. For a few years earlier, the king said, Boniface had promised him, among other things, that the supreme power of the Roman empire would be transferred from the Germans to the French, and indeed that his brother Charles had been expressly named in the agreements as the one to whom that honour would first be assigned. These promises, he said, had now come to nothing, since shortly before, Albert of Austria, a German prince, had openly been confirmed in them by Boniface's decrees.

units.la: Eas rex causas grauius secum considerans, rationem irarum exequendarum perquirit. Neq; difficilis mox via Bonifacij irritandi inuenta. Columna gens Romæ opibus & clientelis insignis; Octauo inter comitiorū arcana, suffragij iure ne legeretur obstiterat. Itaq; eis quoq; Bonifacius, per speciem expilati thesauri ecclesiæ, effecerat, vt ædes & suburbana familiæ publicè diruerentur, & qui eorū Cardinales iam essent, venerando collegio excederet. Interea Stephanus ex ea gente profugus in Gallia agitans, idoneus Philippo visus est, per què initia malorum fierent. Cœptus comiter humaneq; haberi, liberaliusq; quàm fortuna exulantium est. Ad hoc Philippus ne quid impotentiæ praetermitteret, sacerdotales Galliarū titulos à pontificibus antea pro decretis, proq; more sanctæ matris ecclesiæ componi solitos, ipse ordinare citra consensum praesidis Romani statuit.
units.tr: Considering these causes more gravely in his mind, the king sought a way of carrying out his resentment. Nor was a way of provoking Boniface soon found that was hard to come by. The Colonna family, distinguished at Rome by their wealth and clients, had opposed, during the secret deliberations of the eighth year, the law that the vote should not be taken. And so Boniface, on the pretext of having plundered the treasury of the church, had also brought it about that their houses and suburban estates were publicly demolished, and that those of their number who were already cardinals withdrew from the venerable college. Meanwhile Stephen, a fugitive from that family who was wandering in Gaul, seemed to Philip a suitable instrument through whom the beginnings of the troubles might be made. He was received courteously and kindly, and more generously than the fortunes of exiles usually allow. In addition, so that Philip might leave nothing undone in his insolent arrogance, he resolved to appoint, without the consent of the Roman pontiff, the ecclesiastical offices of the Gallican churches, which had formerly been arranged by the popes, by decree, and in the custom of holy mother Church.

units.la: Quæ vbi summus antistes intelligit, grauissimè tulit iniuriam pessimi exempli, id quod erat, existimans, si vel antecessorum rectè constituta temerè rescinderentur, vel autoritate pontificiâ laicus princeps prophanasset. Augebatur indignitas ipsius Bonifacij, supra quàm dici potest ambitiosa magnitudine animi, & contumeliarum insolentis. Itaque quo partes suæ iustiores vulgo noscerētur, lege potius agere quàm armis instituit. Præla-tos Gallicos maiores conuenire Romā vniuersos iubet, ad publicam synodum celebrandam. Hi nec regno decederent, Philippi prohibitione in- tercluduntur. Quibus rebus ad Octauum delatis, increpatur rex primùm per literas, deinde quum castigationem contumaciæ paruipenderet, sacrorum participatione arcetur. Neque eo minus prælatis regni ipse Lutetiam accersitis, causam quoq; suam approbare nititur.
units.tr: When the highest bishop understood this, he took the insult very badly, judging it a case of the worst example: that the well-established decisions of his predecessors might be rashly annulled, or that a lay prince might profane them with papal authority. The affront to Boniface himself grew beyond what can be said, owing to his ambitious greatness of spirit and his intolerance of insults. So that his cause might be more widely known as the more just, he chose to proceed by law rather than by arms. He ordered all the greater prelates of Gaul to come to Rome to hold a public synod. But they were prevented by Philip's prohibition from leaving the kingdom, and so were shut in. When these things were reported to Boniface, the king was rebuked first by letter. Then, since he made little of the rebuke for his obstinacy, he was excluded from participation in the sacred rites. Nevertheless, Philip summoned the prelates of the kingdom to Paris, and there he strove to win approval for his own cause.

units.la: Pontifex ne nullam non rationem coercendi Pulchri tentaret, Flandrorum partes tueri aggreditur. Ea tum gens, quod superbius imperatum sibi diceret, Gallicum iugum detrectabat. Cum superis quoque Germanis amicitiam interiorem coniungit, iussò Alberto quibuscunque posset viribus, fines Belgarum quatenus Philippici iuris essent, incurIare.
units.tr: So that the pope might leave no means untried for restraining the Fair King, he undertook to defend the party of the Flemings. That people, because they said that more arrogant orders had been imposed on them, were then refusing the French yoke. Boniface also joined the Germans of the upper regions in close friendship, and at his command Albert was to attack the borders of the Belgians, as far as they were subject to French law, with whatever forces he could muster.

units.la: Sed nihil ea Gallum à consilio dimouerunt. Missi clanculum in Italiam qui Campanos, si qui forsan priuatas ob iras infensi essent Antistiti, corruptos auro traherent in sententiam, cæteraque comprehendendi eius idonea maturè apparárent. Neque euentus infando commento defuit, Anaginæ agens pontifex, à Sarra Columnio duce Gallicæ multitudinis non prouiso irrumpente, summa luce circumuenitur, liberæque custodiæ traditum, oppidani immodicè (vt æquum erat) funesto scelere conturbati, triduo demum elapso, receptis animis exemerunt. Ipse Romam regressus, dum vindictæ modos altiùs inuestigat, morbum, vt creditur, ex ægritudi-ne nactus, interijt.
units.tr: But nothing turned the Frenchman from his plan. Men were secretly sent into Italy to draw the Campanians over to his side with gold, in case any of them, perhaps from private anger, were hostile to the bishop, and to make other preparations suitable for seizing him promptly. Nor did the outcome lack an unspeakable plot. While the pope was staying at Anagni, Sciarra Colonna, leader of the French forces, burst in unforeseen and surrounded him in broad daylight, and he was handed over to free custody. The townsfolk, disturbed beyond measure (as was right) by the deadly crime, after three days had passed, recovered their spirits and freed him. He himself returned to Rome, and while he was investigating more deeply the means of vengeance, he caught a disease, as is believed, from the sickness, and died.

units.la: Vndecimus Benedictus Octauum, Clemens quintus Benedictum, munere summi pontificatus insequitur. Reyterandum Gotthonem quoad priuatus erat, appellabant Burdegalensem Archiflaminem. Is enim variantibus nonnihil patrum sententijs, inter alios duos Pulchro ab suarum partium Cardinalibus nominatus extiterat; quem rex quoniam id temporis plurimùm poterat, si ita sedisset, solenniter nuncuparet. Philippus insperatæ dignationis lætitia gestiens, Reyterandum accersit, in suaque manu papalia Comitia, prolaris epistolis Cardinalium, repositá edocet; cæterum postulata quædam sex capitib. comprehensa, recipi sibi prius quâ res conficí posset, oportere. Gottho nihil minus quàm quæ iactabantur, vel speras, vel cogitans, illudiíque sibi existimas, cunctari primùm: vbi serio agere principem comperit, actis in præsens gratijs, capita se regiæ petitionis præstiturum promittit. Data accep-taque fide placita curantur. Raymundum cardinalis Gallici duodecim summum ecclesiæ Romanæ sacerdotem in gratiam regis consalutant: Italicos statim patres, vt idem facere vellent, epistolis, nunciisque celerrimis adhortati. Gottho vt primùm quæ abrege acta de se fuerant, Italis quoque probari cognouit, senatum statim Cardineum vniuersum, regesque Transalpinos aliquot conuenire Lugdunum iubet, ad peragenda inaugurandi solennia. Id edictum tametsi prælatis Ausoniæ non perinde arriderèt, pontificiam aulam trans Alpes concessuram gementibus: coiere tamen in ciuitatem designatam non infrequentes: ibi declaratus ex more maximus ecclesiæ Christianorum episcopus, quintiqué Clementis appellationem fortitús, mox Philippum censuris (namque id primum postulatorum caput extiterat) quibus innexum à Bonifacio diximus, exoluit, reliqua promissorum tempestiuè se effecturum affirmans.
units.tr: Benedict XI followed Boniface as the eleventh pope, and Clement V followed Benedict. Before he was a private man, they called Bertrand de Got, archbishop of Bordeaux, Gotho. For, while the opinions of the Fathers varied somewhat, he had been named by the cardinals of Philip's party, among two others, as the candidate most acceptable to Philip; and since the king at that time had the greatest power, he would proclaim him solemnly if he were to be seated. Philip, rejoicing at this unexpected honour, summoned Gotho, showed him the papal election in his own hand, and explained the letters of the cardinals. However, he said, certain demands, comprised in six articles, must first be accepted by him before the matter could be completed. Gotho, hoping for or imagining nothing of what was being bandied about, and thinking himself mocked, at first hesitated. When he found that the prince was in earnest, he gave thanks for the present favour and promised that he would fulfil the articles of the royal petition. Faith was given and received, and the agreed matters were arranged. The twelve French cardinals saluted Raymond as supreme priest of the Roman Church, in the king's favour, and at once urged the Italian fathers, by letters and the swiftest messengers, to do the same. When Gotho learned that what had been done on his behalf by the king was also approved by the Italians, he at once ordered the whole college of cardinals and several transalpine kings to assemble at Lyons, to carry out the solemn rites of his inauguration. Although this edict did not equally please the prelates of Italy, who groaned that the papal court would be surrendered beyond the Alps, they nevertheless gathered in no small numbers in the designated city. There he was declared, as is customary, greatest bishop of the Christian Church, and taking the name Clement V, he soon absolved Philip from the censures (for this had been the first of the demands) with which, as we said, Boniface had bound him. He affirmed that he would in due time carry out the remaining promises.

units.la: Sed nec ea Philippus posthabenda ratus, Pictauos, in cóuentum accersito Cle-mente, de cæteris desiderij sui partibus referri iussit medium. Summa petitio erat, de abolenda in perpetuum memoria Bonifacij. Neq; prætextu caruit flagitatio impudès, articulis quadraginta ingenio causidicorum excogitatis, quibus Octaui mores, præter alia facinora de hæretica impietate suggillabantur. Hic vero hærere æstuaréque Clemens, quid nam consilij in re tam inexplicabili caperet. Namque inde occurre-bat Sacramenti interuentu firmata promissio: huic innocentia Bonifacij, qui vt neque forsan insons prorsus criminum haberetur; ita non vllum extare de obiecto admisso iudicium: quin exemplis, decretis, constitutionibusque declaratum abunde reliquisse, quanto studio, quantaque fide gubernacula culminis apostolici procurasset.
units.tr: But Philip thought these matters not to be neglected either. He summoned Clement to an assembly at Poitiers and ordered the remaining parts of his desire to be laid before it. The chief demand was that the memory of Boniface be abolished for ever. The shameless demand lacked no pretext: forty articles, devised by the cleverness of lawyers, by which the character of Boniface, besides other crimes, was branded with heretical impiety. Here Clement was in turmoil and hesitated over what course to take in so intractable a matter. For on one side there presented itself the promise confirmed by the intervention of an oath; on the other, the innocence of Boniface. Though he might perhaps not be altogether free of crimes, no judgment existed concerning the offence charged against him. Indeed, he had left it abundantly declared, by examples, decrees and constitutions, with how much zeal and how much faithfulness he had managed the helm of the apostolic summit.

units.la: Sollicito inter has curas Quinto, opportune Nicolaus cardinalis Pratensis intervenit: cui, quod arbiter omnium arcanorum haberetur, nudatur ordine omnia. Is, vt erat ingenio ad subita etiam quaeque moderanda dexterrimo, primum confirmato pontificis animo, scire se quid potissimum illi consilij profuturum speraret, affirmat; regias in primis spes ali dissimulanter augeriqué placere, tum doceri cupidū principem, quo magis rata fiant: quae ad Bonifacij cineres attinent, videri futurum consultius, si tanta res non nisi publici consilij senatusconsulto firmetur. Quam sententiam vbi Gallus approbauerit, sedem conuentui Viennam inter Allobroges deligat, aliamve ciuitatem quampiam & liberam, & ad excedendum regiis finibus opportunam. Placuit Quinto cardinalis suggestio. Itaque de voluntate Philippi Viennam maximo Christianorum conuentu edicto, Octauoque de opposita impietate ex sententia patrum absoluto, ipse ibi paucos commoratus dies Auenionem in Roberti regis prouinciam sese contulit. Nunc tandem ad Henricum nostrum deflectat oratio.
units.tr: While Clement was anxious amid these cares, Nicholas, cardinal of Prato, opportunely intervened. Because he was regarded as the keeper of all secrets, everything was laid bare to him in order. He, being by nature most adroit at moderating even sudden matters, first strengthened the pope's mind and affirmed that he knew what counsel he hoped would most profit him. It pleased him, above all, that the royal hopes should be nourished and increased in a dissembling manner, and then that the prince, who was eager to learn, should be taught, so that they might become more certain. As for matters concerning the ashes of Boniface, it would, he said, be more prudent if so great a matter were confirmed only by a decree of public council. When the Frenchman approved this opinion, he chose Vienne among the Allobroges as the seat of the assembly, or some other free city suitable for going beyond the royal borders. Clement approved the cardinal's suggestion. Thus, at Philip's wish, a very great assembly of Christians was summoned to Vienne, and Boniface was acquitted, by the opinion of the fathers, of the impiety laid against him. Clement himself stayed there a few days and then betook himself to Avignon, in the province of King Robert. Now at last let my discourse turn to our Henry.

units.la: Anno a Christo M. CCCVIII. rege Romanorum Alberto per insidias nepotis occiso, nuntiatum est, principes, quorum legendi Caesaris ius est, de sufficiendo Imperatore parum conuenturos. Philippus discordiam Germanorum coeptis suis optime conducturam existimans, secretiorum modo consiliorum arbitros coire iussos, de noua dispositione interrogat. Venisse aliquando tempus suo quoque seculo exornandi regni Gallici: Sextum antea postulatorum caput, quod ad eum diem consulto noluisset Clementi prodere, id vero nunc expromere statuisse, de Carolo fratre substituendo in imperium, deque ea dignitate per senatusconsultum in perpetuum transponenda in Galliam. Esse Clementem iam pridem in potestate, possetque rem & iure & exemplo nixam facile transigi. Cui enim fiat iniuria, si vacantis imperij permutetur conditio? Idem fecisse pontifices olim alios. Denique fatorum seriem conuenire cum eiusmodi proposito, vt quemadmodum principatus ille de Graecis quondam in Francos, sicut ei videbatur, deque ea gente ad Italos, ac postremum ad Theutones translatus crederetur, ita rursus ad Francorum posteritatem remigret. Mouit vniuersos proceres relatio regia, laudatoque nobilitandi Gallorum regni desiderio, de consilij sententia decretum fit, & vt Philippus & Carolus primo quoque tempore ante etiam quam Germani irent in suffragium, Clementem numeroso comitatu adeant, rumore quidem dispersio, quasi ad persequendam Bonifacij criminationem veniant: reuera autem vt protinus quam Auenionem inierint, pontificem de sexta & ad id tempus ignota petitione commonefaciant. Eam occultationem nihil fuisse aliud, quam de Imperatorio apice publice transponedo in Celtas. Abdere vero rem placuisse eatenus, quam apud Bonifacium quoque tentauissent, vt ne viuum regnantemque Albertum affecisse videretur iniuria. Nec repugnaturum Clementem quantumuis audaci flagitationi, videlicet iam instructo exercitu veriusquam famulitio territum. Edicto per vniuersam ditionem dimisso, generosi clientes ad regium iter apparati conueniunt, equitum sex milia fuisse traduntur.
units.tr: In the year of Christ 1308, King Albert of the Romans having been killed by the treachery of his nephew, it was announced that the princes, who have the right to elect the Caesar, would hardly agree on the choice of an emperor. Philip, thinking that the discord of the Germans would best serve his undertakings, ordered his confidants in secret counsels to meet, and asked them about a new arrangement. The time had come, he said, to adorn the French kingdom in his own age too. He had now resolved to bring out the sixth article of demands, which until that day he had deliberately not wished to disclose to Clement: that his brother Charles should be substituted in the empire, and that this dignity should be transferred to France for ever by decree of the senate. Clement was already long in his power, and the matter, resting on both law and precedent, could easily be carried through. For to whom would injury be done, if the condition of the vacant empire were changed? Other popes had done the same in former times. Finally, the sequence of fates, he said, agreed with such a plan: just as that sovereignty had once passed, as he thought, from the Greeks to the Franks, and from that people to the Italians, and lastly to the Teutons, so again it should return to the posterity of the Franks. The royal proposal moved all the nobles. With praise for the desire to ennoble the kingdom of the Gauls, a decree was passed by the opinion of the council that Philip and Charles, at the earliest opportunity, even before the Germans went to vote, should approach Clement with a large retinue. It was spread abroad by rumour that they were coming to pursue the accusation against Boniface; in truth, as soon as they entered Avignon, they were to remind the pope of the sixth petition, which was unknown until then. That concealment was nothing other than the public transfer of the imperial crown to the Celts. They had decided to hide the matter so far as they had also tried it with Boniface, so that no injury might seem to have been done to Albert, who was living and reigning. Clement, they expected, would not resist, however bold the demand, being frightened by an army already drawn up rather than by any servile submission. With a summons sent throughout the whole realm, noble vassals gathered, prepared for the royal journey; six thousand horsemen are said to have been there.

units.la: Enimuero sicuti recte institutis diuinus fauor arridet, ita improbe consulta iuxta Sexti Pythagorici sententiam, funestus insequitur exitus. Permanauit certe ad Pontificem quamuis latitantis conciliabuli astutia. Quare denuo accersito Pratense, intimorum (vt diximus) omnium socio, ac iam ante exoso Philippum ob insectationem Bonifaciane memoriae; quae si tolleretur e medio, & acta quoque illius, in quibus Cardinalatus censebatur, quem Octauus illi contulerat, conuulsum iri verebatur, nouam huiusmodi ambiguitatem aperit. Ille ad innatam sapientiam versus, quam maximis itineribus, inquit, & antequam Gallicae petitionis mentio in senatu fiat, nunciandum in Germania censeo, de successore quammaxime mature surrogando. Quū Clemens, quē igitur praecipuum crederet tantaque successioni idoneum quaesiuisset; Pratensis, ecclesiarum ne libertatis respectu, an studio Gibellinarum partium,
units.tr: Indeed, as divine favour smiles on rightly ordered undertakings, so, according to the saying of Sextus the Pythagorean, a deadly outcome follows wicked plans. Certainly the cunning of the hidden conspiracy leaked out to the pope. So, summoning Pratensis again, the companion of all his intimates (as we said), who was already earlier hateful to Philip for his attacks on the memory of Boniface, the pope opened up this new uncertainty. He feared that if Boniface's memory were removed, his acts would also be torn up, including those by which the cardinalate, which Boniface had conferred on him, was reckoned. Turning to his innate wisdom, Pratensis said: "I think word should be sent into Germany with the greatest speed, and before any mention of the French petition is made in the senate, so that a successor is chosen as early as possible." When Clement asked whom he therefore believed to be the outstanding man, fit for so great a succession, Pratensis, whether out of regard for the liberty of the churches, or from zeal for the Ghibelline party,

units.la: {y} Cardinalis Pratensis, pontificis cōsiliarius. partium, an consuetudinis in urbe quondam institutæ memor, Henricum (ait) Luceburgiæ comitem nulli Germaniæ principum cedere arbitror, siue religionem, siue fidem, seu certè magnitudinem animi spectaueris. Neque dubium, si eo celsitudinis benignitate tua proueƈtus fuerit, nulla non re vel pontificijs obtemperaturum iussis, vel immunitatem ecclesiæ propugnaturum. Sanè clanculum & dissimulanter cunƈta fieri oportet, ne si publico senatu in patrumque conspectu cogitata retexeris, qui cardinales Philippo studet, proditis illico rebus, vota nostra conturbent. Itaque quas ipse literas dabis in Alemanniam, pusilla modò formula placet obsignari, quasi non scriptas de rebus grauissimis. Ego seorsum prolixas de tota re alias exarabo. Iuuit assertionem Cardineam Henrici quoque integritatis gloria, quam ex rebus fortiter probeq; gestis fama iam pridem exorta, ad Clementem quoque pertulerat.
units.tr: Cardinal Pratensis, counsellor to the pontiff: "Whether mindful of the liberty of the churches, or of the zeal of the Ghibelline party, or of the custom once established in the city, I judge that Henry, Count of Luxembourg, yields to no German prince, whether you look to his religion, his faith, or at least his greatness of spirit. There is no doubt that if your kindness raises him to that height, he will obey the pontifical commands in every matter and defend the immunity of the Church. Indeed, everything must be done secretly and quietly. If you disclose your plans in a public senate, before the eyes of the fathers, the matter will at once be betrayed to the cardinal who favours Philip, and he will upset our wishes. So the letters you give to Germany should be sealed in a short form, as if they were not written about the most weighty affairs. I will write long letters on the whole matter separately." The fame of Henry's integrity, which had long since arisen from his brave and honourable deeds, had also reached Clement and supported the Cardinal's assertion.

units.la: Delatis ad Germanos epistolis, reqq; intellecta, Comitiorum solennia maturantur, valueréque adeò pontificiæ Cardinalisq; literæ (qui & illud adiecerat, nisi bonis consilijs protinus obsecundarent, Cæsarei fastigij apicem, iure ne an iniuria, relicto Rheno transiturum in Galliam) sed & maximè spectata virtus Henrici profuit, vti cunctorum suffragijs, ac ne vno quidem repugnante, Romani regni sceptra florenti iuueni deferrentur. Autores habeo Luceburgi transacta fuisse comitia. Quod ascribendum putaui magis, ne ignorauisse eam rem crederer, quàm vt morem locumq; vetustum tam tumultuario præsertim tempore prætermissum, existimarem. Ille vt contra opinionem hominum per Celtas, perque comitatum pontificis renunciatus rex fuit: Pulchellus qui iam festinabat compellare Clementem, illusum se animadvertens, domum irritus spei repetijt, nunquam postea bene de eo pontifice sentiens.
units.tr: When the letters had been delivered to the Germans and their contents understood, the solemn electoral assembly was hurried on. The papal and cardinal's letters prevailed (the cardinal had added that unless they promptly complied with good advice, he would carry the summit of the imperial dignity, rightly or wrongly, across the Rhine into France). Yet the outstanding virtue of Henry also helped, so that by the votes of all, and with not a single dissenter, the sceptres of the Roman kingdom were conferred on the flourishing young man. I have authorities that the assembly was held at Luxembourg. I thought this should be noted, so that I might not seem ignorant of the matter, rather than because I judged that an ancient custom and place had been neglected, especially in so tumultuous a time. Thus, contrary to men's expectation, he was proclaimed king through the French and through the pontiff's following. The handsome young man, who had been hurrying to address Clement, seeing that he had been mocked, returned home disappointed, and never afterwards thought well of that pontiff.

units.la: Luceburgius, qui nihil minus quàm Cæsarea gubernacula sibi credendo cogitauerat, omnium primum gratias immortali Deo lectoribúsq; agendas cēsuit. Mox ad ea quæ & tempus & res & maleuolorum conatus ferebant conuersus, mittit in oram Narbonensem, qui a Clemente postulent, vti ratam sibi facere surrogationem pro more dignaretur. Principes legationis, Sabaudiæ comes (nomen vt in plerisque sequentibus non traditur) & Guido Namurcæus, Flandri comitis frater, ambo ex propinquis regijs: hi à Clemente, totóque cœtu Cardineo comiter humaneque habiti, mense Aprili, comprobationem actorum in Germania, causa cognita impetrarunt. Decretum vti è cardinalibus Pratensis & Fliscus prima quaque occasione in Italiam proficisci maturarèt gentibúsque cis alpes habitantibus, apostolica vice præciperent, ne quid impedimenti morarúmque, quo minus potestas novo regi petendæ vrbis foret, astruerent, quin obedienter atque hospitaliter aduentum illius curarent excipere. Sunt qui legem adiectam fuisse probationi affirmèt, vt intra primum biennium ad motus Italiæ compescendos, Romam solita expeditione properaret, simulque ipse summos Imperatorij nominis fasces acciperet, quum tres proximè antecedentes principes eum honorem prætermisisse constaret.
units.tr: Luxembourg, who had thought of entrusting the imperial government to himself least of all, judged that thanks must first be given to the immortal God and to his readers. Then, turning to those matters which both the time, the affair and the efforts of ill-wishers demanded, he sent to the Narbonne coast men to ask Clement to deign, according to custom, to confirm his election for him. The leaders of the embassy were the Count of Savoy (his name is not given in most of what follows) and Guido of Namur, brother of the Count of Flanders, both from the royal kin. Treated courteously and kindly by Clement and the whole cardinalate, they obtained in April, after a hearing of the case, the approval of the acts in Germany. A decree was issued that the cardinals Pratensis and Fliscus should hasten to set out for Italy at the first opportunity, and should, by apostolic authority, instruct the peoples living on this side of the Alps not to allege any hindrance or delay that might prevent the new king from seeking the city of Rome, but to take care to receive his arrival obediently and hospitably. Some affirm that a condition was added to the approval, namely that within the first two years he should hasten to Rome on the usual expedition to quell the disturbances of Italy, and at the same time receive the highest insignia of the imperial name, since it was established that the three immediately preceding princes had neglected that honour.

units.la: Sabaudo reuerso, voluntatéque Clementina perspecta, conuentus Aquisgranum indicitur. Coiere anno insequente ad id concilium inter alios proceres dux Brabantiæ, comes Flandriæ & comes Raynaldus. Ibi peractis solennibus, generoso vertici regium diadema archiepiscopus Agrippinæ, more maiorum, ad octauum idus Ianuarij, imposuit. Quem diem & constitutiones ecclesiæ celebrari ob memoriam Magorum iusserunt, & tum publica lætitia celebriorem reddidit.
units.tr: When the Count of Savoy had returned and Clement's will had been ascertained, a diet was summoned at Aachen. In the following year, among other magnates, the Duke of Brabant, the Count of Flanders and Count Reginald came together for that assembly. There, the solemnities having been performed, the archbishop of Cologne placed the royal diadem on the noble head, according to ancestral custom, on the eighth day before the Ides of January. The Church's constitutions ordered that this day be celebrated in memory of the Magi, and public rejoicing then made it more celebrated.

units.la: Anno à Christo genito M. CCC.IX, ad diem v i.idus Maij, cælum ardere visum, discurrente flammæ vortice è plaga Boreali in Meridiem. Quo typo aduentum Henrici portendi, Italorum multi crediderunt.
units.tr: In the year from the birth of Christ 1309, on the sixth day before the Ides of May, the sky seemed to burn, with a whirl of flame sweeping from the northern quarter towards the south. Many Italians believed that this sign portended the coming of Henry.

units.la: Interea Carolus Siciliæ rex secúdus, Gallicæ originis, cis fretum regnans, rebus humanis excessit. Plures huic filij, nempe maior natu Carolus, Martellus cognomine, & Robertus. Martellus viuo etiam dum patre, mortem (sed filio relicto) obijt. Qua in specie, exq; facto ipso, larga disputandi materia Iureconsultis est nata: Nepós ne antecedere iure possit patruum in successione auita. Sed & responsis prudentum & pontificia pronunciatione quadam Robertus annixus, compendium hæreditatis obtinuit, paternaq; necè comperta, mox Auenionem properat. Ibi nullis non modis Clementis amicitia comparata, adeò promouit, vt & rex vtriusque appellaretur Siciliæ, & quicquid præterea alieni æris patri, auóque per belli quondam tempora ecclesia Romana crediderat, illi ferretur acceptum: summa aureorum sex milia superauisse putatur. Tantis beneficijs Robertus se obnoxium sentiens, actis ad tempus gratijs, operam curamque Clementi omnem gratitudinis ostendendæ pensandæque dignationis detulit. Hic Quintus qui Luceburgium, vt supra tetigimus, paulò ante regem Romanum declarauerat, siue suspectam habens Henrici potentiam, siue contractæ amicitiæ Vasconico more pertæsus, Siculum Romandiolæ comitem facit. Eamque Robertus prouinciam Giliberto Zantillio Vice comiti demandauit. Quæ res perpulchram Gibellinis Imperatorij iugi detrectandi potestatem tribuit, vel tantula rebellandi occasione gestientibus.
units.tr: Meanwhile Charles II, king of Sicily, of French origin, who reigned on this side of the strait, departed this life. He had several sons, namely the eldest, Charles, surnamed Martel, and Robert. Martel died while his father was still alive, but he left a son. On this point, and on the fact itself, a wide matter for dispute arose among the jurists: whether a grandson can by right precede his uncle in succession to the grandfather's inheritance. But Robert, relying both on the answers of the learned and on a certain papal pronouncement, obtained the benefit of the inheritance, and, having learned of his father's death, soon hastened to Avignon. There, having secured Clement's friendship by every means, he so advanced his cause that he was called king of both Sicilies, and whatever other debt of money the Roman Church had lent to his father and grandfather during the wars of former times was credited to him; the sum is thought to have exceeded six thousand gold pieces. Feeling himself bound by such great benefits, Robert expressed thanks for a time, and then devoted all his effort and care to showing gratitude and repaying the favour to Clement. Clement, who had a little earlier declared Luxembourg Roman king, as we touched upon above, either because he held Henry's power in suspicion, or because he was weary of a friendship entered into in the Gascon manner, made the Sicilian Count of Romagnola. Robert entrusted that province to Gilbert Zantillio, the vice-count. This matter gave the Ghibellines a splendid opportunity of constantly refusing imperial rule, especially those eager for rebellion however slight the occasion.

units.la: Luceburgius nihil eorum negligendum ratus, quæ ad amplitudinem Augusti principatus pertinent, summa ope annisus est, vt quam celerrime documentum aliquod præberet, quantus & quàm propensus sibi esset animus pontificiæ dignitatis excolendæ. Dimisso edicto per prouincias, vt quisquis nobilium Augustale beneficium obtineret, die constituto vellet adesse, solennemq; profectionem, Romanæ mitræ capiendæ causa, pro conditione, próque consuetudine sua curaret exornandam. Ipse vniuersa Germania Ioanni filio demandata, cum non adeo grandi comitatu iter ingressus, alpibúsq; propinquans, Laufani constitit, reliquam exercitus partem opperiens. Eo mox legationes ex Italia salutandi causa certatim occurrunt. At Guelphorum factio in Hetruria, cis alpináque degentium, quam semper ante hac Teutonicæ felicitati aduersatam constat, in multo maximum metum incidit, & fama numerosi exercitus, & reliquæ Italiæ proniore consensu. Præcipue verò Florentini, inter spem metúmque ancipites, hostiliter ne an deditione fortissimum ducem exciperent. Præualuit tamen sententia, vi potius quàm abiecta formidine agedum censentium. Itaq; quo vel conturbaretur inauguratio, vel lentiùs certè succederet, conscripta per totam ciuitatem iuuentute, accitisq; militibus alijs voluntarijs, præsidium haud contemnendum efficiunt. Ad hoc pecuniam, frumentum cæterasque res comparant, vel stipendio, vel obsidioni necessarias. Deniq; fœdus cum Siculo Roberto, ciuitatibúsq; Hetruscis ac cisalpinis aliquot faciunt. Pisanorum longè diuersa sententia, hi quo sese Gibellinarum partium, atq; adeò Cæsarei nominis quàm maximè studiosos Henrico in ipso Italiæ ingressu cóprobarent, donum regi aureorum milia x l submiserunt.
units.tr: Luxembourg, judging that none of those things which pertain to the greatness of the Augustan principate should be neglected, strove with all his might to give some proof quickly of how great and how inclined his mind was to cultivate the pontifical dignity. He issued an edict through the provinces that whoever among the nobles held an Augustal benefice should be present on an appointed day, and that each should prepare, according to his rank and custom, a solemn departure in order to receive the Roman mitre. He himself entrusted the whole of Germany to his son John, and set out with no very large retinue; approaching the Alps, he halted at Lausanne, awaiting the rest of the army. Soon embassies from Italy hurried there eagerly to greet him. But the faction of the Guelfs, living in Tuscany and on this side of the Alps, which had always before been known to oppose the German good fortune, fell into very great fear, both at the rumour of a numerous army and because of the more ready consent of the rest of Italy. The Florentines in particular, wavering between hope and fear, were uncertain whether to receive the most valiant leader as an enemy or by surrender. Nevertheless the opinion of those who urged resistance by force rather than abject fear prevailed. Therefore, so that the inauguration might either be disturbed or at least proceed more slowly, they enrolled the youth throughout the whole city, summoned other volunteer soldiers, and made a garrison by no means to be despised. To this end they procured money, grain and other things necessary either for pay or for a siege. Finally they made an alliance with the Sicilian Robert and with several Tuscan and cisalpine cities. The Pisans held a quite different view: to show themselves most zealous for the Ghibelline party, and indeed for the imperial name, at the very entrance of Henry into Italy, they sent the king a gift of forty thousand gold pieces.

units.la: Eo veluti viatico prœditus (quippe cuius ærarium, vt veris agamus, virtute esset quàm nummis instructius) Septembris exitu mouit è Laufano, superatóque monte perquam arduo, Senisium vocant accolæ, Taurinum est inuectus. Illinc decimo die quàm accesserat, Insubres ingreditur, ibi quoque magno apparatu acceptus, Astensium dissidia haud exilia summa cura composuit. Constabat id temporis regius comitatus equitum duobus milibus, quum reliquum perinde expectaretur. Manfititaque apud Astam toto bimestri atque amplius, & reliquam, vt dixiimus, copiarum partem opperiens, & de incunda Insubrium ciuitate cōsultas. Gnidottus Turritus sapientia atq; opibus clarus, genti ea tempestate præerat. Is audito in primis aduentu, veteri cepit, ne diuersæ factionis pars (Gibellini erant violetia illius acti in exilium) occasione Germani aduentantis in recuperanda dignitate vteretur. Itaq; præsidium ad vrbis suæ tutelam comparat duorum milium atque amplius. Ipsi fœdus atque hospitium erat cum toto Guelphorum genere, per Italiam agentium. Sed & operâ dabat quibuscunque poterat artibus, ne mœnibus reciperetur Heinricus, Gibellinæ scilicet factionis patronum, vt paulò ante scripsimus, futurum metuens. Neq; tamen obtinere potuit, quin bona ciuitatis pars regis amatior, simul cardinalis Fliscus, tum legatus Apostolicus, Clementináque mandata conficere cupiens, Luceburgium vltro inuitarent. Rex Romanus, dolentibus Gnidotti oculis, pridie Mediolanum Dominici natalis inuehitur, diéq; sequente octauo, Antistes eius dicœcesos, in Ambrosij beatissimi delubro mysterijs vacantis, Henrici verticem secunda corona redimiuit. Augustæ quoq; quam vnà secum aduexerat, idem honor habitus. Affuere solennib. omnium ferè Italiæ ciuitatû legati, Gibellinarû modo partium, ita vt Fluentini duntaxat oratores desiderarentur. Insubriû quoq; interim discordiâ quanta fieri potuit cura
units.tr: Provided with this viaticum (for his treasury, to speak the truth, was better equipped by courage than by money), at the end of September he set out from Lausanne, and having crossed a very steep mountain, which the inhabitants call Senis, he was carried to Turin. From there, on the tenth day after he had arrived, he entered the Insubrian territory, and there too he was received with great pomp; and he settled with the greatest care the no small discord of the Asti. At that time the royal retinue numbered two thousand horsemen, while the rest was expected in the same way. He stayed at Asti for the whole of two months and more, awaiting, as we said, the rest of the forces, and consulting about entering the Insubrian city. Guidotto della Torre, famous for his wisdom and wealth, presided over that people at that time. He, having heard first of all of the coming, in his old fear, began to take care lest a part of the opposing faction (they were Ghibellines, from whose violence he had been driven into exile) should use the occasion of the German's arrival to recover their dignity. Therefore he prepared a garrison of two thousand men and more for the protection of his city. He himself had an alliance and friendship with the whole Guelf race travelling through Italy. He also laboured by whatever arts he could so that Henry, the patron, as we wrote a little earlier, of the Ghibelline faction, might not be admitted within the walls, fearing that he would become so. Yet he could not prevent a large part of the city, who loved the king the more, together with Cardinal Fliscus, who was then the apostolic legate and wished to carry out Clement's commands, from inviting Luxembourg of their own accord. The king of the Romans, with Guidotto's eyes grieving, was carried into Milan on the day before the Lord's Nativity; and on the following day, the eighth, the bishop of that diocese, who was busy with the rites in the shrine of the most blessed Ambrose, crowned Henry's head with the second crown. The same honour was given to the empress, whom he had brought with him. The legates of almost all the cities of Italy were present at the solemnities, only the Ghibelline party, so that only the envoys of the Florentines were missed. Meanwhile he also settled, with as much care as possible, the discord of the Insubrians

units.la: Clementis inconstan tia erga Caesarem. Henricus Luxemburgensis Italicam expeditionem suscepit. Florentinorum rebelles. Henricus Laufanna in Italiam movet. Guidotus Turritus Mediolani praefectus. Caesar Mediolanum donatum. cura sedauit, adeo vt & Maphæü Vicecomitē cum sodalibus, & ciuitatis Archiflaminem, cæterosq; proscriptos, reductaret in vrbem. Eò tum quoq; legati frequentes ciuitatum Italiæ gratulatum accedunt, ita vt tota passim Ausonia, Bononiam excipio, & Paduam, vicarij Augustales dimitterentur, acciperenturq; comites.
units.tr: Clement's inconstancy towards the Emperor. Henry of Luxemburg undertook the Italian expedition. The Florentine rebels. Henry moves from Lausanne into Italy. Guidotto Torriani, prefect of Milan. The Emperor is given Milan. By his care he calmed the discord so thoroughly that he brought back into the city Matteo Visconti with his companions, the archbishop of the city, and the other exiles. Then too, envoys from the cities of Italy came in large numbers to offer congratulations, so that all over Italy, except Bologna and Padua, the imperial vicars were being dismissed and counts were being received.

units.la: Inter hæc Gnidottus exosus felicitatem Maphæi, quibuscunq; rationibus poterat, vindicare priscam fortunâ molitur. Ac in sapientia Vicecomitis infaustis cœptis fuisset occursum (namq; rem omnē ordine primoribus regiæ aulæ expositum) maximus in ciuitate tumultus extitisset, non partibus modò noxius, sed & formidolosus Principi, qui iam securior, bonâ exercitus parte per finitima loca neglectim dispersirat. Sunt qui dicant, Maphæum quò certius animū Turriti pernoscceret, simulasse societatem partium accusauisseq; multis modis supercilium Cæsarum, quod id genus Reipub. principatum nomine, seruitutem re ipsa præseferret. Satius esse æquabilem libertate omnib. viribus propugnare, quàm ingenuos ac fortes animos Germanico iugo supponere. Reciperet modò animā, seq; in priscā præfecturā ipse reponeret, nec detrectaturū populum ne nūc quoq; gubernacula quondā sibi cognita. His atq; eiusdemodi dictis perui-ctū Gnidottū cuncta simpliciter credisse, promisisseq; Maphæo, & vafro aduersario & restituto in gratiam, quem impensè cauendū esse, veteri docemur adagio. Illū, Gnidotto prodito, fabulā omnem denarrauisse Septimo. Neq; defuisse impiæ criminationi fidem, ita vt die dicta, Turritoq; adesse iusso, cognitio paraketur. Sed is iudicio consiliorum intellecto, furtim ad Guelphos transijt.
units.tr: Meanwhile Guidotto, hating Matteo's good fortune, tried by every means he could to recover his former position. Had Visconti not met his ill-advised undertaking (for he had set out the whole affair in order to the chief men of the royal court), a great tumult would have broken out in the city, harmful not only to the parties but also dangerous to the prince, who by now felt more secure and had scattered a good part of his army carelessly through the neighbouring places. Some say that Matteo, so that he might know more surely the mind of Torriani, pretended to share his party and accused the arrogance of the Caesars in many ways, saying that such a government wore the name of a commonwealth but in fact showed the face of slavery. It was better, he said, to defend equal liberty with all one's strength than to put free and brave spirits under the German yoke. Guidotto should only take heart and restore himself to his old prefecture; the people would not refuse him, since they still knew him as their former governor. Guidotto, won over by these and similar words, believed everything without reservation and made promises to Matteo, a crafty opponent who had been restored to favour, and whom, as the old proverb teaches, one must be very careful of. Matteo, having betrayed Guidotto, reported the whole story to the Emperor. The impious accusation found credence, so that on the appointed day, with Torriani ordered to appear, a hearing was prepared. But Guidotto, having learned the judgement of the councillors, secretly went over to the Guelphs.

units.la: Iisdem diebus Cremona, Gnidotti exactione comperta, simul Florentinorum adducta instinctu, rebellis Henrico efficitur, sed & qui Brixianorum Gibellini erant, successibus Imperatoris auditis, Guelphos urbe exegerunt. Idē Parmæ factū. Quibus rebus Cæsar cognitis, mittit qui eas quoq; rixas consopitet, exulibus reductis in patriā. Sed breui post tempore Guelphica pars, Felsineorū Florentinorumq; confisa praesidio, Brixia Gibellinos inuicem depulit, ex professo; hostis Imperatori efficitur.
units.tr: About the same days, Cremona, once Guidotto's exactions were discovered and at the same time the urging of the Florentines was brought to bear, became rebellious against Henry. Those of Brescia who were Ghibellines, when they heard of the Emperor's successes, drove out the Guelphs from their city. The same happened at Parma. When the Emperor learned of these things, he sent men to quiet these quarrels too, and the exiles were brought back to their country. But shortly afterwards the Guelf party, trusting in the protection of the Bolognese and the Florentines, drove the Ghibellines out of Brescia in turn, and openly became an enemy of the Emperor.

units.la: Anno à Christo genito MCCCXI, mense Aprili, Imperator Henricus obsessa iamdiu Cremona, Genevensem episcopum, cognatione sibi deuinctum, cum turmis ad Patauinos coercendos mittit, quos à Bononiensibus stetisse diximus. Abeo Vicentia, quæ Paduani iuris erat, bello capitur. Præsidium in arce consistens, fuga dilapsum. Ea victoria ipsos quoque Patauinos metu vsque adeo perculit, vt suppliciter sese fidei in primis tradiderint, aureorum milia centum ob contumaciam pendere, Cæsareumq; præfectum recipere iussi. Idem Antistes profectus Venetias, tributum pro vetere consuetudine postulauit. Appulso honor ingens habitus, adnumeratáq; in tiaram Romanā, talenta Veneta mille. Eadem in ciuitate ipsum insigne confectum, solido ex auro, coronam variis maximiq; precij gemmis adornatibus: sellam quoq; argenteam, auroq; circumlitam, fabricatam ibi tradunt.
units.tr: In the year of Christ 1311, in April, the Emperor Henry, while Cremona had long been under siege, sent the bishop of Geneva, bound to him by kinship, with troops to restrain the Paduans, whom we have said had sided with the Bolognese. From there he took by war Vicenza, which belonged to the jurisdiction of Padua. The garrison holding the citadel fled. This victory struck the Paduans themselves with such fear that they humbly surrendered themselves to the faith of the Emperor, were ordered to pay a hundred thousand gold pieces as a penalty for their obstinacy, and to receive an imperial prefect. The same bishop went on to Venice and demanded tribute according to the old custom. On his arrival he was given great honour, and a thousand Venetian talents were counted into the Roman tiara. In that same city, they say, the insignia itself was made: a crown of solid gold, adorned with various gems of great value; and a silver chair, gilded over with gold, was also made there.

units.la: Interea sedente ad Cremonam Henrico, obsessi, qui parum muniti erant ad obsidionem ferendam, simul Archiepiscopi Rauennatis interuentu, sese sub conditione tributi pendendi, vltro dediderūt. Eidem mandatum Antistiti, muros ciuitatis castellaq; demoliri.
units.tr: Meanwhile, while Henry was sitting before Cremona, the besieged, who were too poorly fortified to endure a siege, surrendered of their own accord on condition that they would pay tribute, at the same time through the intervention of the archbishop of Ravenna. The same bishop was ordered to demolish the walls and castles of the city.

units.la: Cæsar Cremonensi bello perfecto, ad Brixiam quoque circumsidendam festinat, non aliâs pari instructus exercitu: qui parcissimè numerant, equestrium Germanorum validæ armaturæ sex milia fuisse tradunt. Namque vt rumor per transalpinas quasq; prouincias de Mediolano, cæterisq; ciuitatibus subiugatis increbuit, vix dici potest, quanta & quàm fida multitudo militū certatim adfluerat, pars emerendi stipendij studio: cæteri amore vnċti regis adducti. Præ certo creditur Henricum, si in primis abstitisset, relictaq; Brixia processisset in Hetruriā, nō Thuscos modò, qui recētis defectionis sibi conscij, iram iustissimi vindicis formidabant, sed & quantā apexecute non interest, parte Italiæ sub iugum missurum: quippe qui parum prouisi essent contra obsidionē, quorumq; nutarent iam animi, iustitia clementiaq; noui regis, impulsi. Sed is dum cisalpinæ pertinaciūs imminet, maiorum rerum occasionem praetermisit. Adeò vincere maximos duces promptius scire compertum est, quàm vti victoria. Quippe virtus attenuata periculis, nullam non in partem de prouidendo circumspectat: eadem rebus sublata secundis, seqraq; sui, quæ futura sunt negligit.
units.tr: When the Cremonese war was finished, the Emperor hastened to besiege Brescia as well, with an army not equal to any other he had had. Those who count most sparingly say there were six thousand German heavily armed horsemen. For when rumour of Milan and the other subjugated cities spread through the lands beyond the Alps, it can hardly be told how great and how loyal a crowd of soldiers flocked in eagerly: some from desire to earn pay, others drawn by love for their anointed king. It is firmly believed that if Henry had not stopped at first, and had left Brescia and advanced into Tuscany, he would have put under the yoke not only the Tuscans, who, conscious of their recent revolt, feared the anger of a most just avenger, but also a large part of Italy. For the defenders were ill provided against a siege, and their spirits were already wavering, moved by the justice and clemency of the new king. But he, while pressing more stubbornly on affairs this side of the Alps, let slip the opportunity of greater things. So it is found that great commanders know better how to win than how to use victory. For courage, worn down by dangers, looks about on every side to make provision; the same courage, lifted up by success and careless of itself, neglects what is to come.

units.la: Eodem anno ciuitates Hetruscæ, Guelpharum partium, Florentia, Bononia, Senæ, Luca, Pistorium, fœdus inter se aduersum Henricum sanciunt. Florentini præsidium equitum Hispani generis cccc, quos à Roberto acceperant, misere Bononiam, itidemque Senam & Lucam, si forte ea regione Germanus statuisset incedere. Sed & quicquid Gibellinorum in ciuitatibus Guelphis versabatur, exactum.
units.tr: In the same year the Tuscan cities of the Guelf party, Florence, Bologna, Siena, Lucca and Pistoia, made a league among themselves against Henry. The Florentines sent four hundred horsemen of Spanish origin, whom they had received from King Robert, to Bologna, and likewise to Siena and Lucca, in case the German should happen to march into that region. And whatever Ghibellines lived in the Guelf cities was driven out.

units.la: Sub hæc perstante Cæsare in obsidenda Brixia, variæ utrinque clades acceptæ: inter cæteros autem proceres, & frater regis & equitum magister Walramus, magnæ indolis, ictu sagittæ percussus interijt. Corpus apud diuum Barnabam conditur, quod templum nodum ciuitate clausum fuisse, Iacobus philosophus in supplemento autor est. Eo infortunio, sublatos paulò ante Cæsarianorum animos resedise, ob eximij iuuenis necem, Brixiani credentes, frequentius iam incautiúsque excurfare cœperunt. Etenim die quodam licentius euagantes, intercepti, fusi fugatique sunt. Cæsorum numerus ducenti. Capti ex ciuitatis primoribus quadraginta, inter quos Galeatius, cognomento Brusatus, obsessorum tribunus. Is quia fidem regi non multò ante datam infregerat, quadrigarum violentia, diuetsam in partem miserum distrahentium corpus, perfidiæ pœnas exoluit. Cæteri captiuorum securi percussi. Nihilo magis proficiente ad euincendam contumaciam exemplo seueri supplicij, quin hostes cælesti quoq; fauore adiuti videbantur, strue tadauerum odoréque diuturni exercitus incubantis, corrupto aere, ita ut plurimi Teutonum varios in morbos inciderint, cogerentúrque aut miseri è vita excedere, aut inglorij, neq; id citra discrimen, repetere patriam. Procerum ea extinctorum tabe præcipuus Guido Namurceus, cuius supra meminimus, Flandrorum quodam tribunus in Curtracensi prælio, atq; ob id rerum gestarum claritate spectatus: Quam ob luem magna purpuratorum pars Heinricum de soluęda obsidione solicitat. Illo magis intolerabilem ac minime perseueraturam necessitatem hostium, quam laborem exercitus obseruante: quare decedere non nisi compos voti statuit. Quibus rebus intellectis, obscesi effecti supplices, Cardinalis quoque Flisci auxilio veniam consequuti, ad diem xvi kalendarum Octobrium, fidei Principis se dediderunt. Rex ciuitate potitus, murisque protinus ac turribus demoliri iussis, tributum aureorum viginti millium, præterea obsides centum, quos ex omni ciuium multitudine selegisset, belli iure imperat. Magno stetit ea victoria, nempe vix quarta exercitus parte superstite.
units.tr: While the Emperor persisted in besieging Brescia, losses were suffered on both sides. Among the other nobles, the king's brother and master of the horse, Walram, a man of great promise, was struck by an arrow and died. His body was buried at the church of St Barnabas, which, as the philosopher James writes in his supplement, was closed off from the city by a wall. Because of this misfortune the spirits of the imperialists, which had been raised a little before, subsided, and the people of Brescia, believing that the young man's death had quelled them, began to make sorties more often and with less caution. For on a certain day, roaming too freely, they were cut off, routed and put to flight. Two hundred were slain, and forty of the leading men of the city were taken, among them Galeazzo, surnamed Brusato, tribune of the besieged. Because he had broken faith with the king, which he had pledged not long before, he paid the penalty of his treachery: his miserable body was torn apart by four chariots driven in different directions. The rest of the prisoners were beheaded. The example of severe punishment did nothing more to break their obstinacy; indeed the enemy seemed helped even by heaven's favour. The heaps of corpses and the stench from the long-encamped army corrupted the air, so that very many of the Germans fell into various diseases and were forced either to die miserably or to return home without glory, and not without danger. Of the nobles, the principal one carried off by this plague was Guy of Namur, whom we mentioned above, a tribune of the Flemings at the battle of Courtrai, and therefore noted for the fame of his exploits. Because of this pestilence, a great part of the nobles urged Henry to abandon the siege, judging the enemy's necessity more unbearable and less lasting than the army's toil. Therefore he resolved to withdraw only when he had obtained his wish. When these things were known, the besieged, made suppliant, obtained pardon also through the help of Cardinal Fieschi, and on the sixteenth day before the kalends of October surrendered themselves to the good faith of the prince. The king took possession of the city; he ordered the walls and towers to be demolished at once, and by the law of war he imposed a tribute of twenty thousand gold pieces and, besides, a hundred hostages, to be selected from the whole body of the citizens. That victory cost dearly, since scarcely a quarter of the army survived.

units.la: Cremonam hinc ut redijt, incepit consultare de componendis rebus in posterum. Placuit ordinata Longobardia, præsidibúsque per ciuitates impositis, Ligures petere, Mediolanum, ut diximus, procurante Mapheo, Veronam comite Scalari, Parmam Gilberto Corregio, Pascarino Bonoposo Mantuam. Quæ res parum salutaris postea ciuibus extitit: quos præfectos legum seruandarum causa in præsens præposuerat, superbè, auareque postmodum imperantibus. At illis & in primis occupatio, & aureolorum copia, ut in perpetuum confirmarentur, quæ temporis causa concessa fuerant, effecerunt Guelphorum ciuitates vbi aduentare Heinricum accipiunt, obsideri iussis itineribus Ligurum, remorari transitum illius conabantur.
units.tr: From there, when he returned to Cremona, he began to consider how to settle affairs for the future. It was decided that Lombardy should be put in order, with governors set over the cities, and that the Ligurians should be sought out. Milan, as we have said, was entrusted to Matteo; Verona to Count Scaliger; Parma to Gilbert of Correggio; Mantua to Passerino Bonaccolsi. This arrangement later proved not very wholesome for the citizens, because those whom he had set over them as prefects, to keep the laws for the time being, afterwards ruled proudly and greedily. But for these men, above all the seizure of power and the abundance of gold coins, which had been granted for a time only, made them wish to be confirmed for ever. So the Guelf cities, when they learned that Henry was coming, ordered the roads of the Ligurians to be blockaded and tried to hold up his passage.

units.la: Iisdē diebus Clemens de repetenda vrbe Romana ab Heinrico compellatus per literas, ipse consilio ecclesiæ generali distentus, Pratensi Cardinali petendæ Italiæ inaugurandiqué regis, singulari mandato negotium impartitum.
units.tr: At the same time, Clement, who had been urged by letter by Henry to return the city of Rome, was himself occupied with the general council of the Church; so the business of seeking Italy and inaugurating the king was assigned by a special mandate to Cardinal Prato.

units.la: Cæsar ad diem vndecimum Calendarum Octobrium, maximo apparatu Genuam est inuectus: Principem dominumque solenni more appellantibus: mox componendæ discordiæ ratio habita. Itaque Opicino Spinulæ socijsq; impridem exulantibus confecta restitutio: Quæ res ingentem illi dilectionem ciuium peperierunt. Ipsi milia aureorum dono data centum, regiæ verò coniugi viginti: Ea quum insequente mense grauiter ægrotare cœpisset, res humanas reliquit. Elata tumulataq; solennem inter pompam apud beatissimi Francisci cœnobium, pudicitiæ singularis religionisque spectatæ fœmina.
units.tr: The emperor came to Genoa on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October with great pomp, and the people addressed him in the solemn manner as prince and lord. Soon afterwards the means of settling the city's discord was considered. The restoration of Opicino Spinola and his companions, who had long been in exile, was accomplished, and this won him enormous affection from the citizens. He was given a gift of 100,000 gold pieces, and his royal wife 20,000. In the following month she began to fall gravely ill and departed this life. She was carried out and buried with solemn ceremony at the monastery of blessed Francis, a woman of singular chastity and proven piety.

units.la: Anno à Christo genito M CCCX II, ad die quartum calendarum Martij, Genua profectus Henricus classe triremium triginta, Pisas aduehitur. Quæ ciuitas nullo non genere apparatus eo vel exquisitissimo regem accepit dominum quoque inter publicas blicas. blitcas acclamationes cōsalutans. Censebatur tū in primis exercitus mille quingentis trāsalpinis equitib. Præcipui Germanicorū procerū, archiepiscop9 Treuirorū Baldeuinus, cuius supra meminimus, episcopus Eburonū, frater Barri comitis, è ppinquis regijs: dux Bauarus, comes Sabaudus, vtrq; è ppinquis regijs, comes Forestt, Guido Viennēsis Delphini frater, Hēricus Flandrorū comitis filij, comes Vienne, prætectus prætorio, quem nostri Aulæ magistrū appellant, vir maximi in re militari nominis.
units.tr: In the year of Christ 1312, on the fourth day before the Kalends of March, Henry set out from Genoa with thirty galleys and was brought to Pisa. The city received the king with every kind of display, the most exquisite sort, and greeted the lord with public acclamations. The army was then reckoned at 1,500 horsemen from beyond the Alps. The chief men among them were: the German nobles, Baldwin, archbishop of Trier, mentioned above; the bishop of Liège, brother of Count Barri, one of the king's close kin; the duke of Bavaria and the count of Savoy, both close kin of the king; the count of Forez; Guy of Vienne, brother of the Dauphin; Henry, son of the count of Flanders; and the count of Vienne, praetorian prefect, whom we call the Master of the Court, a man of very great reputation in war.

units.la: Eodē anno, mēse Aprili, Robertus Siculus, cuius supra mentio est habita, de Romano Henrici itinere certior factus, quū nulla aliunde lacessendi regis exraret occasio, simul ita facere ab Vrsina factione iussus, Ioannē fratre mittit ad Vrbē cū equitū sexcentorū præsidio: literis subinde scriptis ad ciuitates Hetruriæ Guelpharū partium, de summittendis opportunè Romam auxilijs. Ricardo Lunensi comiti, quem Robertus Thuscis imposuerat, datum negotium, Latij maturè incundi, idq; cum phalange peditum duorum millium sexcentorum. Hi ad diem xv i calendarū Iunij Romam peruecti, Vrsinos conuenerunt, moxq; de sententia consilij, Capitolium, Hadriani molem, ac Vaticanum armatis insederunt: Petro Sabaudo senatore vrbis coniecto in vincula: Columniis aliisq; Cæsarianarum partium Lateranum; Mariam maiorem, amphitheatrum, Rotundam, sanctamq; Sabinam occupantibus.
units.tr: In the same year, in April, Robert of Sicily, mentioned above, learned of Henry's journey to Rome. Having no other pretext for harassing the king, and at the same time ordered by the Orsini faction to do so, he sent his brother John to the city with a garrison of 600 horsemen. He also wrote letters to the cities of Tuscany that belonged to the Guelph party, urging them to send help to Rome in good time. Richard, count of Lunigiana, whom Robert had set over Tuscany, was given the task of occupying Latium promptly, with an infantry force of 2,600. They reached Rome on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June, joined the Orsini, and by decision of their council occupied the Capitol, Hadrian's Mole and the Vatican with armed men. Peter of Savoy, senator of the city, was thrown into chains. The Colonna and others of the Caesarian party were driven out and took refuge in the Lateran, while the rest occupied St Mary Major, the amphitheatre, the Rotunda and Santa Sabina.

units.la: Inter hæc Pisis Henricus equitib. bis mille & hoc amplius cōstipatus, recta per Thuscos Romā cōtendit: Viterbium absq; negocio capit, ibiq; dies aliquot constituit, occasionē inuadēdi Vaticani expectās. Postquā tēpus idoneū visum est perrūpendis insidiis, Viterbio promouet, occurrentesq; Vrsinos leuib. præliis vertit in fugā: simul popularibus in ciuitate rem strenuē gerentibus, ante diem calendarum Iunij, vrbem visenda pompa introiit, protinusq; de expugnandis Roberti clientum reliquiis cōsultat. Itaq; missis, qui singula factionis præsidia deturbarent, pro certo creditur, quicquid ibi Apulorū Ibericorumq; fuerat, depulsurū, nisi prælio quodā, 6 & 20 Maij die cōmisso, cum alij Ducum quidā, tum Leodiorum occubuisset episcopus. Hūc enim pfractis (is erat ardor hominis) viarū custodiis, in castellū Angelicū properantē, Robertini Florali ex area p obliquū progressi, circumueniūt, fugāt, funduntq;. Cæsarianorū qui capti occisiūe fuerāt, numerus millium duorum traditur. Eburonum, quē iam ante dicebamus, antistitem, in equū ab victore raptū, vehentemq; Hispanus quispiā cōspicatus, cuius paulō ante fratre Alemāni cōfecerat, cū nō alia fraternę necis vltionē euenturā speraret, letali percussum vulnere, vt paucis post diebus moreretur effecit. Eius interitu principis, qui & virtute & auctoritate eminuisset in regia, longē maximus pauor Cæsarianos inuasit, Robertinis econtrario lætitiā tristi casu afferente.
units.tr: Meanwhile Henry, at Pisa, with more than 2,000 horsemen around him, made straight for Rome through Tuscany. He took Viterbo without difficulty and stayed there for some days, waiting for an opportunity to attack the Vatican. When the time seemed right for breaking through the ambushes, he advanced from Viterbo and routed the Orsini who came to meet him in light skirmishes. At the same time the popular party in the city acted bravely, and before the Kalends of June he entered Rome with a splendid procession. He at once consulted on how to destroy the remnants of Robert's clients. He sent men to dislodge each of the faction's garrisons, and it was firmly believed that he would drive out whatever Apulians and Spaniards were there, had a certain battle, fought on 20 May, not cost the lives of several leaders, among them the bishop of Liège. This man, with the ardour that was his nature, broke through the road blockades and hurried towards the castle of Sant'Angelo; but Robertine troops advanced obliquely from the Florali square, surrounded him, and put him and his men to flight and rout. The number of Caesarians captured or killed is given as 2,000. The bishop of Liège, whom we mentioned earlier, was seized on horseback by the victor. A Spaniard who saw him being carried off, and whose brother a German had killed shortly before, hoped for no other revenge for his brother's death, struck him with a mortal wound, so that he died a few days later. With the death of this prince, who had stood out in the royal court for both courage and authority, very great terror seized the Caesarians, while for the Robertines the sad event brought joy.

units.la: Porrò Luceburgius, ne tēpus omne vrbanis rixis attereret, statuit absoluere res, quarum causa potissimum vrbē petiuerat. Itaq; de sententia Cardinalium, cōuentu in Lateranū, ad diem Sextilii calend. indicto, Ostiēsiq;, Flisco & Arnoldo Cęsareas infulas sacrato capiti imponētibus, quod felix faustumq; sit, prægrādi apparatu, singulariq; spectantiū gaudio, Augusti nomē apicemq; fastigij imperialis accepit. Peracta inauguratione, Bauarus cum parte procerum perfunctum se officio comitādi exiltimans, assumpto commeatu in Germaniam abiit. Ipse Tybur paucis post diebus concedens, multa ibi veneratione incolarum exceptus, Pisas repetit.
units.tr: Furthermore, Luxembourg, so as not to waste all his time on quarrels within the city, decided to settle the matters for which he had chiefly come to Rome. So, by the decision of the cardinals, an assembly was called in the Lateran for the day before the Kalends of August. The bishop of Ostia, Fliscus and Arnold placed the imperial crown on his consecrated head, with the words "may it be happy and auspicious", amid great pomp and the singular joy of the onlookers, and he received the name Augustus and the summit of the imperial dignity. When the inauguration was complete, the duke of Bavaria, thinking he had fulfilled his duty of escort, took leave with some of the nobles and went away to Germany. The emperor himself withdrew to Tivoli a few days later, was received there with great reverence by the inhabitants, and then went back to Pisa.

units.la: Guelphicæ ciuitates Hetruriæ, vbi quæ Romę acta fuerant, deq; principe decedente intelligunt, iter illius rursum intercludere nitebantur. Ac veriti ne parum instructi copiosō agmini minūs resistere valeant, socios in Vrbe degentes per literas cōmonefaciunt, vt & nouum amplecterentur consilium, & properare mox in Thuscos maturarent. Interim Cæsar Gallia repetita per agrū Perusinum exercitu infesto ꝑgreditur, cunctaq; ferro atq; igne deuastat, Castellione vi capit, Cortonæ, Aretiiq; reuerenter occursum venienti, portaeq; apertæ: inde crebris cū Guelphica gente prœliis feliciter gestis, variisque Florentinorum castellis euersis, agrisque vastatis, inopia pabuli proficisci cōpellitur. Ad eum Bonatiano in prædio (id loco vocabulum) agentem, legati à rege Siciliæ Friderico mari deportati, donum aureorum millia viginti adferunt, fœdus amicitiamque petentes. Postulatis eorum assensum.
units.tr: The Guelph cities of Tuscany, learning what had been done at Rome and that the prince was departing, tried again to block his way. Fearing that they, being poorly prepared, could not withstand a large army, they warned their allies living in Rome by letter both to adopt the new plan and to hurry into Tuscany soon. Meanwhile the emperor, having returned to Gaul, advanced with a hostile army through the territory of Perugia, laying everything waste with fire and sword. He took Castiglione by force, while Cortona and Arezzo received him respectfully and opened their gates to him. Then, after many successful battles with the Guelph people and after overthrowing various Florentine castles and devastating their fields, he was forced to leave for lack of fodder. At a farm near Bonatiano (that is the name of the place), where he was staying, envoys from King Frederick of Sicily arrived by sea, bringing a gift of 20,000 gold pieces and seeking an alliance and friendship. He granted their requests.

units.la: Postquam Cæsar Pisas accessit, legibusque cohercere hostes aggressus, quos bello persequutus fuerat, & asperrima edicta in Thuscos Roberti partium promulgauit,& suos inuicem clientes pulchris beneficijs deuinctiores effecit. Quippe Spinulæ, cuius supra mentio est habita, Marchionique Montisferrati, cum alia dignationum genera, tum ius monetæ cudendæ tribuit: tum de Roberto castigando tractatum. Causa cognita, deque consilij sententia ob læsam maiestatem Romani imperij, paterno illum regno prouincialique Comitatu excidisse pronuntians. Quæ decreta postmodum defuncto Henrico, Pontifex maximus Ioannes xx ii pro potestate rescidit: estq; ea res in publica monumenta redacta.
units.tr: After the emperor came to Pisa and turned to restraining by law the enemies he had pursued in war, he issued very harsh edicts against the Tuscans of Robert's party, and made his own clients more firmly bound to him by generous favours. Thus, to Spinola, mentioned above, and to the marquis of Montferrat he granted, along with other kinds of honours, the right of coining money. He also began to deal with the punishment of Robert. After the case was heard and by the decision of his council, he pronounced that Robert had forfeited his paternal kingdom and provincial county, for injuring the majesty of the Roman empire. These decrees were afterwards rescinded by Pope John XXII, in the exercise of his power, after Henry's death, and the matter was recorded in the public documents.

units.la: Sub idem tempus Henricus Flander magister equitum Cæsaris, Pisanum agrum cum turmis circumuagari coepit, arcemq; fortissimam Petram sanctam, Florentinis & Lucensibus suspectantibus, expugnauit.
units.tr: About the same time Henry of Flanders, the emperor's master of horse, began to roam the Pisan countryside with squadrons of cavalry, and took the very strong fortress of Petra Santa, while the Florentines and Lucchese looked on with suspicion.

units.la: Imperator nihil actum ratus verbosis sententijs, nisi facta consequerentur, ad hoc Hetrusco bello finem commodissimè posse imponi, si ducem caputq; damnandæ audaciæ contudisset, traijcere in Campaniam ad ipsum Robertum armis perdomandum statuit. Idque vt ante diximus, cum Friderico foedere, missisq; in Germaniam, qui supplementum legionum conscriberent, placuit vti die constituta expeditam classem in Ligustico sinu explicaret. Numerus Cæsariani exercitus ad armatorum quatuor millia traditur. Accessit eo & Genuensium classis, triremium septuaginta, à Friderico quoq; Aragone triremibus quinquaginta submissis. Pisis Cæsar nonis Augusti decessit: quo die Fridericū quoq; Messana Rhegium traiecisse postea compertum est: eamq; ciuitatem expugnauisse, cum oppidis aliquot aliis.
units.tr: The emperor judged that nothing would be accomplished by wordy judgements unless deeds followed. He therefore decided that the Tuscan war could most conveniently be brought to an end if he crushed the leader and head of this audacity, and that he would cross into Campania to subdue Robert himself by arms. This, as we said before, was agreed with Frederick by treaty, and men were sent to Germany to raise reinforcements of legions. It was resolved to deploy the fleet in the Ligurian gulf on the appointed day. The number of the Caesarian army is given as about 4,000 armed men. The Genoese fleet of seventy galleys also joined, and fifty galleys were sent by Frederick of Aragon. The emperor left Pisa on 5 August. On that same day Frederick, it was later discovered, had crossed from Messina to Reggio and taken that city, together with several other towns.

units.la: Henricus iter per Hetruriam faciens, vbi ad Montem apertum accessit (idnomen loco tribuere accolæ) ægrotare manifesto incipit: tametsi iam inde à relictis Pisis initia morbi irrepentis animaduerterat. Sed ipse qua erat integritate animiq; magnitudine, ne die dicta temere abfuisse crederetur, fidei quàm valetudinis rationem habere maluit. Inter medicamenta autem balneæ Maceratanæ indicatæ fuere. Itaq; eo loci profectus, procuratoque de Medicorū sententia corpore, sese Bonocouentum contulit: ibi mox ingrauescente malo, excessit è vita, ad diem nonum calendarum septembrium, diuo apostolo Bartholomæo celebrem, anno quàm imperium accepisset, quinto, mense octauo. Defuncto Cæsare, id quod fieri in funere magnorum Ducum assolet, luctus incredibilis omnem comitatum perculit. Itaque familiares defecti Principe, pars Teutonicos lares repetiit, cæteri regium corpus protinus Pisas, vt viuus iusserat, singulari fide ciuitatis adductus, deportarunt: ibi quoque non à sociis modo, sed ab oppidanis quoq; maiorem in modum defletus, solenni atq; exquisitissima pompa effertur.
units.tr: Henry, travelling through Etruria, reached a place called Montaperto (the locals give the place this name), and there he began to fall visibly ill, although he had already noticed the first signs of the creeping sickness since leaving Pisa. But with the integrity and greatness of spirit that were his, he preferred to honour his word rather than his health, lest he be thought to have rashly failed to appear on the appointed day. Among the remedies the baths of Macerata were recommended. So he went there, and after his body had been treated on the advice of the physicians, he made his way to Buonconvento. There the illness soon grew worse, and he departed this life on the ninth day before the Kalends of September, a day celebrated for the blessed apostle Bartholomew, in the fifth year after he had received the empire, in the eighth month. When the emperor had died, the grief that usually accompanies the funerals of great leaders struck his whole retinue with incredible force. So his household, bereft of their prince, partly returned to their German homes, while the rest, moved by the singular loyalty of the city, at once carried the royal body to Pisa, as he had ordered while still alive. There too he was mourned greatly, not only by his companions but also by the townspeople, and he was buried with solemn and most exquisite pomp.

units.la: Vitam instantissimi Principis, qua acceperamus (vt puto) traditione narrauimus, quem non Italia modò, nullis neq; aduersis frangi potuisse, neq; secundis efferri, manifesto cognouerat: sed & barbaros laetitia inuicti Ducis extincti obtinuit. Qui eo viuo nihil prorsus rerum nouarum tentare ausi, defuncto, cuncta per Italiā (vt postea constitit) miscuerunt. Neq; Pisanis cæterisq; optimatibus dubium erat, nisi maturatus fuisset interitus, regnum Roberto bello ablaturum, quippe cui perexiles essent ad propugnandum copiæ: ita vt ne signa quidem collaturus, quin cognito mox Imperatoris aduentu, nauigio aduolaturum Narbonam. Quòd si Campaniæ obtinendæ facultatem dij tribuissent, infinitum esset, quantum ille rex & opportunitate commeatuum & innata virtute moliri efficere potuerit.
units.tr: We have related, as we received it by tradition (I think), the life of this most determined prince, whom it was clear that neither Italy alone could break in adversity nor elate in success. Even the barbarians were held in check by the joy at the death of the unconquered duke. While he lived they dared attempt nothing new, but once he died they threw everything into confusion throughout Italy, as later became plain.
