Quorum plures comprehensi, & in præsentia cleri & populi conuicti fuerunt, & inter cætera nefandi erroris sui flagitia confessi sunt, quòd etiam ab esu carnium in Quadragesima non abstinerent, & quòd annualem censum transmittere solebant Mediolanum, vbi diuersarum hæresium primatus agebatur.
units.tr: In the year of the Lord 1231, a persecution was carried out against the heretics, enemies of the faith and foes of the truth, whose great multitude lay hidden among the people of God, in cities, towns and villages, subverting and leading astray as many of the Church as they could. Many of them were seized and convicted in the presence of the clergy and people, and among other shameful things of their unspeakable error they confessed that they did not abstain from eating meat in Lent, and that they used to send an annual tribute to Milan, where the chief place of various heresies was held.

units.la: Eodem anno Ludouicus dux Bauariæ interfectus obiit. Fuit autem transfixus cultello præacuto, quem nos possumus appellare sicam, à quadam persona (vt dicebatur) vili & ignobili, quales mittere solet quidam potens, qui dicitur senex de Montania. Comprehenso autem interfectore, cum multis suppliciis torquerent eum & cogerent ad confitendum, cuius instinctu vel iussu tantum facinus attentare præsumpsisset, nihil ab eo poterant extorquere: & sic per omnia laniatus & discerptus periit.
units.tr: In the same year Duke Louis of Bavaria was killed and died. He was pierced with a very sharp knife, which we may call a dagger, by a certain person (as it was said) base and ignoble, of the kind that a certain powerful man, who is called the Old Man of the Mountain, is accustomed to send. The killer was seized, and although they tortured him with many punishments and forced him to confess at whose instigation or command he had presumed to attempt so great a crime, they could extract nothing from him. And so, mangled and torn in every part, he died.

units.la: Anno domini M.CCXXXIII, frater Cunradus de Margburg, per multa tempora pœna crucis prædicator, à malignis hominibus interfectus est.
units.tr: In the year of the Lord 1233, Brother Conrad of Marburg, for many years a preacher of the cross, was killed by wicked men.

units.la: Ipsis temporibus Elisabeth provincialis comitissa Turingiæ, filia regis Vngariæ, vxor quondam Ludouici Lantgrauij, qui in itinere crucis apud Brundusium vita decessit, mulier sancta & religiosa, post mortem mariti signis & miraculis clarescere cœpit.
units.tr: At this same time Elizabeth, provincial countess of Thuringia, daughter of the king of Hungary and former wife of Landgrave Louis, who died on the crusade at Brindisi, a holy and devout woman, began to become famous for signs and miracles after her husband's death.

units.la: Anno domini M. CCXXXV, cum Fridericus Imperator esset in Italia, & cum aliquo tempore mansisset ibidem, filius suus Henricus rex patri suo se opposuit. Fridericus reuersus in Alemanniam circa festum Iohannis baptistæ, filium Henricum captiuauit, & eum in Apuliam transmisit vinculatum, ibiq; in captiuitate mortuus est & sepultus, anno domini M.CCXXXVI.
units.tr: In the year of the Lord 1235, when Emperor Frederick was in Italy and had remained there for some time, his son King Henry opposed his father. Frederick returned to Germany around the feast of John the Baptist, took his son Henry captive, and sent him in chains into Apulia, where he died in captivity and was buried, in the year of the Lord 1236.

units.la: Imperator & episcopus Argentinensis circa initium Quadragesimæ, pacificè conuenerunt de feodo, super quo prius longo tempore inter eos contentio vertebatur.
units.tr: Around the beginning of Lent the emperor and the bishop of Strasbourg met peacefully concerning the fief, over which a dispute had long been waged between them.

units.la: Eodem tempore apud Fuldense monasterium Iudæi quosdam pueros Christianos, in quodam molendino, vt ex eis sanguinem elicerent ad suum remedium, peremerunt. Vnde ciues eiusdem ciuitatis multos ex Iudæis occiderunt. Sed cum puerorum corpora in castrum Hagenowe delata, & ibidem venerabiliter tumulata fuissent: Imperator tumultum, qui tunc contra Iudæos ortus est, aliter sedare non valens, multos viros potentes, magnos & literatos ex diuersis partibus conuocans, diligenter à sapientibus inquisiuit, vtrum sicut fama communis habet, Iudæi Christianum sanguinem in parasceue necessarium haberent: firmiter proponens, si hoc ei de vero constaret, vniuersos imperij sui Iudæos fore perimendos. Verùm quia nihil certi super hoc experiri poterat, seueritas imperialis propositi, accepta tamen à Iudæis magna pecunia, acquieuit.
units.tr: At the same time, at the monastery of Fulda, Jews killed some Christian boys in a mill, in order to draw blood from them for their own remedy. As a result, the citizens of that town killed many of the Jews. But when the bodies of the boys had been brought to the castle of Hagenau and honourably buried there, the emperor, not being able to quell the uproar that had then arisen against the Jews by any other means, summoned many powerful, great and learned men from various parts and diligently inquired of the wise whether, as common report has it, the Jews needed Christian blood on Good Friday. He firmly declared that if this were established as true, all the Jews of his empire would be put to death. But since nothing certain could be found out about this, the imperial severity of purpose gave way, though only after a large sum of money had been received from the Jews.

units.la: Anno domini M.CCXXXVII, Imperator profectus est in Austriam, cui ministeriales ducis de marchia Stirensi se tradiderunt. Inde venit ad ciuitatem Viennæ, quæ similiter ipsius dominio se subiecit: vbi etiam Cunradum filium suum, de vxore transmarina genitum, eligi fecit in regem, quem elegerunt archiepiscopus Moguntinus & Treuerensis & rex Bohemiæ, & dux Bauariæ, qui & Palatinus comes Rheni, consentientibus cæteris qui aderant, tamen paucis, & relicto ibi præsidio militum, rediit ad partes Rheni.
units.tr: In the year of the Lord 1237, the emperor set out for Austria, and the ministerial officials of the duke of the Styrian march surrendered themselves to him. From there he came to the city of Vienna, which likewise submitted to his lordship. There he also had his son Conrad, born of his overseas wife, elected king. He was chosen by the archbishops of Mainz and Trier, the king of Bohemia, and the duke of Bavaria, who was also the Count Palatine of the Rhine, with the consent of the others present, though few in number. Leaving a garrison of soldiers there, he returned to the parts of the Rhine.

units.la: Anno domini M.CCXXXVIII, Henricus comes provincialis Alsatiæ decedens sine hærede, feoda plurima quæ tenebat ab imperio & episcopatu & ab aliis ad dominium suæ proprietatis sunt reuocata, quia frater eius in ipsis feodis nihil iuris habebat, & vxori eius nihil aliud remansit nisi pauca prædia quæ eiusdem erant: quæ pauco tempore post enixa est filium.
units.tr: In the year of the Lord 1238, Count Henry, provincial count of Alsace, died without an heir. Many fiefs which he held from the empire, the bishopric and others were reclaimed to the lordship of their owners, because his brother had no right in those fiefs; and to his wife nothing remained except a few estates that belonged to her. A short time afterwards she gave birth to a son.

units.la: Hic Fridericus postposito iuramento quod fecerat Innocentio papæ, vsurpauit sibi bona ecclesiæ, & tenuit ea violenter vsq; ad papam Greg. à quo fuit excommunicatus: sed facta compositione, absolutus fuit. Transactoque breui tempore, compositionem violauit, vsurpando sibi bona ecclesiæ, & tenuit ea violenter, vsque ad mortem Honorij & Celestini papæ, per auxilium ciuium Romanorum, qui eum contra Apostolicum fouebant. Cùm autem infra discordiam Innocentius papa quartus electus & exaltatus fuisset, & in vrbe Roma non posset resistere Friderico, transtulit se occulte in ciuitatem Ianuensem. Ianua recedens, venit in ciuitatem Lugdunensem, ibiq; conuocatis Cardinalibus, & multis pontificibus & prælatis ecclesiarum, præfixit & statuit Concilium, & citauit Fridericum, vt in Concilio compareret, super obiectis coram principibus responsurus. Qui non comparuit, sed responsales pro se transmisit minus sufficientes. Innocentius autem papa celebrato Concilio, mediantibus patriarchis Antiochiæ & Aquileiensi, Imperatori Constantinopolitano & multis maioribus ecclesiæ, recitauit damna & grauamina, excessus plurimos & crimina Friderici: & lata sententia excommunicauit eum, & priuauit eum imperio & omni honore.
units.tr: Frederick, disregarding the oath he had sworn to Pope Innocent, seized the goods of the Church and held them by force until the time of Pope Gregory, by whom he was excommunicated. Then a settlement was reached and he was absolved. After a short time, however, he broke the settlement, again seizing the goods of the Church and holding them by force until the death of Popes Honorius and Celestine, with the help of the citizens of Rome, who supported him against the Apostolic See. While the schism was still going on, Innocent IV was elected and raised to the papacy. Unable to resist Frederick in the city of Rome, he secretly withdrew to the city of Genoa. Leaving Genoa, he came to the city of Lyons. There he called together the cardinals and many bishops and prelates of the churches, appointed a council and set its date, and summoned Frederick to appear at the council and answer the charges before the princes. Frederick did not appear but sent in his place representatives who were not competent. When the council had been held, Pope Innocent, through the mediation of the patriarchs of Antioch and Aquileia, the Emperor of Constantinople and many of the greater men of the Church, recited the losses and grievances, the many excesses and crimes of Frederick. Then, having pronounced sentence, he excommunicated him and deprived him of the empire and of every honour.

units.la: Principes verò Alemanniæ, scilicet archiepiscopus Moguntinus, & Coloniensis & Treuerensis, cum cæteris episcopis, Argentinensi, Metensi, Spirensi & aliis,
units.tr: The princes of Germany, namely the archbishops of Mainz, Cologne and Trier, together with the other bishops, those of Strasbourg, Metz, Speyer and others,

units.la: elegerunt apud Herbipolim, Henricum Lantgrauium Turingiae in regem. Electione vero facta, idem rex praefixit principibus curiam solennem apud Francfurt. Cum autem Fridericus depositus Imperator filium suum Cunradum regem in Alemannia haberet: ille curiam praefixam in Francfurt praevenire cupiens, & impedire volens, collegit magnum exercitum, & venit ad campos apud Francfurt. Henricus vero rex qui curiam praefixit, cum episcopis & fautoribus ecclesiae collegit etiam magnum exercitum & insequebatur Cunradum regem usque ad eosdem campos, ibique facta est pugna & maximus conflictus inter praedictos duos reges, in festo B. Oualdi, & Deus dedit victoriam ecclesiae & regi Henrico. Cunradus autem rex fugiens, amisit multos milites & maxima bona, & imposuit Sueuis, qui cum eo venerant, & 10 cum ipsis multis amissis fugerant, quod ipsi eum infideliter prodidissent. Sueui proinde ira moti, conspiraverunt cum ecclesia & rege Henrico, moventes bellum in regem Cunradum & suos fautores per Sueuiam, & circa Danubium & Mogum & ubique.
units.tr: elected Henry, Landgrave of Thuringia, as king at Würzburg. After the election, the same king appointed a solemn assembly of the princes at Frankfurt. Now, Frederick, the deposed emperor, had his son Conrad as king in Germany. Wishing to forestall the assembly appointed at Frankfurt and to prevent it, he gathered a large army and came to the fields near Frankfurt. King Henry, who had appointed the assembly, also gathered a large army with the bishops and supporters of the Church, and pursued King Conrad as far as those same fields. There a battle and a very great clash took place between the two kings, on the feast of Saint Oswald, and God gave the victory to the Church and to King Henry. King Conrad, however, fled, losing many soldiers and very great possessions. He blamed the Swabians who had come with him, and who, after many of their number had been lost, had fled with him, for having betrayed him treacherously. The Swabians, moved by anger, therefore joined in a conspiracy with the Church and King Henry, waging war against King Conrad and his supporters throughout Swabia, around the Danube and the Main, and everywhere.

units.la: Episcopus vero Argentinensis, nomine Henricus de Stahelecke, obsedit in Alsatia munitiones, oppida & castra, quae Fridericus & filius suus possidebant: & expugnavit firmissima & nobilissima duo castra...... & Kronenburg, quae funditus destruxit, & alia munita castra igne consumpsit. Fautores vero eiusdem episcopi expugnaverunt ex altera parte Rheni nobile castrum Mulberg & castrum Husen & multa oppida. Posthaec expugnavit idem episcopus castrum Ortenberg & subiugavit sibi oppidum 20 Offenburg & Kinzigerthal & Gengenbach.
units.tr: The bishop of Strasbourg, Henry of Stahleck, besieged in Alsace the fortifications, towns and castles which Frederick and his son held, and he stormed the two strongest and most noble castles ...... and Kronenburg, which he utterly destroyed, and he burned the other fortified castles. His supporters, on the other side of the Rhine, took by storm the noble castle of Mulberg, the castle of Husen and many towns. After this the same bishop took the castle of Ortenberg and brought under his control the town of Offenburg, the Kinzig valley and Gengenbach.

units.la: Cunradus autem rex, filius Friderici, videns, quod non poterat resistere fautoribus ecclesiae, duxit filiam ducis Bauariae, spe consilij & auxilij: sed parum profuit ei, quia Sueui fugaverunt eum de civitate in civitatem, & cum rege Henrico obsederunt civitatem Vlmam in Sueuia, sed non expugnaverunt: propter magnum frigus & defectum pabuli oportebat eos recedere de civitate. Rex autem Henricus ab Vlma recedens, venit in Turingiam, & mortuus est, anno ab incarnatione domini M.CCXLVII, & non regnauit per annum unum.
units.tr: King Conrad, son of Frederick, seeing that he could not resist the supporters of the Church, married the daughter of the duke of Bavaria, in hope of counsel and aid. But this profited him little, for the Swabians drove him from city to city, and together with King Henry they besieged the city of Ulm in Swabia, but did not take it; because of the great cold and the lack of fodder they had to withdraw from the city. King Henry, leaving Ulm, came into Thuringia and died in the year of the Lord's incarnation 1247, having reigned not quite one year.

units.la: Mortuo vero Henrico rege, Innocentius papa pro alio rege laborabat, & inter principes non inuenit aliquem, qui se de regno vellet intromittere contra Fridericum 30 & filium suum Cunradum. Tandem dux Brabantiae, filium sororis suae, Wilhelmum comitem Hollandiae, domino papae & episcopis Alemanniae praesentauit. Quem episcopi elegerunt in regem apud Coloniam, promittentes ei iuramento praestito, rebus & personis fideliter assistere. Qui cum episcopis, comitibus & nobilibus obsedit Aquisgranum & firmissimum castrum Werde in fluvio Rheni, & Ingelnheim: quae omnia sibi subiugauit. Colonia, Moguntia & Argentina ecclesiae assistebant: sed Wormatia, Spira, & aliae civitates & oppida Rheni, Sueuiae & Bauariae, & Metis, fauebant Friderico & filio suo sub vinculo excommunicationis: & eorum fauore Cunradus natus Friderici tenuit bellum contra ecclesiam, & terram aduersariorum suorum devastauit incendio & rapina, usque ad mortem patris sui Friderici.
units.tr: After the death of King Henry, Pope Innocent was anxious about another king, and among the princes he found no one who was willing to intervene in the kingdom against Frederick and his son Conrad. At last the duke of Brabant presented to the lord Pope and the bishops of Germany William, count of Holland, the son of his sister. The bishops elected him king at Cologne, promising on oath to stand faithfully by him with their property and persons. With the bishops, counts and nobles, he besieged Aachen and the very strong castle of Werde on the Rhine, and Ingelheim, and he subjected all of these to himself. Cologne, Mainz and Strasbourg supported the Church, but Worms, Speyer and the other cities and towns of the Rhine, of Swabia and of Bavaria, and Metz, favoured Frederick and his son under the bond of excommunication. With their favour Conrad, Frederick's son, carried on war against the Church, and he laid waste the lands of his enemies with fire and plunder, until the death of his father Frederick.

units.la: Anno domini M.CCL, Fridericus Imperator cum post suam ab imperio depositionem inter civitates Lombardiae Parmam, tanquam magis exosam sibi, forti manu obsideret: a legato domini papae & a Parmensibus est deiectus, & amissis thesauris suis & rebus aliis in Apuliam rediens, ibi graui infirmitate correptus, defunctus est.
units.tr: In the year of the Lord 1250, Emperor Frederick, after his deposition from the empire, was besieging with a strong force Parma among the cities of Lombardy, since it was more hateful to him than the others; but he was driven out by the legate of the lord Pope and by the people of Parma. Having lost his treasures and his other possessions, he returned to Apulia, and there, seized by a grave illness, he died.

units.la: Anno domini M.CCLI, Cunradus rex filius Friderici, vt mortuo patre Siciliae regnum suscipieret, per mare in Apuliam devenit, & capta Neapoli, muros illius funditus destruxit. Sed cum sequenti anno introitus sui in Apuliam infirmari coepisset, clystere, quod a Medicis iudicabatur ad salutem, veneno mixto intulit sibi mortem. Post haec Wilhelmus rex a Frisonibus occisus est.
units.tr: In the year of the Lord 1251, King Conrad, son of Frederick, in order to take up the kingdom of Sicily after his father's death, came by sea into Apulia, and having taken Naples he utterly destroyed its walls. But when in the following year his entry into Apulia began to make him ill, he took a clyster, which the physicians judged would bring him health, but poison was mixed in it and brought him death. After this King William was killed by the Frisians.

units.la: Haec audiens episcopus Coloniensis, ad Angliam perrexit, & inde duxit Richar- 50 dum ducem Cornubiae, quem ipse & episcopus Moguntinensis elegerunt in regem: quibus dedit multam pecuniam, & caeteris episcopis Alemanniae & nobilibus terrae. Et cum adhuc opulentus esset in diuitiis, vehebatur per principes Alemanniae ad singulas civitates & oppida imperij super fluuium Rheni: & ab omnibus civitatibus, ob reuerentiam principum qui cum eo aderant, honorifice est receptus. Cum autem Richardus rex peruenisset vsq; ad ciuitatem Basileam, defecit ei substantia: tunc reliquerunt eum principes Alemanniæ solùm, dicentes: quòd eum non dilexerunt propter personam, sed ratione substantiæ, & dederunt ei libellum repudij, & per aliam viam reuersus est in regionem suam: cuius regis memoria cum sonitu periit. Tunc vacauit regnum Romanorum, annis xxiii, vsq; ad tempora domini Rudolfi Dei gratia Romanorum regis.
units.tr: Hearing this, the bishop of Cologne went to England and from there brought back Richard, duke of Cornwall, whom he and the bishop of Mainz elected as king. To him and to the other bishops of Germany and the nobles of the land he gave a great deal of money. And while he was still rich in wealth, he was carried by the princes of Germany to the individual cities and towns of the empire along the Rhine, and from all the cities he was received with honour, out of reverence for the princes who were with him. But when King Richard had come as far as the city of Basel, his resources failed him. Then the princes of Germany left him alone, saying that they had not loved him for his person, but for the sake of his wealth; they gave him a bill of divorce, and he returned by another road to his own country. That king's memory perished with a great noise. Then the kingdom of the Romans was vacant for twenty-three years, until the time of the lord Rudolf, by the grace of God king of the Romans.

units.la: Vacante autem regno prædicto, Cunradinus, Cunradi regis filius, filij Imperatoris Friderici, pollens diuitiis & honore, adhuc adolescens de morte patris sui Cunradi, & aui sui Friderici Imperatoris dolens, cùm esset infra dies luctus, consilio vsus suorū, volens & patrem & auum vlcisci, licet esset teneris sub annis collegit exercitum magnum, venit in Italiam, volens inuadere regnum Siciliæ, quod ad eum ex successione hæreditaria asseruit pertinere, tempore Clementis papæ quarti. Hoc audiens Carolus, qui tunc ex donatione Apostolica sibi assumpsit regni Siciliæ gubernacula gubernanda, collegit vice versa exercitum, & inito cum proceribus, qui cum eo aderant, consilio, qualiter & quomodo ipsi Cunradino & suis resistere possent. Fauore tamen & auxilio domini Clementis papæ congregati sunt, ac acies hinc inde ordinatę, aggressi sunt confligtum & bellum magnum, & facta est cædes magna hominum, & obtinuit prima facie fidę Cunradinus & sui victoriam. Et cum Teutonici insistentes spolio, fugarent aduersarios, adhuc Cunradino existente in tentoriis, superuenit quędam acies Caroli, Cunradinum captiuare conantes: & cum se desolatum vidit, fugiebat. Demum captus & capite truncatus est, anno Domini M. CCLXVIII, de cuius morte tota dolet Germania.
units.tr: While the aforesaid kingdom was vacant, Conradin, son of King Conrad and grandson of the Emperor Frederick, wealthy and honoured, still a young man, grieving for the death of his father Conrad and of his grandfather Frederick the Emperor, while he was still within the days of mourning, acting on the counsel of his followers, wishing to avenge both his father and his grandfather, though he was of tender years, gathered a great army and came into Italy, intending to invade the kingdom of Sicily, which he claimed belonged to him by hereditary succession, in the time of Pope Clement IV. Hearing this, Charles, who at that time had taken up the government of the kingdom of Sicily by apostolic grant, in turn gathered an army, and after taking counsel with the nobles who were with him, considered how and in what way they might resist Conradin and his men. Nevertheless, gathered with the favour and aid of the lord Pope Clement, they drew up their battle lines on both sides, engaged in combat and a great war, and there was a great slaughter of men. At first sight Conradin and his men gained the victory. And while the Germans, intent on plunder, were routing their opponents, Conradin still remained in his tents; then a certain battle line of Charles came upon him, trying to capture Conradin, and when he saw himself abandoned he fled. At last he was captured and beheaded, in the year of the Lord 1268, and all Germany grieves for his death.

units.la: Cùm autem regnum Romanorum vacaret à tempore Richardi regis, qui Romani imperij (licet profecisset modicum) assumpsit gubernacula gubernanda, & nullus Alemanniæ principum, propter metum aliquorum Alemanniæ, sibi Romani regni regimen assumere vellet, qui partem Imperatoris & suorum contra ecclesiam fouebant: & medio tempore in partibus Alemanniæ & aliarum circumiacentium per diuersos spoliatores viarū & nobiles ipsius terræ fuerint insolentiæ perpetratæ quamplurimæ, tempore Gregorij papæ decimi, apud quem per diuersos Alemanniæ nobiles & alios transeuntes sæpe & sæpiùs querimonia super tanta importunitate vertebatur: inito consilio præcepit principibus Alemanniæ electoribus duntaxat, vt de Romanorum rege, sicut sua ab antiqua & approbata consuetudine intererat, prouiderēt, infra tempus eis ad hoc de papa Gregorio statuto: aliàs ipse de consensu Cardinalium, Romani imperij prouidere vellet desolationi.
units.tr: Now the kingdom of the Romans had been vacant since the time of King Richard, who took up the reins of government of the Roman empire (though he achieved little), and none of the princes of Germany wished to assume the rule of the Roman kingdom, out of fear of certain Germans who supported the emperor's party and his followers against the Church. Meanwhile, in the regions of Germany and the neighbouring lands, very many outrages were committed by various highwaymen and nobles of that country. At the time of Pope Gregory X, complaints about such great lawlessness were constantly and repeatedly brought before him by various nobles of Germany and other travellers. Having taken counsel, he instructed the princes of Germany, the electors only, to provide for a king of the Romans, as was their right by ancient and approved custom, within a period fixed for them by Pope Gregory; otherwise he himself, with the consent of the cardinals, would wish to provide against the desolation of the Roman empire.

units.la: Mandato autem Apostolico viso ab ipsis principibus & recepto, conuenerunt apud Franckenfurt, de electione Romanorum regis tractaturi. Qui vtique se electores diuersis inter se tractatibus & diuerticulis habitis, non poterant de electione concordare, reducentes sibi inuicem memoria vniuersorum nobilium per omnem gyrum Alemanniæ regionis. Qualiter autem vltimò concordabant in dominum Rudolfum comitem de Habesburg, eligendum in Romanorum regem, in sequenti opusculo patebit.
units.tr: When the apostolic mandate had been seen and accepted by these princes, they gathered at Frankfurt to deal with the election of a king of the Romans. But the electors, holding various discussions and side-meetings among themselves, could not agree on the election, each recalling to the others the claims of all the nobles throughout the whole circuit of the German region. How at last they agreed on Count Rudolf of Habsburg as the one to be elected king of the Romans will be made clear in the following little work.

units.la: CVm Albertus de Argentina historias Germanicas illius seculi, quod Rudolfi Habspurgensis electionem & Caroli quarti morte intercessit, sincera fide literarū æternitati commendarit, resq; multas ab aliis vel intactas, vel nō tā plenè tractatas scripserit: equidem sæpius fortunam eius miseratus sum, quæ cū non nisi membris truncatū ac toto pene corpore tabidū, in hominum conspectū prodire passa esset. Quod.n.istius lucubrationis fragmentū in publicū abierat, id infinitis pene verborū & sententiarū mendis adeo corruptū erat, vt quàplurimis locis sensus nullus, quibusdam et falsus & depravatus inesset, atq; ideo velut exangue & putre corpus, conceptu laborarit. Cuspinianum certè, virū in historiarum rep. clarissimum, hasce boni auctoris mancas pagellas non magni fecisse constat: unde & lectorē cautum esse iubet, ne his nimium fidendo in errorē agatur. Ac sanè fateri debeo, me illius ductu, in historia Basilien si alicubi (quàquam in re non vsq; adeo magni momenti) impegisse. Verumenimuerò q scriptor hic ἀδὸξος permâsit, eiq; tantum non fides derogata sit, eum certè nauum non sua culpa contraxit, sed temporum & vetustatis invidia, quæ exemplaria longos vitiata per annos, tantū non aboleuerat. Neq; n.cuiquā dubium esse potest, auctorem illum quo antehac habitu comparuit, ex veteri codice lacero, aut squalore & carie corrosio velobliterato, trāscriptū esse: quod si hac iniuria nō persensissēt, maiore & fide & dignitate polluisset. Cuspin. equidē duo se M. Alberti antiqua exēplaria nactū esse memorat: vnū quod præ vetustate vix legi potuerit: alterū, à priore diuersum, fenestratū atq; mancū.
units.tr: Since Albert of Argentina, with sincere fidelity, committed to the eternity of letters the German histories of that century which lay between the election of Rudolf of Habsburg and the death of Charles IV, and wrote about many matters either untouched by others or not treated so fully, I have often pitied his fortune. It was allowed to come before the eyes of men only mutilated in its limbs and nearly wasted over its whole body. For the fragment of this work that had gone out to the public was so corrupted by almost endless errors of words and sentences that in very many places there was no sense, and in some a false and distorted one, so that, like a bloodless and rotting body, it struggled to be grasped by the mind. Cuspinian, certainly a man most famous in writing history, is known not to have thought much of these meagre pages of a good author; whence he also warns the reader to be careful, lest by trusting them too much he be led into error. And indeed I must confess that, following his lead, I stumbled somewhere in the history of Basel (though in a matter not of very great importance). But although this writer has endured an inglorious [ἄδοξος] fate, and his credit has been almost taken from him, he certainly did not contract this blemish through his own fault, but through the malice of time and antiquity, which had so corrupted the copies over long years that they had almost destroyed them. For there can be no doubt that the author, in the form in which he has appeared hitherto, was copied from an old, torn codex, or one eaten away by squalor and decay or blotted out; and had this injury not been suffered, he would have been served up with much greater trustworthiness and dignity. Cuspinian indeed reports that he obtained two ancient copies of Master Albert: one which could scarcely be read because of its age, and the other, differing from the first, full of gaps and incomplete.

units.la: Latatus igitur sum, cùm liber is totus ac integer, quantumuis à recentiore quodam transcriptus, in manus meas incidisset: quanquam primo intuitu (eo quòd nullum auctoris nomen præ se ferret) Albertum esse ignorarim. Nec diffido, quin alij quoq; patriæ amantes, quando eum sui temporis historias, si non eleganter & ornatè, verè tamen atq; syncerè, tradidisse animaduerterunt, voluptatem indefructuosam sint percepturi, atq; eum aliis mediæ ætatis scriptoribus fide neutiquam inferiorem habituri. Contuli aut prædicti huius scriptoris apographum, cū vetusto è membranis codice, quem (vt reor) bibliotheca cœnobij Nouientensis seu Ebersheimensis, siti in Alsatia, in insula Illæ fluminis, conseruarat. Eum clariss. vir, D. Ioannes Pistorius, Marchionum Badensium & Hochbergensium medicus, amicus optimus, iuuandi mei instituti caussa, Carolsburgo ad me perferri curauit. Is codex meo per omnia fere consentiebat, nisi quòd principium libri, de comitum Habspurgensium è Romana gente origine (quam sanè opinionem & alij quoque docti non satis verisimilem censent) in meo desiderabatur, his verbus incipiente: Rudolfus comes de Habspurg, cùm esset apud Fridericum Imp. &c. Eo autem prorsus erant similes, quòd vterq; continuo orationis filo nullis argumentis (vt in impresso fragmento) interseritis, descriptus erat, prætermissis vtriusq; nonnullis quæ in eodem fragmento leguntur. Hæc tamen audacius eiicere nolui, sed vt quæ in manuscriptis codicibus nō extant, à reliquo contextu dignoscerentur, ab initio signo ☞, ad calcem vero signo ☞, notāda esse duxi. Denique in vtroq; exēplari antecedebat Fragmentū historicum, à Dagoberto Franc. rege, vsq; ad Rudolfi tempora, quibus Albertus historiam inchoat, deductū: sequebatur vero comentarius ille de rebus gestis Bertoldi episcopi Argent. quibus tractatibus ego quoq; auctorem huncce vestitum in theatrū exire volui.
units.tr: I was therefore glad when the book, whole and entire, though copied by some more recent hand, came into my hands; although at first glance, since it bore no name of its author, I did not know it was Albert. Nor do I doubt that other lovers of their country, when they perceive that he has handed down the histories of his own time, if not elegantly and ornately, yet truly and sincerely, will also take profitable pleasure in him, and will judge him by no means inferior in reliability to other writers of the Middle Ages. I compared the copy of this aforementioned writer with an old codex on parchment, which (as I think) the library of the monastery of Neuwiller, or Ebersheim, situated in Alsace on an island of the river Ill, had preserved. That most distinguished man, Johannes Pistorius, physician to the margraves of Baden and Hachberg, my best friend, had it brought to me from Karlsburg to help my undertaking. This codex agreed with mine almost in every respect, except that the beginning of the book, concerning the origin of the counts of Habsburg from the Roman family (an opinion which other learned men also judge not very probable), was missing from mine, the text beginning with these words: Rudolf count of Habsburg, when he was with Emperor Frederick, etc. The two were altogether similar in this, that both were transcribed in one continuous flow of narrative without any interposed headings (as in the printed fragment), and both omitted some passages that are read in that fragment. I did not wish, however, to cast these out too boldly, but thought they should be marked, so that what is not found in the manuscript codices could be distinguished from the rest of the text: at the beginning with the sign ☞, and at the end with the sign ☞. Finally, in both copies a historical fragment preceded, carried from King Dagobert of the Franks down to the times of Rudolf, where Albert begins his history; and there followed that commentary on the deeds of Bishop Berthold of Strasbourg. With these treatises I too wished to bring this author, now clothed, out onto the stage.

units.la: Porrò quòd ad auctorem, dubitatio aliquando incidit, num is, de Basiliensium rebus tā multa referens, è vetusta & equestri illa vrbis nostræ familia ortum duceret, quæ cognomine de Argentina, ante CCC annos floruit, & aliquot dignitate & muneribus insignes viros produxit. De quorum numero fuere equestri baltheo decorati, Albertus de Argentina, circa annum 1236, in vrbe Basil. imperij aduocatus, & Wernherus anno 1263 ciuium magister, quorum hic (vt Colmarienses fasti memorant) à Richeimēsibus rusticis postea occisus fuit. Item Ludouicus, anno 1318 summi templi mysta seu canonicus. Verūm eas mihi nebulas discussit, locus in historia Ludouici quarti, quo scribit, se ab episcopo Argentinensi Auinionem ablegatum fuisse, vt & eum pontifici Romano excusaret, eiq; Ludouici decretum per omnē Germaniam promulgatum, afferret, quo palam asseruebat, pontifici in exauctorando Cæsare nihil iuris esse, &c. Inde coniicio, fuisse hunc Albertum episcopo Argentinensi familiarem, fortè Doctorem (quod magistri nomen insinuat) aut sacerdotem: cuiusmodi plures Argentina habuit, qui res eius vrbis & episcopatus literis ad posteros transmiserunt. Quales sunt Fridericus Closnerus qui historiam à Rudolfo Habspurgensi, vsq; ad annum salutis 1362 perduxit: & Iacobus Kœngelshofius qui res Argentinensium ab vrbis origine vsque ad principium seculi à nato Christo decimi quarti, collegit.
units.tr: As to the author, a doubt sometimes arises whether he, who relates so much about the affairs of Basel, was descended from that old and knightly family of our city which took the name "de Argentina" and flourished three hundred years ago, and produced several men distinguished by rank and office. Among their number were those decorated with the knight's belt: Albert of Argentina, around the year 1236, advocate of the imperial city of Basel, and Werner, in 1263 master of the citizens, who (as the annals of Colmar record) was afterwards killed by the peasants of Richeim. Likewise Ludwig, in 1318 a member of the cathedral chapter. But those clouds were dispelled for me by a passage in the history of Ludwig IV, where he writes that he was sent by the bishop of Strasbourg to Avignon, both to excuse him before the Roman pontiff and to bring the decree of Ludwig, promulgated throughout all Germany, in which he openly asserted that the pontiff had no right in deposing the emperor, etc. From this I conjecture that this Albert was a familiar of the bishop of Strasbourg, perhaps a doctor (which the title of master suggests) or a priest; of which kind Argentina had several, who handed down the affairs of that city and diocese to posterity in writing. Such are Friedrich Closener, who brought the history from Rudolf of Habsburg down to the year of salvation 1362, and Jakob Koenigshofen, who gathered the affairs of the people of Strasbourg from the origin of the city to the beginning of the fourteenth century after the birth of Christ.

units.la: M. ALBERTI ARGENTINENSIS CHRONICON INTEGRVM, A RVDOLPHO HABSPVRGENSI, ADVSQVE CAROLI quarti Imperatoris obitum, id est annum dominicae incarnationis, M.CCC.LXXVIII.
units.tr: M. ALBERTI ARGENTINENSIS CHRONICON INTEGRUM, FROM RUDOLF OF HABSBURG TO THE DEATH OF THE EMPEROR CHARLES IV, that is, to the year of the Lord's incarnation 1378.

units.la: VDOLPHVS comes de Habspurg ex antiquis progenitoribus ab vrbe Roma traxit originem. Olim namque duobus fratribus, propter potetis Romani occisionem, eliminatis ab Vrbe: pater eorum nobilior Romanus, dans cuilibet eorum immensam pecuniam, ipsos iussit in partes abire remotas. Qui se in superiori Alemannia receperunt. Antiquior autem ad emptionem praediorum & munitionum, iunior vero ad habendam vasallorum multitudinem contendebat. Patre autem in Vrbe existente post aliquot annos cum intellexisset, filios cum pace stare in Alemannia, ipsos visitabat. Et cum vidisset teneris empta praedia, eius prudentiam nimium commendauit. Requirens autem a iuniore, quid cum sua substantia egerit, ille se omnem in vnam munitionem fortissimam collocasse, respondit: & iussis omnibus vasallis suis, cum eorum liberis masculis optime armatis ad munitionem pertinentibus, & ab eo infeodatis, venire ad mõtem, vbi castrum Habesburg est collocatum, illuc patrem traducens, illam fortium multitudinem, quos & omnes eorum posteros masculini sexus suos & posteritatis suae fideles vasallos illis confitentibus patri, probauit. Quo viso, pater in illius animosa nobilitate gauisus, reuersus ad Vrbem, magnum thesaurum destinauit eidem. Ex quibus duobus fratribus omnes de Habespurg postea processerunt.
units.tr: Rudolf, count of Habsburg, traced his origin from ancient ancestors who came from the city of Rome. Once, after a Roman potentate had been killed, two brothers were driven out of the city. Their father, a nobleman of Rome, gave each of them an immense sum of money and ordered them to go to distant parts. They withdrew into Upper Alemannia. The elder devoted himself to buying estates and fortifications, the younger to gathering a great number of vassals. Some years later the father, still in Rome, learned that his sons were living in peace in Alemannia, and he went to visit them. When he saw the estates the elder had bought, he greatly praised his prudence. He then asked the younger what he had done with his fortune. The younger replied that he had put all of it into one very strong fortress. He ordered all his vassals, with their adult sons, who were well armed, belonged to the fortress and held their fiefs from him, to come to the mountain where the castle of Habsburg now stands. He then led his father there and showed him that band of brave men, who all acknowledged the father and pledged themselves, with all their male descendants, as faithful vassals of his line. The father, delighted with this spirited nobility of his son, returned to Rome and sent him a great treasure. From these two brothers all the lords of Habsburg afterwards descended.

units.la: Rudolfus verò cum esset apud Fridericum Imperatorem secundum in Lombardia, qui & ipsum Rudolfum leuauit de sacro fonte: Astronomus Imperatoris ipsi Rudolfo, quamuis iuueni frequenter assurgens, ipsum prae caeteris cunctis spectabilibus & clarissimis honorauit. Scisciatus autem a Caesare Astronomus, cur illi iuueni prae caeteris tantum exhiberet honorem: respondit, quòd ad eum imperij honor & principis potestas in posterum deueniret. Turbato ex hoc Caesare, & iuueni illi indignanti, Astronomus dixit: Non indignemini ei; quia antequam incipiat eius dominium, ex vobis, qui iam decem habetis filios, & ex eis qui succedat in imperio penitus nullus erit. Verum Rudolfus abinde recessit, propter imperatoris indignationem.
units.tr: While Rudolf was with Emperor Frederick II in Lombardy, the emperor, who also lifted him from the sacred font at his baptism, the emperor's astronomer often rose to greet the young Rudolf and honoured him above all the other notable and distinguished men. When the Caesar asked the astronomer why he showed this young man so much honour above all others, he replied that the honour of the empire and the power of the prince would in time pass to him. The Caesar was disturbed by this, and the young man was indignant. The astronomer said: "Do not be angry with him. Before his rule begins, of you, who already have ten sons, none at all will succeed to the empire." Rudolf, however, withdrew from there because of the emperor's displeasure.

units.la: Male autem succedente principi, depositio ab Innocentio quarto, & dolis cleri praevalentibus contra eum, ipsoque tandem in regno suo Siciliae in Panormo defuncto: principes Germaniae, virtute translationis ad ipsos factae ex morte Ottonis tertij Imperatoris, Richardum regem Angliae inclytum in regem Romanorum eligere decreuerunt: qui regi Franciae inuidens, illico eidem quandam ciuitatem obsedit, & in obsidione iaculo est occisus: statimque postea electo per principes Langtrauio Turingiae, deinde Wilhelmo comite Holandiae, qui Rhenum ascendens Briscum venerat, & descendens Frisiam inuaserat, ipse inibi est occisus. Sic post Fridericum imperium tegnumque Romanorum xxx annis vacauit. Richardus enim & Wilhelmus, quia non duraverunt in regno, non fuisse censentur, & ambo caruerunt benedictione imperiali.
units.tr: Since the prince's affairs went badly, he was deposed by Pope Innocent IV, and the clergy's intrigues prevailed against him. He died at Palermo in his kingdom of Sicily. The princes of Germany, by the right of transfer to them upon the death of Otto III the emperor, decided to elect the famous Richard, king of England, as king of the Romans. Envious of the king of France, Richard at once besieged a certain city, and he was killed by a dart during the siege. Soon afterwards the princes elected Landgrave Henry of Thuringia, and then William, count of Holland. William came up the Rhine as far as Brisach, then went down and invaded Friesland, and there he himself was killed. Thus after Frederick the imperial office and the kingship of the Romans stood vacant for thirty years. Richard and William are not counted as kings, because they did not hold the kingdom for long, and both lacked the imperial blessing.

units.la: Innocentius autem papa quartus,qui Fridericum deposuit, Carolum Martellum comitem Prouinciæ,fratrem scilicet regis Franciæ, constituit Siciliæ regem : contra quem Cunradinus nepos Friderici ex Cunrado filio suo,veniens in Italiam cum duce Auftriæ,& magna multitudine Germanorum, cum Carolo iniuit conflictum: vi&oq; per Germanos Caroli exercitu & fugato, Germani prædam fugientium infequentes,Cunradinum cum duce & paucissimis reliquerunt. Quod videns Carolus, qui fe in montem cũ magna parte exercitus fui receperat,vt videret recessus Germanorum:Cunradinum quasi desolatum inuasit. Quo cum duce & quibusdam aliis capto,indeq; abducto, exercitus eius dispersus ob prædam , miferabiliter fugatus est & occisus.Scripsit autem Carolus Clementi tum papæ existenti, quid faciundum effet de Cunradino capto.Qui rescripsit eidem,quia ei suebat:Vita Cunradini,mors Caroli:mors Cunradini,vita Caroli. Quo scripto viso,statim Carolus Cunradinum cum duce Auftriæ & cæteris decollauit.
units.tr: Pope Innocent IV, who had deposed Frederick, appointed Charles of Anjou, count of Provence and brother of the king of France, king of Sicily. Against him Conradin, the grandson of Frederick through his son Conrad, came into Italy with the duke of Austria and a great multitude of Germans, and joined battle with Charles. Charles's army was conquered and routed by the Germans, but the Germans, pursuing the plunder of the fleeing enemy, left Conradin behind with the duke and very few others. Seeing this, Charles, who had withdrawn to a mountain with a large part of his army to watch the Germans' retreat, attacked Conradin as if he had been abandoned. The duke and some others were captured and led away, and Conradin's army, scattered in pursuit of plunder, was miserably put to flight and killed. Charles then wrote to Pope Clement, who was reigning at the time, asking what should be done with the captured Conradin. The pope wrote back, as was his habit, with a saying: The life of Conradin is the death of Charles; the death of Conradin is the life of Charles. On seeing this reply, Charles at once beheaded Conradin, the duke of Austria and the rest.

units.la: Quod Petrus rex Arragonum,Cunradini proauunculus ægre ferens,habitis machinationibus occultis cum incolis infulæ Siciliæ, per mare potenter infulam ingrefsus,occisis Francigenis, & fugato Carolo, infulam Siciliæ occupauit : quam eius posteritas postea tenuit,& eius abnepotes hodie detinent fine lite. Carolus autem Neapolim & reliquam partem quæ est citra mare, vnà cum comitatu prouinciæ,cum posteris suis quietè possedit,semper resistendo Germanis:sub quo Guelforũ,de parte ecclesiæ:& Gibellinorum,de parte imperij sunt nomina inchoata.
units.tr: King Peter of Aragon, Conradin's great-uncle, took this badly. After secret plots with the inhabitants of the island of Sicily, he entered the island by sea with a strong force, slaughtered the French, put Charles to flight, and seized the island of Sicily. His descendants held it afterwards, and his great-great-grandsons hold it today without dispute. Charles, however, quietly possessed Naples and the rest of the land on this side of the sea, together with the county of Provence, with his heirs, always resisting the Germans. Under him the names Guelphs, for the party of the Church, and Ghibellines, for the party of the empire, came into use.

units.la: Erat autem mater Caroli,filia regis Castellæ, cuius regni arma sunt,castra: regni autem Franciæ,lilia. De quo Carólo, antequam mater eius regi Franciæ nuberet, prophetizatum dicitur in hæc verba:Castra floribus coniungentur,& ex equa equus generabitur generosus,qui pugnabit contra pullos Aquilarum,& præualebit eis. Papa autem Alexander contra Petrum Arragoniæ ac filios & regna eius in rantum processit, quòd multis annis in regnis eius nunquam sunt celebrata diuina, etiam nominantes cum regem,damnando.Qui Petrus rex in senio duos filios suos, vnum Arragoniæ,alium Siciliæ reges constituens,sibi huiusmodi titulum adscripsit:Petrus Arragonensis natus,pater duorum regum,dominus maris & miles imperterritus. Tandem sedes Apostolica cum vltrò reuocasset processus,iuuenes qui in eisdem regnis tempore interdicti 30 successerant,vel succreuerant,ante non visam celebrationem diuinorum deriserunt: propter quod post multa tempora Bonifacius papa octauus decretalem Alma condebat.
units.tr: The mother of Charles was a daughter of the king of Castile, whose kingdom bears castles in its arms, while the kingdom of France bears lilies. Concerning this Charles, before his mother married the king of France, it is said that a prophecy was uttered in these words: The castles will be joined with the flowers, and from a mare a noble horse will be born, who will fight against the chicks of the eagles and will prevail over them. Pope Alexander proceeded against Peter of Aragon, his sons and his kingdoms to such an extent that for many years no divine services were celebrated in his kingdoms, and even the king was condemned by name. In his old age King Peter appointed his two sons, one king of Aragon and the other of Sicily, and he gave himself this title: Peter of Aragon, born, father of two kings, lord of the sea and fearless knight. At last the Apostolic See of its own accord revoked the sentences. The young men who had succeeded or grown up in those kingdoms during the interdict mocked the celebration of divine services, which they had never seen before. Because of this, many years later, Pope Boniface VIII issued the decretal Alma.

units.la: Post Fridericum creuit potentia & superbia sedis Apostolicæ,ac Minorũ & Prædicatorum,quos eò quòd Fridericum & suos detestabantur,ipsa sedes apostolica præ cunctis Ordinibus priuilegiis exaltauit in tantum, quòd nunc ipsa sedes & clerus vix defensantur ab illis.
units.tr: After Frederick, the power and pride of the Apostolic See grew, and so did those of the Minorites and the Preachers. Because these orders detested Frederick and his followers, the Apostolic See itself exalted them above all other orders with privileges, to such a degree that now the See itself and the clergy can hardly be defended against them.

units.la: In diebus illis Henricus de Stahelegge,episcopus Argentinensis, quem Imperator forsan viuens læserat,Kronenburg,Haldenburg,Illewickersheim, & quædam alia castra Imperij demoliuit.
units.tr: In those days Henry of Stahelegg, bishop of Strasbourg, whom the emperor had perhaps wronged while he was alive, demolished Kronenburg, Haldenburg, Illewickersheim, and certain other castles of the empire.

units.la: Creuit autem Rudolfus de Habspurg temporibus prædictis, astutia & honore: qui cum litem duram haberet cum abbate sancti Galli,& duę lites aliæ sibi etiam succrescerent,venit ad domum abbatis, qui eum persequebatur odio capitali,sedens ad mensam eius edentis,inscius & non vocatus. Abbas verò miratus,ipsum honorificè & gratanter recepit.Facto sic simul prandio,illico in tantum sunt amici effecti, nullo se interponente,quòd abbas cum exercitu,ad inuadêdum alios comites aduersarios, in auxilium cum eo perrexit.Dixit enim comes ad suos:Quicunq; tres lites habet,duas si poterit reformet:hoc est consilium meum.
units.tr: Rudolf of Habsburg grew in cunning and honour in the times mentioned above. He had a hard dispute with the abbot of St. Gall, and two other disputes were also developing for him. He came to the house of the abbot, who was pursuing him with deadly hatred, and sat down at the abbot's table while he was dining, unknown to him and uninvited. The abbot, astonished, received him with honour and gladly. When they had dined together, they at once became such friends, with no one interceding, that the abbot went with him with an army to help attack the other adversary counts. For the count said to his men: "Whoever has three disputes, let him settle two if he can. This is my advice."

units.la: Cùm autem quadam vice idem comes, animo quædam inuadendi,in Ensensheim seruitores congregaret paulatim,& illis panem de siligine,& vinum durissimum 50 ministraret,quidamq; milites ex illis,panem album & bonum vinum super mensam comitis emerent sibiipsis: comes leuata mensa illos milites licentiauit secretè,dicens: se non indigere ipsorum.Illis verò caussam licentię quærentibus,ipsos quòd non contentabantur iis,quibus meliores contentarentur,arguendo confudit.
units.tr: On one occasion the same count, intending to attack someone, was gradually gathering servants at Ensisheim, and he was feeding them rye bread and very harsh wine. Some of the knights among them bought white bread and good wine for themselves and put them on the count's table. The count lifted the table and quietly dismissed those knights, saying that he had no need of them. When they asked the reason for their dismissal, he confounded them by pointing out that they were not content with what those better than they were content with.

units.la: Habuit autem comes de Kuffenberg sororem ipsius Rudolfi: quo defuncto fine liberis,
units.tr: The count of Kuffenberg had a sister of Rudolf himself. When he died without children,

units.la: Sororis Rud. Habspurgen sis. liberis, eadem soror Ottoni de Ochsenstein data est in vxorem: ex qua domini de Ochsenstein & Strasberg postmodum prodiere.
units.tr: the same sister was given in marriage to Otto of Ochsenstein, from whom the lords of Ochsenstein and Strasberg afterwards sprang.

units.la: Obiit autem antiquus comes de Kiburg, ipsius Rudolfi auunculus, solam relinquens filiam, quam ipsi recommisit, qui eam Eberhardo, filio patrui sui, dedit in vxorem, retinens sibi dominium in Kiburg, Winterthur, Diessenhofen, Baden, Mellingen, Arowe, Friburgum Vehtlandiæ, & quædam alia: assignans tandem eidem patrueli, postquam aliquandiu cum duce Burgundiæ auunculo suo morabatur superius dominium, quod socer eius a matre sua, sorore ducis Zeringiæ habuit, sc. Burgdorff, Thune & alia, quæ illius posteritas hodie tenet. Alia vero ipse Rodolfus suæ posteritati reliquit. Ipse vero patruelis & eius posteritas deinceps no de Habspurg, sed de Kiburg sunt vocati, eo quod illud dominium aliud præcessit, tempore, diuitiis & honore.
units.tr: The old count of Kyburg, Rudolf's own uncle, died leaving only a daughter, whom he entrusted to Rudolf. Rudolf gave her in marriage to Eberhard, the son of his paternal uncle, and kept for himself the lordship of Kyburg, Winterthur, Diessenhofen, Baden, Mellingen, Aarau, Freiburg in Uechtland, and certain other places. After the cousin had lived for some time with his maternal uncle, the duke of Burgundy, Rudolf finally assigned to him the superior lordship which his father-in-law had from his mother, a sister of the duke of Zähringen: Burgdorf, Thun and others, which his descendants hold today. Rudolf left the other lands to his own descendants. The cousin and his line were afterwards called not of Habsburg but of Kyburg, because that lordship came before the other in time, wealth and honour.

units.la: Erat autem antiquum castrum Kiburg olim in Brisgaugia, ex opposito nunc castri Friburgensis, cumq; olim dux Zeringiæ a sororio suo comite de Kiburg precibus obtinuisset, vt annueret ducem facere domum venationis in monte castri Friburgensis: vxor territa dixit marito comiti: Bene dixit frater meus, quod domum venationis ibi facere velit, quia venabitur & expellet vos per ipsam domum de partibus istis, & omni honore: quod & breuiter postea factum est.
units.tr: There was once an old castle, Kiburg, in the Breisgau, opposite the present castle of Freiburg. When the duke of Zähringen had obtained from his brother-in-law, the count of Kiburg, his consent to build a hunting lodge on the mountain of the Freiburg castle, the count's wife was frightened and said to her husband: "My brother did well to say he wants to build a hunting lodge there, for he will hunt you out of these parts, and drive you from all your honour, through that very house." This came about shortly afterwards.

units.la: Mortuo autem tempore Friderici, Berchtoldo duce Zeringiæ, anno M.CC.XVIII, calendis Maij: vni sororio de Kiburg cessit illud dominium in Burgunden: alteri Egeboni cum barba, comiti de Vrach, cessit inferius dominium. Quo mortuo, cum reliquisset duos filios, scilicet Chunradum seniorem, cui cessit dominium in Brisgaugia: & Egenonem, cui cessit dominium in Sueuia, a quo comites de Fürstenberg procefserunt. Chunradus vero comes Friburgensis moriens, reliquit duos filios: Egenonem seniorem, cui cessit dominium Friburgense: & Henricum, cui cessit Neuwenburg & Badenweiler. Qui Henricus cum Neuwenburg venisset, animo recipiendi in crastino ab hominibus fidelitatem: in sero sub macellis cuiusdam burgensis vxorem stuprauit, propter quod Neuwenburgenses illi fidelitatem facere renuerunt.
units.tr: After the death of Frederick, Berthold, duke of Zähringen, died in the year 1218, on 1 May. The upper lordship passed to one of the Kiburg brothers-in-law, to Burgundy; the lower lordship passed to the other, Egeno with the beard, count of Urach. When he died he left two sons: Conrad the elder, to whom the lordship in the Breisgau passed, and Egeno, to whom the lordship in Swabia passed, and from him the counts of Fürstenberg descended. Count Conrad of Freiburg, dying, left two sons: Egeno the elder, to whom the lordship of Freiburg passed, and Henry, to whom Neuenburg and Badenweiler passed. This Henry, when he came to Neuenburg intending to receive the homage of the townsmen the next day, in the evening, behind the butchers' stalls, raped the wife of a certain citizen; because of this the Neuenburgers refused to do him homage.

units.la: Erat autem in diebus illis partialitas inter nobiles Basilienses, hodieq; durans, inter Psittacos & Stelliferos, quæ ex eo sumpsit originem. Cum olim milites Basilienses ad torneamenta hastiludia, vel parlamenta alia cum multitudine egrederentur, & diceretur: Qui sunt isti? Tum dicebatur: Scalarij & Monachi Basilienses, qui erant excellentiores. De quo alij commoti, consilio habito, fecerunt vexillum albæ stellæ magnæ in rubeo campo, quod in Torneamentis & alibi efferebant: sub quo signo erant progenies de Eptingen, Vicedomini, Vfheim, Kraften, Reichen, Pfaffen, aliqui de Ramstein, Am Rortmarck, postea dicti de Neuwenstein, Macerell, Frick, & plures alij. Alij vero fecerunt viridem Psittacum in albo campo: ij erant Scalarij, Monachi, de Rheno, Marschalci, Camerarij, & multi alij, qui semper in ciuitate Stelliferos præcesserunt. Erant autem omnes comites & nobiles vicini, de alterutra partium earundem. Omnes enim de progenie Noui castri am See, marchiones de Hochberg & domini de Rotelen fuerunt Psittaci. Comites vero de Habspurg & de Pfirt, item Henricus cui cessit Neuwenburg & Badenweiler supradictus, fuerunt Stelliferi.
units.tr: At that time there was a factional split among the Basel nobles, which lasts to this day, between the Parrots and the Starbearers, and it took its origin from the following. Once, when Basel knights rode out with a large company to tournaments, jousts or other gatherings, and someone asked, "Who are those?", the answer was given: "The Scalarii and the Basel Monks", who were the more distinguished. Because of this, others were moved, and after taking counsel they made a banner with a large white star on a red field, which they carried at tournaments and elsewhere. Under this sign were the families of Eptingen, Vicedomini, Ufheim, Kraften, Reichen, Pfaffen, some of Ramstein, Am Rortmarck, afterwards called of Neuenstein, Macerell, Frick, and many others. Others made a green parrot on a white field. These were the Scalarii, the Monks, von Rhein, the Marshals, the Chamberlains, and many others, who always took precedence over the Starbearers in the city. All the nearby counts and nobles were on one side or the other of these factions. For all of the family of Neuenburg am See, the margraves of Hochberg and the lords of Rötteln were Parrots. The counts of Habsburg and of Pfirt, and likewise the aforementioned Henry, to whom Neuenburg and Badenweiler passed, were Starbearers.

units.la: Orta autem briga inter Henricum comitem de Badenweiler & Neuwenburgenses, cum pro domino receptare nolentes, cui Henrico Rudolfus de Habspurg pro viribus assistebat: quidam incolæ oppidi dicti Wilre & plures alij, clam pro Henrico episcopo Basiliensi, de Nouocastro dicto, miserunt, qui veniens media nocte, intromissus, castrum Neuwenburg iuxta portam superiorem, quod comes tenebat, confregit. Erat autem idem episcopus filius Vlrici comitis Noui castri: qui Vlricus moriens reliquit fratrem, qui habuit Nouum castrum & dominia Gallica: ipse vero habuit comitatum Noui castri & dominia Teutonica. Qui Vlricus reliquit quatuor filios antiquos, de Nidowe, de Strasberg, de Arburg & Henricum episcopum prædictum. Iste reliquit multas filias, datas dominis de Tockenburg, de Valckenstein, de Rotelen, de Regenspberg, de Grandisone, ex quibus multæ progeniesprocesserunt.
units.tr: A quarrel arose between Count Henry of Badenweiler and the Neuenburgers, since they would not receive him as their lord, and Rudolf of Habsburg supported Henry with all his strength. Some inhabitants of the town called Wilre, and many others, secretly sent for Henry, bishop of Basel, from the so-called Neuenburg. He came at midnight, was admitted, and broke into the castle of Neuenburg by the upper gate, which the count held. This bishop was the son of Count Ulrich of Neuenburg. This Ulrich, on dying, left a brother who held Neuenburg and the French lordships, while he himself held the county of Neuenburg and the German lordships. Ulrich left four elder sons: of Nidau, of Strassberg, of Arburg, and the aforementioned bishop Henry. The bishop left many daughters, who were given to the lords of Toggenburg, of Falkenstein, of Rötteln, of Regensberg and of Grandson, and from them many families descended.

units.la: Inualuit autem bellum contra Newenburgenses in tantum, quod pluribus annis nec agri, nec vineæ, imo nec vnus hortus, culti fuerunt: multisq; occisis & captis, vltra quinquaginta pedibus sunt truncati. Ipsi vero auxilio episcopi oppidum Blamenta...
units.tr: The war against the Neuenburgers grew so fierce that for many years neither fields, nor vineyards, nor even a single garden were cultivated. Many were killed and captured, and more than fifty had their feet cut off. But they, with the help of the bishop, took the town of Blamenta...

units.la: { } Fragment of notes in the margin are listed under notes. doltzheim, prædicti Rodolfi, item turrim in Otmarsheim, destruxerunt. Nobiles autem oppidi, dicti Sermentzer, & alij cum comite existentes, nimis læserunt Burgenses, quibus duo fortalitia in Ougheim & castrum Gerneck, item vnum castrum Froschbach, per comitem ædificatum iuxta Rhenum prope Bantzenheim, vbi tunc alueus Rheni fuerat, demolita fuerunt.
units.tr: { } Fragment of notes in the margin are listed under notes. doltzheim, belonging to the aforesaid Rudolf, and likewise the tower at Otmarsheim, they destroyed. The nobles of the town called Sermentzer, along with others who were with the count, did great harm to the townsmen. There were demolished two fortresses at Ougheim, the castle of Gerneck, and likewise one castle at Froschbach, built by the count on the Rhine near Bantzenheim, where the bed of the Rhine had then been.

units.la: Multa etiam alia acciderunt, quod duravit vsq; ad creationem Rudolfi, in regem promoti, qui tandem conquerentibus illis de stupro, oppidum ad ius regni Romani recepit, finens tamen, quòd comes per se captos excoriaret ad unguem. Insuper rex decimam partem omnium bonorum oppidanorum recepit, quam comiti assignavit.
units.tr: Many other things happened, and this lasted until the election of Rudolf as king. When those who complained of the rape finally appealed to him, he took the town under the right of the Roman kingdom, providing however that the count might flay those he had captured down to the last nail. Besides this, the king took a tenth part of all the townsmen's goods, and assigned it to the count.

units.la: In diebus illis, electo Wernhero archiepiscopo Moguntino ad Vrbem pro confirmatione proficisci volente, Rudolphus comes prædictus per electum literis rogatus, ipsum ab Argentina vsq; ad Alpes euntem, eoq; feliciter confirmato redeuntem conduxit. Qui archiepiscopus grates sibi agens, optavit vt nunquam moreretur, nisi comiti de tanto officio respondisset. Itaq; Moguntinus feliciter procedens & prospere ad ecclesiam suam est reversus. Quod postea fecit idem episcopus, qui pro creatione regis Romanorum principes quorum intererat ad oppidum Franckfurt convocavit. Interea accidit, quòd Psitaci Basilienses Stelliferos expulerunt: propter quod Rudolfus comes congregatis suis amicis, cum Stelliferis & eorum fautoribus iuxta capellam Binningen Basileam obsedit. Congregatis autem principibus electoribus in Franckfurt, rege Bohemiæ dempto, & inter se de periculo diutinæ vacationis Imperij, & de perditione iuris principum inuicem conquerentibus, ac de persona eligenda, quæ imperio expediret, tractantibus: Moguntinus Rudolphi comitis de Habspurg magnanimitatem ac sapientiam commendauit: multisq; aliis potentibus nominatis, Moguntinus asserens, sapientiam & strenuitatem diuitiis & potentiæ esse præferendas, pro Rudolpho comite instituit: Colonien-sem quoq; & Treuerensem ad id ipsum inducens. Dux autem Bauariæ, qui clarissimam vxorem suam, ex patre duce Brabantiæ, & ex matre de Hollandia natam, ob falsam adulterij suspicionem decollauerat, pater post Ludouici quarti principis, conuocans Burggrauium de Norinberg præsentem, qui & ipsius Rudolphi extitit consobrinus, ait illi: Si Rudolphus prefatus promoueretur in regem, quomodo essem ab eius læsione securus? Habet ne aliquam filiam, quam mihi daret in vxorem? Et illo asserente, quòd Rudolphus sex haberet filias, & de danda sibi vna, sub omnium bonorum suorum hypotheca ducicauente, dux annuit Moguntino. Quod audientes, dux Saxoniæ, & Marchio Brandenburgensis, qui & ipsi non habebant vxores, receptis cautionibus de dandis sibi Rudolphi filiabus, similiter consenserunt, sicq; concorditer est electus, anno domini M.CC.LXXIII, XII pridie calendas Octobris.
units.tr: At that time, Werner, the elected archbishop of Mainz, wished to set out for Rome for his confirmation, and Count Rudolf, asked by letter by the archbishop-elect, escorted him from Strasbourg as far as the Alps, and on his return journey, after the confirmation had been happily obtained, escorted him back again. The archbishop, giving thanks, wished that he might never die unless he had repaid the count for so great a service. So the Mainz archbishop, proceeding happily and prosperously, returned to his church. Afterwards this same bishop summoned to the town of Frankfurt the princes who had an interest in the election of the king of the Romans. Meanwhile it happened that the Basel Parrots expelled the Starbearers. Because of this, Count Rudolf gathered his friends and, together with the Starbearers and their supporters, besieged Basel near the chapel of Binningen. When the electoral princes had assembled at Frankfurt, the king of Bohemia being set aside, they discussed among themselves the danger of a long vacancy of the empire, and complained to one another of the loss of the princes' rights, and considered the person to be chosen who would be useful to the empire. The archbishop of Mainz commended the magnanimity and wisdom of Count Rudolf of Habsburg. When many other powerful men had been named, the archbishop of Mainz, asserting that wisdom and vigour should be preferred to wealth and power, nominated Count Rudolf, and brought the archbishops of Cologne and Trier to the same view. The duke of Bavaria, who had beheaded his most illustrious wife, born of the duke of Brabant as father and of a Dutch mother, on a false suspicion of adultery, and who was the father of the later Prince Louis IV, summoned the burgrave of Nuremberg, who was present and was also a cousin of Rudolf himself, and said to him: "If this Rudolf is promoted to king, how could I be safe from his injury? Does he have any daughter whom he would give me as a wife?" When the burgrave replied that Rudolf had six daughters, and the duke, pledging all his goods as security, asked for one of them, the duke agreed to the archbishop of Mainz. Hearing this, the duke of Saxony and the margrave of Brandenburg, who also had no wives, likewise consented, after receiving assurances that Rudolf's daughters would be given to them. And so he was unanimously elected, in the year of the Lord 1273, on 18 September.

units.la: Burggrauius autem de Nurinberg acceptis de electione principum literis, Basileam ad Rudolphi exercitum properauit, & venit ibi repente in media nocte: & excitato comite, dixit sibi, quòd esset rex nouus electus. Ille credens se deludi, cōtra Burggrauium commouebatur. Ille verò dixit: Absit quòd vos deludam, valetissimum dominorum: & sibi expositum seriem rei gestæ. Rex verò audiens, filias suas nupturas tantis principibus, & de prosperitate sua digne gauisus, Burggrauium in ciuitatem Basileam ad episcopum & ad Psitacos eius inimicos, pro amica reformatione direxit. Audiens autem episcopus, quod erat factum, se percutiens ad frotem, dixit: Sede fortiter dñe Deus, vel locum occupabit Rudolphus tuū. Ambæ igitur partes cū magnatibus illarum partium, cū rege & regina Alberti sorore comitis de Hohenberg, Aquisgranum pro ipsorum coronatione, egregiè sunt profecti, rebus per omnia bene gestis.
units.tr: The burgrave of Nuremberg, having received letters from the princes announcing the election, hurried to Rudolf's army at Basel and arrived there suddenly in the middle of the night. Having roused the count, he told him that he was the newly elected king. Rudolf, believing he was being mocked, grew angry with the burgrave. The burgrave said: "Far be it from me to mock you, most worthy of lords," and explained to him the course of events. The king, hearing that his daughters were to marry such great princes, and rightly rejoicing at his good fortune, sent the burgrave into the city of Basel, to the bishop and to the Parrots, his enemies, to propose a friendly reconciliation. When the bishop heard what had happened, he struck his forehead and said: "Sit firmly, Lord God, or Rudolf will take your place." Then both parties, with the magnates of those regions, set out splendidly for Aachen for the coronation, with the king and the queen, the sister of Count Albert of Hohenberg, and everything had gone well in every respect.

units.la: Ex his itaq; tribus filiabus multi duces Bauariæ, Saxoniæ, & Marchiones de Brandenburg processerunt. Dedit quoq; rex vnam filiarum Carolo tertio, nepoti Caroli Martelli prædicti regis Siciliæ, ex qua reges Vngariæ, Clementia regina Franciæ & mater Delphinorū, & Andreas rex Siciliæ, processerunt. Non dico rex insulæ Siciliæ, quam semper Aragonij tenuerunt. Habuit autem & rex à prædicta vxore de Hohenberg, tres filios, Albertum Rudolfum & Hartmannum: qui Hartmānus postea prope Rhinaw in Rheno submersus, Basileæ cum matre prædicta & adhuc vno filio parvulo, in choro maioris ecclesiæ Basiliensis sunt sepulti. Tempore autem electionis regis, iuerat fuerat Albertus ad comitem Tirolis, ad recipiendam Elisabet filiâ suam. Et intelligens comes electionem regis, Alberto filiam illico copulauit. Erat autem ipsa Elisabet soror quondâ Chunradini ex matre, quæ defuncto Chunrado rege recepit comitē Tirolis. Vacauerunt autem imperio à tempore occisionis Chunradini; ducatus Austriæ, Styriæ, & Carinthiæ. Rex aût de ducatu Carinthiæ, quē aliàs ipse comes occupauit, recepta ab eodem magna pecunia, inuestiuit eundem, qui postea non comes, sed dux Carinthiæ vocabatur.
units.tr: Of these three daughters came many dukes of Bavaria and Saxony, and the margraves of Brandenburg. The king also gave one of his daughters to Charles III, grandson of the Charles Martel mentioned above, king of Sicily, and from her descended the kings of Hungary, Clementia, queen of France and mother of the Dauphins, and Andrew, king of Sicily. I do not mean the king of the island of Sicily, which the Aragonese always held. The king also had three sons by his aforesaid wife of Hohenberg: Albert, Rudolf and Hartmann. Hartmann was later drowned in the Rhine near Rheinau, and he, with his mother just mentioned and another small son, was buried in the choir of the cathedral church of Basel. At the time of the king's election, Albert had gone to the count of Tyrol to receive his daughter Elizabeth. When the count learned of the election, he at once married her to Albert. This Elizabeth was the half-sister of the late Conradin, and after the death of King Conrad she had taken the count of Tyrol as her husband. The duchies of Austria, Styria and Carinthia had been vacant of an imperial holder since the killing of Conradin. The king invested with the duchy of Carinthia, which the count had otherwise occupied, the same man, who on receiving a large sum of money from him was afterwards called not count but duke of Carinthia.

units.la: Ducatum autem Austriæ quem occupauit Ottocharus rex Bohemiæ, cōtulit Alberto & Rudolfo filiis suis, & veniens cum exercitu, est in Vienna ciuitate Austriæ capitali receptus: habitisq; multis tractatibus, Ottocharus qui Bohemiam, Austriā, Moraviam, & quasi Hungariam, & totam quasi terram vsq; ad Prussiam, & vsq; ad mare, tenuit, à rege sua feuda recepit. Venit autem ad regem cum ineffabili pompa & ostensione potentiæ & diuitiarum. Rex autem longus & gracilis statura valde, aquilum habens nasum, indutus grisea rusticali tunica, cum alto galero, in cōmuni strata sedens, Ottocharum indutum pretiosissimè, genu flexū, more regio inuestiuit de feudis. De quo indignatus Ottocharus, & per vxorem suam, quę Polona extitit, durè tentus, pro eo quòd se in tantum subiecit, coepit regem infestare & Austriam occupare.
units.tr: The duchy of Austria, which King Ottocar of Bohemia had occupied, he bestowed on his sons Albert and Rudolf, and when he came with an army he was received in Vienna, the capital of Austria. After many negotiations, Ottocar, who held Bohemia, Austria, Moravia, and almost Hungary, and nearly the whole land as far as Prussia and to the sea, received his fiefs from the king. He came to the king with unspeakable pomp and display of power and wealth. The king, who was very tall and thin, with an aquiline nose, dressed in a grey peasant's tunic with a high hat, sat on the common road, and Ottocar, dressed most splendidly, knelt and, in royal fashion, was invested with his fiefs. Ottocar was indignant at this, and, being hard pressed by his wife, who was a Pole, because he had submitted so far, began to harass the king and seize Austria.

units.la: Obierat autem diebus illis prædictus H. de Nouocastro, episcopus Basiliensis, cuius gesta (qualiter tempore prædecessoris sui Berchtoldus de Pfirt, administrator episcopatus fuit, & illo defuncto, quasi sine electione, sed solo Capituli consensu, non audentis contradicere, episcopatum tenuit, quamuis quasi illiteratus: qualiter quadam vice citatus per papam personaliter, nūcium post magnum honorem sibi exhibitum, coēgit quasi, vt papam ad eundem diem coram eodem episcopo citaret, ad castrum suum Birsecke: qualiter tunc comes Ferretarum, ex quadam indignatione suorum, quandam permutationem terrae suae fecit cum episcopo, ad munitionem & vallem Telschberg, & ob hæc sui in eum iracundè irruentes, pro eo quòd eos infideliter alienauerit, ipsum facti pœnitentem, cùm vidisset tātum suorum dolorem, coēgerint quasi ad rescissionem contractus: & quod castrū Zouger & aduocatiam in Sergowe, quæ ipse comes tenebat, episcopo resignauit, ac Ferretum, Altkilch & alia abeo, propter rescissionem permutationis, in feudum recepit: qualiter duo milites de Buttenheim, ea quæ ab ecclesia Basiliensi habuerunt à prædicto comite de Habspurg in seudum recognouerant, & episcopus postea in præsentia regis eisdem dixit: Vos alienastis vos à beata virgine, & ego vos ab ea tollo, Sathanæ committendos: qualiter postea quilibet eorum alter alteri suam cognouit vxorem, qualiter postea Landser regi vendiderunt, & in rebus & in personis perierunt, ita quòd nullus est superstes ex eis, & alia ipsius episcopi acta) causa breuitatis relinquo.
units.tr: In those days the aforesaid Henry of Neuenburg, bishop of Basel, had died. I omit, for the sake of brevity, his deeds: how in the time of his predecessor Berthold of Pfirt he was administrator of the bishopric, and how, when Berthold died, he held the bishopric almost without an election, by the sole consent of the chapter, which dared not oppose him, although he was almost unlettered; how once, cited in person by the pope, after he had been shown great honour, he more or less compelled the papal messenger to summon the pope to appear before this same bishop on the same day at his castle of Birseck; how then the count of Ferrette, in anger at his own people, made an exchange of his land with the bishop for the fortress and valley of Telsberg, and how his people, rushing furiously upon him because he had alienated them disloyally, when they saw his repentance and so great a grief among them, forced him almost to rescind the contract; and how he surrendered to the bishop the castle of Zwingen and the advocacy in Sorgau, which the count himself held, and received back Pfirt, Altkirch and others from him in fief, because of the rescinding of the exchange; how two knights of Buttenheim acknowledged that they held from the church of Basel in fief what they had from the aforesaid count of Habsburg, and the bishop afterwards said to them in the king's presence: "You have alienated yourselves from the blessed Virgin, and I hand you over to Satan"; how afterwards each of them knew the other's wife; how afterwards they sold Landser to the king, and perished both in property and in person, so that none of them survived; and the other deeds of this bishop.

units.la: Erat autem in diebus illis quidā frater Henricus de Isena Sueuus, de ordine Minor. filius fabri, lector domus Moguntinæ, Theologus & Nigromanticus, qui dum quadam vice dæmonem cuidam bonæ mulieri in specie viri diu cohabitantem, per chateres eiecisset: dæmon non valens vltra illam accedere, dixit dæmon: Ab initio meæ ruinæ solitus eram cohabitare mulieribus, nunquam dilectiorem habui: nunquam ergo desistam, quin illum qui te mihi abstulit in eam altitudinem perducam, qua obliuiscatur penitus Dei sui. Hic Henricus cum pro Petro diutis Canonico Basil. & præposito ecclesiæ Moguntinensis, pro episcopatu Basiliensi iuisset ad papam, papa sibi, videlicet Henrico, non illi, de episcopatu prouidit. Hic regi familiarissimus est effectus.
units.tr: In those days there was a certain Brother Henry of Isny, a Swabian of the Franciscan order, son of a smith, lecturer at the house of Mainz, a theologian and a necromancer. Once, when by means of charms he had driven out a demon that for a long time had lived with a certain good woman in the form of a man, the demon, unable to approach her any further, said: "From the beginning of my fall I was accustomed to dwell with women, and I never had one more dear to me. I will therefore never cease until I bring him who has taken you from me to such a height that he completely forgets his God." This Henry, when he had gone to the pope on behalf of Peter, canon of Basel and provost of the church of Mainz, for the bishopric of Basel, the pope provided Henry himself, not Peter, with the bishopric. He became a very close friend of the king.

units.la: Rex autem congregato forti exercitu, Bohemiam contra Ottocharum est profectus, cum quo ipse Basiliensis episcopus cū c dextrariis iuit in propria persona. Transeuntes autem sylvam Bohemiæ per inuasores, quasi fugientes, damna plurima sunt perpessi. Episcopus autem Basiliensis tenens extremam exercitus custodiam, inuasores iterum venientes inuasit, qui in amnem fugientes more solito, transire credebant. Episcopus verò personaliter in flumen prosiliens, quem sui sequebantur, cepit eos, quos nudos ligans super equis secum duxit ita diu, quousq; fuerunt à muscarum corrosione perempti: nec amplius à talibus fuerunt infestati. Dicebatur autem de magna multitudine inimicorum latitantium in sylua. Quod cùm rex dixisset episcopo: statim episcopus procurauit, quòd ducētigaleati vltra flumen iuxta regis exercitum processerunt. Quærenti autem regi, qui essent illi galeati & ignoti, episcopus respondit: pro vobis sunt illi. Rex habens tædiū de illis, rogauit episcopū vt abiret: qui iubente epo abierūt.
units.tr: The king, having gathered a strong army, set out for Bohemia against Ottocar, and with him went the bishop of Basel in person, with a hundred war-horses. As they crossed the Bohemian forest, they suffered much damage at the hands of raiders, as if in flight. The bishop of Basel, who held the rear guard of the army, attacked the raiders when they came again, and they, fleeing into a river as was their habit, believed they could cross it. The bishop, leaping into the river in person, followed by his men, captured them; binding them naked on horses, he led them with him until they were destroyed by the gnawing of flies, and they no longer harassed anyone in this way.
