It was said that a large number of enemies were hiding in the forest. When the king said this to the bishop, the bishop at once arranged for two hundred helmeted men to cross the river beside the king's army. When the king asked who these helmeted, unknown men were, the bishop replied: "They are for your sake." The king, being weary of them, asked the bishop to send them away, and at his command they departed.

units.la: Venit autem Ottocharus cum exercitu innumerabili contra regem. Rex autem non in signis regalibus, sed in armis non signatis & rubiginosis prodiit in cōflictum. Venit autem quidā Valens ad regem, cupiens ab eo donum, eo animo vt sibi seruiret. Quod cum rex renueret, venit ad Ottocharū: & illius dono recepto, promisit regē, quātumcunq; se abscondentem, positurum ad terram. Videns Ottocharus exercitum regis, & quòd eum (quod credidisset) vitare nolebat, accessit dictum Zewusch Bohemum potentem, cuius fratris filiam ipse Ottocharus dolose cognouit, & patrem eius in turri igne occidit, dicens illi, quòd ignosceret, si quid vnquam mali egerit contra ipsum, vt perpetuò ditaret eundem. Ille vero respondit, quòd pro eo fideliter pugnare non posset: segregans se cum Ottocharo cum electis duobus millibus Bohemorum.
units.tr: Ottocar came against the king with an innumerable army. The king came forward into the battle not under royal insignia but in unmarked and rusty armour. A certain Valens came to the king, wishing to receive a gift from him, with the intention of serving him. When the king refused, he went to Ottocar, and having received a gift from him, promised to lay the king low, however much he might hide. When Ottocar saw the king's army, and saw that he (as he had believed) did not wish to avoid it, he went to the aforesaid Zewusch, a powerful Bohemian, whose niece Ottocar himself had treacherously known, and whose father he had killed in a fire in a tower, telling him that he would be forgiven for anything wrong he had ever done against Ottocar, and would be enriched for ever. But Zewusch replied that he could not fight faithfully for him, and separated himself from Ottocar with two thousand picked Bohemians.

units.la: Appropinquantibus autem timorosè & paulatim exercitibus ad conflictum, Rudolfus de Rheno miles Basilensis, sonora voce cătauit, quod per ambos exercitus audiebatur: Domina sancta Maria, domina sancta, quod tempore Litaniæ rustici cantant. Præordinauerat autem Henricus marchio de Hochberg, quòd quandocunque ipse tempore conflictus acclamaret, ipsi fugiunt, fugiunt, idiplum cæteri etiam acclamarēt: quod & factum est, per quod territi sunt Bohemi. Henricus quoq; Schorlin Sueus, episcopi Basil. seruitor, habēs equum indomitum, præsurā bormis seu aciei exercitus regis sufferre nō valens, tacto equo cum calcaribus, primus Bohemos invasit. Dixitq; rex: Tempus est vt ille iuuetur. Initoq; conflictu, prædictus Valens, qui donū ab Ottocharo recepit, cognoscens regem quamuis abscōditum per scapulas procliues, occiso equo regis, regem prostrauit in terrā. Quo Valēte ab aliis occiso, cum seruitores regis pro illius erectione se occupare vellent, dixit rex: non curetis de me, non est vis de vno homine, sed progredimini ad conflictum, & iuuetis alios. Illi dimisso rege prostrato, trudentes & progredientes viriliter, Ottocharum occiderunt: imò eo capto, ipsum finito conflictu quidam Bohemus occidit, cuius reliquam prædictus Zewusch postea recepit vxorem, quem Wenceslaus rex, Ottocharī filius, postea decollauit. Reliquit enim Ottocharus filiū & filiā, quibus Romanus rex prædictus Rudolfus suos liberos copulauit, dans Wenceslao vnam filiarum suarum, & sorori eius filium suum Rudolphum, cui sorori dominium de Kiburg quod ipse rex sibi retinuerat, morganitico iure donauit. Rudolfus verò dux postea moriens vnicum filium Ioannem ducem, Alberti regis occisorem, reliquit. Wenceslaus verò rex Bohemiæ absq; briga viuens quietè & sine armis in lecto moriēs, filium & duas filias ex prædicta vxore reliquit. Filius factus rex per traditionem clam in lecto occisus est. Vnam filiarum habuit Hēricus dux Karinthiæ, quem pro rege receperunt Bohemi: qui tamen propter infestationes Alberti regis, qui & ipse filium suum Rudolphum primogenitum ibi regem constituerat, possessionem pacificam habere nequiuit. Aliam verò filiam Wenceslai, diu postea occisi, successiuè Adolpho & Alberto regibus, & creato Heinrico comite de Lutzelburg Romanorum Imperatore, recepit in vxorem, & regnum Bohemorum cum ea, Ioannes filius Imperatoris eiusdem. Occiso itaq; Ottocharo, Rudolphus rex in Austriam pergens, diu quousq; omnia bene disposuit, permansit in Vienna.
units.tr: As the armies drew near to battle, fearfully and slowly, Rudolf of Rhein, a knight of Basel, called out in a loud voice, so that it could be heard through both armies: "Holy Lady Mary, holy Lady," which the peasants sing at the time of the litany. Henry, margrave of Hochberg, had arranged beforehand that whenever he himself shouted during the battle, "They flee, they flee," the others too should shout the same; and this was done, by which the Bohemians were terrified. Henry Schorlin the Swabian, servant of the bishop of Basel, having an unbroken horse and unable to endure the onslaught of the king's vanguard or battle line, spurred his horse and was the first to attack the Bohemians. And the king said: "Now it is time for that man to be helped." When the battle had begun, the aforesaid Valens, who had received the gift from Ottocar, recognising the king, although he was hidden, by his shoulders, which sloped, killed the king's horse and threw the king to the ground. When Valens had been killed by others, and the king's attendants wished to hasten to lift him up, the king said: "Do not trouble about me; there is no strength in one man. Go forward to the battle and help the others." They, leaving the fallen king, pressing on and advancing manfully, killed Ottocar; indeed, when he had been captured, a certain Bohemian killed him after the battle was over. His widow was afterwards taken by the aforesaid Zewusch, and Wenceslaus, the king, Ottocar's son, afterwards beheaded Zewusch. Ottocar left a son and a daughter, and King Rudolf, the aforesaid Roman king, married his own children to them, giving one of his daughters to Wenceslaus, and giving to the sister his son Rudolf, to whom he granted by morganatic right the lordship of Kyburg, which the king himself had kept for himself. Duke Rudolf, dying afterwards, left an only son, John, the duke, the murderer of King Albert. King Wenceslaus of Bohemia, living quietly and without strife, and dying in bed without arms, left a son and two daughters by the aforesaid wife. The son, made king, was killed secretly in bed by treachery. Henry, duke of Carinthia, had one of the daughters, and the Bohemians received him as king; yet, because of the attacks of King Albert, who had also established his own eldest son Rudolf there as king, he could not hold the kingdom in peace. The other daughter of Wenceslaus, who was killed long afterwards, was successively taken as wife by the kings Adolf and Albert, and when Henry, count of Luxemburg, had been made emperor of the Romans, John, son of that same emperor, received the kingdom of the Bohemians with her. So, with Ottocar killed, King Rudolf went into Austria and remained at Vienna until he had arranged everything well.

units.la: Erat autem quidam potes comes Vngarus, nomine Vwan, qui regem & Austriam plurimùm infestauit, pluries pacta inita inter ipsos infringens. Pro quo rex verbis pacificis mísit in dolo, & cùm venisset Viennam, timorǫ; magnus irruisset super eum, accedens mensam, bibit de cypho regis, dicens: Modò sum securus, quia bibi cum probiore viuente in hoc mundo. Verùm statim post mensam arreptus, sub glacie est submersus. Videns autem quidam de Liele magister militum regalis curiæ arreptionem, irruit in gladium suum pro illius comitis defensione. Rege verò dicente: desiste, quid ad te? ipse videns perfidiam regis, mœrens quieuit. Quidam verò miles probissimus, qui eundem comitem iubente rege illuc conduxerat, videns quæ fiebant per se impediri non posse, quasi amens factus, postea præ verecundia latitauit.
units.tr: There was a certain powerful Hungarian count named Vwan, who greatly harassed the king and Austria, repeatedly breaking the agreements made between them. Against him the king sent peaceful words, but with deceit in them. When Vwan came to Vienna, great fear fell upon him. He approached the table and drank from the king's cup, saying: "Now I am safe, since I have drunk with a better man living in this world." But immediately after the meal he was seized and drowned under the ice. Meanwhile a certain Liele, master of the soldiers of the royal court, seeing the count seized, rushed upon his sword in defence of him. But the king said: "Desist, what is it to you?" He, seeing the king's treachery, grieved in silence. A certain most valiant soldier, who had brought that count there at the king's command, seeing that what was happening could not be prevented, became as if mad, and afterwards hid himself out of shame.

units.la: Cùm autē in Vienna nocte famuli euntes pro vino spoliarentur, & resistentes vulnerarentur: Fridericus comes de Liningen, qui cum rege erat, quadā nocte, assumēs Gruem militem suum dictum Franich/personaliter cum milite solo iuit pro vino, circuiens vndiq; cum cantharo tanquam garcio, omnes ribaldos in eum irruentes occidit, & omnibus illis amputatis capitibus, Franich miles cuiuslibet caput posuit super ventrem occisi. Mane autem facto, plures ciuium filij occisi reperti sunt in plateis, & magnus clamor factus est per ciues coram rege, de occisione filiorum suorum, ipso in ciuitate stante. Quis autem fecisset, nemo sciuit. Progrediente autem rege ad Missam, & sequente cum Friderico comite, viderunt vnum in strata occisum, non tamen caput supra ventrem habentem: & clàm dicente Friderico ad Gruem, se illi non recte fecisse: rex audiens duorum colloquium, tacuit. Sed post in camera sua quęrens à Friderico & audiens ab eo facti seriem, ipsum commendauit: de cuius Friderici consobrini regis gestis nobilibus, integra historia opus esset. De Viuiano etiam ciue Basil. socero prædicti Schorlin, quanta in prædicto conflictu peregerit, & de mirabilibus factis eius, ad præsens relinquo.
units.tr: When servants going out for wine were robbed at night in Vienna, and those who resisted were wounded, Count Friedrich of Liningen, who was with the king, took his soldier named Gruem, called Franich, one night and went out for wine with only that soldier, personally, circling on all sides with a jug like a serving boy. He killed all the ruffians who rushed at him, and after cutting off all their heads, the soldier Franich placed one man's head upon the belly of each dead body. In the morning many sons of the citizens were found slain in the streets, and the citizens raised a great outcry before the king over the killing of their sons, the king being in the city at the time. Nobody knew who had done it. But as the king went on to Mass, with Count Friedrich following, they saw one man slain in the street who did not have his head upon his belly. When Friedrich quietly told Gruem that he had not acted rightly, the king, overhearing the conversation of the two, said nothing. But afterwards, in his chamber, he asked Friedrich, and hearing from him the sequence of events, he commended him. The noble deeds of this cousin of the king, Friedrich, would need a whole history. About Viviano also, the citizen of Basel and father-in-law of the aforesaid Schorlin, how much he accomplished in that conflict and his wonderful deeds, I leave for the present.

units.la: Reliquit autem rex cum filio suo duce Alberto multos Sueuorum in Vienna, quorum vnius scil. de Walsee liberi postea propter eorum virtutem constantiæ ditissimi sunt effecti: ita quòd, qui per pedes venerant in Austriam, finaliter decem milium marcarum redditus habuerunt.
units.tr: The king left many Swabians in Vienna with his son, Duke Albert. Among them the children of one man, namely of Walsee, were afterwards made very rich on account of their steadfast courage, so that those who had come into Austria on foot finally had revenues of ten thousand marks.

units.la: Veniente autem rege Nurenberg, Henricus Schorlin, filiam hospitis sui speciosissimam, violenter corrupit & stuprauit. Cùm autem populus commotus, à rege propter hoc iudicium postularet: rex diu protrahes, cum se nemo interponeret, tandem dixit commotus: de isto iudicabo, & in hoc loco iudicans, quàm diu vixero iudicabo. Perterriti autem nobiles & populus ciuitatis, videntes quanta ille affectione diligebatur à rege, Henrico Schorlin puellam in coniugem legitimam copulabat, & ducentas marcas argenti eis dabat, & sic clamor contra Henricum cessabat.
units.tr: When the king was coming to Nuremberg, Henry Schorlin violently seduced and debauched the very beautiful daughter of his host. When the people, stirred up, demanded judgment from the king for this, the king delayed for a long time. No one intervened, and at last he said, roused: "I will judge concerning this man, and in this place, judging, I will go on judging as long as I live." The nobles and people of the city, terrified and seeing how much he was loved by the king, gave the girl to Henry Schorlin in lawful marriage, and gave them two hundred marks of silver, and so the outcry against Henry ceased.

units.la: Rediens autem rex ad Rhenum cum episcopo Basil. castrum & oppidum Brunndruti, quod comes montis Biligardi tenuit, quod antiquitus fuisse dicebatur ecclesiæ Basil. obsedit. Quo tum victo, ecclesia Basil. deinde quiete possedit. Construxit etiam ipse episcopus de auxilio regis castrum Goldenfels, vltra Brunndrut, in territorio Gallicorum, terram quæ circa est attrahedo. Cumq; comes Nouicastri, dicens se aduocatū super oppidum Biele, terrā vsq; ad Biele in sua potestate teneret, prædictus eps castrum Schloßberg ædificās, illam terram per duas leucas ecclesiæ suæ dominio attrahebat. Itè in valle S. Immerij castrū forte Arguel ædificans, inibi meatum Gallicorum præclusit.
units.tr: Returning to the Rhine with the bishop of Basel, the king besieged the castle and town of Brunndrut, which the count of Montbéliard held and which was said in ancient times to have belonged to the church of Basel. When it was conquered, the church of Basel afterwards possessed it in peace. The bishop himself, with the king's help, also built the castle of Goldenfels beyond Brunndrut, in the territory of the French, drawing in the land that lies around it. And since the count of Neuchâtel, calling himself advocate over the town of Biel, held the land as far as Biel in his power, the aforesaid bishop, building the castle of Schlossberg, drew that land within two leagues under the lordship of his church. Likewise, in the valley of St. Immer, building the castle perhaps called Arguel, he closed off the passage of the French there.

units.la: Idem episcopus post multos bonos actus & strenuos, & vtiles ecclesiæ Basilienfi, ad Maguntinum archiepiscopatum promotus, Petrum Diuitis, mediante fauore Papæ, ad ecclesiam Basilien-sem promouit.
units.tr: The same bishop, after many good and vigorous deeds useful to the church of Basel, was promoted to the archbishopric of Mainz, and by the favour of the Pope he advanced Peter Diuitis to the church of Basel.

units.la: Rex autem nullum motum habens ad Italiam, forsitan quia vidit cæteris multis malè succeßisse: misit prædictum Henricum episcopum Basilien-sem, cum membranis sigillo suo sigillatis, ad ciuitatem Romanam, qui ibidem sedi Apostolicæ Romandiolam & quædam alia, in damnum graue imperij dedit: ibi habitis quibusdam tra-ctatibus nomine regio sigillauit.
units.tr: The king, having no inclination toward Italy, perhaps because he saw that many others had fared badly there, sent the aforesaid Henry, bishop of Basel, to the city of Rome with documents sealed with his own seal. There he gave Romagna and certain other lands to the Apostolic See, to the grave loss of the empire, and after certain negotiations he sealed them in the royal name.

units.la: Ipse quoq; Henricus factus archiepiscopus strenuè multa peregit: volensq; visitare episcopatum Constantiensem, Rudolfus de Habspurg episcopus Constantiensis, filius patrui regis, sibi restitit. Quibus ambobus postea coram rege constitutis, & instante archiepiscopo pro visitatione: episcopo verò dicente, modicum esse episcopatum suum & pauperem: illo verò dicente, se bene scire qualis esset: episcopus respondit: Bene credo, quia soleis vestris sæpiùs percurristis eum, quàm ego vnquam potuerim equitare. Vltimò tamen dixit rex, eum admitti debere & admissus fuit ad visitationem. Fuerunt autem tres fratres de Habspurg, filij patrui regis, sc. Rudolfus episcopus Constant. Gotfridus dominus in Lauffenberg, & Eberhardus qui dicebatur de Kiburg.
units.tr: Henry himself, once made archbishop, did many things vigorously. Wishing to visit the diocese of Constance, he was resisted by Rudolf of Habsburg, bishop of Constance, son of the king's uncle. Both of them were afterwards brought before the king. The archbishop insisted on the visitation, and the bishop said that his diocese was small and poor. The archbishop said he knew well what it was like. The bishop replied: "I well believe it, since you have gone over it with your shoes more often than I could ever have ridden it." In the end, however, the king said that he ought to be admitted, and he was admitted to the visitation. There were three brothers of Habsburg, sons of the king's uncle: Rudolf, bishop of Constance; Gottfried, lord of Laufenberg; and Eberhard, who was called of Kyburg.

units.la: Habuit autem archiepiscopus maiorem affectionem ad milites quàm ad clerum. Vnde quadam vice habens festum, cum clerici citiùs quàm milites sederent ad mensam, dixit archiepiscopus: bini & bini milites recipiant vnum clericum pro puluinari.
units.tr: The archbishop had greater affection for soldiers than for the clergy. Hence, on one feast day, when the clerics sat down at table sooner than the soldiers, the archbishop said: "Let soldiers, two and two, take one cleric each for a pillow."

units.la: Vnde & super eius morientis sepulchrum scripsit quidam versus, Nudipes Antistes, non curat Clerus vbi stes: Dum non in cœlis stes vbicunq; velis. Indista autem curia Coloniæ per regem, & adducto per eum genero suo, duce Bauariæ, in die hastiludij progrediuntur centum milites, ad hastiludium parati, omnes ducentes mulierem decapitatam in armis, in despectum ducis Bauariæ. Quod videns rex, & ducem de accessu suo arguens, curia dimissa recessit.
units.tr: Hence someone also wrote verses upon his tomb as he lay dying: "Barefoot bishop, the clergy does not care where you stand; since you do not stand in heaven, you may stand wherever you wish." The Cologne court, summoned by the king, and with the duke of Bavaria, his son-in-law, brought there by him, proceeded on the day of the joust. A hundred soldiers, ready for the joust, all came leading a beheaded woman in armour, in contempt of the duke of Bavaria. Seeing this, the king rebuked the duke for his coming, dismissed the court, and withdrew.

units.la: Rex quoq; postea oppidum Petterlingen situm versus Laufannam obsedit, & oppidum Murten, de manibus comitis Sabaudiæ eruens, ad regnum retraxit. Rex quoq; Bernam sibi rebellantem obsidens, & quincere non valens, sed quotidiana lite infestans: tandem Rudolfum filium suum clam cum quadringentis equitibus misit, qui se ponens in insidiis, quosdam abductores pecorum solito more præmisit: quos illi insequentes usq; ad locum insidiarum, capti sunt & occisi. Ipsi vero Ludouicum comitem de Honberg, patrem valentissimi Wernharij, primum aggredientium cuspidibus recipientes, necârunt: sicq; Berna regi est reformata.
units.tr: Afterwards the king also besieged the town of Petterlingen, situated toward Lausanne, and, snatching the town of Murten from the hands of the count of Savoy, brought it back into the kingdom. The king also besieged Bern, which was rebelling against him. Unable to conquer it, but harassing it with daily fighting, he at last secretly sent his son Rudolf with four hundred horsemen. Rudolf placed himself in ambush and sent ahead some cattle-raiders in the usual way. When the pursuers followed them as far as the place of the ambush, they were captured and killed. But the ambushers, receiving with their spears Count Ludwig of Honberg, the father of the most valiant Werner, who was first among the attackers, killed him. And so Bern was restored to the king.

units.la: Cumq; etiam rebellantem sibi Columbariam obsedisset, quidam vero quondam Imp. Friderico simillimus, in inferioribus Rheni partibus seiplum Fridericum fingês, ac Barones & ciuitates sibi aggregas, usq; Wetzflar venisset: rex pertimiscens, admissa cum Columbariensibus concordia, cum gente descendens, ac se illu velle tanq; Imp. venerari fingens, ipsum apprehensum quæsiuit unde venisset, & quis esset, & eu cremauit.
units.tr: When he had besieged Colmar, which was rebelling against him, a certain man very like the former Emperor Friedrich appeared in the lower regions of the Rhine. Pretending to be Friedrich himself and gathering barons and cities to his side, he came as far as Wetzlar. The king, alarmed, made peace with the men of Colmar and came down with his troops. Pretending that he wished to venerate him as emperor, he seized the man and asked where he had come from and who he was, and then had him burned.

units.la: Dicitur quoq;, quòd cum rex Fraciæ illis diebus monasterium S. Dionysij, quod imperio pertinebat, nimis grauaret, & pluries à rege Rudolfo rogatus nō desisteret: tandē rege scribente Franco inter singula, quòd desisteret, alioquin in partibus suis ipsum visitaret, per vires & viros, quos sibi felix Germania germinauit: Francus se nolens inbrigare cum illo, à grauaminibus cessauit & quieuit.
units.tr: It is also said that in those days the king of France was grievously burdening the monastery of St. Denis, which belonged to the empire, and would not desist even when often asked by King Rudolf. At last King Rudolf wrote to him, among other things, that he should desist, or else he would visit him in his own territories with the forces and men which fortunate Germany had brought forth for him. The Frenchman, unwilling to become entangled with him, ceased his oppression and kept quiet.

units.la: In diebus illis cum Petrus Basiliensis episcopus habens litem cum Gallicis vicinis, succubuisset in conflictu, inlitum præsertim Basiliensium magna multitudine captiuata: rex Rudolfus pro illorum recuperatione veniens, Bisuntium potenter obsedit: vbi manicas wambasij sui fractas, cum nouis peciis reparans, dedit exemplum aliis ita faciendi. Dux autem Burgundiæ cum omni quasi potentia Gallicorum, cum exercitu maximo se posuit contra regis exercitum, ne regi victualia possent afferri: ita quòd vno die regis exercitus in victu defectum maximum est perpessus. Videns autem rex rapas in campo, rapam unam rasam comedit. Quod videntes alij, admirati de eo, omnes quodammodo rapis sunt saturati.
units.tr: In those days Peter, bishop of Basel, had a dispute with the French neighbours and was defeated in the conflict, and a great multitude of the Basilians was captured, especially of the soldiers. King Rudolf came to recover them and powerfully besieged Besançon. There, having mended the broken sleeves of his doublet with new pieces, he gave the others an example of doing likewise. The duke of Burgundy, with almost all the power of the French, set himself with a very great army against the king's army, so that provisions could not be brought to the king, and on one day the king's army suffered the greatest shortage of food. Seeing turnips in the field, the king ate one turnip raw. When the others saw this and marvelled at him, they all, in a manner, were satisfied with turnips.

units.la: Rex autem retrocedens ad Gallicorum exercitum in valle positum iuxta ripam, in montem desuper se recepit, ita quòd vnus exercitus in alterum posset respicere: & in sero tractans cum satrapis suis, de ineundo mane conflictu, cum quidam ex eis miraretur, addens, de quo viuere vellent? rex ipsum inanem habere curam, respondit dicens: Si ipsos vicerimus, victualibus eorum vescemur: si nos vicerint, cùm nobiles sint, dabunt victum captiuis. Ipsisq; sic tractantibus, nox accessit.
units.tr: The king, however, withdrew to the height above the French army, which was posted in the valley beside the bank, so that one army could see the other. In the evening, while he was discussing with his nobles the battle to be joined the next morning, one of them was surprised and added: what would they live on? The king, saying that he had no concern for that, replied: "If we defeat them, we shall eat their provisions; if they defeat us, since they are noblemen, they will give food to the prisoners." While they were talking in this way, night fell.

units.la: Erat autem tumultuosum murmur in exercitibus, ut moris est. Et ecce quidam de Suitia, quorum rex mille ducentos habuit, soliti currere in montanis, descendentes montem, irruerunt in castra Theobaldi comitis Ferretarum, qui fuit adiutor in acie Gallicorum, & aliquibus occisis, ipsius spolia deferendo, & plurima laniado: ita quòd in valle facta est commotio clamorosa. Gallicis quoq; tractantibus de præcludendo regi discessu, cùm arbitrarētur, se propter eorum multitudinē, & quia non erat aptus descensus ad eos, securos à conflictu: quidam ex eis dixit, Nolco regē talem, etsi debeat manibus & pedibus repere, nos inuadet. Sicq; timentes, diluculo solennes ad regem pro concordia nuntios destinârunt. Cumq; rex aliud nollet, nisi ante omnia captiuis liberè restitutis: dux & maiores Burgundiæ se Basileam corporaliter præsentârunt, ibi de concordia tractantes. Vasalli imperij quoq; præstita fidelitate, sunt de regalibus inuestiti. Dicitur etiam, regem in ipso exercitu dixisse, se in qualibet mundi parte cum electis quatuor galeatorum, & quadraginta peditum armatorum de Alemannia millibus, stare inuictum: æstimans, hos omnem multitudinem aggressuros.
units.tr: There was, as is usual, a noisy murmuring in the armies. And behold, some men from Switzerland, whose king had twelve hundred, accustomed to running in the mountains, came down from the heights and attacked the camp of Count Theobald of Ferrette, who had been an ally of the French in the battle. After killing some, they carried off his spoils and cut many to pieces, so that a loud commotion arose in the valley. The French, meanwhile, were discussing how to cut off the king's retreat, believing that he could not escape from them because of their numbers and because the descent to them was not easy. Some of them said: "I do not want a king like that. Even if he has to crawl on hands and feet, he will attack us." Fearing this, they sent envoys at dawn to the king with solemn requests for peace. The king would agree to nothing except that, above all, the prisoners be freely restored. Then the duke and the chief men of Burgundy presented themselves in person at Basel, where they negotiated the peace. The vassals of the empire, having sworn their fealty, were also invested with the royal fiefs. It is also said that the king declared in the army itself that he would stand unconquered in any part of the world with four chosen mounted knights and forty thousand armed foot soldiers from Germany, reckoning that these would attack the entire multitude.

units.la: Mortua autem domina Anna de Hohenberg regina, & in choro ecclesiæ Basiliensis cum duobus filiis sepulta: rex filiam sororis regis Francię in senio iuuenem recepit vxorem, quæ tamen post mortem regis rediit satis egens.
units.tr: Queen Anna of Hohenberg died and was buried in the choir of the church of Basel with her two sons. The king, though old, took as his wife a young daughter of the sister of the king of France; she, however, after the king's death, returned to her own family, quite destitute.

units.la: Rex autem Rudolphus cum Anna de Hohenberg, sorore Alberti de Hohenberg, berg, habuit tres filios: inter alios Rudolphum, Albertum & Hartmannum. Qui Hartmannus apud Xeynow, in Rheno periit, & cū matre & paruulo fratre Carolo in choro Basiliensis ecclesiae est sepultus. Item habuit sex filias, quarum vnam habuit dux Bauariae superioris, alteram dux Bauariae inferioris, tertiam dux Saxoniae: quartam dux Vratislaviae: quo defuncto, recepit Marchionem in Brandenburg. quintam habuit rex Wenceslaus Bohemiae, filius Ottochari, per ipsum Rudolphum regem occisi: sextam habuit Carolus primogenitus regis Siciliae siue Apuliae.
units.tr: King Rudolf, with Anna of Hohenberg, sister of Albert of Hohenberg, had three sons, among them Rudolf, Albert and Hartmann. Hartmann perished in the Rhine at ChSeynow [Xeynow] and was buried with his mother and little brother Charles in the choir of the church of Basel. He also had six daughters: one married the duke of Upper Bavaria, another the duke of Lower Bavaria, a third the duke of Saxony, a fourth the duke of Breslau; when he died, she took a margrave of Brandenburg. King Wenceslaus of Bohemia, son of Ottokar, whom King Rudolf himself had killed, took the fifth. Charles, the firstborn son of the king of Sicily or Apulia, had the sixth.

units.la: Ex Rudolfo filiorum primogenito & sorore Wenceslai, descendit Ioannes Bohemiae dux, occisor praedicti Alberti.
units.tr: From Rudolf's firstborn son and the sister of Wenceslaus descended John, duke of Bohemia, the killer of the aforementioned Albert.

units.la: Ex Alberto, qui habebat Elisabet, filiam comitis Tirolis, antequam pater promoueretur in regem, quem comitem ipse rex postmodum duce Carinthiae creauit, creati sunt: 1 Rudolfus primogenitus, qui factus est rex Bohemiae, & filiam regis Franciae ducēs, sine liberis est defunctus. 2 Item Fridericus, in Romanorum regem in discordia electus & coronatus: quia ex filia regis Arragonū sola relicta filia, quae postea comiti Carinthiae data est, sine liberis est defunctus. 3 Item dux Leopoldus strenuissimus, qui relictis duabus filiabus, ex filia comitis Sabaudiae, quarū vna postea data est duci de Sueinitz Silesiae, alia domino de Cusin Franciae, sine aliis liberis defunctus. 4 Item Otto dux, ex filia ducis Bauariae inferioris duos relinquens filios, Fridericum & Leopoldum, qui mortui sunt sine liberis. 5 Item dux Austriae, qui ex filia comitis Ferretarum habet filios & filias: quorum Rudolfus primogenitus habet filiam Caroli Imper. & Bohemiae regis. 6 Item Agnes, ducens Andream regem Vngariae, sine liberis est defuncta: quae hodierno die ducit vitam sanctam & beatam. 7 Item ducissa Lotringesis, ex qua Rudolfus filius, & Rudolfus nepos, & domina de Chabilone sunt nati. 8 Item Catharina desponsata Henrico Imp. coq; defuncto duci nupta Calabriae, filio regis Ruperti Siciliae, sine liberis est defuncta. 9 Item comitissa de OEtingen.
units.tr: From Albert, who had Elizabeth, daughter of the count of Tyrol, before his father was raised to the kingship (whom count the king himself later made duke of Carinthia), the following were born: (1) Rudolf the firstborn, who became king of Bohemia and, marrying a daughter of the king of France, died without children; (2) likewise Frederick, elected and crowned king of the Romans in a dispute, who, having left only one daughter by the daughter of the king of Aragon (later given to the count of Carinthia), died without children; (3) likewise Duke Leopold, most valiant, who, leaving two daughters by the daughter of the count of Savoy, one of whom was afterwards given to the duke of Sweidnitz in Silesia and the other to the lord of Cusin in France, died without other children; (4) likewise Duke Otto, who, by the daughter of the duke of Lower Bavaria, left two sons, Frederick and Leopold, who died without children; (5) likewise the duke of Austria, who by the daughter of the count of Ferrette has sons and daughters, of whom the firstborn Rudolf has a daughter of Emperor Charles and king of Bohemia; (6) likewise Agnes, who married Andrew, king of Hungary, and died without children; she today lives a holy and blessed life; (7) likewise the duchess of Lorraine, by whom were born a son Rudolf, a grandson Rudolf, and a lady of Chabilon; (8) likewise Catherine, betrothed to Emperor Henry, but after his death married to the duke of Calabria, son of King Robert of Sicily, and died without children; (9) likewise the countess of Oettingen.

units.la: Ex filia Rudolfi regis in inferiori Bauaria.†
units.tr: From the daughter of King Rudolf in Lower Bavaria.†

units.la: Ex superiore Bauaria nati sunt, Rudolfus primogenitus, dux & palatinus Rheni, Ludouicus Romanorum Imperator quartus, & Langgrauia Hassiae. Ex Rudolfo, & Metza filia Adolfi regis Romanorum, eius coniuge, descenderunt: Adolfus, Rudolfus & Rupertus minor, quem Arnestum nominant, cuius mater fuit de OEtingen & de Wirtenberg: qui Arnestus filiam regis Siciliae duxit vxorem. Ex Rudolfo & filia ducis Carinthiae, descendit vxor Romanorum & Bohemiae regis. Ex Ludouico Imperatore descenderunt: ex Polona, Ludouicus & Stephanus filij, & marchionissa de Missen: ex Holanda autem, descenderunt Romerius marchio Brandeburgēsis, Wilhelmus comes Holandiae, & Albertus, & duae filiae, quarum vnam habet frater regis Vngariae, aliam Mastufus dominus Veronensis. Ex Ludouico primogenito marchione in Brandenburg & filia regis Daciae, descendit filia nupta regi Norwegiae: ex filia vero ducis Carinthiae, ablata Ioanni Bohemi propter impotentiam, nati sunt filij & filiae. Ex Stephano & filia regis Siciliae, & postea ex filia Burggrauij de Nureberg, multi filij & filiae sunt creati. Ex marchionissa Missenensi plures filij & filiae creati sunt.
units.tr: From Upper Bavaria were born: Rudolf the firstborn, duke and count palatine of the Rhine; Louis IV, emperor of the Romans; and the landgrave of Hesse. From Rudolf and Mechtild, daughter of King Adolf of the Romans, his wife, there descended Adolf, Rudolf, and the younger Rupert, whom they call Ernest, whose mother was of Oettingen and of Württemberg; this Ernest married a daughter of the king of Sicily. From Rudolf and the daughter of the duke of Carinthia descended the wife of the king of the Romans and of Bohemia. From Emperor Louis descended: by the Polish woman, the sons Louis and Stephen, and the margravine of Meissen; by the Dutch woman, however, descended Romerius, margrave of Brandenburg, William, count of Holland, and Albert, and two daughters, one of whom the brother of the king of Hungary has, and the other Mastino, lord of Verona. From Louis the firstborn, margrave in Brandenburg, and the daughter of the king of Denmark, descended a daughter married to the king of Norway; from the daughter of the duke of Carinthia, taken from John of Bohemia on account of his impotence, sons and daughters were born. From Stephen and the daughter of the king of Sicily, and afterwards from the daughter of the burgrave of Nuremberg, many sons and daughters were born. From the margravine of Meissen many sons and daughters were born.

units.la: Ex Saxona, Rudolfi regis filia, plures Saxoniae duces sunt creati.
units.tr: From Saxony, daughter of King Rudolf, several dukes of Saxony were born.

units.la: Ex ducissa Vratislaviae, postea marchionissa in Brandenburg, Volmarus & quidam alij Marchiones nati sunt.
units.tr: From the duchess of Breslau, afterwards margravine in Brandenburg, Volmar and some other margraves were born.

units.la: Ex regina Bohemiae, ipsius Rudolfi regis filia, & ex Wenceslao rege, descenderunt, Wenceslaus filius, qui rex factus sine liberis est defunctus. Item duae filiae, quarū vnam habuit Henricus dux Carinthiae, ex qua descenderunt duae filiae: aliam habuit Ioannes rex Bohemiae & marchio Moraviae, vnde Carolus Imperator descendit. Ex Carolo Romanorum Imperatore, & sorore regis Franciae, descenderunt duae filiae: vna regina Vngariae, quae sine liberis est defuncta, alia ducissa Austriae.
units.tr: From the queen of Bohemia, daughter of King Rudolf himself, and from King Wenceslaus, there descended: Wenceslaus, the son, who became king and died without children; and two daughters, one of whom Henry, duke of Carinthia, had, from whom two daughters descended; the other John, king of Bohemia and margrave of Moravia, had, from whom Emperor Charles descended. From Charles, emperor of the Romans, and the sister of the king of France, two daughters descended: one, queen of Hungary, who died without children; the other, duchess of Austria.

units.la: Ex regina Siciliae, ipsius Rudolfi filia, descenderunt Carolus successor patris etiam rex Siciliae, sed per patrem Rupertum & per papā eiectus, & de adiutorio Alberti regis Romanorum auunculi sui Hungariae rex creatus. Item Delphina, ex qua duo Delphini filij sunt nati. Item Clementia regina Franciae, quae absq; liberis est defuncta. Ex Carolo rege Hungariae praedicto descenderunt, nunc Carolus primogenitus, rex Hungariae: item Andreas rex Siciliae, iugulatus per Iohannam vxorem & patruelem suam.
units.tr: From the queen of Sicily, daughter of Rudolf himself, there descended Charles, successor of his father and also king of Sicily, but expelled by his father Rupert and by the pope, and, with the help of Albert king of the Romans, his uncle, made king of Hungary. Also Delphina, from whom two sons of the Dauphin were born. Also Clementia, queen of France, who died without children. From the aforementioned King Charles of Hungary there descended, now Charles the firstborn, king of Hungary; also Andrew, king of Sicily, strangled by Joanna, his wife and cousin.

units.la: De animoso & probo comite Alberto de Haigerloch & Hohen- berg, qui dicebatur esse vnus de XII pugilibus.
units.tr: The Spirited and Upright Count Albert of Haigerloch and Hohenberg, who was said to be one of the twelve champions.

units.la: ALBERTVS comes de Hohenberg & de Haigerloch, frater praedictae reginae, dominae Annae, duos comitatus habuit antiquos valde, scilicet Haigerloch & Hohenberg: & siti sunt in corde Sueuiae, & dicebantur comites de Hurmingen, & illi comites fuerunt potentes in Sueuia & Alsatia. In Elsatia habuerunt castrum, quod dicitur Ortenberg, & magnas villas & totam vallem quae dicitur Albrechts thal, cum omnibus pertinentiis. In qua valle duo domini & fratres de Hurmingen, quorum vnus fuit laicus, constuxerunt claustrum solenne ordinis sancti Benedicti, in honorem sancti Michaelis, & procurauerunt eximi ab omnibus exactionibus & muneribus quibuscunque, a Sixto papa: excepto quod annuatim debent praesentare ad cameram papae vnum marmotinum, hoc est, denarium aureum, qui bene noscitur in Curia, & est minoris valoris, quam paruulus florenus de Florentia. Nomen claustri, Latine Hugonis curia, Teutonice Hugeshofen. Praedicti vero duo domini ambo mortui sunt, & in dicto claustro sepulti, vbi corpora eorum hodierna die requiescunt. Quod dominium Albertus comes postea dedit Rudolfo de Habspurg, in dotem dominae Annae, praedictae sororis suae.
units.tr: Albert, count of Hohenberg and Haigerloch, brother of the aforesaid queen, the lady Anne, held two very ancient counties, namely Haigerloch and Hohenberg. They lie in the heart of Swabia, and their counts were called counts of Hurmingen. Those counts were powerful in Swabia and Alsace. In Alsace they held a castle called Ortenberg, large estates, and the whole valley called Albrechtsthal, with all its appurtenances. In that valley two lords and brothers of Hurmingen, one of whom was a layman, built a solemn monastery of the Order of St Benedict, in honour of St Michael. They obtained from Pope Sixtus exemption from all exactions and services whatsoever, except that each year they must present to the papal chamber one marmotinum, that is, a gold penny, which is well known at the Curia and is of less value than the small florin of Florence. The monastery is called in Latin Hugonis curia, in German Hugeshofen. The two lords both died and were buried in that monastery, where their bodies rest to this day. Count Albert afterwards gave this lordship to Rudolf of Habsburg as a dowry for the lady Anne, his sister.

units.la: Albertus vero praedictus multa bona fecit tempore suo, & laudabilia. Fuit bellicosus, animosus & probus: & cantatum fuit a quodam magistro, qui dicebatur Kumier, quod idem Albertus esset sustentaculum Romani imperij totius Sueuiae. Qui Albertus fuit occisus in proprio comitatu suo, per quendam ducem Bauariae, iuxta castrum Lintstetten, pessime derelictus a seruitoribus suis: quorum progenies hodie praedicto domino est nota, qui fugitiue recesserunt a domino suo, sicut canes quibus alligantur vesicae, quibus impositae sunt fabae. Progenies fugientium dicuntur, die Lemmer von Wittingen/ & duxerunt agnum per ista. Et sicut legitur, quod vna ouis interficit totum gregem: ita dominus eorum interfectus fuit per fugam ipsorum. Vtinam fuissent lupi rapaces, qui devorassent corpora eorum.
units.tr: Albert, the aforesaid, did many good and praiseworthy things in his time. He was warlike, spirited and upright, and a certain master called Kumier sang that this same Albert was the mainstay of the Roman empire throughout Swabia. This Albert was killed in his own retinue by a certain duke of Bavaria, near the castle of Lintstetten, abandoned in a most wretched way by his servants. Their descendants are well known to the present lord: they fled from their lord like dogs to whom bladders are tied, with beans placed on them. They are called the offspring of the fugitives, "die Lemmer von Wittingen", and they led the lamb away through these places. And as it is read, one sheep infects the whole flock; so their lord was destroyed by their flight. Would that they had been ravening wolves, to devour their bodies.

units.la: Ex praedicto Alberto descenderunt, Albertus & Rudolfus. Albertus dicebatur Röschmann Rudolfo existente Albertus mortuus est. Rudolfus multa & laudabilia fecit: & potentior Sueuiae fuit, qui tunc vixit. Et habuit tres comitatus, scilicet Rotenburg, Haigerloch, Hohenberg, exceptis pluribus munitionibus, Horwe, *Nordlingen, Werfch, der Busch, Buggingen. Obsedit etiam Rudolfus Eberhardum de Wirtenberg, & filium suum Vlricum vnicum, cum machinis & aliis instrumentis, cum quibus castra & munitiones inuaduntur, & duo sibi castra destruxit, & eum obsedit pluribus septimanis cum magnis expensis: quorum vnum dicebatur Hohenek, aliud vero Pfullentz, & Grauenwiler ita destruxit, quod domini de Wirtenberg nunquam audebant eum depellere de loco.
units.tr: From the aforesaid Albert descended Albert and Rudolf. Albert was called Röschmann; Albert died while Rudolf was still living. Rudolf did many praiseworthy things and was the most powerful man in Swabia of his time. He held three counties, namely Rottenburg, Haigerloch and Hohenberg, besides several fortresses: Horw, Nördlingen, Werth, der Busch, Buggingen. Rudolf also besieged Eberhard of Württemberg and his only son Ulrich, with siege engines and other instruments by which castles and fortresses are assailed. He destroyed two of their castles, one called Hohenegg and the other Pfullendorf, and he so destroyed Grafenwiler that the lords of Württemberg never dared to drive him from the place. He besieged them for several weeks at great expense.

units.la: Ex Rudolfo & domina de Werdenberg descenderunt Albertus, Rudolfus, Hugo, Henricus, & vna filia. Albertus missus fuit in Constantiam per patrem suum Rudolfum causa studij, vbi stetit honorifice pluribus annis, & multum profecit in artibus: factus est canonicus maioris ecclesiae, & rector cuiusdam ecclesiae in Austria quae dicitur Ruspach, & rector trium ecclesiarum in Sueuia, quarum pater eius fuit patronus. Postea missus fuit Parisios, vbi stetit pluribus annis cum magnis sumptibus, & profecit in magnum clericum: & legebat iura ad tempus multis audientibus. Postea licentiatus fuit in Decretis, non causa dominij, sed causa veritatis scientiae. Postea rediens in patriam, receptus est in canonicum Argentinensem. Mortuo autem domino Rudolfo episcopo Constantiensi, electus est in episcopum; sed in discordia non habuit processum, quia maior pars Capituli & burgenses erant contra eum, qui timuerunt potentiam patris.
units.tr: From Rudolf and the lady of Werdenberg descended Albert, Rudolf, Hugo, Henry, and one daughter. Albert was sent to Constance by his father Rudolf for the sake of study. He stayed there with honour for several years and made great progress in the arts. He became a canon of the cathedral church and rector of a certain church in Austria called Ruspach, and rector of three churches in Swabia, whose patron his father was. Afterwards he was sent to Paris, where he stayed for several years at great expense and became a learned clerk; for a time he lectured on law to many listeners. Afterwards he was licensed in Decretals, not for the sake of a lordship, but for the sake of the truth of knowledge. Afterwards, returning to his country, he was received as a canon of Strasbourg. When the bishop Rudolf of Constance died, he was elected bishop; but in the dispute he did not prevail, because the greater part of the chapter and the townsmen were against him, since they feared the power of his father.

units.la: Postea factus est Cancellarius domini Ludouici Imperatoris, & eius aduocatus prouincialis totius Elsatiae, in cuius seruitio multa peregit, & in solennibus negotiis missus fuit per Imperatorem in Franciam, tunc in Prouinciam ad papam, modo ad regem Angliæ, tunc ad ducem Austriæ. Postea videns Imperatorem esse pigrum, & non multum promotum ab eo, transtulit se Auinionem, ibi diu stetit per longum tempus, vbi prouisum fuit sibi de episcopatu Herbipolensi, à papa Clemente sexto: sed non obtinuit, propter potentiam illius de Hohenloh, concorditer electi à toto Capitulo. Post mortem domini de O Etingen, qui fuit famosior physicus mundi, papa Clemens sextus prouidit prædicto domino Alberto de episcopatu Frisingensi, quem potenter & sine impedimento tenet. Qui fuit virtutibus plenus, sociabilis, affabilis, largus, sed minus humilis, quia nimia humilitas parit contemptum.
units.tr: Afterwards he became chancellor to the lord Emperor Louis, and his provincial advocate for all Alsace, and in that service he accomplished much. On weighty business he was sent by the Emperor into France, then into Provence to the pope, and later to the king of England, and then to the duke of Austria. Afterwards, seeing that the Emperor was sluggish and not much advanced by him, he transferred himself to Avignon and stayed there a long time. There, by Pope Clement VI, provision was made for him of the bishopric of Würzburg; but he did not obtain it, because of the power of the man from Hohenlohe, who had been elected unanimously by the whole chapter. After the death of the lord of Oettingen, who was the most famous physician in the world, Pope Clement VI provided the aforesaid lord Albert with the bishopric of Freising, which he holds powerfully and without hindrance. He was full of virtues, sociable, affable and generous, but less humble, because excessive humility breeds contempt.

units.la: Rudolfus secundogenitus fuit probus, virilis, sed crapulosus. Ex quo & domina sua de Nassowe, descendit vnus filius, qui sepultus est in collegio Ehingensi, iuxta Neccarum, quod pater ipsius construxit.
units.tr: Rudolf, the second-born, was upright and manly, but a glutton. From him and his lady of Nassau descended one son, who is buried in the college at Ehingen, beside the Neckar, which his father had built.

units.la: Hugo vero tertiogenitus, animosus, bellicosus, mitis, virtuosus, sociabilis & audax, non curans de futuris contingentibus, sed excessit in multiloquio, contra dogma Catonis:
units.tr: Hugo, the third-born, was spirited, warlike, mild, virtuous, sociable and bold, not worrying about future contingencies, but he went too far in talkativeness, against the saying of Cato:

units.la: Virtutem primam esse puta compescere linguam.
units.tr: Think that the first virtue is to restrain the tongue.

units.la: & Aristotelis: O quàm speciosum est & honestum in homine, abstinere à multiloquio? A quo & filia Ferretarum comitis, descendit filius.
units.tr: and of Aristotle: O how fine and honourable it is in a man to refrain from talkativeness! From him and the daughter of the count of Ferrette descended a son.

units.la: Henricus vero quartogenitus, animosus, bellicosus & prodigalissimus ergà seruitores suos, ita quòd omnes munitiones & villas eis distribuit, exceptis paucis villis & vna munitione optima super Danubio quà tenuit, scilicet Fridingen vel Newen Hohenberg. Qui dominus Henricus occisus fuit, & cum eo optima iudicia Sueuiæ, in episcopatu Curiensi, per dominos de Bellmont & adiutores eorum, in montanis. Qui sepultus fuit honorificè in claustro quod dicitur Salmansweiler, anno Domini, M. CCC. LII.
units.tr: Henry, the fourth-born, was spirited, warlike, and extremely lavish towards his servants, so that he distributed to them all his fortresses and estates, except a few villages and one excellent fortress on the Danube which he kept, namely Fridingen or Neu-Hohenberg. This lord Henry was killed, and with him the best judgements of Swabia, in the bishopric of Chur, by the lords of Belmont and their helpers, in the mountains. He was honourably buried in the monastery called Salmansweiler, in the year of the Lord 1352.

units.la: Quedam fabula de quodam notario Alberti comitis de Hohenberg.
units.tr: A certain tale about a notary of Count Albert of Hohenberg.

units.la: FVIT quidam notarius domini Alberti comitis de Hohenberg, qui dicebatur Cappadocier, sociabilis, curiosus & subtilis, non curans pecuniam, qui fuit rector cuiusdam ecclesiæ in Schera, nomine Tieringen. Rex verò Rudolfus libentissimè confabulabatur cum eo, in cuius curia frequenter morabatur propter dominum suum, cuius sororem rex habuit in vxorem. Quadam vice rex indixit curiam principibus in Franckfurt, Cappadocier veniens à longè, & vadens ad Cancellariam, inuenit mensam paratam, & Cancellarium & notarios splendidè prædentes. Sedit verò & ipse ad mensam, & pauca cibaria dabantur sibi, licet magnam haberet famem: & superiùs in mensa erant magnæ scutellæ, impletæ optimis cibariis. Ipse verò vocauit vnum de seruis suis, & dixit ad eum: Redeas ad modicum tempus, & voca me festinanter, & dicas quòd dominus meus miserit pro me. Ille verò interim circumuoluit secretè mensale, & fine rotæ calcaris sui fortiter firmauit. Seruus verò intrauit, & festinanter vocauit dominum suum. Ille surgens festinanter & mensale cum omnibus ferculis & scyphis traxit in terram, & exiuit ad dominum suum. Rex verò percipiens, quæsiuit ab eo dicens: Quid modò fecisti? Ille respondit: Dum veni ad mensam Cancellarij & notarij vestri, habuerunt fercula diuersa, & dabatur mihi quod sanæ mentis & corpore infirmus bene comedissem: tunc egi quòd ipsos mecum oportuit ieiunare. Rex verò ridens, respondit: optimè fecisti. Ille verò postea gratulanter & honorificè tractatus fuit à Cancellario & omnibus notariis regis.
units.tr: There was a notary of Lord Albert, Count of Hohenberg, called Cappadocier, a sociable, inquisitive and clever man who did not care about money. He was rector of a church in the Schera, named Tieringen. King Rudolf liked to chat with him very much, and he often stayed at the king's court on account of his lord, whose sister the king had taken as his wife. On one occasion the king summoned a diet of the princes at Frankfurt. Cappadocier came from far off and, on his way to the chancery, found a table laid, with the chancellor and the notaries dining splendidly. He too sat down at the table, but only a few dishes were given to him, although he was very hungry. Higher up the table there were large platters filled with the finest food. He called one of his servants and said to him: "Go back for a short time, and come to me quickly and say that my lord has sent for me." Meanwhile the servant secretly wrapped the tablecloth around the wheel of his master's spur and fastened it firmly. The servant then came in and quickly called his lord. Cappadocier got up at once, dragged the tablecloth with all the dishes and cups to the ground, and went out to his lord. The king, seeing this, asked him: "What have you just done?" He replied: "When I came to the table of your chancellor and notaries, they had various dishes, and I was given what might have been enough for a healthy man to eat well; so I made them all go hungry with me." The king laughed and replied: "You did very well." Afterwards he was treated with great respect and honour by the chancellor and all the king's notaries.

units.la: Item, quæsitus fuit à rege, si haberet ecclesiam bonam. Ille respondit, fortem & bonam ecclesiam habere, & bonas campanas, sed quòd dominus suus nimis frequenter acciperet sibi fructus ecclesiæ. Quod rex audiens, promisit se acturum, quòd dominus permitteret fructus cum ecclesia.
units.tr: Likewise, the king asked him whether he had a good church. He replied that he had a strong and good church and good bells, but that his lord took the church's revenues far too often. When the king heard this, he promised that he would arrange for the lord to leave the revenues with the church.

units.la: Alia fabula de eodem.
units.tr: Another tale about the same man.

units.la: ITEM, Rex quadam die erat in Vlma, vbi oleum nucum erat in carissimo foro. Cappadocier dixit, dominum suum habere plures arbores nucū in comitatibus suis, quàm in tota Elsatia & tota Westaugia: idq; iurando affirmauit coram multis dominis,& aliis. Aliqui credebant eum mentiri,& dixerunt regi. Rex verò vocauit Cappadocier,& dixit: Quid dicis de arboribus nucum sororij mei? Respondit: Ego dico,& dixi per iuramentum dominum meum plures habere arbores nucum, quam in tota Elsatia & Westaugia sunt: sed sunt coryli, quæ sunt arbores nuces proferentes, si non magnas,tamen paruas. Rex ridens dixit: Sicut te dimitto, ita te inuenio. Multa talia fecit prædictus.
units.tr: Once, when the king was at Ulm, where walnut oil was very dear in the market, Cappadocier said that his lord had more walnut trees in his counties than there were in all of Alsace and all of Westaugia; and he affirmed this on oath before many lords and others. Some believed he was lying and told the king. The king then summoned Cappadocier and said: "What do you say about the walnut trees of my brother-in-law?" He replied: "I say, and have sworn, that my lord has more walnut trees than there are in all of Alsace and Westaugia. But there are hazels, which bear nuts; if not large trees, still small ones." The king laughed and said: "As I let you go, so I find you." The aforesaid man did many such things.

units.la: Alia fabula de quodam milite, qui dicebatur Iacobus Müller de Thurego.
units.tr: Another tale about a knight called Jacob Müller of Zurich.

units.la: RVDOLFVS comes de Habspurg fuit inimicus capitalis Iacobi dicti Müller, militis Turicensis, antequam fuit electus in regem. Cui quadam vice obuians, cum nullo modo posset effugere manus comitis, sapiens fuit, & festinanter descendit equum,& proiecit gladium suum in terram,& extraxit braccam,& sedit in viam quasi merdando. Comes verò & seruitores sui venerunt, vehementer exeuaginando gladios suos, volentes eum occidere. Ille verò extensis manibus clamauit comiti: Non decet dominationi & honestati vestræ occidere merdantem: detis mihi pacem quousque attraham braccam. Comes respondit: Sit ita. Ille verò dixit: Tunc bracca mea nunquam plus veniet ad culum meum. Comes verò hoc audiens, furore repletus, recessit ab eo,& idem postea factus est seruitor eius specialis.
units.tr: Count Rudolf of Habsburg was the mortal enemy of Jacob, called Müller, a knight of Zurich, before he was elected king. Once, when Jacob met him and could in no way escape the count's grasp, he acted wisely: he quickly got off his horse, threw his sword on the ground, pulled down his breeches and sat down in the road as if he were defecating. The count and his servants came up, drawing their swords and wanting to kill him. He, with his hands outstretched, cried to the count: "It is not fitting for your lordship and honour to kill a man at his stool. Give me peace until I pull up my breeches." The count replied: "So be it." Then he said: "Then my breeches will never again come up to my backside." When the count heard this he was filled with rage and withdrew from him; and afterwards that same man became his special servant.

units.la: De morte & sepultura Henrici, dicti Frauwenlob, magni dictatoris.
units.tr: On the death and burial of Henry, called Frauenlob, the great poet.

units.la: ANNO domini M.CCC.XVII, in vigilia sancti Andreæ, sepultus est Henricus dictus Frauwenlob in Maguntia, in ambitu maioris ecclesiæ, iuxta scalas honorificè valde: qui deportatus fuit à mulieribus ab hospitio vsq; ad locum sepulturæ, & lamentationes & querelæ maximæ auditæ fuerunt ab eis, propter laudes infinitas, quas imposuit omni generi fœminco in dictaminibus suis. Tanta etiam ibi copia fuit vini fusa in sepulchrum suum, quòd circumfluebat per totum ambitum ecclesiæ. Cantica canticorum dictauit Teutonicè, quæ vulgariter dicuntur Vnser Frawen Lied/ & multa alia bona.
units.tr: In the year of the Lord 1317, on the eve of St Andrew's day, Henry called Frauenlob was buried with great honour at Mainz, in the precinct of the greater church, near the steps. He was carried by women from the inn to the place of burial, and very great lamentations and complaints were heard from them, on account of the endless praises which he had bestowed on every kind of woman in his poems. There was also such a quantity of wine poured over his tomb that it flowed all round the precinct of the church. He composed in German the Song of Songs, which is commonly called "Unser Frawen Lied", and many other good things.

units.la: Rex quadam vice transiens pontem Turegi, cùm vidisset stantem quendam senem sanguineum, cum canorum multitudine pilorum, dixit ad quendam confabulantem sibi: O quot bonos dies in vita sua peregisse potuit ille canus? Quod audiens ille, dixit suauiter: Domine, fallimini, quia nunquam habui bonum diem. Quod quasi audiens rex, quæsiuit ab illo, quid factum fuisset ab eo? Respondit & dixit: Se egentem in iuuentute vetulam, deformem mulierem ratione pecuniæ & diuitiarum recepisse vxorem, cum qua diu viuente iracunda, ipsumq; præ timore aliarum mulierum corrodétem, dixit, se sic vitam miserabilem peregisse. Qua, ipso iam sene facto, defuncta, illico aliam iuniorem recepi, nec illi in lecto complacere possum, vitam cum ea rixosam & duriorem peregi. De quo rex in risum est prouocatus.
units.tr: Once, when the king was crossing the bridge at Zurich, he saw an old man standing there, ruddy-faced, with a great many white hairs. He said to someone talking with him: "Oh, how many good days could that grey-haired man have spent in his life!" Hearing this, the man said pleasantly: "Sire, you are mistaken, for I have never had a good day." The king, as if he had heard something of interest, asked him what had happened to him. He replied and said that, being poor in his youth, he had taken as his wife, for the sake of money and riches, an old, ugly woman; and while she lived she was ill-tempered, and, gnawing at him out of fear of other women, she made him spend his life wretchedly, as he said. When she died, now that he himself was old, he at once took another, younger wife, but he could not please her in bed, and he had lived a quarrelsome and harder life with her. At this the king was moved to laughter.

units.la: Dicitur autem, quòd cùm diues quidam mercator, sagacior præ omnibus in mercatura, semper gerens negotia sua verisimiliter pro vtiliori, continuè defecisset: quadam vice eum rogauit rex, quærens, si vellet recipere eum pro socio mercaturæ, & consilium suum sequi. Quo annuente, quilibet eorum posuit centum marcas. Dixit autem rex: Volo omnino, quòd Argentinæ emptas haleces traducas Coloniam, & ibi vina empta reducas Argentinam. Cui cōsilio ille socius, quamuis nimis & merito territus, acquieuit. Erat autem eo tempore Argentinæ tanta multitudo halecum, quòd quasi pro nihilo vendebantur: & cùm venisset Coloniam, accidit quoddam periculum in lacu, vbi haleces piscantur, quòd non erat spes illo anno de halecibus capiendis, ita q; mercator valde in halecibus lucrabatur. Accidit autem quòd tanta multitudo vini descenderat per Rhenum ad partes inferiores, quòd vina leuiori foro & precio vendebantur Coloniæ, quàm in Alsatia. Vina itaq; tunc super curribus Argentinâ ducens (cùm interim vineæ repentina geliditate perirent) illa pretio vendidit triplicato: ita quòd rex & ipse maximè sunt lucrati. Dixit ergo rex: Oportet quandoq; contraria, non semper lucri verisimilia inchoare.
units.tr: It is said that a certain rich merchant, the shrewdest of all in trade, who always conducted his business on what seemed the more profitable course, kept suffering losses. Once the king, enquiring, asked him whether he would take him as a partner in trade and follow his advice. When the merchant agreed, each of them put in a hundred marks. The king said: "I want you, without fail, to carry herrings bought at Strasbourg to Cologne, and there to bring back wine bought there to Strasbourg." The merchant, though greatly and rightly alarmed, agreed to this plan. At that time there was such a glut of herrings at Strasbourg that they were sold for next to nothing. When he arrived at Cologne, a misfortune befell the lake where herrings are fished, so that there was no hope of catching herrings that year, and the merchant made a great profit on his herrings. It also happened that so much wine had come down the Rhine to the lower regions that wine was sold at Cologne for less money and in a smaller measure than in Alsace. So the king's partner, carrying the wine from Cologne on carts to Strasbourg (while meanwhile the vineyards were ruined by a sudden frost), sold it at three times the price; and so both the king and he himself made a great profit. Then the king said: "One must sometimes begin with what is contrary, not always with what seems likely to bring profit."

units.la: Venit autem quadam vice quidam mercator clam ad regem in Nürenberg, indicans regi, quòd hospiti ibidem noto & famoso commiserit ducentas marcas argenti ad conseruandum, quas hospes se recepisse negabat. Rex autem scisicitans, in quali sacco esset argentum mercatorem abscondit. Venientibus autem ciuibus, & inter illos hospite ad alloquendum regem, rex alloquens iocosè hospitem sibi notum, videns eum pulchram valde habere mitram in capite, sicut tùc moris erat: dixit rex, se oportere mitram eandem habere: & ipsam extraxit de capite illius. De quo hospes ridens, gaudebat. Propositio autem sermone ciuium, rex pro consilio intrauit cameram, & clam quendam de ciuitate cum mitra pro interfignio misit ad vxorem hospitis, quòd ipsa hospiti talé saccum cum argento illico destinaret. Quod cum illa fecisset, nuncius illeregi præsentauit argentum. Quo ostenso mercatori, & illo dicente suum esse: rex abscondo argento, & vocato ad se hospite solo, ei querelam exposuit mercatoris. Quo negante præcisè, mercatore verò asserente instanter: rex producto sacco hospitem nimis territum de fraude conuicit. Redditoq; mercatori argento, hospitem prædiuitem in substantia bonorum multauit.
units.tr: Once a merchant came secretly to the king at Nuremberg, informing him that he had entrusted two hundred marks of silver for safekeeping to a well-known and notorious innkeeper there, but the innkeeper denied receiving it. The king, enquiring in what kind of sack the silver was, hid the merchant. When the citizens came, and among them the innkeeper to speak to the king, the king, addressing the innkeeper jokingly as someone he knew, saw that he wore a very fine cap on his head, as was then the custom, and said that he must have the same cap; and he took it off his head. The innkeeper laughed at this and was pleased. But after the citizens had spoken, the king went into his chamber as if to consult, and secretly sent a certain man from the city with the cap as a sign to the innkeeper's wife, telling her to send such a sack with the silver to her husband at once. When she had done so, the king's messenger presented the silver to him. The silver having been shown to the merchant, who said it was his, the king hid the silver, and, calling the innkeeper to him alone, laid the merchant's complaint before him. When he flatly denied it, while the merchant insisted strongly, the king produced the sack and convicted the innkeeper, who was greatly frightened, of fraud. The silver was returned to the merchant, and the innkeeper, who had been very rich in property, was fined heavily.

units.la: Rex quadà vice à Henrico marchione de Hochberg, qui parcè dicebatur vesci, quid comederet, requisiuit. Quo respondente, quòd & ipse & sui comederent vnum pulmentum cum carnibus, & ipse & vxor eius vnum caponem, & qui plus habere vellet, acciperet alibi: rex respondit, Verè non malè comedis, si sic facis.
units.tr: Once the king asked Henry, margrave of Hochberg, who was said to eat sparingly, what he ate. He replied that he and his household ate one stew with meat, and that he and his wife ate one capon, and whoever wanted more could get it elsewhere. The king answered: "Truly, you do not eat badly, if you live like that."

units.la: Deficiente tandem rege præsenio, & dicentibus sibi Medicis, quòd vltra certos dies durare nequiret, ipse dixit: Eamus Spiram ad alios reges inibi in maiori ecclesia sepultos. Et manés in oppido Germersheim iuxta Spirã, ibiq; moriens Spiram ductus, & in sepulchro regali honorificè est sepultus: anno regni eius XVIII, cuius epitaphium in silice superposito sculptum, tale est.
units.tr: When the king was at last failing with fever, and the physicians told him that he could not last beyond a few days, he said: "Let us go to Speyer, to the other kings buried there in the great church." He stayed in the town of Germersheim, near Speyer, and dying there was taken to Speyer and honourably buried in the royal tomb in the eighteenth year of his reign. His epitaph, carved on a stone laid over the tomb, reads as follows.

units.la: Anno Domini, M.CC.LXCI, pridie calend. Octobris, Obiit Rudolfus de Habspurg, Romanorum rex.
units.tr: In the year of the Lord 1291, the day before the Kalends of October, Rudolf of Habsburg, king of the Romans, died.

units.la: Mortuo itaq; Rudolfo, & veniente Alberto duce Austriæ filio eius (pro quo eligendo principes Electores miserant) cum magnis expensis usque Hagenow: Adolfus comes de Nassauwe in regem Romanorum à principibus Alemanniæ concorditer est electus: à quo idem Albertus de feodis suis, præsertim ducatu Austriæ, investitus, in Austriam est reuersus. A quo duce cum postea missis legatis rex peteret, filio suo ducis filiam copulari: dux respondit: Se, si posset ex filia sua facere principem, hoc facturum. Vel, quòd rex filiam suam vni ex filiis ducis coniungeret, quem se principem facturum promitteret. Ex quibus & aliis inter regem & ducem odium est subortum. Rex autem Metzam filiam suam Rudolfo duci Bauariæ Palatino in vxorem copulauit, qui ex ea genuit tres filios: Adolfum, Rudolfum, & Rupertum. Intoxicatus autem dux Albertus in Austria, & diu per pedes suspensus, oculum perdens cuasit.
units.tr: After Rudolf's death, Duke Albert of Austria, his son (for whose election the electors had sent envoys), came at great expense as far as Hagenau. Adolf, count of Nassau, was unanimously elected king of the Romans by the princes of Germany. From him Albert received investiture of his fiefs, especially the duchy of Austria, and returned to Austria. Later the king sent envoys asking the duke to join his son in marriage to the duke's daughter. The duke replied that if he could make his daughter a princess, he would do so; or else the king should join his own daughter to one of the duke's sons, whom the duke promised to make a prince. From these and other causes hatred arose between the king and the duke. The king, however, gave his daughter in marriage at Metz to Rudolf, Palatine duke of Bavaria, who by her had three sons: Adolf, Rudolf and Rupert. Duke Albert, poisoned in Austria and long hung up by the feet, lost an eye and died.

units.la: Iisdem temporibus Bonifacius papa octauus Columnenses persequebatur ad vn- guè, Cardinalibus de Columna depositis, aliisq; plurimùm molestatis. Fouens autem rex Franciæ Columnenses, papam persequebatur odio capitali: propterea quòd papa in odium Fráci regem diligebat Adolfum. Rex autem Angliæ propter antiquam dominiorum guerram, cupiens aggredi Francum, centum millia marcarum argéti pro auxilio sibi promisso, sed nõ præstito, Adolfo principi destinauit: qui rex Rom. infideliter agens, se non disposuit ad bellum, sed à marchione Missenesi, nepote olim Friderici Imp. ex filia, odio habente filium suum, eúdem Marchionatum emit, & tempore breui possedit, exceptis quibusdam munitionibus: quia filius Marchionis, Fridericus nomine, eiecto principe, occupauit eundem. Princeps autem Misniam potenter ingressus, crudelia multa peregit. Vnum enim castrum vincens, c l, qui domino suo castrum manu tenuerant, decollauit.
units.tr: At the same time Pope Boniface VIII pursued the Colonna family relentlessly, deposing the Colonna cardinals and harassing many others. The king of France, favouring the Colonna, pursued the pope with deadly hatred, while the pope favoured Adolf out of hatred for the French. The king of England, wishing to attack the Frenchman because of their old quarrel over their domains, sent Prince Adolf 100,000 marks of silver as the aid he had promised, but never delivered. Adolf, the king of the Romans, acting faithlessly, did not prepare for war. Instead he bought the margraviate of Meissen from the margrave, a nephew through a daughter of the late Emperor Frederick, who hated his own son, and for a short time he possessed it, except for certain fortresses, because the margrave's son, Frederick by name, had expelled the prince and seized the same territory. The prince entered Meissen with force and committed many cruelties. For, capturing one castle, he beheaded 150 men who had held the castle against their lord.

units.la: Cuono autem de Berghem miles, præses principis in Alsatia elatus, infestans C. de Liechtenberg episcopum & etiam ciues Argent. cótra eos principe incitauit. Illi aùt oppidũ Cunonis Germersheim, destruxerút, & post obitũ regis idem eps castrũ Crap Cunoni destruens, lapides quadros ad constructionem oppidi Liechtenaw traduxit.
units.tr: Cuno of Bergheim, a knight and president of the prince in Alsace, grew arrogant. Attacking Conrad of Lichtenberg, the bishop, and also the citizens of Strasbourg, he incited the prince against them. They destroyed Cuno's town of Germersheim, and after the king's death the same bishop destroyed Cuno's castle of Crapp and carried its square stones to build the town of Liechtenau.

units.la: Princeps autem Columbariam, quæ sibi fidelitatem fecerat, rebellatem, obsedit: cui inter alios aderant episcopus Basil & comes Ferretarum. Multi autem baronum, scilicet de Liechtenberg & Rapoltstein,& alij episcopi Argentinensis consanguinei, in oppido existentes, cum per quosdam plebeios porta de nocte aperiretur principi, effugerunt,& fugientium multi sunt comprehensi, inter quos Anshelmus de Rapoltz‐stein vix decollationem euasit. Captum etiam Waltherum scultetum Columbariae, & Ioannem filium eius per episcopū Basilien‐sem,rex omnino eos habere volens, sed eis propter officium episcopi vitam reseruans,patrem omni die longo tempore fecit ligari super rotam erecta manu,in signum perfidię,& per vias & ciuitates ante se duci, & tandem in turri seruari: vbi patre extincto,filius post mortem regis est liberatus.
units.tr: The prince besieged Colmar, which had sworn fealty to him and then rebelled. Among others, the bishop of Basel and the count of Pfirt were present. Many barons, namely of Lichtenberg and Rappoltstein, and other kinsmen of the bishop of Strasbourg, were in the town. When some commoners opened the gate to the prince at night, they fled, and many of the fugitives were captured; among them Anselm of Rappoltstein barely escaped beheading. The bailiff of Colmar, Walter, and his son John were also captured by the bishop of Basel. The king, wishing to have them wholly in his power but sparing them out of regard for the bishop's office, had the father bound to a wheel, one arm raised, every day for a long time, as a sign of treachery, and led him before himself through roads and cities; finally he was kept in a tower. There the father died, and the son was freed after the king's death.

units.la: Intenderat autem princeps facere brigam duci Austriae:propter quod multi Australium superbiebant contra ducem.Dixerat enim dux:Si dominus meus Romanorum rex stipendiarius est Anglici factus, & ego minore dedecore stipendiarius ero Franci. Plures autem electorum principum & specialiter Gerhardus Moguntinus, principem ipsis aestimantem ingratum,duci, quod venire ad Rhenum,nuntios & literas destinârūt. Dux autem timens se à rege in Austria visitari, allata secum pecunia, partes Rheni & Sueuiae est ingressus: malens in partibus consanguineorum suorum potius regi litem inferre,quàm in Austria visitari. Rex autem ascendens, Cunradū de Liechtenberg episcopū Argent.duci fauentē,in Rubiaco oppido diu potėter obsedit.
units.tr: The prince had intended to make war on the duke of Austria, and because of this many Austrians were proud and rose against the duke. For the duke had said: "If my lord, the king of the Romans, has become a mercenary of England, I shall with less disgrace become a mercenary of France." Several of the electoral princes, and especially Gerhard of Mainz, who considered the prince ungrateful, sent messengers and letters to the duke, urging him to come to the Rhine. The duke, fearing that the king would visit him in Austria, took the money he had with him and entered the regions of the Rhine and Swabia, preferring to wage war against the king among his kinsmen rather than be visited in Austria. The king, marching up, besieged for a long time the town of Rubiacum, where Conrad of Lichtenberg, bishop of Strasbourg, was holding out in the duke's favour.

units.la: Fuerant autem quatuor duces Bauariae fratrueles, Rudolfus & Ludouicus fratres,superioris:Stephanus & Otto inferioris Bauariae duces. Veniente autem Ottone in auxilium regis, Albertus strenuissimus comes de Hohenberg in Sueuia ei obstaculum ponens,ab eo est in conflictu occisus.
units.tr: There were four dukes of Bavaria, cousins: Rudolf and Louis, brothers, dukes of Upper Bavaria; and Stephen and Otto, dukes of Lower Bavaria. When Otto came to the king's aid, Albert, the most valiant count of Hohenberg, opposed him in Swabia and was killed by him in battle.

units.la: Cum dux Austriae veniens de Sueuia cum exercitu,iuxta oppidum Kentzingen castrametaret,rex in Rubiaco eundem locum accessit. Cumq; propter flumen Elrză exercitus se mutuò inuadere non possent,oppidumq; regi aperiretur:dux cum hostili exercitu Sueuorum & Rhenensium equitum descendens,Moguntiam venit, ibiq; à quibusdam principibus quasi congregatis,regemq; tanquam inutilem Reipublicae & imperij destructorem destituentibus,in Romanorum regem est electus. Cumque regi Adolfo post eum descendenti, adesse nimiam multitudinem populi assistentis sentiret;se doluit descendisse,& ascendens iuxta montem Dornsperg, prope Wormatiam,expectauit.Rex autem feruens,metuensq; Australem autugere, non expectato peditum exercitu suo,cum equitibus suis celeriter sequebatur. Argutus autē à suis, dicentibus,aciem equitum esse minus fortem,noluit assentire. Aspiciens autem exercitum ducis,quem credidit non masurum,dixit:Verum dixistis, nostrum exercitum nimis breuem esse. Illis verò dicentibus,modò neglectum esse, inierunt conflictum. Erat enim rex animosus valde. Australes autem habito consilio,exercitum suum declinauerant,vt acies regis obuium haberet solem. Ipsisq; aggredientibus,multisq; hinc inde occisis & praecalore extinctis,inter quos Otto dominus de Ochsenstein vexilliifer Alberti,& Ludouicus Monachi,pater valentis Petri custodis Lutenbacensis, cum aliis,caloribus sunt extincti.Rex ipsum Albertum aggrediens dixit:Non euadetis,sed hic imperium dimittetis. Ille verò dicens,hoc est in potestate Dei, regē iuxta oculum vulnerauit gladio.Prostratus autem rex in terram per comites syluestres & alios quos laeserat,per quendam armigerum descendentem de equo leuata regi galea,modico in collo vulnere est occisus.Quod videns dux,nullum amplius occidi,sed capi praecepit.Sicq; Adolfus,cū octo annis regnasset,nolens expectare suos,stultitiae furia est occisus,& in monasterio Frowenfeld, ad quod praesente Alberto venerunt, est sepultus. De quo scripti sunt versus. Anno milleno,trecentis bis minus annis In Iulii mense rex Adolfus ruit ense Per manus Austrani, Procesi & Martiniani.
units.tr: When the duke of Austria came from Swabia with an army and encamped near the town of Kentzingen, the king came to the same place at Rubiacum. Since the armies could not attack each other because of the river Elz, and the town was opened to the king, the duke came down with a hostile army of Swabian and Rhenish horsemen and went to Mainz. There, with some princes gathered as it were, and with them deposing the king as useless to the commonwealth and a destroyer of the empire, he was elected king of the Romans. When Adolf, coming down after him, perceived that a huge multitude of people was supporting the duke, he regretted having descended. Going up beside the mountain Dornsperg, near Worms, he waited. The king, hot-headed and fearing that the Austrian would flee, did not wait for his infantry but pursued quickly with his horsemen. Argutus, however, told him that the line of horsemen was too weak, but he would not agree. When he saw the duke's army, which he thought would not hold, he said: "You were right, our army is far too small." When they replied that it was now too late, since the matter had been neglected, they joined battle. The king was very spirited. The Austrians, having taken counsel, had shifted their army so that the king's line had the sun in its face. As they attacked, many were killed on both sides and some were struck down by the heat. Among them were Otto, lord of Ochsenstein, Albert's standard-bearer, and Louis of Monchen, father of the valiant Peter, keeper of Lutenbach, who died from the heat along with others. The king, attacking Albert himself, said: "You will not escape; here you will give up the empire." Albert replied: "This is in God's power," and wounded the king near the eye with his sword. The king was thrown to the ground by the forest counts and others he had injured. A squire dismounted and, lifting the king's helmet, killed him with a slight wound in the neck. Seeing this, the duke ordered that no one else be killed but that they be taken alive. Thus Adolf, having reigned eight years and unwilling to wait for his men, was killed by the fury of folly, and was buried in the monastery of Frauenfeld, to which they came in Albert's presence. Verses were written about him: "In the year thirteen hundred less two, in the month of July, King Adolf fell by the sword, by the hands of the Austrian, Procesus and Martinian."

units.la: Victo autem regis exercitu,cùm rex per garciones spoliatus, omnino nudus iaceret, Moguntinus scilicet Gerhardus de Eppenstein occisi consanguineus, & machinator facti,videns regem,fleuit,dicens:cor validissimum periisse. Dux autem timens eundem G.Moguntinum variare promissa sua,dixit ei: A me non recedetis,meo negotio non perfecto.
