units.tr: After the king's army was defeated, the king lay on the ground, stripped by his attendants and entirely naked. Gerhard of Eppenstein, archbishop of Mainz, a kinsman of the slain man and the author of the deed, saw the king and wept, saying: "A most mighty heart has perished." The duke, fearing that Gerhard of Mainz would fail to keep his promises, said to him: "You shall not leave me until my business is finished."

units.la: Occiso itaq; Adolfo, Albertus dux Austriae occisor, ab omnibus principibus est electus, & Aquisgrani solenniter est coronatus. Quem papa Bonifacius diu odio prosequens, & laesae maiestatis crimine reum dicens, tandem similiter in odiu regis Franciae approbauit. Quem Albertum cum papa contra regem Fraciae instigare vellet, ille se hoc non facturum, nisi sibi & haeredibus suis regnum & imperium confirmaretur per sedem, respondit. Quod si hoc sibi fieret, aut se Francum expulsurũ de regno, aut se per hoc moriturum, promisit. Noluit enim in haeredum destructionem se tanto periculo exponere, pro incerto. De quo cum multum tractaretur per Sedem, tandem in contrarium resedit consilium. Recesserunt enim, quantum a tempore promotionis Rudolphi regis patris sui illa fuerit progenies exaltata: in seruitute redigi se timentes. Dixit ei papa: Non fiet viuente ista Iesabel: denotans Elizabet reginam, quae ex matre soror extitit Chunradini.
units.tr: Adolf having thus been killed, Albert, duke of Austria, his slayer, was elected by all the princes and solemnly crowned at Aachen. Pope Boniface, who had long pursued him with hatred, calling him guilty of treason against the majesty of the empire, at last likewise approved of him out of hatred for the king of France. When the pope wanted to incite Albert against the king of France, Albert replied that he would not do it unless the kingdom and empire were confirmed to him and his heirs by the Holy See. He promised that if this were done for him, he would either drive the Frenchman from the kingdom or die in the attempt. For he did not want to expose himself and his heirs to such danger for an uncertain prize. When this was much debated at the See, at last the opposite counsel prevailed. For they drew back, fearing that a family so exalted since the rise of Rudolf, his father, would be reduced to servitude. The pope said to him: "It shall not happen while this Jezebel lives," referring to Queen Elizabeth, who was the sister of Conradin on her mother's side.

units.la: Hic Bonifacius alludens suo tempori, centesimum annum statuit Iubileum, quod ante eum nunc aliquis attentauit: in quo, sc. millesimo trecentesimo, Roma multitudo maxima Christicolarum confluebat. Hunc Bonifacium Colunenses de auxilio Franci Anagniae captiuârunt, qui tetus, necdũ illos absoluere voluit: imò amplius maledixit, & prae ira manus corrodes, tandè liberatur per Rom. Egredien de Anagnia, coeuersus ad eã dixit: Si nõ meminero tui, obliuioni detur dextera mea. Verũ breuiter expirauit.
units.tr: Bonifacius, adapting himself to his own times, appointed a jubilee every hundredth year, a practice someone had attempted before him. In the year 1300 a very great multitude of Christians flocked to Rome for it. The Colonnesi, with the help of the Frenchman, captured this Boniface at Anagni. He raged, gnawing his hands in anger, and did not want to absolve them; he cursed them even more. Finally he was freed by the Romans. As he went out of Anagni, he turned to the town and said: "If I do not remember you, may my right hand be forgotten." But he soon breathed his last.

units.la: Hic est Bonifacius, de quo dicitur, q. Caelestino praedecessori suo, viro vtiq; sancto, de quo Curia doluit se in lucris non proficere, per longam cannam loquebatur ad lectum, Caelestine cede, Caelestine cede: quo etiam cedente, & Bonifacio tanquam certissimo creato, tamen populus adhuc Caelestinū venerabatur vt papa. Bonifacius hoc sub excommunicationis poena prohibens, constitutione edidit, quo papam posse renunciare papatui declarauit: quia multi asserentes contrariu, eum papam negabant. Hic condidit sextum Decretalium, in quo claritate & venustate dictionis omnes qui vnquam in iure scripserant, antecessit. Edidit etiam constitutionem Super cathedram, grauem Minoribus & Praedicatoribus. Quo mortuo, Benedictus XI successor, qui fuit Praedicator, fecit constitutionem, Inter cunctas, per quam reuocauit aliam. Quo etiam sub papa Alberto rege mortuo, creatus est Clemens V Vasco, qui constitutionem Super cathedram renouauit. Ex tunc curia fuit a Roma translata: primò enim fuit in Burdegali, postea super Rhodanum. hic concurrit cum Heinrico Imperatore.
units.tr: This is the Boniface of whom it is said that he spoke to his predecessor Celestine, a man certainly holy, at whose resignation the Curia grieved because it gained nothing from it, through a long cane, toward the bed: "Celestine, give way, Celestine, give way." Even after Celestine had given way, and Boniface had been installed as one most certainly pope, the people still venerated Celestine as pope. Boniface, forbidding this under penalty of excommunication, issued a constitution by which he declared that a pope could resign the papacy, because many, asserting the contrary, denied that he was pope. He also compiled the Sixth Book of the Decretals, in which he surpassed in clarity and elegance of expression all who had ever written on law. He also issued the constitution Super cathedram, a burden on the Minorites and the Preachers. When he died, his successor Benedict XI, who had been a Preacher, made the constitution Inter cunctas, by which he revoked the other. Also, when Pope Albert the king had died, Clement V of Gascony was created, and he renewed the constitution Super cathedram. From then on the Curia was moved from Rome: first indeed to Bordeaux, and afterwards to the Rhône. Here he came into conflict with the Emperor Henry.

units.la: Iste Albertus rex monoculus, potens in regno Alemanniae, & inibi filiis suis omnia quae potuit attrahens, partes alias non curauit. Habuit n. sex filios: Rudolfum primogenitum, qui cum relicta, secunda scilicet vxore Wenceslai regis Bohemiae (filio eiusdem regis mortuo) contrahes, & rex Bohemiae effectus, sine liberis est defunctus. Fuit aut eadem relicta de Polonia: prior. n. vxor soror fuit Alberti regis. Item habuit Fridericum, elegantem, formosum & fortè: Leopoldum bellicosum & prudentè, Henricū, Albertū & Ottonè. Vnam filiarum suarum Andreae regi Vngariae copulauit: cuius Andreae pater olim de regno Vngariae eiectus, Venetiis filiā ditissimi ciuis ducens, ex ea hunc Andreā genuit. Qui veniēs ad curiā huius Alberti adhuc ducis Austriae, & recepstus in rege Vngariae, petiit Alberti filiam. Quod cum dux renueret, dicens, eū mercatoris filium: ipse Vngarus Viennam in omni parte obsedit, & ad dandū sibi filiā ducem coegit, dans filiae Presburg & multas alias munitiones iure morganitico: cuius fratres postea Henrico & Friderico ducibus Austriae, Carolus rex Vngariae ab ipsis Presburg extorsit. Quo Andrea sine liberis defuncto, relicta in loco occisionis patris, sc. Kōnigsfelden vitā coelibem diu duxit. Item aliam filiā nomine Elsam dedit duci Lotaringiae, quae ex eo ducem Rudolfum Lotaringiae procreauit. Tertiam filiā dedit Woldemaro marchioni Brandenburgensi: quo mortuo sine liberis, ipsam dedit duci in Presla Poloniae. Item relictam comitis de Strasberg, sororem Ottonis de Ochsenstein, consobrinam regis, ipse rex Albertus dedit Rudolfo marchioni de Baden. Item vnam filiarum eiusdem relictae Rudolfo iuniori de Baden, senioris filio, & aliam Walthero domino de Horburg matrimonio copulauit: quae filiae sine liberis obierunt.
units.tr: This King Albert, one-eyed, powerful in the kingdom of Germany, drew to his sons all that he could within it and did not care for other regions. For he had six sons: Rudolf the firstborn, who married the widow, that is, the second wife, of King Wenceslaus of Bohemia (the son of that same king, now dead), and became king of Bohemia, and died without children. This widow was from Poland, for his first wife was the sister of King Albert. He also had Frederick, elegant, handsome and brave; Leopold, warlike and prudent; Henry, Albert and Otto. He joined one of his daughters in marriage to Andrew, king of Hungary. Andrew's father, once expelled from the kingdom of Hungary, had taken in Venice the daughter of a very wealthy citizen and by her begot this Andrew. Andrew came to the court of this Albert, who was still duke of Austria, and was received by the king of Hungary, and sought Albert's daughter. When the duke refused, saying that he was a merchant's son, the Hungarian besieged Vienna on every side and forced the duke to give him his daughter, and he gave the daughter Pressburg and many other fortresses by Morganatic right. Afterwards Charles, king of Hungary, extorted Pressburg from Albert's sons, Henry and Frederick, dukes of Austria. When Andrew died without children, his widow, in the place where her father had been killed, namely Königsfelden, lived a long celibate life. He gave another daughter, named Elizabeth, to the duke of Lorraine, who by him begot Duke Rudolf of Lorraine. He gave a third daughter to Waldemar, margrave of Brandenburg; when he died without children, King Albert gave her to the duke in Pressburg of Poland. Also, King Albert himself gave the widow of the count of Strasberg, the sister of Otto of Ochsenstein, cousin of the king, to Rudolf, margrave of Baden. He also joined one of the daughters of that same widow in marriage to Rudolf the younger of Baden, son of the elder, and another to Walther, lord of Horburg. These daughters died without children.

units.la: Hic Albertus cum magna potentia descendens, comitatus Holandię & Selandiae, qui vacauerunt imperio, & quos comes de Henegowe occuparat, apprehendere volens, praemonitus à fratruele sua de Kiburg, vxore comitis de Cleuen, quòd omnes inferiores principes contra eum conuenerant: sic quod infecto negotio est reuersus. - Mortuo autem (vt præscribitur) Andrea rege Hungariæ, & Ottone duce inferioris Bauariæ recepto in regem, & postea per magnates regni capto, & commisso custodiæ comitis Transilvaniensis, & per vxorem eiusdem comitis absentis, consanguineam ipsius Ottonis liberato, & ad Prussiam, deinde Bauariā remisso: mortuoq; illis diebus Carolone rege Siciliæ, ac Carolone quarto filio regni hærede, per Robertū patruum suum regni occupatore exclusō, ac regno Hungariæ (vt prømittitur) vacante, eidemq; Caroloni quarto, filio sororis regis Alberti, ad instātiam Roberti, de regno Hungariæ per papam prouiso: Albertus rex eundem nepotem in regnum Hungariæ traducens, ipsum potentem effecit: quæ eius potētia postea pluries liberis Alberti regis in perniciem conuersa est. Ipse namq; Carolo strenuè se tenens, eiectis pluribus magnatibus 10 regni, potentissimus est effectus. Accepit autem filiam regis Cracouiæ, filiam sororis regis Lithuaniæ gentilis, in vxorem. Quæ vxor quadam vice, volente quodam ipsum regem interficere sedentem in mensa, per gladium: ipsa manibus suis protegens caput regis, tres digitos amisit. Ille autem malefactor per quendam repente fuit occisus.
units.tr: This Albert, descending with great power, wished to seize the counties of Holland and Zeeland, which had been vacant of the empire and which the count of Hainault had occupied. He was forewarned by his cousin of Kyburg, wife of the count of Cleves, that all the lesser princes had united against him, so he returned with the business undone. Now, when Andrew, king of Hungary, had died (as was said above), and Otto, duke of Lower Bavaria, had been received as king and afterwards seized by the magnates of the kingdom, and entrusted to the custody of the count of Transylvania, and freed by the wife of that same count, who was absent and a blood relative of Otto, and sent back to Prussia and then to Bavaria; and when, in those days, Charles, king of Sicily, died, and Charles the Fourth, heir of the kingdom, was excluded by Robert, his uncle, who seized the kingdom, and the kingdom of Hungary was vacant (as was said above), and it was provided to that same Charles the Fourth, son of King Albert's sister, from the kingdom of Hungary by the pope at the instance of Robert: King Albert brought his nephew into the kingdom of Hungary and made him powerful. His power afterwards was often turned to the ruin of King Albert's sons. For Charles, holding himself boldly, after several magnates of the kingdom had been expelled, became very powerful. He took as wife the daughter of the king of Cracow, the daughter of the sister of the pagan king of Lithuania. On one occasion, when a certain man wished to kill the king while he was sitting at table, with a sword, his wife, protecting the king's head with her hands, lost three fingers. That wicked man was suddenly killed by someone.

units.la: Alberto autem in regem electo, vixit adhuc relicta olim Rudolfi ducis Austriæ, fratris Alberti: qua morante tunc in Brugga, misit frater eius Wenceslaus rex Bohemiæ pro ea, volens eam copulare regi Hungariæ: quæ cum filio suo duce Iohanne veniens in Bohemiam, inibi est defuncta, anno MCCCI. Rex autem Albertus omnino volens rehabere Ioannem fratruelem suum, ipsum sibi remissum cū filiis suis, quousq; tandem ab ipso est occisus, enutriuit. 20
units.tr: When Albert had been elected king, the widow of the late Rudolf, duke of Austria, brother of Albert, was still alive. While she was staying then in Bruges, her brother Wenceslaus, king of Bohemia, sent for her, wishing to marry her to the king of Hungary. Coming into Bohemia with her son, Duke John, she died there in the year 1301. King Albert, wishing wholly to recover his cousin John, had him sent back to him with his sons, and reared him until at last he was killed by him.

units.la: Orta autem discordia inter Albertum regem & Wenceslaum Bohemum, super quibusdam terris: Albertus cum tribus millibus galeatorum de Sueuia & Rheno, & cum I millibus Hungarorum & aliorum, Bohemiam poteter ingressus, eam decem septimanis ignis incendio deuastauit, sed nullam munitionem euicit. Quo egresso, mortuoq; postea Wenceslao, & post eum filio suo, vix per annū in Bohemia regnante, in lecto fraudulenter occiso, dictoq; Rudolfo, filio Alberti, facto rege inibi, sine ple defuncto, ac Henrico duce Carinthiæ genero Wenceslai & auunculo Alberti, sibi Bohemiæ regnum ascribente, sed non possidente: iterū Albertus rex animo obtinendi idem regnum, Bohemiam cum potentia est ingressus. Sed Baronibus regni terram pro iuniore filia Wenceslai tenentibus, rex infecto negotio est reuersus: qui iterum 30 postea paratus ingredi Bohemiam, morte est præuentus.
units.tr: Then a quarrel arose between King Albert and Wenceslaus of Bohemia over certain lands. Albert, with three thousand men-at-arms from Swabia and the Rhine, and with a thousand Hungarians and others, entered Bohemia and laid it waste with fire for ten weeks, but took no fortress. When he left, Wenceslaus died, and after him his son, who reigned in Bohemia scarcely a year and was fraudulently murdered in bed. Rudolf, son of Albert, was made king there; he died without issue. Henry, duke of Carinthia, son-in-law of Wenceslaus and uncle of Albert, claimed the kingdom of Bohemia for himself but did not possess it. Again King Albert, intent on obtaining the same kingdom, entered Bohemia with his forces. But since the barons of the kingdom held the land on behalf of the younger daughter of Wenceslaus, the king returned with the business undone. Again, when he was afterwards preparing to enter Bohemia, he was forestalled by death.

units.la: Idem autem Albertus factus rex, tenensq; quasdam munitiones in Misena, quas & Adolphus tenuerat, misso exercitu & capitaneo in Missenam, animo capiendi Marchionatū, initoq; cōflictu, Fridericus Marchio victo regis exercitu, obtinuit terrā suā.
units.tr: This same Albert, having become king, and holding certain fortresses in Meissen which Adolf had also held, sent an army and a captain into Meissen, intending to seize the margraviate. A battle was joined; Margrave Frederick defeated the king's army and retained his land.

units.la: Anno etiam ipsius Alberti regis regni quarto orta est inuidia inter prædictū Gerlacum Maguntinum & nonnullos principes contra regem, ac Moguntino, Treuerēsi, Colonienși & Rodolfo Palatino, filio sororis regis coniurantibus contra regē: ipse rex cum robore descendens, primò Palatinum inuasit, Wissenloch & quædam alia destruendo eidem, postea Moguntinum infestans. Qui conuocato Colonienși ad quoddā castrum suum, cum eum iuxta conspirationem adiuuare non curauerit, ipsum voluit 40 captiuasse, si non per quosdam probos (asserentes, hoc dedecus esse, quòd in domo sua, postquam cibum suum comedisset, hoc faceret) fuisset auersus. Sicq; principibus non ausis sibi inuicem assistere, vel resistere regi, rex post multas oppressiones alias, oppidum Pinguiam obsedit & expugnauit, sed castrum non obtinuit, & terram Ringowe, Altewil, Gisenheim, Ostringen, Nudersheim, &c. per incēdium deuastauit: sed tandem multorum precibus deuictus, eundem Moguntinum sibi sufficienter cautem, ad gratiam reassumpsit.
units.tr: In the fourth year of King Albert's reign, envy arose between the aforesaid Gerlach of Mainz and some princes against the king. Mainz, Trier, Cologne and Rudolf the Palatine, son of the king's sister, conspired against the king. The king himself came down with his strength and first attacked the Palatine, destroying Weisenloch and certain other places, and afterwards harassed Mainz. Having summoned the Cologne prince to a certain castle of his, and finding that he would not help him according to the conspiracy, he wished to have seized him, but he was turned aside by certain upright men, who asserted that it would be a disgrace for him to do this in his own house after he had eaten his food. Thus, since the princes did not dare to support one another or to resist the king, the king, after many other oppressions, besieged and took the town of Bingen, but did not gain the castle, and laid waste the land of Rheingau, Altweil, Gissenheim, Ostringen, Nidderheim and others with fire. But at last, overcome by the entreaties of many, he received the same Mainz back into favour, as sufficiently secured for him.

units.la: Alberto rege facto, Ego comes de Friburg, habens sororem Chunradi de Liechtenberg, episcopi Argent. ad subiiciendum sibi Friburgenses conabatur. Et orta lite inter eos, rex aliquandiu in fauorem episcopi Friburgum obsedit. Ciues autem castrum 50 Friburgense machinis deturbārunt. Veniens autem episcopus ad deuastandum Friburgenses illisq; exeuntibus, inierunt conflictum: multisq; Friburgēsium occisis, quidam carnifex episcopum super dextrario in rubea Wambasia circumeuntem, & exercitum suum ad pugnandum incitantem, cuspide perforauit. Quo occiso, comes & sui per ciues postea continuè debilitati sunt & depressi. Post Cōradum, frater eius Fridericus dericus præpositus Argent. valentissimus in armis, in literatura nullus, ad amicorum instârias, quasi inuitus, in episcopum est promotus. Quo (postquam annis aliquot ecclesiam suam viriliter rexit) defuncto: rex Albertus Ioannem episcopum Eistetensem cancellarium suum, illegitimè natum, pro episcopatu Argent. obtinendo, Ioanni de Ochsenstein scholastico Argentinensi, consobrino regis, ad Romanam curiam destinauit. Papa autem nō Scholastico, sed eidem Cancellario de episcopatu Argent. prouidit. Quem rex tanquam suum manu tenuit, & vix à scholastici amicis defendit: episcopo multa pro illis faciente & magna donante. Hic Ioannes in structuris & emptionibus benefecit ecclesiæ, & postea filiis regis, præterquam in fine Bauaro, adhæsit.
units.tr: When Albert became king, Count Egino of Freiburg, whose sister was married to Conrad of Lichtenberg, bishop of Strasbourg, tried to bring the people of Freiburg under his power. A quarrel arose between them, and for some time the king besieged Freiburg in support of the bishop. The citizens, however, battered the castle of Freiburg with siege engines. The bishop came to lay waste the Freiburgers, and when they came out, they engaged in battle. Many Freiburgers were killed, but a certain executioner pierced the bishop with a spear as he rode about on a horse, wearing a red tunic, and urged his army to fight. After he was killed, the count and his men were continually weakened and humbled by the citizens. After Conrad, his brother Frederick, provost of Strasbourg, very strong in arms but without any learning, was reluctantly promoted to the bishopric at his friends' urging. When Frederick died after he had ruled his church bravely for some years, King Albert sent John, bishop of Eichstätt, his chancellor, who was born out of wedlock, to the Roman court to obtain the bishopric of Strasbourg, and he also sent John of Ochsenstein, scholastic of Strasbourg and the king's cousin. The Pope, however, provided the bishopric not to the scholastic but to the chancellor. The king held him as his own and scarcely defended him against the scholastic's friends, while the bishop did much for them and gave generously. This John did good service to the church in building and purchasing, and afterwards he attached himself to the king's sons, except at the end, when he joined the Bavarian.

units.la: 10 Rex quoq; in principio creationis suæ, cum Chunrado de Ochsenstein episcopo, Theobaldum comitem Ferretarum invasit, eius terram vastando. Qui comes, dando filiâ suam Ottoni de Ochsenstein, regi reformatur. Aliâ filiam dedit Vdalrico de Wirtenberg comiti: ex quibus duabus nūc dñi de Wirtenberg & Ochsenstein puenerunt.
units.tr: 10 At the beginning of his reign, the king also, together with Conrad of Ochsenstein, bishop, attacked Count Theobald of Pfirt, laying waste his land. This count, by giving his daughter to Otto of Ochsenstein, was reconciled to the king. He gave another daughter to Count Ulrich of Württemberg; from these two daughters the lords of Württemberg and of Ochsenstein are now descended.

units.la: Mortuo aūt Petro Diuitis episcopo Basil. Petrus de Treuiri physicus per Sedem in episcopum est promotus. Prædictus Petrus diuitis cùm esset de parte Stelliferorum Basil. omnes suos & suas Psitacis copulauit. Hic ordinauit, q; cum uno anno Basileæ Psitacus magister esset civium, eodem anno Stellifer esset Zunftarū magister; & anno sequenti econuerso: & q; tot milites & tot probi cives in Consilium de vna parte, sicut de reliqua, sumerentur. Qui episcopus cū quadam vice quedā in consilio Basil. peteret: Ioānes de Arguel, cui plebs adhęsit, contradicens, ab epo dicente: ego facia tibi erui oculos tuos, illa vice de loco Cōsulū est expulsus. Cui et ciui de Argdel Petrus Scalarij senior, miles valentissimus, in cōsilio sibi resistenti, respōdit: nescis q in una domo paterfam. & scrofa morentur, sed aliter & aliter teneātur? De huius Scalarij cōmendatione integra historia opus esset. Hic Petrus de Treuiri episcopus multa bona fecit ecclesiæ Basil. & magna fecisset, si non inibi molestatus fuisset. A Hartungo n. monachi canonico Basilensi alapa est percussus. Hunc Hartungum monachi consiliis & armis strenuum, qui regi & Rudolfo patri suo feruenter adhæsit, ipse rex Albertus post multas preces, personaliter Capitulum ingrediēs, vix ad canonicatum promouit: regemq; iratū honorare nolebant, nisi pro tribus peteret: qui eorū largitate tres promouens cōmendauit.
units.tr: After the death of Peter Diviticus, bishop of Basel, Peter of Trier, a physician, was promoted to the bishopric by the Apostolic See. This Peter Diviticus, while he was on the side of the Stellifers of Basel, joined all his men and women to the Psittacs. He ordained that in one year the Psittacus should be master of the citizens of Basel, and in the same year the Stellifer should be master of the guilds, and in the following year the reverse; and that as many knights and as many worthy citizens should be taken into the council from one side as from the other. When this bishop once sought something in the council of Basel, John of Arguel, whom the common people supported, objected, and the bishop said: "I will have your eyes put out." On that occasion John was expelled from his place among the magistrates. To him, when he resisted in council, the citizen of Arguel, Peter Scalarius the elder, a most valiant knight, replied: "Do you not know that the householder and the sow may live in one house, but are kept in different ways?" A full account of the praise of this Scalarius would require a whole history. This Peter of Trier, bishop, did many good things for the church of Basel and would have done great things had he not been harassed there. For Hartung Mönch, canon of Basel, struck him on the cheek. King Albert himself, after many prayers, entered the chapter in person and scarcely got this Hartung, a man vigorous in counsel and arms, who had adhered warmly to the king and to his father Rudolf, promoted to a canonry. The canons did not wish to honour the angry king unless he asked on behalf of three men; he, by distributing largesse among them, recommended three men, whom he promoted.

units.la: 30 Eps quoq; in Suevia per comitē Mōtisfortis captus, nō p rege, sed p pecuniā liberatur. Habuit rex tractatū emendi oppidū Liestal à comite de Honberg. Comes aūt obmisso rege, vēdidit & tradidit idem oppidum eidem episcopo & ecclesiæ Basil. quę hodie tenet illud. Ex quo rex contra episcopum, Capitulum, ecclesiam & civitatem Basilien sem cōmotus fuit odio capitali. Idem aūt Petrus, occasione artis medicæ, in archiepisc. Moguntin. postmodum Otto de Gradisone Gallicus in epm Basil. per sedē sunt pmoti.
units.tr: 30 A bishop also, in Swabia, was captured by the Count of Montfort and was freed for money, not by the king. The king had negotiated to buy the town of Liestal from the Count of Homberg. But the count, passing over the king, sold and handed over the same town to this bishop and to the church of Basel, which still holds it. From this the king was stirred up against the bishop, the chapter, the church and the citizens of Basel with deadly hatred. The same Peter, by occasion of his medical skill, was afterwards promoted by the Apostolic See in the archbishopric of Mainz; and Otto of Grandson, a Frenchman, was promoted to the bishopric of Basel.

units.la: Hic Otto episcopus cum rex ipsum nollet de suis regalibus investire, & alias esset infestus eidē: quadam vice rege existēte Basileæ in curia monachorū, in mōte S. Petri, assumptis seruitoribus suis, accessit regē, ac genu flexus coram eo, per Hugonē ad Solem, sciente Gallicum, per regē se petiit investiri. Rex n. Gallicū, episcopus verò Teutonicum nesciuerunt. Venit aūt episcopus eo animo, q; si eū renuisset investire, q; eum voluit occidisse. Petente ergo Hugone in Teutonico à rege, epm humiliter investiri: rege verò respondente vulgariter: quid vellet iste scholaris? episcopus non intelligens dictū regis, sed credens eū recusasse preces suas iratus dixit: Qui dit? qui dit? in Gallico.
units.tr: This Bishop Otto, since the king did not wish to invest him with his royal rights, and was otherwise hostile to him, once, when the king was at Basel in the monks' court on St Peter's Mount, took his servants with him, approached the king, knelt before him, and through Hugo ad Solem, who knew French, asked to be invested by the king. For the king knew no German... Rather: the king did not know French, and the bishop did not know German. The bishop came with the intention that, if the king refused to invest him, he would kill him. When Hugo, speaking in German, asked the king to invest the bishop humbly, the king answered in the vernacular: "What does this scholar want?" The bishop, not understanding the king's words but thinking he had refused his request, said angrily: "What did he say? What did he say?" in French.

units.la: 40 Hugo verò videns furiā episcopi (erat n. iuuenis & animosus) manuerē dixit episcopo in Gallico: Domine, dominus noster rex dicit, quòd eras libenter velit vos investire, & omnia facere, ad quæ ecclesiæ Basiliensi tenetur. Et episcopus inclinans se, dixit, Grammersi, & recessit. Rex videns motum episcopi, post recessum episcopi illico recessit, non ingrediens amplius Basileam, sed contra illos durius est incensus.
units.tr: 40 Hugo, seeing the bishop's fury (for he was a young and spirited man), gestured to the bishop and said in French: "My lord, our lord the king says that he would gladly invest you and do everything that the church of Basel is bound to." And the bishop, bowing, said "Grammercy," and withdrew. The king, seeing the bishop's agitation, left immediately after the bishop withdrew, and did not enter Basel again, but was kindled all the more fiercely against them.

units.la: Eo tempore progenies Zerkinden, Vorgassen, de Raperc, de Lorrach, de Schowerberg, Pinzerna, Basileæ fouebant episcopum. Rex autem castrum Furstenstein, Wernheri & Ioannis de Raperc, per suos obsedit.
units.tr: At that time the families of Zerkinden, Vorgassen, of Raperc, of Lörrach, of Schönberg, and the Pinzerna supported the bishop at Basel. The king, however, besieged the castle of Fürstenstein, belonging to Werner and John of Raperc, with his men.

units.la: Ioannes aūt dux fratruelis regis, quem rex in curia sua cū filiis suis nutriuit, asserens munitiones dominij de Kiburg ad se spectare, tanquā matri suę per Rudolfum regem olim morganitico iure donatū, libenter habuisset sua: instans ferventer, vt sibi saltem munitiones aliquas assignasset. Ad quod cum rex induci nequiret, & insuper multos accensus. Baronum bonis suis & iuribus spoliaret, instante frequenter regina, ut liberos suos sibi commendatos haberet, ac ipsius Ioannis prodigalitatem nimiam accusante: tandem ipse Ioannes dux, cum baronibus Rudolfo de Wart, Walthero de Eschibach, & Vdalrico de Palma, regem interficere cogitavit.
units.tr: Duke John, the king's cousin, whom the king had raised in his court with his sons, claimed that the fortifications of the lordship of Kyburg belonged to him, having been given to his mother by King Rudolf long before by morganatic right, and he would gladly have had them as his own. He pressed eagerly that at least some of the fortifications should be assigned to him. When the king could not be persuaded to this, and moreover was stirred up against many barons and despoiled them of their goods and rights, and when the queen often urged him to keep his children, who had been committed to him, and accused John of excessive prodigality, at last Duke John, with the barons Rudolf of Wart, Walter of Eschibach and Ulrich of Palma, planned to kill the king.

units.la: Ascendente autem regina versus Rinfeldam, cum iuxta minorem Basileam venisset, exiuit ad eam currens Otto episcopus Basil. iuxta currum, eius gratiam pro rege placando imploransque dicente Cuhrado Monachi milite Basiliensi ad vectores currus, quod percuterent equos, illisque percutientibus, episcopus luto fuit perfusus. Crastino autem rege existente apud locum suum Balnearum, ac Ioanne episcopo Argen. rogante regem, ut praedicto duci de munitionibus suis aliquid assignaret: rege vero respondente, quod vellet ipsi duci committere centum galeatos in expeditionem regis versus Bohemiam, & post reversionem vellet sibi aliqua assignare, hoc quoque per eum ad ducem perlato: dux dicens, se nihil habere, & commissionem getis sibi faciendi esse onerosam, ego respondit: se morte & suorum ablatione ad patria iudicare. Waltherus quoque de Eschibach, cum a rege sibi ablata repeteret, dicens: se regis consanguineum, & patrem suum in servitio regis occisum: nec proficeret, quo pariter ipsum posset submergere, dixit regi. Prandentibus autem illis cum rege eiusque filiis: rex cuilibet filiorum & Ioanni duci unum crinile rosarum posuit super caput. Dux autem flens, suum crinile posuit super mensam: ipseque & sui consortes praenominati comedere noluerunt in mensa.
units.tr: When the queen was going up toward Rinfelden, and had come near Little Basel, Bishop Otto of Basel ran out to her beside the carriage, imploring her favour and begging her to appease the king on his behalf. Conrad Mönch, a knight of Basel, said to the carriage drivers that they should strike the horses; and as they struck, the bishop was splashed with mud. The next day, when the king was at his place of the baths, and Bishop John of Strasbourg begged the king to assign something from his fortresses to the aforesaid duke, the king replied that he wished to commit to the duke a hundred helmeted men for the expedition against Bohemia, and after their return he would assign him something; and this answer, carried by John to the duke, was refused: the duke said he had nothing and that the commission of doing such deeds was burdensome. To him the other replied that he would judge him worthy of death and of the loss of his property. Walter of Eschibach too, when he demanded back what had been taken from him by the king, saying that he was the king's kinsman and that his father had been killed in the king's service, was told by the king that it would not help him, and that the king could drown him as easily. As they dined with the king and his sons, the king placed a garland of roses on the head of each of the sons and of Duke John. The duke, weeping, put his garland on the table, and he and his aforesaid companions refused to eat at the table.

units.la: Cum autem post prandium rex vellet equitare ad reginam in Rinfeldam, venisset quoque ad flumen Rufam: Ioannes dux & sui, primi in navi ascenderunt, quae ibi unica erat. Sequebatur autem vice transeunte rege & equitante per fata, sicut in more habuit, colloquente sibi dicto de Casteln, milite: accesserunt Ioannes dux & sui, primusque Rudol. de Wart dixit: Quam diu istud cadaver equitare permittemus? ac Rulassingen famulo eius frenum equi regis apprehendente: Ioan. dux cultrum extrahens, collo regis infixit. Rudol. vero de Wart regem gladio perforavit: Vdalricus vero de Palma facie & caput gladio diuisit. Waltherus vero de Eschibach, licet regem facto non laeserit, interfuit tamen. Sic Albertus Rom. rex potens, filius Rudolfi regis, in terra sua, anno domini M.CCC.VIII, cal. Maii, in meridie anno regni sui decimo, est occisus. In quo loco occisionis solenne monasterium Konigsfeld, ordinis Minorum, est constructum, in quo rex primo sepultus, Spiram postea est translatus, in quo etiam loco plures filiorum suorum sepulti sunt.
units.tr: When after dinner the king wished to ride to the queen at Rinfelden, and had come to the river Reuss, John and his men went first aboard the boat, which was the only one there. The king was following, crossing and riding through the meadows, as was his custom, talking with the said knight de Castell, when John and his men came up, and first Rudolf of Wart said: "How long shall we let this corpse ride on?" As the servant Rulassingen seized the bridle of the king's horse, Duke John drew a knife and plunged it into the king's neck. Rudolf of Wart pierced the king with a sword; Ulrich of Palma split his face and head with a sword. Walter of Eschibach, although he did not wound the king, was present at the deed. Thus Albert, powerful king of the Romans, son of King Rudolf, was killed in his own land in the year of the Lord 1308, on 1 May, at noon, in the tenth year of his reign. At the place of the killing the famous monastery of Königsfelden of the Franciscan order was built, where the king was first buried, and afterwards was transferred to Speyer; in this place also several of his sons are buried.

units.la: Occisores autem fugati, primo venerunt in castrum Froburg: dolo autem elusi per comitem de Nidow dominum castri, postea sunt dispersi. De Palma, n. miles fortis diu Basileae in domo Conversarum latitans, tandem obiit: in vita sua castro suo Altpuren obsessio per Lupoldum regis filium, & victo: in quo decapitati sunt quinquaginta. Castra vero Schnabelberg & aliis bonis Waltheri de Eschibach destructis, ipse in terra comitis de Wirtenberg pastor pecorum est effectus: post annos 35 in morte se pandens, honorifice est sepultus. De Wart vero, postea in castro Valckenstein aliquandiu latitasset, voles ire ad sedem Apost. veniens ad Ilam oppidum Theobaldi comitis de Blamont, pādente eum historione comiti & uxori suae, quae fuit de Veringe, illaque cum lacrymis dicente: absit quod ego sim, qui dominum & consanguineum meum interfecit: per ipsum comitem fuit captus, cum famulo suo Rulassingen, recepta pro eo pecunia duci Lupoldo sunt assignati. Unde & mercator dictus est idem comes. Rulassingen iuxta Ensisheim est positus super rota. Rud. de Wart vero, iuxta locum occisionis regis ductus ad iudicium, cum non daretur ei advocatus pro se loquens, primo negas occidisse regem, obtulit se duello. Secundo dixit, in eo nullum fuisse crimen commissum, qui occidendo dominum suum Adolfum Rom. regem, reus laesae maiestatis fuisset. Sed ex quo ipsi occisores fuerunt per sententiam Henrici Imp. damnati, quando ipse Henr. in regem Rom. fuerat creatus, ut ferebatur: sententiatu fuit, nulla alia sententia contra ipsum Rud. de Warte opus esse, nec suas defensiones esse attendendas. Sicque ligatus ad caudam equi, tractusque ad locum supplicii, fractis dorso & membris, flexus est super rota. Eius uxor de Palma veniens noctu sub rota, prostrata ad terram ad modum crucifixi in oratione permansit. Ille vero interrogatus, si suam vellet uxorem adesse? respondit super rota, quod non, quia pari modo in uxoris copulatione atque in propria pateretur. Quae relicta, multis annis postea Basileae beatissima duxit vitam.
units.tr: The assassins, put to flight, first came to the castle of Froburg, but the count of Nidau, lord of the castle, deceived them by treachery, and afterwards they were scattered. De Palma, a brave knight, lay hidden for a long time at Basel in the house of the Conversae, and at last died there. In his lifetime his castle of Altpuren was besieged by Leopold, the king's son, and taken, and fifty men were beheaded in it. The castles of Schnabelberg and the other goods of Walther of Eschibach were destroyed, and he himself became a herdsman of flocks in the land of the count of Württemberg. After thirty-five years, disclosing himself on his deathbed, he was honourably buried. As for de Wart, after he had lain hidden for some time in the castle of Falkenstein, he set out to go to the Apostolic See and came to the town of Ilam, belonging to Count Theobald of Blamont. The story was unfolded to the count and to his wife, who was of Veringen, and she said with tears: "Far be it from me that I should be the one who killed his lord and kinsman." He was captured by the count himself, together with his servant Rulassingen; after money had been received for him, they were handed over to Duke Leopold. For this reason the same count was also called "the merchant". Rulassingen was broken on the wheel near Ensisheim. Rudolf de Wart, however, was brought before the court near the place where the king was killed. Since no advocate was given him to speak on his behalf, he first denied having killed the king and offered to settle the matter by duel. Secondly, he said that no crime had been committed in that case, since whoever killed his lord Adolf, king of the Romans, would be guilty of treason. But since the assassins themselves had been condemned by the sentence of Emperor Henry, when Henry had been created king of the Romans, as it was reported, he was sentenced: no other sentence was needed against Rudolf de Wart, and his defences were not to be heeded. And so, tied to a horse's tail and dragged to the place of execution, with his back and limbs broken, he was bent upon the wheel. His wife, de Palma, came by night and lay prostrate on the ground beneath the wheel, in the manner of one crucified, and remained there in prayer. When he was asked from the wheel whether he wished his wife to be present, he answered no, because he would suffer in her bond to him just as he suffered in his own. Left behind, she afterwards led a most blessed life at Basel for many years.

units.la: Ioannes vero dux post multas occultationes, tandem in forma Beghardi veniens Pisas, fas, ab Imp. Henrico inibi captus, & post Imperatoris mortem pluribus annis ibi tentus, tandem mortuus inibi honorifice est sepultus. Occiso autem rege, cum obsessi in Furstenstein se mane voluissent captos dedisse, in crepusculo noctis veniens nuncius, in vertice montis clamas: Domine de Raperg, rex est occisus. Eo[que] audito, et exercitus, qui & de hoc ipso ante medium noctis nuncii habuerat, territus, summo mane recessit.
units.tr: Duke John, after many concealments, at last came to Pisa disguised as a Beghard, and was captured there by Emperor Henry. After the Emperor's death he was held there for many years, and at last he died and was honourably buried there. When the king was killed, the besieged in Furstenstein wished to surrender to their captors that morning; but at the twilight of night a messenger came, and shouted from the top of the mountain: "Lord of Raperg, the king is killed!" When this was heard, the army, which had also received word of this before midnight, was terrified and withdrew early in the morning.

units.la: Obsessi autem venientes Basileam, contra Monachos mouebantur: ac dissensione facta, & Nicolao ad pueros per Petrum Scalarij vulnerato, ac rumore facto in populo: Otto eps Basil. apprehendens paneriu ciuiu, curiam Monachorum ad S. Petrum accessit, & ingressus omnis populus, Monachis & eorum liberis per muros & cloacas fugatis, omnia pretiosa domus tollens, quinquaginta plaustra vini effundens, non quievit, quousque omnia sunt destructa. Congregati aut multi amicorum super castro Basileę, descendentes animo subueniędi illis, fugati à plebe, ingressi{q} domu Rubei leonis, insequente plebe per tecta discurrere, & de tecto Stebelini ad tectu ad Clauę vltra via saltare coacti sunt. Cessante autem furia populi, collectis{q} viribus Scalariorum & Monachorum, prędictæ progenies non credentes se vltra mensem excludi, iurantes egredi per duo milliaria à ciuitate Basil. ad gratiam consulu, annis 14 exulârunt. Eps autem Otto, qui initio occisionis regis bene potuisset agere facta sua, recepta pecunia cum regina & eius liberis cōcordauit.
units.tr: The besieged men, on coming to Basel, stirred up trouble against the monks. A quarrel arose, and Nicholas was wounded toward the boys by Peter Scalarius, and a commotion broke out among the people. Bishop Otto of Basel, seizing the citizens' banner, came to the monks' court at St Peter's, and the whole populace entered. The monks and their children fled through the walls and sewers, and the mob carried off all the valuable goods of the house and poured out fifty wagonloads of wine. They did not rest until everything was destroyed. Many friends gathered above the castle of Basel and came down intending to help them, but they were driven off by the common people. Entering the house of the Red Lion, they were pursued by the crowd and forced to run across the roofs, leaping from the roof of Stebelin to the roof at Clave across the street. When the fury of the people subsided, the forces of the Scalari and the monks were gathered, and the aforementioned families, not believing they would be shut out for more than a month, swore to leave the city of Basel to a distance of two miles and to seek the favour of the consuls. They were exiled for fourteen years. Bishop Otto, who at the beginning of the king's killing could well have acted on his own deeds, received money and came to terms with the queen and her children.

units.la: Orta autem dissensione inter episcopum & Theobaldum comitem Ferretarum, & episcopo cum ciuitate volente egredi in terram comitis: comes munitionem Blu- menberg propriam, in feudum recipiens ab episcopo, reformatur eidem.
units.tr: A dispute arose between the bishop and Count Theobald of Pfirt, and when the bishop with the city wished to enter the count's land, the count, receiving his own fortress of Blumberg as a fief from the bishop, was restored to it.

units.la: Mortuo autem Orthone episcopo, Gerhardus de Wippingen, ex matre de Grandisone, per Clementem papam v, Basiliensi ecclesię est præfectus.
units.tr: When Bishop Orthone died, Gerhard of Wippingen, whose mother was from Grandson, was set over the church of Basel by Pope Clement V.

units.la: Occiso itaq; Alberto rege, Hainricus comes de Lutzelburg, strenuus & acer, eodem anno in festo omnium Sanctorum, à principibus concorditer in Franckfurt est electus, & Aquisgrani in sequeti anno in Epiphania coronatus. Ascendens aut Rhenum, cum venisset Spiram, venit Eberhardus comes de Wirtenberg cum cc equis in magna superbia, qui cum de multa tyrannide in homines imperij commissa, non concordaret, à rege indignanter recessit: propter quod idem comes postea ad mandatum regis in Italia existentis, p Cun. de Winsperg præsidem regis, ciuitatę Esslingam & reliquas ciuitates Sueuię adeò est destructus, quòd sibi vix tres ex omnibus suis munitionibus remanserunt: quem de castro Asperg obsessum, cum multo tremore fugietem, Hesso Marchio de Baden in oppido Beisckheim recepit, vbi in turri latitabat vsq; ad mortem Imperatoris. Qui comes depauperatus, cum concepisset Imper. gratiam in Italia quæsiuisse, postea mortuo Imp. paulatim reuixit. Venientibus aut nunciis Argent. ad regem ac proponentibus, se per dnos suos Argentinenses, pro gratia regis & priuilegiorum innouatione transmissos: nec Spirę nec Argent. ab ipso responsum habebant. Ascendentes aut versus Columbariam ad regę, edocti à quodam secretario regis, dixerūt ci: ciues vestri Argent. hoc petunt. Quos rex, dicens, se ante non intellexisse quorum fuissent nuncij, cum dominos Argent. nominassent, fauorabiliter exaudiuit. Ascedens aut homagia & fidelitate dominorum & ciuitatum capiens, cum no abundaret, concepit in Italia proficisci: & veniens iterum Spiram, Fridericum ducē Austriæ, Alberti regis occisi filium, post plures tractatus & tentationes, si possent Alberti liberi ab Austria separari (dicente cōsilio regis, quinq; reges propter ducatu Austrię occisos, ac Friderico respondente: & iste, si carere noluerit, poterit esse sextus) tandē de ipso ducatu & aliis dominiis quæ pendent ab imperio, eum investiuit: addito, q duces regi vltra montes cum ducentis galeatis seruirent. Delato autem corpore Alberti regis nauigio Spiram: rex obuiam pergens funeri ad Rhenum, reginam Vngarię, occisi filiam, sub brachiis in ciuitatem traduxit, sed omnino voluit corpus Adolphi regis inibi similiter sepeliri. Quo allato uno die sic Albertum & Adolphum Rom. reges occisos: Henricus rex Spirę in sepulchris regiis sepeliuit, Alberto in vxoris olim Friderici Imp. Adolpho verò in eiusdem filiæ sepulchris, sepultus.
units.tr: After King Albert had been killed, Henry, count of Luxembourg, a vigorous and keen man, was elected unanimously by the princes at Frankfurt in the same year, on the feast of All Saints, and was crowned at Aachen in the following year, at Epiphany. Going up the Rhine, when he came to Speyer, Count Eberhard of Württemberg came to him with two hundred horses in great arrogance. Because he did not agree about the great tyranny committed against the men of the empire, he withdrew indignantly from the king. On account of this the same count, afterwards, by command of the king, who was then in Italy, was so utterly ruined through Cuno of Winsberg, the king's deputy, together with the city of Esslingen and the other cities of Swabia, that barely three of all his fortresses remained to him. Besieged at Asperg, he fled trembling, and was received by Margrave Hesso of Baden in the town of Beisckheim, where he lay hidden in a tower until the death of the Emperor. This count, impoverished, had sought to win the Emperor's favour in Italy, and after the Emperor's death he gradually recovered. When messengers from Strasbourg came to the king and set forth that they had been sent by their lords, the Strasbourgers, to seek the king's favour and the renewal of their privileges, they had no reply from him, neither at Speyer nor at Strasbourg. Going up toward Colmar to the king, and instructed by a certain royal secretary, they said to him: "Your citizens of Strasbourg ask this." The king, saying that he had not understood before whose messengers they were when they named the lords of Strasbourg, heard them favourably. Ascending, he received the homage and fealty of the lords and cities; but since he did not have enough, he resolved to set out for Italy. Coming again to Speyer, after many negotiations and attempts, he finally invested Frederick, duke of Austria, son of the slain King Albert, with the duchy itself and the other dominions that depend on the empire. The king's counsel had said that five kings had been killed on account of the duchy of Austria, and Frederick replied: "And this one too, if he is unwilling to be spared, can be the sixth." It was added that the dukes would serve the king beyond the mountains with two hundred mailed knights. When King Albert's body was brought to Speyer by boat, the king went out to meet the funeral at the Rhine and led the queen of Hungary, the slain man's daughter, under his arms into the city; but he also wished the body of King Adolf to be buried there likewise. When it had been brought, on the same day both kings of the Romans, Albert and Adolf, were thus buried: King Henry laid them in the royal tombs at Speyer, Albert in the tomb of the late wife of Emperor Frederick, and Adolf in the tomb of that same daughter.

units.la: Audito aut eo tempore, q Elsa puella circiter viginti annorum, grādis & bruna, olim Wenceslai regis Bohemiæ filia, neptis Rod. regis, Ioanni, filio Henrici regis, annorū circiter x 1, nuptui, & cum ea ipso Iohanni regnum Bohemię traderetur, eaq; Spiram cum excelleti decentia veniente, ac principe propter falsam suspicionē fornicationis cohocatur. 1309. illi copulare filium dubitare: illa moræ anxia, cum causam protractionis omnino scire vellet, & à suis causam suspicionis difficulter audisset, dixit: Absit q; dominus rex filiū suum mihi deneget ex hac causa, quia virginitatē meam per aspectum corporis comprobabo. Examinata ergo per honestas matronas, & reperta virgo, fuit filio regis soleniter copulata. Quos coniuges Petrus de Treuiri, archiepiscopus Mogun. Bohemiam traducens, Pragæ in regem & reginam, prout antiquitus ad Mogutinū pertinet, coronauit. Solennitas aūt nuptiarū Spiræ, paratis sedibus, propter cōtentionē antiquam Mogūtini & Coloniensis, quorū quilibet ad dextrā principis sedere voluit, est turbata.
units.tr: At that time it was heard that Elsa, a girl of about twenty years, tall and dark, formerly daughter of King Wenceslas of Bohemia and granddaughter of King Rudolf, was to be given in marriage to John, son of King Henry, who was about eleven years old, and that with her the kingdom of Bohemia would be handed over to John himself. When she came to Speyer with remarkable dignity, the prince, on account of a false suspicion of fornication, hesitated to join his son to her. She, anxious about the delay, and wishing to know fully the reason for the postponement, had with difficulty heard from her people the cause of the suspicion, and said: "Far be it that the lord king should deny me his son on this ground, since I will prove my virginity by an examination of my body." She was examined, then, by honest matrons, found to be a virgin, and was solemnly joined to the king's son. Peter of Trier, archbishop of Mainz, conducted the couple to Bohemia and crowned them king and queen at Prague, as belongs anciently to Mainz. But the solemnity of the wedding at Speyer, with the seats prepared, was disturbed by the old contention between Mainz and Cologne, each of whom wished to sit at the prince's right hand.

units.la: Mãsit verò ibi rex sex hebdomadibus cum principibus electoribus & aliis principibus & ciuitatum nunciis, de suo transitu & de præstãdis seruitiis in Italiam, disponendo, vbi & ad eum venerant Matheus Mediolani & Theobaldus Brixiæ magnates, & plurimi Lombardorum. Prædictum Theobaldum Brixiensem inibi militauit.
units.tr: The king, however, remained there for six weeks with the electoral princes and other princes and the envoys of the cities, arranging his crossing and the services to be rendered in Italy. There came to him also Matteo of Milan and Theobald of Brescia, great men, and very many of the Lombards. This Theobald of Brescia served in the army there.

units.la: Post hæc rex patriam suam Lutzelenburg accedens, & cum dominis terræ illius & amicis de auxilio tractans, cum vxore sua, filia ducis Brabantiæ, ac fratribus suis, Balduino videlicet archiepiscopo Treuerēsi, ac Walramo de Lutzelburg milite egregio, ascendēs, per terram comitis Sabaudiæ, qui sororem reginæ habuit in vxorem, Lombardiam viriliter est ingressus. Ingressi sunt autem cum eo, Lupoldus Austriæ, Rudolfus Bauariæ duces, archiepiscopus Treuirensis, Leodiensis, Basiliensis, & plures alij episcopi, comes Sabaudiæ, comes Flandriæ, multiq; alij comites, & omnium quasi totius Alemanniæ stipendiarij ciuitatum. Et veniens Astam, post receptionem suam de eis dubitans, meliores ex eis secum Mediolanum perduxit. Receptus est autem pacifice Mediolani per Guidonem de Turri Guelfum, dominium ciuitatis habentē, credidit enim eum citò recessurum. Misit autē rex pro melioribus in tota Italia, de vtraq; parte Gibellinorum & Guelforum, tentans, si quo modo posset inter eos cōcordiam ordinare. At illis post magnam deliberationem dicentibus, hoc impossibile esse: rex desistens, illos negotio imperfecto reliquit.
units.tr: After this the king went to his homeland of Luxembourg, and, discussing aid with the lords of that land and his friends, he set out with his wife, the daughter of the duke of Brabant, and his brothers, namely Baldwin, archbishop of Trier, and Walram of Luxembourg, an outstanding knight. He passed through the land of the count of Savoy, who had the queen's sister as his wife, and bravely entered Lombardy. With him went Leopold of Austria and Rudolf of Bavaria, dukes; the archbishops of Trier and Liège and Basel, and several other bishops; the count of Savoy, the count of Flanders, and many other counts; and the hired soldiers of almost all the cities of the whole of Germany. Arriving at Asti, and doubting some of them after their reception, he led the best of them with him to Milan. He was received peacefully at Milan by Guido della Torre, the Guelf, who held lordship of the city, for he believed that he would soon withdraw. The king sent for the leading men throughout all Italy, from both the Ghibelline and the Guelf parties, trying whether in some way he could bring about harmony between them. But when they said after long deliberation that this was impossible, the king desisted and left them, the business unfinished.

units.la: Videns autem Guido, regem diu & potenter in Mediolano morari, & de traditione & nece regis & suorum per se & suos cogitans: quendam de Sodomia damnatum educere decreuerant ad cremandum, vt Alemannis egredientibus ad videndū, clausis portis regem occiderent desolatum. Et irruentibus illis cum populo ad palatium regis: primi fratres Teutonici S. Mariæ, signati armis & vexillo ordinis, qui decreuerant non exire cum cremando, cum quibusdam aliis, irruentem populum viriliter inuaserunt: defensoq; palatio regis, ad portam vbi iacuit Lupoldus dux Austriæ cum ducentis galeatis, cum magno labore properates, proiecta in vicū vasorum & alia obstacula, remouerunt, ictusq; lancearum & lapidum de domibus sustinentes, & violenter aperta porta: cum dux & alij ad regis palatium peruenissent, ad mandatum regis Guidonem & suos inuadentes, nemini pepercerunt. Illoq; extra ciuitatem fugato, suisq; occisis, cum comes Sabaudię, qui fuit Guelfus, conquestus esset regi, quòd Teutonici illos sine misericordia occidissent: rex respondit, quòd ipsos in pecuniam noluerunt talliare. Quibus victis & eiectis, rex de Mediolanensibus pro sua dispositione voluntate: Matthæum Vicecomitem ponendo ministrum, qui & liberi sui etiam post mortem Cæsaris, illius terræ dominium tenuerunt: rexq; postea Gibellinis adhæsit.
units.tr: Guido, however, seeing that the king was staying long and powerfully in Milan, and thinking of the betrayal and death of the king and his men by himself and his people, had decided to bring out a certain man condemned for sodomy to be burned, so that, when the Germans went out to watch, the gates could be closed and they could kill the king left defenceless. And when they rushed with the people to the royal palace, first the Teutonic brothers of St Mary, marked with the arms and banner of their order, who had resolved not to go out to the burning, together with some others, bravely attacked the surging crowd. Defending the royal palace, they hurried with great effort to the gate where Duke Leopold of Austria lay with two hundred helmeted men; they threw aside the tubs and other obstacles that had been cast into the street, and bearing the blows of spears and stones from the houses, they forcibly opened the gate. When the duke and the others reached the king's palace, at the king's command they attacked Guido and his men and spared no one. Guido was put to flight outside the city and his men were killed. When the count of Savoy, who was a Guelf, complained to the king that the Teutonic brothers had slaughtered those men without mercy, the king replied that they had refused to be taxed for money. Having defeated and expelled them, the king, according to his own disposition, set Matteo Visconti over the Milanese as their governor; he and his sons, even after the death of the Emperor, kept lordship of that land. Afterwards the king attached himself to the Ghibellines.

units.la: Wernherus autem comes de Honberg, relictus in Lōbardia à rege, quot & quantas incredibiles habuerit victorias, & quàm feliciter nomine Imperatoris triumphārit, integra historia non caperet.
units.tr: As for Count Werner of Honberg, left in Lombardy by the king, the whole history would not hold how many and how great incredible victories he won, and how happily he triumphed in the name of the Emperor.

units.la: Postea rex obsidendi animo ad Cremonam transiuit, qui eū & suos missos renuerant receptare. Territi autem Cremonenses, ferendo funes in collis, obuiam ibant regi. Habita igitur Cremona, & multis aliis ciuitatibus Lōbardiæ, Brixiam obsistentem inuenit: quam cum Mediolanensibus, Veronensibus & aliis ciuitatibus, suaq; militia, per integram æstatem potenter obsedit: vbi Walramus frater regis iaculo est occisus. Huius obsidionis & exercitus multitudine fœtorem & pestilentiam esse factam, quid opus est narrare? Cùm multę ciuitates ibidem quasi cum domicilio residerent, vt hąc gradientes per dua milliaria fœtorem senserint. Exercitus ambitus habebat tria miliaria: nec erat numerus captiuorū, & continuè occisorum, nec vnquā mors cōmuniot videbatur. Omnes aūt Guelfi eidem ciuitati in hominibus & victualibus auxilium præbuerunt.
units.tr: Afterwards the king, intending to besiege it, passed over to Cremona, which had refused to receive him and his envoys. The frightened Cremonese, carrying ropes, went out to meet the king. Having taken Cremona and many other cities of Lombardy, he found Brescia resisting; with the Milanese, the Veronese and other cities, and his own army, he powerfully besieged it for the whole summer, where Walram, the king's brother, was killed by a javelin. Why need I relate that by the multitude of this siege and army a stench and pestilence arose? Since many cities were settled there almost as if in permanent dwellings, those approaching could smell the stench from two miles away. The army encircling it covered three miles; nor was there any number of prisoners, and the slaughter was continual, nor did death ever seem to cease. All the Guelfs, however, gave help to the same city with men and provisions.

units.la: Habebant autem intrinseci pro se montem, contiguum ciuitati. Et ecce quodam die mane ascendens montem virilis regis exercitus, vicit multitudinem ascedentium ex aduerso, in quo conflictu, Theobaldus, Brixiæ dominiu tenens, auctor huius belli, quem rex Spiræ militauerat, letaliter est vulneratus. Allato autem eo regi, rex eum intuendo cognoscens, mirabiliter est gauisus. Cùm autem ille ope Medicorum curari non posset, vt durius puniretur, per quatuor tauros membratim est laniatus, & quælibet partium postea super rotam, & caput versus portam ciuitatis lancea figebatur. Quæsitus autem ille adhuc viuens, cur tantum nefas attentauerit contra regem? respondit: Se regis superbiam ferre non potuisse. Intrinseci autem videntes quæ fiebant de illo, captiuorum de exercitu regis magnum numerum iuxta mœnia suspenderunt: Obtento autem monte ab extrinsecis, tandem illi deficientes se & ciuitatem regis gratiæ obtulerunt, funes ferentes in collis. Rex autem demolita porta & parte muri, ingressus est, vltra murum.
units.tr: Those inside had for their side a hill adjoining the city. And behold, one morning the king's army climbed the hill with manly courage and overcame the crowd coming up from the opposite side. In this clash Theobald, who held lordship of Brescia, the author of this war, whom the king had employed at Speyer, was mortally wounded. When he was brought to the king, the king, recognising him as he looked upon him, rejoiced wonderfully. Since he could not be cured by the help of physicians, to be punished more severely he was torn limb from limb by four bulls, and each part was afterwards set upon a wheel, and his head was fixed on a spear towards the city gate. Being questioned while still alive as to why he had dared such a crime against the king, he answered that he could not bear the king's arrogance. Those inside, seeing what was being done to him, hanged a great number of the king's captured soldiers along the walls. But when the hill was taken by those outside, at last they, failing, offered themselves and the city to the king's grace, carrying ropes. The king, having broken down the gate and part of the wall, entered beyond the wall.

units.la: Post hæc circa hyemem Ianuam profectus cum regina, honorificè est receptus: vt Beatrix regina moriens, sepulta est ad Minores. Ibi pluribus mensibus rex permanens, postea iuit Pisas. Pisis autem mensibus aliquot manente eo, Ioannem ducem Austriæ, occisorem Alberti regis, clam venientem de papa & volentem regis gratiam quærere, captum in hospitio per quendam de Salah, intuitu ducum Austriæ, commisit Pisanis. Antea enim ipsius Alberti damnauerat occisores. Qui diu ibidem honorificè tentus, in captiuitate diem clausit extremum.
units.tr: After this, about winter, he set out for Genoa with the queen, and was received with honour; where Queen Beatrice died and was buried among the Minorites. The king remained there for several months, and afterwards went to Pisa. While he remained at Pisa for some months, he handed over to the Pisans John, duke of Austria, the murderer of King Albert, who had come secretly from the Pope and wished to seek the king's favour; he had been captured in an inn by a certain man of Salah, out of regard for the dukes of Austria. For earlier the king had condemned the murderers of Albert himself. Held there for a long time with honour, he ended his days in captivity.

units.la: Venerunt autem subinde nuncij solennes Romanorum pro rege. Erat autem ingressus Italiam de assensu & approbatione Clementis papæ quinti, qui & ei Hostiensem episcopum, cum tribus aliis Cardinalibus, pro impendendis vnctionis & confirmationis insignibus, destinauit. Rex igitur properauit ad Vrbem, quem Robertus rex Apuliæ, tenens Romam, nisus est impedire, pro eo, quòd rex eum, per nuntios suos Mediolani inuestituram feudorum petentem, inuestire distulit, quousque veniret ad Vrbem.
units.tr: Then, soon afterwards, the solemn envoys of the Romans came for the king. He had entered Italy with the assent and approval of Pope Clement V, who had also sent to him the bishop of Ostia, with three other cardinals, to perform the anointing and the rites of confirmation. The king therefore hastened to the City, which Robert, king of Apulia, who held Rome, tried to prevent; for the king, when Robert through his envoys at Milan had sought the investiture of the fiefs, had postponed investing him until he should come to the City.

units.la: Stephanus verò de Columna & sui potentiores Laterani tenebant vnam turrim super pontem Tyberis: alias enim tenuerant Vrsini, qui quasi omnes adhærebant Roberto regi. Misit autem Robertus Ioannem fratrem suum cum magna gente, ad obstruendum iter regi: qui ad fractionem pontis regi parati machinis & aliis, quàm plurimum laborabant, quibus in hoc Stephanus resistebat. Veniente autem rege, gens Roberti retrocessit ad S. Petrum. Rex autem in vigilia Pentecostes pontem transiens, multos fecit milites. Guelfi enim ex turri quam habebant super pontem, in regem & suos instar grandinis direxerunt sagittas. Laterani autem honorificè est receptus: & super castro, quod Militia dicitur, manens, quasi quotidie ex parte Roberti & fautorum suorum multas pugnas pariter & conflictus sustinuit.
units.tr: Stephen of Colonna and his more powerful men of the Lateran held one tower above the bridge over the Tiber; for the Orsini, who almost all adhered to King Robert, had held the others. Robert sent his brother John with a great force to block the king's way; they, prepared with machines and other means, laboured very hard to break the bridge, and Stephen resisted them in this. When the king came, Robert's men withdrew to St Peter's. The king, crossing the bridge on the vigil of Pentecost, made many knights. For the Guelfs from the tower they held above the bridge directed arrows like hail against the king and his men. He was received with honour at the Lateran, and, remaining above the castle called the Militia, he endured almost daily many battles and clashes on the side of Robert and his supporters.

units.la: Misit autem pro quinquaginta melioribus in Lateranum, qui & pro eo miserant, petens ab eis, vt sibi sua vrbis fortalitia aperirent. Qui cum se difficiles redderent, alii qui verò prætendentes fingerent, se esse Roberti vasallos: rex ab ipsis discedens, eos fecit includi, quousq; sibi & liberos in obsides, & fortalitia assignarent, turrimq; prædictam illico assignarunt. Sicq; nunc Capitolium, nunc hac nunc illac contratas habentes, continuè pugnârunt, quousq; totaliter occupaâr̃ut Lateranum. Occisis autem in eiusmodi pugnis quadam vice episcopo Leodiensi, regis consanguineo, & abbate Wissenburgensi, cum Henricus dictus de Blanckenberg id regi Hendo nunciaret: rex ipsum redire cum fletu ad sinum matris dicebat.
units.tr: He sent for the fifty leading men in the Lateran, who had also sent for him, asking them to open to him the fortresses of their city. When they made themselves difficult, and others pretending to be Robert's vassals, the king, withdrawing from them, had them shut up until they assigned to him their children as hostages and the fortresses, and they at once handed over the aforesaid tower. And so, now holding the Capitol, now this district, now that, they fought continually, until they had totally occupied the Lateran. In such fighting, on one occasion, the bishop of Liège, the king's kinsman, and the abbot of Weissenburg were killed; when Henry called Blankenberg reported this to the king, the king said that he should return to the bosom of his mother, weeping.

units.la: Differentibus aût Cardinalibus, quorum vnus obierat coronationem regis, & deprehenso quodam cum literis papalibus, quibus ipsis Cardinalibus papa regis coronationem interdixerat, eisdemq; destructis ex persuasione Hostiensis, qui & Gibellinus fuit, & Stephani de Columna: multitudo Romanorum irruit in palatium regis. Et requirente rege, quid vellent? Illi se velle occidere voratores dixerunt, qui stipendia militum devorarent: & sic territi Cardinales, regi in ecclesia sancti Ioannis, calendis Augusti, vnctionis & coronationis Imperialis insignia impenderunt (erant autem alba omnia eius indumenta, cum equo albo) præstito per eum iuramento, secundum formā, quam Imp. coronandi ecclesiæ Romanæ præstare solent. Postea aût nûquam assurrexit Cardinalibus, sicut antè, nec quèquam in suâ mēsam locabat. Pœnituit autem papam, videntem eius potentiam ac rancorem inter Robertum & ipsum principem: imò & inter Philippum regem Franciæ, & ipsum regem. Turbauit enim Francum, quem ipse rex se in scribendo præposuit: ipsiq; tres papa, Robertus & Philippus in eius exterminium cogitabant. Cæsar autem ab Vrbe recedens, inibi reliquit Hugonē de Buchegge comitem, cum trecentis galeatis: qui cum Stephano prædicto viriliter se tenês, & frequenter cū Guelfis confligens, vrbē S. Petri, quā Cæsar habere non potuit, acquisiuit.
units.tr: The cardinals disagreed, one of them having died before the king's coronation. A certain man was caught carrying papal letters by which the pope had forbidden the cardinals to crown the king. When these letters were destroyed, at the urging of the Hostiensis, who was also a Ghibelline, and of Stefano Colonna, a crowd of Romans burst into the king's palace. When the king asked what they wanted, they replied that they wished to kill the gluttons who devoured the soldiers' pay. Frightened by this, the cardinals in the church of St John on the calends of August gave the king the insignia of anointing and imperial coronation. (All his garments were white, and he had a white horse.) He first swore the oath that the emperors-elect are accustomed to swear to the Roman Church, in the prescribed form. Afterwards, however, he never rose for the cardinals as he had before, nor did he seat anyone at his table. The pope then regretted seeing his power and his rivalry with Robert and with the prince himself, and indeed with Philip, king of France, and the king. For he had stirred up the Franks, whom the king had placed before himself in his writings, and the pope, Robert and Philip were all plotting his destruction. The emperor, leaving the city, left behind Count Hugo of Buchegg with three hundred men-at-arms. Holding firm with the aforesaid Stefano, and often fighting with the Guelfs, Hugo gained the city of St Peter, which the emperor had not been able to take.

units.la: Cæsar autem Florentiam, habētem vltra centum millia armatorum (omnes n. Guelfi illuc subsidium destinârant) cum pauca gente obsedit. Infirmus autem factus aliquantulum, in villam vicinam sub monte, causa meliotis æris collocauit, & ascendentes inimici in montem, vexârunt Cæsarem lapidibus & sagittis. Et dicēte Cæsare: Ah quòd neminem habeo cui hæc cordi existant: multi ascendentes de turba Cæsaris, difficulter è monte inimicos fugârunt, interficiendo ducētos, & vltrà. Decrescente autem turba Cæsaris, misit pro reliquis in Vrbe, & sic Hugo de Buchegge cum reliquis Romæ, vrbe Stephano cōmissa, ad Cæsarē pperauit, in itinere duobus conflictibus feliciter triumphādo: plures enim q; ipsi fuerāt in obsidione Florentiæ, Cæsari præsentarūt captiuos.
units.tr: The emperor besieged Florence with only a small force, although the city had more than a hundred thousand armed men (for all the Guelfs had sent help there). Having fallen somewhat ill, he moved into a nearby village below the mountain for the sake of better air. The enemy went up the mountain and harassed the emperor with stones and arrows. The emperor said, "Ah, I have no one who cares for these things." Many of the emperor's men climbed up and, with difficulty, drove the enemy off the mountain, killing two hundred and more. But as the emperor's force dwindled, he sent for the rest from the city. So Hugo of Buchegg came hurrying to the emperor from Rome with the others, leaving Stefano in charge of the city, and on the way he triumphed successfully in two skirmishes. For they presented to the emperor more prisoners than there had been men at the siege of Florence.

units.la: Post hæc Cæsar Pisas rediens, citato inibi Roberto rege, & habitis processibus debitis, in eum tanquam in maiestatis læsæ reum, ac proditorem & hostem imperij, prevationis omnium dominiorum & decapitationis, si vnquam veniret in imperij fines, sententiam promulgauit. Quam sententiam Clemens papa post mortem Cæsaris revocauit, prout notatur in Clem. de reiudicata. c. pastoralis cura.
units.tr: After this the emperor returned to Pisa. There King Robert was summoned, and after the proper proceedings had been held, the emperor pronounced sentence against him as guilty of treason, a traitor and an enemy of the empire, declaring that he should be stripped of all his lordships and beheaded should he ever come within the borders of the empire. Pope Clement revoked this sentence after the emperor's death, as is noted in the Clementines, de reiudicata, c. pastoralis cura.

units.la: Conuenit autem Cæsar cum rege Siciliæ, de danda filia sua filio Siculi: & disposuit seiturum Neapolim, & in partes illas. Rex quoq; Robertus disposuit recedere de regno Cæsare veniente, & in prouinciam se transferre. Decreuit autē Cęsar, se Apuliam & terram Roberti, Siculo commissurum. Præceperat etiam omnibus ciuitatibus, episcopis, & aliis magnatibus Alemanniæ, vt transmitterent nouam gentem, quæ iam erat in itinere veniendi. Venerat etiam mater Imper. filia comitis Flandriæ cum filia Siculo danda, vsq; Basileam, ad Cæsarem profectura. Ducebatur etiam domina Catharina soror ducum Austriæ quondā Alberti Rom. regis filia, Imperatori nuptura. Præmiserat etiam Cæsar prædictum comitem de Blanckenberg ad Vrbem, sibi apud S. Petrum domicilium paraturū: & venit Cæsar cū exercitu suo iuxta Senas, aliquot diebus, ad Senensium sibi rebellium terram ignis incendio deuastando, & captos ex eis in arboribus suspendendo. Et in assumptionis virginis Mariæ vigilia, decantata coram eo Missa, eoq; per quendam Prædicatorem cōmunicato, post missam coepit illico infirmari. Dicebatur enim q; ipse Prædicator venenum sub vngue digiti tenens abscon sum, post cōmunionem potui Cæsaris immisisset, & illico discessisset. Cùm autē consuleretur Cæsari, q; Pisas reuerteretur, ipse se in seruitio domini esse, & non retrocessurū respondit, & procedens, cùm venisset ad villam quæ dicitur Bonconuent, progredi vltrà nequiuit: sed in die B. Bartholomei decessit, quē exercitus Pisas reduxit, vbi cum ineffabili lamentatione est honorificè sepultus, anno domini M.CCC.XIII. Sicq; heu periit columna magnanimitatis & iusticiæ ac flos germinis Germanorum.
units.tr: The emperor had agreed with the king of Sicily to give his daughter to the Sicilian's son, and he planned to go to Naples and those parts. King Robert, too, planned to leave the kingdom when the emperor came and to move into his province. The emperor had decided to entrust Apulia and Robert's land to the Sicilian. He had also ordered all the cities, bishops and other magnates of Germany to send over the new troops who were already on their way. The emperor's mother, the daughter of the count of Flanders, had come with the daughter who was to be given to the Sicilian, as far as Basel, where she was to meet the emperor. Lady Catherine, sister of the dukes of Austria and daughter of the former Roman king Albert, was also being brought to be married to the emperor. The emperor had earlier sent the aforesaid Count of Blankenberg to Rome to prepare a residence for him near St Peter's. The emperor came with his army near Siena and spent some days laying waste the lands of the Sienese, who were rebels against him, with fire, and hanging those of them he captured from trees. On the vigil of the Assumption of the Virgin Mary, after Mass had been sung in his presence and he had received communion from a certain Preacher, he at once began to fall ill. For it was said that this same Preacher, holding poison hidden under his fingernail, had put it into the emperor's cup after communion and at once departed. When the emperor was advised to return to Pisa, he replied that he was in the service of the Lord and would not turn back. Advancing, when he came to the village called Buonconvento, he could go no further, and he died on the feast of St Bartholomew. The army brought him back to Pisa, where he was honoured with burial amid indescribable lamentation, in the year of the Lord 1313. Thus alas perished the pillar of magnanimity and justice and the flower of the German stock.

units.la: Pisani autem cum magnates Cæsaris repatriantes secum retinere non possent: multi tamen militares de exercitu remanserunt cum illis. Et facta est briga magna inter Robertum regem capitaneum Gelforū, & Pisanos, vt & facto postea per annum conflictu ante montem Catinum, vbi omnis pars Gelforum conuenerat, Pisani cum Alemannis vicerunt: & occisi sunt in die illa multa milia Gelforum: & cecidit Ioānes princeps, frater regis Roberti. Super quē sedens comes Niger Pisanus, miles factus est super eum. A tempore n. quondā Chunradini, nullus de progenie eorundem comitū militari voluit, nisi in bello vbi fieret vindicta in stirpe quæ Chunradinum occidit.
units.tr: When the Pisans could not keep the emperor's magnates with them as they returned home, many of the soldiers from the army nevertheless stayed on with them. A great quarrel arose between King Robert, the captain of the Guelfs, and the Pisans. Later, in the course of that year, a battle took place before Monte Catini, where all the Guelf forces had gathered; the Pisans with the Germans won, and many thousands of Guelfs were killed that day, and John, the prince, brother of King Robert, fell. Count Niger of Pisa, sitting upon him, was made a knight over him. For from the time of the former Conradin, no one of the lineage of those counts had wished to be knighted, except in war where vengeance could be taken on the family that had killed Conradin.

units.la: Mortuo itaq; Hainrico Imp. & vocatis principibus in Fráfcurt, Fridericus dux Austriæ, filius Alberti regis, & nepos Rudolfi regis, pro regno laborabat. Cui Petrus Treuerensis, Mogunt. & olim episcopus Basilien. quem Albertus quondam rex lēserat, & Balduinus Treuerensis, & Ioannes Bohemus, se opponunt. Fridericus autem Austra lis alloquitur Rudolphum & Ludouicum duces Bauariæ, Palatinos Rheni, exhibens se ad assistendum eis. At illi æstimantes se tanto negocio impotentes, se Friderici seruiseruitio astrinxerunt. Dux quoq; Saxoniæ, & Voldemarus, Marchio Brandeburgensis, Friderico adhæserunt. Hi enim laici omnes & vxor Bohemi, fuerunt quondam regis Rudolphi nepotes. Item Hainricus de Virnenberg Coloniensis, acto inter alios tractatu fecit, quod filia fratris sui comitis de Virnenberg copulata fuit Hainrico duci Austriæ, fratri Friderici; similiter adhæsit eidem.
units.tr: Therefore, after the death of the emperor Henry, and with the princes summoned to Frankfurt, Frederick, duke of Austria, son of King Albert and grandson of King Rudolf, strove for the kingdom. Against him Peter of Trier, of Mainz, and formerly bishop of Basel, whom the former king Albert had injured, and Baldwin of Trier, and John of Bohemia, set themselves. Frederick of Austria then approached Rudolf and Louis, dukes of Bavaria, and the Palatines of the Rhine, offering to support them. But they, judging themselves too weak for so great a business, bound themselves to Frederick's service. The duke of Saxony and Waldemar, margrave of Brandenburg, also attached themselves to Frederick. For all these laymen, and the wife of John of Bohemia, were grandchildren of the former king Rudolf. Likewise Henry of Virneburg, of Cologne, who had carried on negotiations with the others, arranged that the daughter of his brother, Count of Virneburg, should be married to Henry, duke of Austria, brother of Frederick; and he likewise attached himself to Frederick.
