At the Pope's request the envoys were conducted by the Dauphin through the mountains as far as Lausanne.

units.la: Eduardus autem rex Angliæ valentissimus, renouato contra Philippū prædictum regem Franciæ odio antiquo prætendens, se verum regni hæredē, habitis tractatibus cum Flandrensibus, duce Brabantiæ, comitibus Hollandiæ, Gelriæ, Iuliacensi, Montium, & alijs inferiorum partium magnatibus, qualiter posset ipsum Francū inuadere, cogitauit. Quamuis autē ijdem principes Aquilonis ipsum Francum ipsis graue, exosum haberēt: cū tamen omnes quasi eius essent vasalli, nisi ab Imperatore mouerentur, cuius essent homines ligij, inuadendi eū cum honore occasionem aliquam non habebant. Et ecce rex Angliæ cum reuerentia accedens Principem in villa Rens, super Rhenum sibi facto homagio, colligauit se eidem. Princeps verò ipsum regem, datis super eo literis Imperialibus, generalem Vicarium per Germaniam & Teutoniam deputauit. Scripsit quoq; literas Princeps regi Franciæ, quem Philippum de Valesio nominauit, quòd ab occupatione terrarū Imperij desisteret, ac fideli Imperij Eduardo regi Angliæ, principi suo dilecto super querelis suis iustitiam faceret coram ipso principe: alioquin cùm ipse Philippus feuda quæ teneret ab Imperio, nō recognouisset sicut rex Angliæ, ipsi Eduardo assistere cogeretur in quantum iustitia persuaderet, & diffidare Philippum. Quo diffidato, & monitis inferioribus Principibus, vt assi-
units.tr: King Edward of England, the most powerful of kings, renewing his old hatred against Philip, the aforesaid king of France, and claiming to be the true heir of the kingdom, considered how he might invade the Frenchman, having held negotiations with the Flemings, the duke of Brabant, the counts of Holland, Guelders, Jülich and Mons, and other magnates of the lower regions. Although these northern princes held the Frenchman in dislike and hatred as a burden to themselves, yet since they were almost all his vassals, and since they were bound as liege men to the Emperor, they had no honourable occasion to invade him unless the Emperor moved them. And so the king of England, approaching the prince with reverence at the town of Rhens on the Rhine, did homage to him and allied himself to him. The prince, by imperial letters issued for this purpose, appointed the king his vicar general throughout Germany and Teutonia. The prince also wrote to the king of France, whom he called Philip of Valois, that he should desist from occupying the lands of the Empire, and should do justice before the prince himself to Edward, king of England, the loyal supporter of the Empire and his beloved prince, concerning his complaints. Otherwise, since Philip had not acknowledged the fiefs he held of the Empire, as the king of England had, the prince would compel Edward's support so far as justice required, and would defy Philip. Once Philip was defied, and the lesser princes had been warned to adhere to the Empire, as they were bound to do,

units.la: NB. fterent imperio, vt tenerentur: omnes ijdem principes sunt regi Angliæ colligati. De qua diffidatione Papa Benedictus, ea intellecta, multum iocundabatur.
units.tr: N.B. (they were bound to adhere to the Empire): all these same princes were allied to the king of England. Pope Benedict, when he learned of this defiance, rejoiced greatly.

units.la: Dedit autem rex Angliæ Ludouico principi lxxx milia aureorum, & in duplo tantum, vt cum eo cum magno exercitu terram accederet Franciæ, quod eidem promisit. Fuit autem rex Angliæ recens, & paratus Franciam visitare: sed ex persuasione & astutia Principis, simulantis se illico progredi, non iuerunt. Rex autem Franciæ timens eorum aduentum, se in finibus regni sui versus Flandriam posuit, cum xxx milibus galeatis, decem hebdomadis eorum expectans aduentum, nunquam in aliqua parte terram inimicorum attingens, sed quolibet die duos florenos pro quolibet galeato expendens, exceptis equorum perditionibus, & alijs damnis, ita quod brigarum {10}sarcinam didicit inconsuetam.
units.tr: The king of England gave Prince Louis eighty thousand gold coins, and twice as much again, so that he would come into the land of France with a great army, which the prince promised him. The king of England was ready and eager to visit France, but through the persuasion and cunning of the prince, who pretended that he would set out at once, they did not go. The king of France, fearing their arrival, posted himself with thirty thousand men-at-arms on the borders of his kingdom towards Flanders, waiting ten weeks for their coming. They never entered enemy territory anywhere, but each day he spent two florins for each man-at-arms, apart from the loss of horses and other damages, so that he learned the unaccustomed burden of war.

units.la: Sequenti autem anno rex Angliæ se simulans non iturum in Franciam, cum duodecim galeatorum milibus est ingressus, terramque ipsam per xl miliaria in circuitu ignis incendio, & alias crudeliter vastauit, multasque munitiones non bene fortes funditus demoliuit: Ludouico Marchione de Brandenburg filio Imperatoris, qui tunc eidem regi cum centum galeatis aderat, in ipso exercitu cum incendiarijs regē continuè precedente. A Parisijs autem ipsius Angli exercitus minus vna diæta distabat, quem Francus cum xxx equitum milibus, & omni sua multitudine aggredi non audebat. Et cum ipse Anglus conflictum diebus aliquot expectassets, tandem præ carentia victualium illæsus recessit. {20}
units.tr: In the following year the king of England, pretending that he would not go into France, entered it with twelve thousand men-at-arms. He laid waste that land for forty miles around with fire and in other cruel ways, and utterly demolished many fortifications that were not very strong. Louis, margrave of Brandenburg, son of the Emperor, who was then with the king with a hundred men-at-arms, was in that same army, with incendiaries always going ahead of the king. The English army was less than a day's journey from Paris, but the Frenchman did not dare to attack it with thirty thousand horsemen and all his host. When the Englishman had waited some days for battle, at last, for lack of provisions, he withdrew unharmed.

units.la: Tertio autem anno, rex Angliæ cum omni potentia Flandrensium, & præscriptorum Aquilonis principum se parans, Principi Ludouico pecuniam sibi promissam aliquot diebus post terminum statutum in oppidum Franckfurt destinauit, deside rans eum secum propria in persona transiturum. Princeps autem prætendens lapsum termini, & pactum partium de amittēdo iam datam pecuniam, cum liberatione promisi, nisi intra terminum præfixum pecunia soluereture: pecuniam remisit eandem: prætendens etiam se non cum quingentis galeatis, prout rex exegerat, sed cum duobus milibus sub expensis regis, prout conuētum attulerat, & prout deceret Principem, transiturum: sicque conquerete rege de ipso Principe secundum quosdam, secundum alios ipsis occulte in vnum concordantibus, princeps cum magno vituperio, Alemanorum in partibus remansit. Anglus vero cum prædictis principibus & Flandrensibus ciuitatem Tornacensem regis Franciæ pluribus mensibus potēter obsedit. Francus vero se ponens in vicino, cum maxima hominum multitudine, Angli exercitum non inuasit. Habuit enim Anglus, exceptis equitibus, ter centum millia peditum armatorum. Et post multa discrimina, relicta quondam comitis Holandiæ Monialis, soror Franci, mater comitis Hollandiæ, socrus Ludouici principis, Angli & comitis Iuliacensis de vno exercitu in alium sæpe transiens, treugas ad triennium inter Francum & Anglum & eorum consortes, cum difficultate maxima ordinauit. Dixit autem Papa Benedictus de Franco: Iste pacem noluit, & elongabitur ab eo. {30}
units.tr: In the third year, the king of England, preparing himself with all the forces of the Flemings and the aforementioned northern princes, sent the money promised to Prince Ludwig to the town of Frankfurt, some days after the appointed date, wanting the prince to cross over with him in person. The prince, claiming that the term had lapsed and that the parties had agreed the money already given would be forfeited, with his promise released, unless the money was paid within the fixed term, sent the same money back. He also claimed that he would cross not with five hundred men-at-arms, as the king had demanded, but with two thousand at the king's expense, as the agreement had stated and as befitted a prince. So the king complained of the prince, according to some; according to others, they had secretly agreed together. The prince remained in the parts of Germany with great disgrace. The Englishman, with the aforementioned princes and the Flemings, besieged the city of Tournai, the king of France's, powerfully for several months. The Frenchman, encamped nearby with a very large multitude of men, did not attack the English army. The Englishman had three hundred thousand armed foot soldiers, not counting the horsemen. After many dangers, the widow of the former count of Holland, a nun, sister of the Frenchman, mother of the count of Holland, mother-in-law of Prince Ludwig, of the Englishman and of the count of Jülich, passing often from one army to the other, arranged with the greatest difficulty a truce for three years between the Frenchman and the Englishman and their allies. Pope Benedict said of the Frenchman: "He did not want peace, and he will be estranged from it."

units.la: Post hæc misit Francus nuncium & literas Imperatrici, filiæ sororis suæ, quā dominam Alemanniæ scripsit, vt inter ipsum & Principem concordiam, si posset, ordinaret, & sibi nuncium, de quo princeps consideret, de concordia attentanda destinaret. Et missis hinc inde pluries nuncijs & literis inter Principem & Francum interpositis iuramentis, & cōfectis literis, liga perpetua est firmata: in qua ipse Francus Principem cum sede apostolica reformare iurauit. Et sic Princeps per Francum, & in tota Francia, post hæc & Parisijs scriptus est & nominatus Imperator. Cum autem consiliarij Franci propter processus apostolicos anxij, dubitarent, dicebant nuncij principis: Si estis in propositio nostro, quòd processus non ligent, bene consuluistis domino nostro: sin aliter, tradidistis eūdem. Et sic Princeps commissionem Vicariatus factam regi Angliæ, in parlamento publico & literatorie reuocauit. {40}
units.tr: After this, the Frenchman sent a messenger and letters to the Empress, the daughter of his sister, whom he styled lady of Germany, asking her to arrange concord between himself and the prince, if she could, and to send him a messenger, acceptable to the prince, to attempt a reconciliation. Messengers and letters were sent back and forth between the prince and the Frenchman, oaths were interposed, documents were drawn up, and a perpetual league was confirmed, in which the Frenchman swore to reconcile the prince with the apostolic see. And so the prince was afterwards written to and named emperor by the Frenchman, and in all of France and at Paris. When the French councillors, anxious about the papal processes, hesitated, the prince's envoys said: "If you hold to our proposal, that the processes do not bind, you have served our lord well; but if otherwise, you have handed him over." And so the prince publicly, in parliament and by letter, revoked the commission of vicariate given to the king of England.

units.la: Missisque interim sæpius nuncijs Imperatoris, vnà cum legatis & literis Franci, ad Papam, pro reformatione Principis, Papa Benedictus nunquam Ludouicum principem ad arbitrium Franci, nunc hæreticum, nunc Christianissimum haberi debere, respondit: Et protracto varijs occasionib. negotio: Francus (vt credebatur) quod noluisset, simulauit se velle: Benedictus vero, quod voluisset, simulauit se nolle. Interim conuenientes in villa Rens super Rhenum Imperator & Principes electores, confectis desuper literis & iuramentis prestitis, quod Imperium & eius iura contra omnes, nullo excepto, manu tenerent, & ad ipsum omnes quos possent, arctarent, nulla absolutione vel quauis occasione obstante, firmarunt. Post haec Ludouicus princeps, anno Domini M. CCC. XXXVIII, regni sui XXIIII, imperij vero XI, die octaua mensis Augusti, in Franckfurt vocata Curia, decretum quoddam, de consilio quorundam fratrum Minorum, confectum, sub sigillo suo magno, edidit: in quo & inter alia declarauit, processus quondam domini Ioannis Papae nullos: & quod Papa non posset contra Imperatorem talia attentare, cum iurisdictiones sint distinctae, ianuis suae Curiae affigebat, cum iurium approbatione: vbi & praecepit per principes inuadere praedicatores. Quarum copiam & coniurationis principium cum Papae tulisset, exponendo, episcopu Argentinensem non posse plus resistere Principi suo, quo minus ab eo Regalia, faciendo homagium, recognoscat: ipse visus durè loqui de Principe, cum à me audiuisset benignum sermonem, suum principe plus extulisse, quam si ei centum millia marcarū dedisset, Papa vltra modū ridens dixit: O vult ergo pro beneficio malū reddere. Ex quo risu apparuit, quod ex corde verborū duritia nō processit.
units.tr: Meanwhile, the emperor's messengers, together with the Frenchman's envoys and letters, were often sent to the Pope for the reconciliation of the prince. Pope Benedict replied that Prince Ludwig should never be held, at the Frenchman's discretion, now a heretic, now most Christian. The business being drawn out by various pretexts, the Frenchman (as was believed) pretended to will what he had not wanted, and Benedict pretended not to will what he had wanted. Meanwhile the emperor and the electoral princes met at Rhens on the Rhine; letters were drawn up and oaths sworn that they would uphold the empire and its rights against all, none excepted, and would bind to it all whom they could, no absolution or any other pretext standing in the way; and they confirmed it. After this, Prince Ludwig, in the year of the Lord 1338, the twenty-fourth of his reign and the eleventh of his empire, on the eighth day of August, with the court summoned at Frankfurt, issued a decree drawn up on the advice of certain Franciscan friars and sealed with his great seal. In it he declared, among other things, that the processes of the late lord Pope John were null, and that the Pope could not attempt such things against the emperor, since the jurisdictions are distinct. He had it posted on the doors of his court, with the approval of the laws, and there he also ordered the princes to attack the preachers. The Pope had been given a copy of this and the beginning of the conspiracy, with the explanation that the bishop of Strasbourg could no longer resist his prince, so as not to acknowledge the regalia from him by doing homage. The bishop seemed to speak harshly of the prince, but when he heard a kindly word from me, he praised his prince more than if he had given him a hundred thousand marks. The Pope, laughing excessively, said: "Oh, so he wants to repay kindness with evil." From this laughter it appeared that the harshness of the words did not come from the heart.

units.la: Obijt autem Heinricus dux Bauariae, gener Ioannis Bohemi, relinquens filium paruulū: quo breuiter mortuo, Princeps totā eius terrā, scilicet inferiorem Bauariam, excepta parte, in qua matri Henrici relictus vsufructus ad tempus vitae, illico occupauit: quod nō solum Bohemus, sed & Australes aegrè tulerunt. Duo enim filij quondam Ottonis ducis Austriae, qui fuerant filij sororis praedicti Henrici Bauariae, ad terram aspirabant eandem. Rex autem Cracouiae, qui praedictam relictam etiam non visam, marito viuente amauit, assumpto sibi Bohemo patre, causa videndi ipsam, in Bauariam est profectus, quam inuenerat infirmantem. Ingrediens autem pater, rogauit eam, vt aduenam Cracouium, eam diligentem, salutaret benignè. De quo Cracouio quasi gentili illa probissima valde territa, cum cum salutasset, se vertens ad parietem, nullo verbo dicto amplius, expirauit, cuius terram Princeps similiter occupauit. Histriones autem quidam, super praedictorum nece Bauarorum, intoxicationis fraudem Principi impingebant.
units.tr: Duke Henry of Bavaria, son-in-law of John of Bohemia, died, leaving a young son. When he too soon died, the prince at once seized his whole land, namely Lower Bavaria, except the part in which the life usufruct was left to Henry's mother. This the Bohemians and the Austrians bore with difficulty, not only the Bohemians. For the two sons of the late Duke Otto of Austria, who had been sons of the sister of the aforesaid Henry of Bavaria, aspired to the same land. The king of Kraków, who had loved the aforesaid widow even unseen while her husband was alive, took the Bohemian father with him and went to Bavaria to see her, and found her sick. The father, entering, asked her to greet kindly the newcomer from Kraków, who loved her. The most honourable woman, greatly frightened of that Kraków man as if of a heathen, when she had greeted him, turned to the wall, spoke no further word, and died; and the prince likewise seized her land. Certain buffoons, concerning the deaths of the Bavarians, charged the prince with the fraud of poisoning.

units.la: Eo autem tempore quo Princeps & Anglus amicitiam contraxerant, vt praefertur, actum est quòd filia pulcherrima nouennis Angli, quae ob hoc Monacū missa fuerat, & diu ibi morabatur nuptui dari debere Friderico, filio quodam Ottonis ducis Austriae, cui Princeps de pecunia sibi per Anglū data, dare debuisset XL millia florenorū. Quasi cū non daret, nec Fridericus eam traduceret, Anglus filiā reassumpsit, de quo cum improperaretur, Australibus iterū missis ab Austria in Angliam nuncijs, de eisdē nuptijs est tractatum. Actum etiā fuerat, quòd filia principis nubere deberet Lupoldo Australi, eiusdē Ottonis filio iuueni: verum illi duo fratres vnus post alterū obierunt.
units.tr: At the time when the prince and the Englishman had made their friendship, as has been said, it was agreed that the most beautiful nine-year-old daughter of the Englishman, who had been sent to Munich for this purpose and had long stayed there, should be given in marriage to Frederick, a son of Duke Otto of Austria, to whom the prince, out of the money given him by the Englishman, ought to have paid forty thousand florins. As he did not pay, and Frederick did not bring her over, the Englishman took back his daughter. When he was reproached for this, envoys were again sent from Austria to England, and the same marriage was discussed. It had also been agreed that the prince's daughter should marry Leopold of Austria, a young son of the same Otto; but those two brothers died, one after the other.

units.la: Item eo tempore duces Austriae obierunt, ita quòd de Australibus nemo remansit, nec Albertus arthritide in manibus & pedibus cōtractus, qui ex Ioanna de Phirtconiuge sua Rudolfum filiū paruulum habuit, qui cū non crederetur eius Cōtracti filius, ipse tamen Albertus suū fecit filium esse & sermonibus praedicari. Cùm autē Ludouicus princeps aspirare ad ducatū Austriae diceretur: idē Albertus ac Carolus marchio Morauiae Bohemus, de pdicto Rudolfo puero & filia Marchionis spōsalia cōtraxerūt.
units.tr: At that time the dukes of Austria also died, so that none of the Austrians remained, nor Albert, who was crippled in hands and feet with arthritis and who had a young son, Rudolf, by his wife Joanna of Pfirt. Although the boy was not believed to be the son of this crippled father, Albert nevertheless had him declared his son and proclaimed in speech. Since Prince Ludwig was said to aspire to the duchy of Austria, the same Albert and Charles, margrave of Moravia, a Bohemian, arranged a betrothal between the said boy Rudolf and the margrave's daughter.

units.la: Cùm autem Rupertus rex Siciliae imò Apuliae non haberet filium, misit ad Carolum regem Hungariae, fratruelem suum, vt sibi vnum de filijs suis destinaret, post se dominia sua obtenturum, recognoscens se eundem Carolum supplantasse. Missō itaq; Andrea Hungari filio, Robertus ei neptem suam ex filio copulauit. Mortuo autem eodem Carolo quarto Hūgaro, successit ei filius primogenitus Carolus quintus: idemq; Carolus quintus rex Hungariae filiam Caroli marchionis Morauiae duxit in vxorem. Obierat autem sine liberis masculis, vxor Ludouici marchionis de Brandenburg, primogeniti Principis, quae fuit filia regis Daciae.
units.tr: Since Robert, king of Sicily, or rather of Apulia, had no son, he sent to Charles, king of Hungary, his cousin, asking him to send one of his sons to obtain his dominions after him, acknowledging that he had supplanted the same Charles. Andrew, son of the Hungarian, having been sent, Robert joined him in marriage to his granddaughter through a son. When the same Charles the Fourth of Hungary died, his eldest son, Charles the Fifth, succeeded him, and this same Charles the Fifth, king of Hungary, married the daughter of Charles, margrave of Moravia. Moreover, the wife of Ludwig, margrave of Brandenburg, the eldest son of the prince, who was the daughter of the king of Denmark, had died without male children.

units.la: Cumq; Ioannes comes Tyrolis, filius Bohemi impotens, vxorem suam semifatuam plurimùm molestaret, inter alia eius mordedo mammillas, illa cum Baronibus suis habitis occultis tractatibus, eiecto Bohemo de comitatu, praedictum Ludouicum Marchionem de facto in maritum recepit. Sicq; Ludouicus princeps, filium Ioannis regis Bohemiæ, vxore & dominio spoliauit, inconsuetum & horribile facinus attentando. Filium namq; ad hoc maleficij genus induxit inuitum, quòd videlicet vxorē sui consanguinei in tertio gradu, non separatam ab vllo iudice ecclesiæ, ipsamq; suam consanguineam non vxorem, sed mœcham traduxit. Prætendit autem Princeps, se iuste illum à comitatu eiecisse, de quo (vt tenebatur, & vt sibi per regem Bohemiæ patrem promissum asseruit, sub cautione rehabendi ciuitatem Egram, quod non fieret) nunquam se à Principe petierit inuestiri. O idolorum seruitus auaritia, quæ tantos principes confudisti, ex quibus iterum inter Bohemos & Principem & filios suos non immeritò liuor edax, & odia suscitantur.
units.tr: Since John, count of Tyrol, the impotent son of the Bohemian, greatly troubled his semi-insane wife, biting her breasts among other cruelties, she, after secret negotiations with her barons, expelled the Bohemian from the county and received the aforesaid Margrave Ludwig as her husband in fact. And so Prince Ludwig stripped the son of John, king of Bohemia, of his wife and lordship, attempting an unusual and horrible deed. For he drew the son, against his will, into this kind of wickedness: namely, he treated the wife of his kinsman in the third degree, who had not been separated by any church judge, and treated her, his kinswoman, not as a wife but as an adulteress. The prince alleged that he had rightly expelled him from the county, the Bohemian having (as he was bound to do, and as he asserted the king of Bohemia his father had promised him, on condition that he would recover the city of Eger, which did not happen) never sought investiture from the prince. O avarice, servitude to idols, which has confounded such great princes! From these things, again, between the Bohemians and the prince and his sons, not undeservedly, devouring envy and hatreds are stirred up.

units.la: Progredior autem ad gesta sub Clemente Papa sexto, ad aliqua quæ sub Benedicto gesta sunt, reuersurus.
units.tr: I now proceed to the events under Pope Clement VI, returning afterwards to some things done under Benedict.

units.la: Mortuo namq; Ruperto Siciliæ rege, & prædicto Andrea fratre Hungari regnum comitatumq; Prouinciæ, & omnia Roberti dominia obtinente, eoque apud Papam Clementem pro coronatione laborante: Papa sibi cardinalem dare nisus est, curatorem: quod ille potens nimium, vilipendit. Cardinalis quoq; Petragoricensis (ex cuius sorore olim Ioannes, frater Roberti regis, reliquit filium principem Taranti, pro eodem principe in consistorio allegauit: ipsum tanquam vna linea Ruperto proximiorem, quàm fuerat Andreas, in dominijs præferendum) coronationem plurimùm impediuit. Cumq; ipse Andreas eadem dominia annis aliquot tenuisset, tandem missis Papæ, per regem Hungariæ, fratrem Andreæ, octoginta milibus florenorum, pro coronatione Andreæ, cùm crederet coronari debere: nocte Neapoli, cùm ipse Andreas in camera sua iam ingredi vellet lectum, quidam vocantes eum, dicebant, sibi de fratre suo nuncios destinatos. Quos cùm in crastinum expectare iuberet, & illi pro eius egressu instarent, vxor Andreæ ipsum egredi incitauit. Quo egresso de camera, illi mittentes laqueum in collum regis Andreæ, ipsum crudeliter iugulauerunt, ipsum etiam præcipitantes de muro. Nutrix autem eius, quam de Hungaria secum adduxerat, quæ frequenter reginæ aderat, de mora reuersionis Andreæ aitædiata, egressa cameram, cùm neminem inuenisset, prospiciens per fenestram, videbatur sibi videre regem in terra iacentem, ac territa dicens, Domine: ac repentè descendens, ipsum reperit iugulatum. De quo crimine non solùm vxor & princeps Taranti, sed & Papa & aliqui Cardinalium tenebantur suspecti. Factum est autem hoc facinus, anno Domini, M. CCC. XLV. Sed quid ex hoc sequutum sit, referuans, regrediot ad priora.
units.tr: For when Robert, king of Sicily, had died, and the aforementioned Andrew, brother of the king of Hungary, had obtained the kingdom, the county of Provence, and all of Robert's dominions, and was labouring with Pope Clement for his coronation, the Pope tried to give him a cardinal as guardian, which Andrew, being very powerful, scorned. The Cardinal of Périgord also greatly hindered the coronation. (On behalf of the prince of Taranto, son of John, King Robert's brother, who had left a son by the Cardinal's sister, he argued in consistory that the prince, being one line nearer to Robert than Andrew was, should be preferred in the dominions.) When Andrew had held those dominions for some years, at last, through his brother, the king of Hungary, he sent eighty thousand florins to the Pope for Andrew's coronation, since he believed he ought to be crowned. But one night at Naples, when Andrew himself was about to go into his bedchamber, certain men calling to him said that messengers had been sent to him from his brother. When he ordered them to wait until the morning, and they pressed him to come out, Andrew's wife urged him to go out. As he went out of the chamber, they put a noose around the neck of King Andrew, strangled him cruelly, and threw him down from the wall. His nurse, whom he had brought with him from Hungary and who often attended the queen, was disturbed by the delay of Andrew's return. Going out of the chamber and finding no one, she looked out of the window and seemed to see the king lying on the ground. Terrified, she cried, "Lord!", and running down at once, she found him strangled. Suspicion of this crime fell not only on the wife and the prince of Taranto, but also on the Pope and some of the cardinals. This deed was done in the year of the Lord 1345. But what followed from it I will reserve, and return to earlier matters.

units.la: Temporibus prædictis erant duo fratres Delphini Viennenses, nepotes Caroli tertij regis Apuliæ, ex filia, & pronepotes quondam Rudolphi Romanorum regis: quorum iunior Humbertus nomine, ducens filiam sororis Roberti regis, fratris prædicti Caroli, cum ipso Roberto Neapoli morabatur. Socer autem prædicti Humberti, quem vxor eius clam receperat, Comes Nouellus à nouitate est dictus. Orta est autem briga durissima inter Delphinum seniorem, & Aimonem comitem Sabaudiæ, & tempore Ioannis Papæ multis annis durans: ac tandem Delphino per iaculum in cuiusdam castri prædicti Comitis obsidione occiso, Humbertus frater eius dominiū Delphinatus nanciscens, ita Aimoni comiti reformabatur, quòd pro maiori cautela quilibet eorum vasallus alterius est effectus, sicq; inter eos briga cessauit. Hic Humbertus bene literatus, liberis carens, faciem quasi muliebrem habens, plus sermonibus & studijs, quàm militiæ insistebat. Hunc Benedictus Papa diligens, statim promoto Curiam suam Auinionem dedit eidem. Et quia Papa regi Franciæ exosus erat, multū in Delphini defensione confidit. Cùm autem Papa quandam terram Delphini, vicinam Curiæ, ab eo emisset, si fine liberis decederet, ad Romanam sedem deuoluendam, pro quinque millibus florenorum, ipsiq; Delphino pro vita sua castrum pontis Sorgiæ assignasset, recepta pecunia: homines terræ illius cùm consentire nollent, distracto contractu pecunia Delphino ferè tota remansit.
units.tr: In the times mentioned, there were two brothers, the Dauphins of Vienne, nephews through their mother of Charles III, king of Apulia, and great-grandsons of the late Rudolf, king of the Romans. The younger, named Humbert, who had married the daughter of the sister of King Robert, brother of the aforementioned Charles, lived with Robert at Naples. Humbert's father-in-law, whom his wife had secretly received, was called Count Novellus from his recent rise. A most bitter quarrel arose between the elder Dauphin and Aimo, Count of Savoy, which lasted for many years in the time of Pope John. At last the Dauphin was killed by a javelin during a siege of a castle belonging to the Count. Humbert, his brother, obtained the lordship of Dauphiné and was reconciled to Count Aimo, on such terms that, for greater security, each of them became the vassal of the other, and so the quarrel between them ceased. This Humbert was well educated, had no children, and had an almost womanly face; he devoted himself more to words and studies than to warfare. Pope Benedict, who loved him, soon promoted him and gave him his court at Avignon. And because the Pope was hateful to the king of France, he put great trust in the Dauphin's protection. When the Pope had bought from him a certain land of the Dauphin's near the Curia, to fall to the Roman see if he died without children, for five thousand florins, and had assigned to the Dauphin, for his life, the castle of Pont-de-Sorgue, the money having been received, the men of that land refused to consent. The contract being annulled, almost all the money remained with the Dauphin.

units.la: Misit autem rex Franciæ pro Delphino: qui cum bona fide ad Curiam regis venisset, quidam eum salutans in transitu, dixit ei: Facite quicquid petetur à vobis, vel perpetuò estis tentus. Ductus autem Delphinus ad cameram regis, in præsentia consilij audiuit à rege: Auuncule, cupio quòd recipias pecuniam, & sis seruitor meus, annuens omnibus factis meis. Ad quod respondit Delphinus: Domine, cum sitis consanguineus & promotor meus, alias in omnibus vobis consentirem: ex quo ergo largitatem vestram mihi ostenditis, feruenter in omnibus vobis astringar. Rex autem grates ei referens, & annuos redditus eidem promittens, dixit: Cum intendam villam Viennensem citra Rhodanum circundare muro, rogo quod tibi placeat? Cui ille: Non solum illud, sed quicquid volueritis placet. Delphino itaque euadente, rex illico ex opposito Viennae ciuitatem construxit, turrim in ponte ponendo, quod ante prae Delphinis aggredi non audebat.
units.tr: The king of France sent for the Dauphin. When he had come in good faith to the king's court, someone greeting him in passing said, "Do whatever is asked of you, or you are bound forever." The Dauphin was then led into the king's chamber, and in the presence of the council heard the king say, "Nephew, I wish you to accept money and be my servant, agreeing to all my acts." The Dauphin replied, "Sire, since you are my kinsman and patron, I would otherwise consent to everything for you; since you now show me your generosity, I am bound to you in all things with eagerness." The king thanked him and promised him an annual income, and said, "Since I intend to surround the town of Vienne on this side of the Rhône with a wall, what do you wish me to do?" He answered, "Not only that, but whatever you wish pleases me." Thus, with the Dauphin yielding, the king at once built a town opposite Vienne, placing a tower on the bridge, which previously the Dauphins had not dared to attack.

units.la: Post haec idem rex cum auxilio archiepiscopi Viennensis attrahere conabatur Vi-ennam. Veniens autem Delphinus, archiepiscopum expulit. Transeuntes autem ministri regis, dixerunt Delphino: Domine, factum archiepiscopi est facto regis. Quibus ille: Satis habet agere rex vester, vehementer abite: & sic dolus regis est impeditus. Post haec tempore Clementis Papae sexti, cuius & regis Francie vnum cor erat, actum est, quod terra Delphini post mortem eius liberis caretis, pro multa pecunia data & promissa, ad regem devolui deberet: quae tamen terra quasi tota ab Imperio detinetur. Temporibus praedictis rex Lithuaniae gentilis, iuuenis & recens, tempore ipsius Clementis, fratres Teutonicos sanctae Mariae in Prussia & Liuonia plurimum infestauit, multa Christianorum millia occidendo, & conuersos ad fidem reducendo in perfidiam. Venerunt autem Magistro Ordinis, sequenti anno, scilicet sub anno Domini M. CCC. XLV, in subsidium, reges Hungariae, Bohemiae, Marchio Moraviae filius Bohemi, comes Holandiae, & multi dominorum. Sed propter desidiam Magistri, de eis diffidentis, cum venissent in terram Lithuaniae, & diceretur regem Lithuaniae in Prussiam ex alia parte ingressum, reuersi sunt, & infecto negotio discesserunt. Ob quam desidiam depositio Magistro alter virilis est substitutus. Eisdem diebus comes Holandiae, iuuenis & recens, qui fuit frater Imperatricis & reginae Angliae, gener ducis Brabantiae, reuersus a Prussia, ciuitatem Vtrich longo tempore cum innumerabilibus expensis, in odium Frisonum, potenter obsedit. Quibus sibi cum quibusdam pactis reformatis: postea Frisiam ingrediens, a Frisonibus est occisus: cuius reliquam postea ad septem annos accepit filius Ioannis regis Bohemiae, comes de Luxelburg in uxorem. Sicque eodem anno Domini, M. CCC. XLV, ante autumnum comes Holandiae, & Andreas rex Apuliae perierunt. Eo tempore gentiles, scilicet Turci, qui & ante regnum Armeniae ad perfidiam coegerant, & terras Christianorum, scilicet Cyprum insulam, Rhodon Hospitalariorum, & alias vicinias coeperunt virtiliter infestare. Quibus Veneti, rex Cypri, Hospitalarij & alij Christicolae restiterunt: quibus etiam Delphinus cum CCCC cooperiis equis, quasi sub nomine Papae, in subsidium transfretauit: qui praedictum regem Andream Apuliae, consobrinum suum, in itinere iugulatum inuenit. Tempore Benedicti Papae, anno Domini M. CCC. XXXV, sabbato quo cantatur Charitas, cum Berchtoldus episcopus Argentinensis monuisset omnes Rectores ecclesiarum, & alios ad sacerdotium astrictos, vt ad sacros ordines ascenderet, & ob hoc conspirantibus contra eum, cum Gebhardo de Friburg praeposito, Conrado de Kirchel thesaurario, & quasi toto clero appellantibus: inter episcopum & clerum graue scandalum est subortum. Mortuo Gebhardo praeposito Argentinensi, ac Ioanne de Liechtenberg, & Vlrico de Signowe, filio sororis praedicti Berchtoldi episcopi, in discordia ad praeposituram electis, & Vlrico per episcopum, Ioanne vero postea per H. archiepiscopum Moguntinum in discordia confirmatis, C. de Kirckel & pluribus alijs prelatis habentib. rancorem contra episcopum: ecce ipse episcopus in villa Hasclach, circa media noctem per Rodolphum de Hohenstein, & suos complices familiares, C. de Kirckel & Io. de Liechtenberg, fuit captus, & primo ad castrum Waldeck, & postea ad castrum Kirckel adductus honorifice, sed tutissime est detentus, & eductus fuit nudo corpore, anno Domini M. CCC. XXXVII, quinto Non. Septemb. Quod intelligens Papa Benedictus, illico Ioanni Senepiscopo Basilien si, Argentinensis ecclesiae administrationem commisit, quia fuerat filius sororis eiusdem Berchtoldi episcopi, & contra captiuatores praedictos, per excommunicationis sententiam processit. Venit autem ijsdem temporib. Argentinā Albertus dux Austriae, episcopi cōfoederatus de Aquisgrano in peregrinatione, cuius intentio tunc fuerat ad obsidendum Nidwils rc, & alias munitiones Ioannis de Liechtenberg, & Sigismundi fratris sui, propter captiuationem prædictam: quæ obsessio fuerat obmissa, quia asseruerunt prædictum C. de Kirckel fore principalem huius facti. Tandem cum ipse episcopus xvi hebdomadis fuisset captiuatus, post multos tractatus amicorum suorum, sub multis cautionibus, fideiussoribus, & obsidibus, ac variis pactis exitit liberatus, & cum C. de Kirckel concordatus.
units.tr: After this, the same king, with the help of the archbishop of Vienne, tried to draw Vienne to himself. But the Dauphin came and drove out the archbishop. The king's officers passing by said to the Dauphin, "Lord, the archbishop's deed is the king's deed." He replied, "Your king has enough to do; go away quickly." Thus the king's plot was thwarted. After this, in the time of Pope Clement VI, whose heart and that of the king of France were one, it was agreed that the land of the Dauphin should, after his death without children, fall to the king for a large sum of money given and promised, though that land is almost entirely held by the Empire. In the same period, the heathen king of Lithuania, young and newly come to power, in the time of this same Clement, greatly harassed the Teutonic brothers of St Mary in Prussia and Livonia, killing many thousands of Christians and turning converts back to unbelief. In the following year, namely in the year of the Lord 1345, the kings of Hungary and Bohemia, the Margrave of Moravia, son of the Bohemian king, the Count of Holland, and many lords came to the aid of the Master of the Order. But because of the Master's sloth, which made them distrust him, when they came into the land of Lithuania, and it was said that the king of Lithuania had entered Prussia from another side, they turned back and departed with the business undone. Because of this sloth, the Master was deposed and a more vigorous man was put in his place. In the same days, the Count of Holland, young and newly come to power, who was the brother of the Empress and of the queen of England and son-in-law of the duke of Brabant, returning from Prussia, besieged the city of Utrecht powerfully for a long time, at great and countless expense, out of hatred of the Frisians. After certain agreements had been made with them, he entered Friesland and was killed by the Frisians; afterwards the son of John, king of Bohemia, Count of Luxemburg, obtained his widow as wife, together with her remaining dowry for seven years. Thus in the same year of the Lord 1345, before autumn, the Count of Holland and King Andrew of Apulia both perished. At that time the heathen Turks, who had earlier forced the kingdom of Armenia into unbelief, began vigorously to harass the lands of the Christians, namely the island of Cyprus, Rhodes of the Hospitallers, and other neighbouring places. The Venetians, the king of Cyprus, the Hospitallers and other Christians resisted them, and the Dauphin also crossed over to help them with four hundred armoured horse, as if under the name of the Pope. He found his cousin, King Andrew of Apulia, already strangled on the journey. In the time of Pope Benedict, in the year of the Lord 1335, on the Saturday on which the Charity is sung, when Berthold, bishop of Strasbourg, had admonished all the rectors of churches and the others bound to the priesthood to advance to the holy orders, and because of this, Conrad of Kirchel, the treasurer, and almost the whole clergy, conspiring against him with Gebhard of Freiburg, the provost, appealed; a grave scandal arose between the bishop and the clergy. When Gebhard, provost of Strasbourg, had died, John of Lichtenberg and Ulrich of Signau, son of the sister of the aforementioned Bishop Berthold, were elected to the provostship amid discord. Ulrich was confirmed by the bishop, and later John was confirmed by H., archbishop of Mainz, also amid discord. Conrad of Kirchel and several other prelates bore a grudge against the bishop, and behold, the bishop himself was seized at night, about midnight, in the village of Hasslach by Rudolf of Hohenstein and his accomplices and servants, Conrad of Kirchel and John of Lichtenberg. He was taken first to the castle of Waldeck and afterwards to the castle of Kirchel, honourably but most securely held, and was led out stripped of his clothing, in the year of the Lord 1337, on the fifth day before the Nones of September. When Pope Benedict learned of this, he at once committed the administration of the church of Strasbourg to John, bishop of Basel, because he was the son of the sister of the same Bishop Berthold, and he proceeded against the aforesaid captors by a sentence of excommunication. In those same times Albert, Duke of Austria, allied to the bishop, came to Strasbourg from Aachen on a pilgrimage; his intention then had been to besiege Nidwils and other fortresses of John of Lichtenberg and of his brother Sigismund, on account of the aforementioned seizure. That siege had been abandoned, because it was asserted that the aforesaid Conrad of Kirchel was the principal author of the deed. At last, after the bishop had been held captive for sixteen weeks, after many negotiations by his friends, under many securities, guarantors and hostages, and various agreements, he was released and reconciled with Conrad of Kirchel.

units.la: Veniente autem illis temporibus Ludouico principe Columbariam, Argentinensis & Basiliensis episcopi ipsum cum magna multitudine accesserunt, & qualiter circa episcopum Argentinensem actum fuisset, eidem enarrauerunt. Ille autem simulans se dolere, ad attrahendum eos suo seruitio insistebat. Argentinensis autem episcopus congregationem episcoporum prouinciæ Moguntinæ persuasit. Quibus sic Spiræ congregatis, ac Henrico archiepiscopo Moguntino sedis Apostolicæ prouiso, qui & ipse principi se colligauerat, ad inducendum in idipsum Argentinensem plurimum laborante: communi consilio missi sunt, Vlricus episcopus Curiensis, & Gerlacus comes de Nassowe, ex parte episcoporum Moguntinensis prouinciæ, ad Papam & Cardinales, pro reformatione principis Ludouici laborantes, quibus papa Benedictus, præ timore regis Franciæ annuere non audebat, sicq; infecto negotio celeriter ad partes suas sunt reuersi.
units.tr: When Louis the prince came to Columbaria in those times, the bishops of Strasbourg and Basel came to him with a large crowd and told him what had happened to the bishop of Strasbourg. He pretended to be sorry and kept trying to draw them into his service. The bishop of Strasbourg persuaded the bishops of the Mainz province to hold a meeting. When they had gathered at Speyer, with Henry, archbishop of Mainz, appointed by the Apostolic See (who had himself allied with the prince, while the bishop of Strasbourg worked hard to bring him into the same plan), they jointly sent Ulrich, bishop of Chur, and Gerlach, count of Nassau, on behalf of the bishops of the Mainz province, to the Pope and the cardinals, to labour for the reform of Prince Louis. Pope Benedict, however, did not dare to grant their request for fear of the king of France, so the envoys returned quickly to their own regions with the business undone.

units.la: Cùm autem Princeps & Moguntinus prædictum Berchtoldum episcopum Argentinensem ad concordandum cum ipsis, & ad recognoscendum sua Regalia à dicto principe, precibus, muneribus vel minis inducere nequiuissent, ipsi principes asserentes ipsum episcopum dixisse: Si nuntij prædicti infecto negotio à Papa reuerterentur, se velle concordare cum illis, quod tamen ipse episcopus negauit, & quòd ipsi se pro liberatione episcopi, fideiussores & obsides constituerunt, & quòd eos liberare nollet: ligæ pacis generalis Rheni inferioris acriter sunt conquesti, de quo instrumentum publicum produxerunt contra ipsum.
units.tr: Since the prince and the archbishop of Mainz could not persuade Bishop Berthold of Strasbourg, by prayers, gifts or threats, to come to terms with them and to acknowledge his regalia from the prince, they complained bitterly, as allies of the general peace of the Lower Rhine, about the bishop. They claimed that the bishop had said that if the envoys returned from the Pope with the business undone, he would be willing to come to terms with them. The bishop denied this. They also complained that they had given themselves as sureties and hostages for the bishop's release, and that he was unwilling to free them. Of this they produced a public document against him.

units.la: Præmiserat autem illis temporibus episcopus Argentinensis Papæ & Cardinalibus nuntios, & literas pro consilio & auxilio, vel quod sibi indulgeretur, quòd posset principi homagium exhibere, cùm non præsumeret se posse finaliter reluctari. Papa autem dicens, illum coronam Imperialem non à Papa recepisse, respondit, quòd si in huiusmodi consentiret homagium, per hoc posset Romanæ ecclesiæ præiudicium generari, & quòd ipse episcopus in resistendo illi, sine iactura ecclesiæ suæ faceret posse suum. Licet autem multi Cardinalium ad subueniendum episcopo feruenter instarent, Papa paruipendens factum dixit, Isti vellent, quòd facerem perire istum bonum hominem, quem scio reluctari non posse.
units.tr: At that time the bishop of Strasbourg had sent envoys and letters to the Pope and the cardinals, asking for counsel and help, or for permission to pay homage to the prince, since he did not think he could finally resist him. The Pope, however, said that the bishop had not received the imperial crown from the Pope, and replied that if he consented to such homage, this might do harm to the Roman Church; and that the bishop, in resisting Louis, should do what he could without loss to his own church. Although many of the cardinals urged eagerly that the bishop be helped, the Pope made light of the matter and said: "These men would have me let that good man perish, whom I know cannot hold out."

units.la: Tandem cùm Argentinenses & terra Mundat per aduocatum Principis, propter rebellionem episcopi Argentinensis, damnificati fuissent: ecce Argentinenses inito consilio, episcopum nisi concordaret cum principe, diffidarunt. Tunc episcopus in expensis exhaustus, à suis derelictus, metuensq; se à suis oppidis excludi, propter fauorem Argentinensium anxius, licet paulò ante in capitulo suo respondens consulibus Argentinensibus dixit, Potius se velle reuerti in Ordinem suum Teutonicum, quàm Ludouico principi homagium exhibere: de communi consilio omnium suorum fidelium, Spiram principem accedens, scrupulum conscientiæ obmittens, sibi homagium fecit, & regalium suorum abeo, tanquam Imperatore, inuestituram accepit: protestans in Principis præsentia, eo consentiente, quòd nō minùs domino suo Papæ vellet in omnibus obedire: protestans etiam ante accessum, in præsentia multorum Comitum & Baronum, quod huiusmodi homagium faceret non voluntarius, sed coactus. Sicq; in choro maioris ecclesiæ Spirensis, cum Principe & Moguntino Missas audiuit. Papa autem ob hoc episcopum Argentinensem pro excommunicato non habuit, nec eò minus causas delegandas ei scienter commisit.
units.tr: At last, when the citizens of Strasbourg and the territory of Mundat had been harmed by the prince's advocate because of the rebellion of the bishop of Strasbourg, the citizens of Strasbourg, after taking counsel, renounced their allegiance to the bishop unless he came to terms with the prince. Then the bishop, drained of money, abandoned by his own people, and fearing to be shut out of his towns, and anxious because of the favour of the citizens of Strasbourg, went to Speyer to the prince. Although shortly before, when he answered the Strasbourg magistrates in his chapter, he had said that he would rather return to his Teutonic Order than pay homage to Prince Louis, he now, by the common counsel of all his loyal followers, set aside his scruples of conscience and did homage to him, and received the investiture of his regalia from him as emperor. He protested in the prince's presence, with the prince's consent, that he would obey his lord the Pope in all things no less. He also protested before going in, in the presence of many counts and barons, that he was making this homage not willingly but under compulsion. And so he heard Mass in the choir of the cathedral of Speyer, together with the prince and the archbishop of Mainz. The Pope, however, did not on this account hold the bishop of Strasbourg to be excommunicated, nor did he any the less knowingly entrust cases to be delegated to him.

units.la: Obiit autem feliciter Benedictus Papa, octauo anno pontificatus sui, scilicet anno Domini, M. CCC. XLII, de mense Maij, & inclusis Cardinalibus per Senescha]cum prouinciæ, statim electus est, Petrus Rogerij, ordinis S. Benedicti, Cardinalis, qui fuit Rotomagensis archiepiscopus, progenie militaris, qui nominatus est Clemens sextus. Statim ergo vt electus est Petrus, sermonem faciens, & grates Deo referens, qualiter primò in diuitem Abbatem, postea in meliorem episcopatum, tertiò in optimum archiepiscopatum Franciæ promotus fuerit, & has dignitates omnes grauibus reliquerit sarcinis debitorū grauatas, & postea ad Cardinalatum, & postremò ad summam hanc dignitatem peruenerit, nutu diuino, eò quòd priora eum nutrire nequiuerant, per ordinem enarrauit. Hic ab antecessoris sui moribus multùm distans, mulierum, honorum & potentiæ cupidus, ac suorum auidus promotor, ac seipsum & Curiā de Simonia diffamans, ipse Francus Franco feruenter adhæsit. Tempore quoq; coronationis suæ, primogenito Franci, qui cum duce Burgundiæ auunculo suo aderat, magnam pecuniæ summam erogauit. Qui filius Franci, gener Bohemi, intrans Consistorium, pro rege Alemanniæ rogauit, sed in dolo.
units.tr: Pope Benedict died happily in the eighth year of his pontificate, in the year of the Lord 1342, in May. When the cardinals had been shut in by the seneschal of the province, Peter Roger, of the Order of St Benedict, cardinal and former archbishop of Rouen, of a military family, was at once elected, and took the name Clement VI. As soon as Peter was elected, he gave a speech, giving thanks to God, and went through in order how he had first been promoted to a rich abbacy, then to a better bishopric, third to the best archbishopric of France, and how he had left all these dignities burdened with heavy debts; and afterwards how he had risen to the cardinalate and at last to this supreme dignity, by the will of God, because his earlier posts had been unable to support him. He differed greatly from the ways of his predecessor, being greedy for women, honours and power, an eager promoter of his own kin, and he himself brought the papacy and the Curia into disrepute for simony. This Frenchman clung fervently to the French king. At the time of his coronation he paid out a large sum of money to the firstborn of the French king, who was present with his uncle, the duke of Burgundy. This son of the French king, the son-in-law of the King of Bohemia, entered the consistory and made a request on behalf of the king of Germany, but with deceit.

units.la: Hic Papa cum arma progeniei suę haberent quinq; rosas contra morem antecessorum, totidem rosas poni fecit in Bulla. Qui cùm adhuc esset Romomagensis, Parisijs in præsentia Franci & Bohemi, publicum sermonem faciens, ipsos contra principē, quem nominauit Baurum, animauit: interpretans nomen baurus, id est, nesciens tergere barbam, quia tantam dixit esse fœditatem oris sui, quod ipsam abijcere non valeret. Hic omnes ecclesias mundi per petitiones in immensum grauauit. Et cùm quereretur, an pauperes clerici bene examinari deberent: respondit, quòd montes & colles ipsos examinassent. Cui Papæ rex Angliæ de consilio cleri & populi Angliæ rescripsit, quòd in concessiones huius, quas ipse Papa faceret, præsertim aduenis, qui thesauros ecclesiæ deferrent, & in prouisiones prælaturarum, nullatenus consentiret: quia cùm olim reges Angliæ ecclesiarum patroni de consensu sedis Apostolicæ capitulis cōcessèrint electionē, si Papa pacta huiusmodi non seruaret, res in pristinā reuerteretur naturam.
units.tr: This Pope, whose family arms bore five roses, contrary to the custom of his predecessors, had as many roses placed on his bull. While he was still archbishop of Rouen, he gave a public speech at Paris in the presence of the French king and the King of Bohemia, stirring them up against the prince, whom he called Baurus, explaining the name Baurus as not knowing how to wipe one's beard, because, he said, the foulness of his mouth was so great that he could not rid himself of it. This Pope burdened all the churches of the world beyond measure with petitions. When someone asked whether poor clergy ought to be examined well, he answered that they had examined the mountains and hills themselves. The King of England, with the counsel of the clergy and people of England, wrote back to this Pope that he would not consent to any of the grants that the Pope himself might make, especially to foreigners who carried away the treasures of the Church, nor to the provision of prelacies. For since the kings of England, as patrons of the churches, had long ago granted the election by the consent of the Apostolic See under certain conditions, if the Pope did not keep agreements of this kind, the matter would revert to its former state.

units.la: Simulauit autem Papa se reformationem principis affectare: missisq; iterum atq; iterum nuncijs per Principem ad Papam & ad regem Franciæ, illoq; literis & nuncijs intercedente pro ipso, sed vt videbatur in dolo: legati verbis diu tenti, finem habere nō valentes, infecto negotio sunt reuersi. Papa autem munitionem literis ostijs ecclesiæ Auinionensis affixit, contra principem, vt vsq; ad certum diem satisfaceret Deo & ecclesiæ, & ab occupatione iurium Imperij desisteret, & plura alia faceret sub grauium comminatione pœnarum. In quo termino, in Consistorio, & crastino similiter, Latinè & Teutonicè clamari fecit, si aliquis adesset pro Ludouico de Bauaria: nemine tamē comparente. Et licet contra eum intendisset acriter procedere: tamen ipsum Ludouicum reputauit solummodo contumacem. Scripsit etiam princeps Franco, cùm certum esset Papam ad nutum suum regi, si quid contra se fieret, hoc à Franco haberet, & secundum hoc se regeret: & ipse princeps literas Franci principibus ostendebat. Vnde pro tunc Francus scripsit Papæ, quòd nullatenus procederet contra Ludouicū.
units.tr: The Pope, however, pretended to be aiming at the reform of the prince. Envoys were sent again and again by the prince to the Pope and to the king of France, and while the king and the envoys interceded for him in letters and messages, it seemed to be done with deceit. The envoys were long kept with words, and since they could not get an end to it, they returned with the business undone. The Pope then affixed to the doors of the church of Avignon a written warning against the prince, that by a certain day he should make satisfaction to God and the Church, and desist from seizing the rights of the Empire, and do many other things, under threat of severe penalties. Within that time, in the consistory and likewise the next day, he had it proclaimed in Latin and German whether anyone was present to speak for Louis of Bavaria; yet no one appeared. And although he had intended to proceed sharply against him, he nevertheless regarded Louis only as contumacious. The prince also wrote to Philip of France, since it was certain that the Pope would do whatever the king bade, and that if anything were done against him, the Pope would have it from Philip and would govern himself accordingly; and the prince showed the letters of Philip to the princes. Therefore at that time Philip wrote to the Pope that he should on no account proceed against Louis.

units.la: Missisq; iterum per principem literis & nuncijs ad Curiam & ad Francū, ad iscitandum causam impedimenti reformationis, cùm ipse paratus esset omnia facere quæ sibi iniungerentur à Papa: datoq; responso per Francum, quod diceretur per Papam, quòd non peteret eo modo gratiam, quam deberet. Nuncijsq; (prout in mandatis habebant) dicentibus, quòd daretur eis forma Procuratorij, Papæ placens, secundum quam, qualiscunq; esset, se petituros, dicebant. Conceptumq; est procuratorium turpissimum & rigidissimum, quod non credebant Ludouicū sigillaturum, etiamsi captus fuisset. Dabatur enim in eo potestas, Humberto Delphino, auunculo principis, item Augustensis & Babenbergensis ecclesiarum præpositis, item M. Vlrico cancellario suo, in solidum confitendi omnes errores & hæreses. Item resignandi imperium, nec resumendi, nisi hoc fieret de gratia Papæ, & se ac filios suos, ac bona, ac statū suum in manus & voluntatē Papę ponendi, & multa insolita faciedi. Verùm Princeps mandatum huiusmodi non solùm sigillauit, sed etiam corā tabellione, misso per Papam, se seruaturum, necreuocaturum iurauit. De quo Papa ipse & Collegium mirabantur, dicentes intra se: iste homo diffidentia est perplexus. Illisq; quatuor procuratoribus juxta formam mandati iurantibus, ac pro articulis iniunctionis & pœnitentiæ denuò instantibus, nec sine articulis abire volentibus: tandem Papa de consilio Collegij, articulos quos principem facere voluit, qui non tangebant personam eius, sed statum Imperij, assignauit. Quibus articulis principi præsentatis, ipse eorum copiā vniuersis. Principibus, praesertim Electoribus & magnis ciuitatibus destinauit, omnes principes & ciuitates & oppida totius Alemanniae ad Parlamentum publicum super eiusmodi facto in Franckfort conuocando. Electores autem Principes, & inferiorum partium magnates, octo diebus ante huiusmodi terminum Coloniae conuenerunt, huiusmodi articulis se opponere concorditer decernentes.
units.tr: The prince again sent letters and envoys to the Curia and to Philip, to inquire into the cause of the obstacle to reform, since he himself was ready to do everything that the Pope might enjoin on him. The reply came through Philip that it was said by the Pope that the prince did not seek grace in the manner he ought. The envoys, as they had been instructed, said that they were given a form of procuration pleasing to the Pope, and that they would seek according to it, whatever it was. A procuration was drawn up that was most shameful and most rigorous, which they did not think Louis would seal, even if he were captured. For in it power was given to Humbert, dauphin, the uncle of the prince, likewise to the provosts of the churches of Augsburg and Bamberg, and to Master Ulrich, his chancellor, to confess in full all errors and heresies; likewise to resign the empire, and not to resume it except by the grace of the Pope; and to place himself, his sons, his goods and his estate in the hands and will of the Pope, and to do many unusual things. But the prince not only sealed this mandate, but also swore before a notary sent by the Pope that he would keep it and would not revoke it. The Pope himself and the College marvelled at this, saying among themselves: "This man is perplexed by distrust." When the four procurators, according to the form of the mandate, swore and kept insisting on the articles of injunction and penance, and would not leave without articles, at last the Pope, with the counsel of the College, assigned the articles which he wished the prince to accept. These did not touch his person but the state of the Empire. When the articles had been presented to the prince, he sent copies of them to all the princes, especially the electors and the great cities, summoning all the princes, cities and towns of the whole of Germany to a public parliament on this matter at Frankfurt. The electors, princes and magnates of the lower regions, however, met at Cologne eight days before that date and decided by common agreement to oppose these articles.

units.la: Conuenientibus autem in Franckfurt principum & magnatum & ciuitatum, & oppidorum imperialium nuntijs, scilicet sub anno Domini M. CCC. XLIIII, de mense Septembri, & quaerente Principe de ciuitatibus Aquensi, Augustensi & Vberlingensi & aliis, si adessent: & dicto quod sic, & auscultantibus omnibus: Magister Wigkerus protonotarius archiepiscopi Treuerensis iussus per Principem, sic incepit. Gratiose Domine, Domini nostri Principes, Electores, & alij Imperij fideles, pridem Coloniae congregati, recensentes articulos reformationis vestrae, quos Papa requirit, & in quibus intentio apostolicae sedis resedit, concorditer decreuerant, illos articulos in perniciem & destructionem Imperij esse conceptos: & quod nec vos, nec ipsi, virtute iuramenti imperio praestiti, annuere valeatis, & quod ipsi nuncios & literas dirigere velint, Papae & collegio, ut ab his desistant. Quod si nolint, iam aliud terminum in Rens super Rhenum, ad octo dies statuerunt, vbi vobiscum deliberare volunt, qualiter in eventu tali huiusmodi conatibus resistatur.
units.tr: When the envoys of the princes, the magnates, and the imperial cities and towns had gathered at Frankfurt in September of the year of the Lord 1344, the Prince asked the envoys of Aachen, Augsburg, Überlingen and the others whether they were present. When they said that they were, and everyone was listening, the Prince ordered Master Wigker, protonotary of the archbishop of Trier, to begin. He spoke as follows: "Gracious lord, our lords the princes, electors, and other faithful of the Empire, who previously met at Cologne, reviewed the articles of reform that the Pope demands and in which the intention of the Apostolic See lies. They had agreed that these articles were framed for the ruin and destruction of the Empire, and that neither you nor they could consent to them, given the oath sworn to the Empire. They wish to send messengers and letters to the Pope and the college of cardinals, asking them to desist. If they will not, the princes have already set another meeting at Rhens on the Rhine, eight days from now, where they wish to deliberate with you on how such attempts can be resisted if they happen."

units.la: Quo dicto pro illum finito, quaesiuit ipse protonotarius à Moguntino praesente, & à legatis aliorum principum, si ita esset in facto: illisque respondentibus; ita esse: dixit Princeps nuncijs ciuitatum: Vos audistis decretum & consilium principum. Vos igitur nunci exite, nobisque vestram deliberationem referte. Illiq; exeuntes, diuq; deliberantes, ad principes redierunt, & per ciuem Moguntinum de mandato omnium taliter responderunt. Domine (notando Principe) Ciuitates aduerterunt, qualiter Papa cum articulis ad laesionem Imperij nititur. Et cum ciuitates non possint stare nisi cum Imperio, & imperij laesio earum sit destructio: si dominus Papa in talibus persistere vellet, nos inopes omnibus vijs, quas cogitauerunt domini principes Imperij, ad manutenendum iura, honorem & integritatem Imperij, erimus obedire & manu tenere parati. Et quaerente illo ciue à nuncijs, si ita esset, omnibusque nuncijs dicentibus, quod sic: Princeps grates multiplices referens, ait illis: Post octo dies ego & principes conueniemus in Rens super Rhenum, & auunculus noster Carolus marchio Morauiae, & deliberationem nostram cum vobis scripserimus, circa honorem nostrum & Imperij (vt confidimus) faciatis: qui hoc facere concorditer promiserunt.
units.tr: When this speech was finished, the protonotary asked the Archbishop of Mainz, who was present, and the legates of the other princes whether the matter was as stated. When they answered that it was, the Prince said to the envoys of the cities: "You have heard the decision and the advice of the princes. Go out, then, envoys, and bring us back your deliberation." They went out, deliberated at length, and returned to the princes, and through a citizen of Mainz they gave the answer on behalf of all: "Lord" (here the Prince was addressed), "the cities have noted how the Pope is striving with these articles to injure the Empire. Since the cities cannot exist except with the Empire, and injury to the Empire would be their destruction, if the lord Pope were to persist in such things, we, having no means at all except those which the lords princes of the Empire have devised for maintaining the rights, honour and integrity of the Empire, are ready to obey and to support them." When that citizen asked the envoys whether this was so, and all the envoys said that it was, the Prince, giving many thanks, said to them: "After eight days I and the princes will meet at Rhens on the Rhine, and our uncle Charles, margrave of Moravia, will write to you our deliberation. Do what is needed, as we trust, for our honour and that of the Empire." They promised together to do so.

units.la: Post haec conuenientibus Principibus in Rens, & de scribendo Papae conferentibus: Princeps & Bohemus cum filio suo, cum super laesionibus illis factis concordare non possent, in inuidia discesserunt. Nuncij autem principum cum Papae contradictionem articulorum referrent, nec tractandi de aliquo mandatum haberent: Papa cogitans se delusum, maiore dolo & inuidia contra Principem mouebatur, cum Bohemo & filio, ac Treuerensi eorum patruo, ad perpetuum Principis & liberorum suorum exterminium cogitando, qui conceptus biennio parturiens, fecit abortum. 40
units.tr: After this, when the princes had met at Rhens and were conferring about writing to the Pope, the Prince and the Bohemian with his son could not agree about those injuries that had been done, and they departed in enmity. Meanwhile the envoys of the princes reported the Pope's rejection of the articles, and they had no mandate to treat about anything. The Pope, thinking himself deceived, was moved with greater guile and hatred against the Prince, plotting with the Bohemian and his son, and with Trier, their paternal uncle, the utter destruction of the Prince and his children. This scheme, conceived two years earlier, was in labour and produced a miscarriage. 40

units.la: Post haec Eduardus Anglus Papae & Collegio scribens, se Franciae & Angliae regem, ac dominum Hiberniae, qualiter Philippus de Valesio occupator regni Franciae, ipsi Anglo iure hereditario tanquam proximiori in gradu debito, pacem & treugas ab ipso Anglo dolose per Sedem quasi extortas, infregerit, in hominibus & in rebus: non nullos Angli fideles occidendo, aliquas terras, quas tempore treugae initae possederat, spoliando: cum tamen actu fuerit, quod quilibet ipsorum & fideles eorum in ea possessione qua tunc fuerant, manere deberent, & q; ipse Philippus & sedes Apostolica saepe per ipsum Anglum requisiti super reformatione attentatorum, aliud non fecerint, nisi q; legati Sedis, Cardinales videlicet, vel ad auertendum fideles Angli ab eius seruitio nitebatur, & sic pace, quam Philippus non seruauerat, nec Sedes reformari iuxta pmissum procurauerat, ipse Anglus obseruare non posset, sed se & suos defendere cogeretur. Philippus sic diffidando, statim cum magno exercitu Flandrenses expugnabat, comitesque Flandriae, quia ea q ab imperio tenuit, recognouit se à Philippo tenere, à terra Flandriae eiecit. 50
units.tr: After this, Edward of England wrote to the Pope and the college, declaring himself king of France and England and lord of Ireland, and complaining that Philip of Valois, the usurper of the kingdom of France, had broken the peace and truces, which had been extorted from the Englishman through the Apostolic See by deceit, both against persons and against property: he had killed some faithful Englishmen and despoiled certain lands which he had held at the time the truce was made, although by agreement each of them and their faithful ought to remain in the possession they then had. He also said that Philip and the Apostolic See, although often asked by the Englishman to make reparation for these attacks, had done nothing except seek to draw the faithful of England away from his service, through the legates of the See, namely the cardinals. And so the Englishman could not keep the peace which Philip had not observed, nor which the See had failed to secure reform of, as promised, and he was compelled to defend himself and his own. Philip, thus breaking faith, at once attacked Flanders with a great army, and drove the counts of Flanders from the land of Flanders, since they acknowledged that they held of Philip the lands they had held of the Empire.

units.la: Eodem tempore, anno Domini M. CCC. XLVI, in coena Domini, Clemens papa contra Ludouicum principem crudelissimum faciens sermonem, contra ipsum durissime proceprotedens,& eos processus Papæ Ioannis innouans,ipsum hæreticum & schismaticū declarauit,in processu pœnas iuris hæreticorū, & omnes maledictiones antiquas inferendo: in quo etiam monuit Principes Electores, vt Regem eligerent idoneum in Imperatorem, promouendum infra certum tempus expressum, ne Ecclesia diu advocato careat: alioquin circa hoc sedes Apostolica cogitaret.
units.tr: At the same time, in the year of the Lord 1346, on Maundy Thursday, Pope Clement, preaching against Louis the most cruel prince, proceeded very harshly against him, renewed the processes of Pope John, and declared him a heretic and schismatic, inflicting in the process the penalties of heretical law and all the ancient curses. In the same document he also warned the electors to choose a fit king to be promoted as emperor within a certain stated time, so that the Church should not long be without a protector; otherwise the Apostolic See would consider what to do about it.

units.la: Illis etiam temporibus Papa Clemens,H.de Virnenberg archiepiscopū Moguntinensem depositum,Gerlacum filium Ger. Comitis de Nassawe, nepotem quondam Adolphi regis,circa vigesimum annū agentem,in archiepiscopū promouendo. Causa autem depositionis fuerat,q; adhæserat & fauebat Principi, propter quod excommunicatus fuerat, & in excommunicatione animo indurato pluribus annis perseueraverat.Idem namq; H.archiepiscopus, cum ante habuisset litem, cum Roberto duce Bauariæ,filio quondam Rudolphi fratris Principis,propter castrum & oppidū Winsheim/an der Bergstrassen,& ijsdem diebus litem haberet cum marchione Mißnēti, filiastro Principis,& lis ducis & archiepiscopi in principem compromissa fuiller, qui in Franckfurt partibus terminum statuit,ac partes,cum mutuò cum armata gente inibi conuenire nitirentur, ac Princeps circa quatuor millia galeatorū ibi conuocasset: Robertus dux videns,se non posse inibi dominari,cum paucis veniens,& se deprehendi suspicans,repente recessit. Propter quod Princeps Moguntino adiudicauit petita, ducem in multis condemnando expensis. Post hæc Roberto duce se cum patruo reformante,& iterum per Principem partibus termino statuto: Princeps (q; Winsheim pro certa pecunia,pro qua obligatum dicebatur archiepiscopatui Maguntino,eidem duci per Moguntinū restitui deberet,decreuit: de quo Moguntinus cōmotus, Winsheim cum omni iure suo Capitulo resignauit, dicens: se sine illis compromittere nequiuisse.Et ex tunc quæsiuit se absolui à Papa: sed cùm Papa eū nimis astringere vellet,non solùm contra Ludouicum principem, sed etiam contra iura Imperij: nuncij eius infecto negotio sunt reuersi, ipsēq; se cum Duce & Principe reformauit,propter quæ depositus est per Sedem, vt supra.
units.tr: In those same times Pope Clement deposed H. of Virneburg, archbishop of Mainz, and promoted Gerlach, son of Count Gerhard of Nassau, nephew of the late King Adolf, a man about twenty years old, to the archbishopric. The reason for the deposition was that Henry had adhered to and favoured the Prince, for which he had been excommunicated, and he had persisted for several years in excommunication with a hardened mind. For the same Archbishop Henry, having previously had a dispute with Robert, duke of Bavaria, son of the late Rudolf, the Prince's brother, over the castle and town of Weinheim on the Bergstrasse, and at the same time being in dispute with the margrave of Meissen, the Prince's stepson, and since the quarrel between the duke and the archbishop had been referred to the Prince for arbitration, he fixed a day and place at Frankfurt. When the parties tried to meet there with armed followers, and the Prince had summoned about four thousand armoured men to the place, Duke Robert, seeing that he could not dominate there, came with a few men, suspected that he would be seized, and suddenly withdrew. For this reason the Prince adjudged the claims in favour of the Archbishop of Mainz, condemning the duke to pay the costs in many respects. Afterwards, when Duke Robert, together with his paternal uncle, had reformed himself, and the parties were again summoned by the Prince to a fixed date and place, the Prince decided that Weinheim should be restored by the Archbishop of Mainz to the same duke for a certain sum of money, for which it was said to be pledged to the archbishopric of Mainz. The Archbishop of Mainz, moved by this, resigned Weinheim with all its rights to the chapter, saying that he could not have made any compromise without them. From that time he sought absolution from the Pope; but since the Pope wanted to bind him too tightly, not only against Louis the prince but also against the rights of the Empire, his envoys returned with the business unfinished, and he himself reconciled himself with the duke and the Prince. For these reasons he was deposed by the See, as stated above.

units.la: Eisdem diebus B.episcopus Argentinensis per Papā est absolutus præstito iuramento,quòd eidem Ludouico de cætero non assisteret, nisi fuerit cum ecclesia reformatus.
units.tr: In those same days B., bishop of Strasbourg, was absolved by the Pope on swearing that he would no longer support Louis, unless he was reconciled with the Church.

units.la: Eisdem diebus Ioannes rex Bohemiæ, & Carolus marchio Moraviæ filius eius, fuerunt in Curia, de oppressione Ludouici principis,& promotione Caroli cogitantes. Antea autem idem Carolus in Curia existens,in odium Heinrici Moguntini, Pragensem episcopum, subditū Moguntinensi, promoueri in archiepiscopū procurauit, & duos episcopatus in Bohemia sibi subijci, & à Moguntinensis ecclesiæ ditione absolui,& eidem Pragensi ius coronandi regē Bohemiæ, quod antea habuit Moguntinus,concedi: iurans,idioma Bohemicū à Germanico distinctum. De quo postea argutus Ioānes rex Bohemiæ,pater eius,Principibus,q; sine scitu eius factū esset,iurauit.
units.tr: In those same days John, king of Bohemia, and his son Charles, margrave of Moravia, were at the Curia, plotting the oppression of Louis the prince and the promotion of Charles. Previously, Charles himself, while at the Curia, out of hatred for Henry of Mainz, had procured the promotion of Henry, bishop of Prague, a subject of the Mainz see, to the archbishopric, and that two bishoprics in Bohemia should be made subject to him and freed from the authority of the church of Mainz, and that the right of crowning the king of Bohemia, which Mainz had previously held, should be granted to the Prague bishop. He swore that the Bohemian language was distinct from German. Afterwards King John of Bohemia, his father, who was vexed about this, swore to the princes that it had been done without his knowledge.

units.la: Post hæc prouisus Moguntinus Gerlacus de Nassawe,ad villam Rens super Rhenum,ad feriam quartam post Margaretæ, sub anno Domini M.CCC.XLVI, volens apostolico mandato obedire, quantū in eo fuit,ad eligendū Regem, principes conuocauit:vbi conuenientes Balduinus de Lützelburg Treuerensis, Walderamus de Iuliaco Coloniensis,itē Gerlacus de Nassawe nouiter prouisus Moguntinensis, archiepiscopi, itē Rudolfus dux Saxoniæ, & Ioannes rex Bohemiæ,& imperium diu vacasse decernentes, prædictū Carolum marchionē Moravię in regem elegerunt Romanum.Pro quo facto, prædicti Coloniensis & dux Saxoniæ magna pecunia sunt corrupti.
units.tr: After this, Gerlach of Nassau, the newly provided Archbishop of Mainz, called the princes together to the town of Rhens on the Rhine, on the Wednesday after St Margaret's day, in the year of the Lord 1346, wishing to obey the apostolic command as far as lay in him, to elect a king. There, when they had met, Baldwin of Luxembourg, archbishop of Trier, Walram of Jülich, archbishop of Cologne, likewise Gerlach of Nassau, newly provided archbishop of Mainz, also Rudolf, duke of Saxony, and John, king of Bohemia, decreed that the Empire had long been vacant, and elected as king of the Romans the aforesaid Charles, margrave of Moravia. For this deed the aforesaid Cologne and the duke of Saxony were bribed with large sums of money.

units.la: Intenderat autem idem electus in instanti ire Aquisgranum pro coronatione,quā Coloniensis ei nitebatur impendere: cui tamen Aquenses, quantum in eis fuerat intenderant resistere.Imperatrix autem tunc in Holandia scripsit Ludouico principi,q; per gentem suam posset resistere Carolo, ne posset Aquisgranū venire. Occiso enim a Frisonibus anno priore comite Wilhelmo Holandiæ sine liberis, cùm Imperatrix esset senior sororū eius (regina enim Angliæ & comitissa Iuliacensis iuniores fuerūt) gentes autem Wilhelmi occisi,Imperatricem & vnum de filijs suis accipere in dominos decreuerunt. Transcenderat autem in hyeme Imperatrix cum vno filio suo nouenni per Lotharingiam & Franciam, & primò veniens Hennegowe, inibi est recepta:ita tamen quòd de redditibus terrarum nihil reciperet in vsus suos quousq; occisi omnia debita essent persoluta. Promouit autem rex Franciæ Imperatricem,neptem suam forsan non amore Principis, sed quia terras per Anglum timuit occupari. Anxius autem princeps, qui tunc steterat in terra sua Bavaria, propter diutinam uxoris absentiam, cum misisset pro illa, gentes autem illæ vellēt habere seniorem filium Imperatricis pro domino: Princeps Wilhelmum filium suum misit ad terram illam, cū Comite de Katzenelnbogen, post quem idem filius spadonem more garconis equitabat: timor enim erat, propter litem prædictam ipsum deprehendi in via.
units.tr: The same elected man was at once intending to go to Aachen for the coronation, which the Archbishop of Cologne was striving to bestow on him. The Aachen citizens, however, had resolved to resist as far as they were able. Meanwhile the Empress, in Holland, wrote to Prince Louis that he should use his people to block Charles, so that Charles could not come to Aachen. For the year before, Count William of Holland had been killed by the Frisians, leaving no children. The Empress was the eldest of his sisters, since the queen of England and the countess of Jülich were younger, and the people of the slain William resolved to take the Empress and one of her sons as their lords. In winter the Empress had crossed through Lorraine and France with one of her sons, a boy of nine, and first came to Hainault, where she was received. Yet this was on the condition that she should take nothing from the revenues of the lands for her own use until all the debts of the slain man had been paid. The king of France supported the Empress, his niece, perhaps not out of love for the prince, but because he feared the lands would be seized by the Englishman. The prince, anxious because of his wife's long absence, had been staying in his land of Bavaria. After sending for her, and since those people wished to have the Empress's elder son as their lord, the prince sent his son William to that land, together with the Count of Katzenelnbogen. A eunuch rode behind the son in the manner of a page, for because of the said dispute there was fear that he might be seized on the road.

units.la: Cùm autem Carolus electus, ad coronationem iuisse debuisser, eodem mense Iulij episcopus Leodiensis, propter quædam homicidia & iniurias clero allatas, civitatē Leodiensem obsedit, volens ibi ad condemnandum illos pro tribunali sedere, ad quem episcopum tanq; consanguineum & adiutorem suum, idem Carolus properavit, & pater eius. Habuit autem episcopus secum circa septem milia galeatorum. Aderant enim sibi rex Bohemiæ, & Carolus filius eius, item comes Marchiæ, & frater eius. Item Marchio Iuliacensis, Comes Montium, dominus de Waldenburg, & alij multi Barones.
