Miserant autem quædam civitates vicinæ populo Leodiensi x l milia peditū armatorum, qui se posuerunt in locum iudicij, qui sunt extra muros civitatis, se circumvallantes, ne ibidem episcopus posset præsidere. Cùm autem extra locum illum episcopus præsidere niteretur, habitisq; inter partes tractatib. volentēq; populo Leodiensi restituere clerum in personis & rebus, & super iniuria ad arbitrium meliorum episcopi adiutorum satisfacere: episcopo autem contra consilium suorum omnino præsidere volente: ecce quidam ribaldi de populo impetum facientes in aciem equitum, qui versus stratam, ubi popularibus patebat exitus, fuerant ordinati, eosdem equites ad ingressum per eandem stratam ad populū provocarunt. & ingredientibus circa quina gentis galeatis, occisisq; in impetu multis de populo non armatis: populo verò armato in equites impetum faciente, multisq; occisis, & præcipuè domino de Waldenburg valentissimo, quingenti ingressi, cum alij non sequerentur, eò prout poterant evaserunt, toraqz acies episcopi statim confusa recessit. Iuliacensis autem marchio in loco libentissimè permansisset.
units.tr: Since the elected Charles ought to have gone to the coronation, in the same month of July the Bishop of Liège, on account of certain murders and injuries done to the clergy, besieged the city of Liège, wishing to sit in judgment there and condemn those men. Charles hurried to the bishop, whom he regarded as his kinsman and helper, and so did his father. The bishop had with him about seven thousand men-at-arms. For the king of Bohemia was present with him, and Charles his son, also the Count of the Mark and his brother, likewise the Margrave of Jülich, the Count of Mons, the lord of Waldenburg, and many other barons. Some neighbouring cities had sent to the people of Liège forty thousand armed foot-soldiers, who took up position at the place of judgment outside the city walls, surrounding it so that the bishop could not preside there. While the bishop tried to preside outside that place, and negotiations were held between the parties, and the people of Liège were willing to restore the clergy in their persons and goods and to make satisfaction for the injury at the judgment of the better men who were the bishop's helpers, the bishop, against the advice of his own people, insisted entirely on presiding. Then some ruffians from the populace made an assault on the line of horsemen who had been drawn up across the road where the citizens had their exit, and provoked those horsemen to enter by that same road against the people. When about five hundred armed men had entered, and many unarmed citizens had been killed in the attack, the armed populace made an assault on the horsemen, and many were killed, especially the very valiant lord of Waldenburg. Five hundred of them got in, and since the others did not follow, they escaped as best they could, and the whole line of the bishop immediately broke and withdrew in confusion. The Margrave of Jülich would most gladly have stayed in the place.

units.la: Venientibus autem Ioanne rege Bohemiæ & Carolo filio suo Treuerim, statim venerunt noua, de transitu regis Angliæ in terram Franciæ, Francusq; Bohemos pro adiutorio deprecatur: qui illico in Franciam sunt profecti. Anglus autem Normandiam partem Franciæ ingrediens, cum aliquibus egregijs victis civitatibus, alijs verò modicis omnino destructis, spoliisq; in Angliam destinatis, terram illam per l x milliaria in circuitu ignis incendio deuastauit. Post hæc ad civitatem Parisiensem ad vnū miliare transiuit, ibiq; multis diebus glorians, multaq; vastans, non audente Philippo cum longè maiori gente Parisios egredi contra ipsum, tandem præ defectu victualiū recessit: versusq; civitatem Ambianēsem descendit. Egrediebatur autem Philippus, sequens eum cum gente innumerabili equitum & peditum, ad quatuor diætas, & vbi Anglus præcedente nocte iacuit, se posuit Francus sequenti nocte. Sentiens autem Anglus illos sequentes, vno die eò velocius quandam syluam transiuit, manè iuxta syluam quasi abscensus se ad conflictum disponens. Transiens autem Francus cum exercitu suo, cum credidisset Anglum ad vnam diætam transijsse, ecce reperit eum ad conflictum paratum. Anglus enim omnes equos suos cum Garconibus a se iuxta syluam collocans, pedestribus se commisit, curribus se circundans, ne equites Franci alibi quàm in cornu anteriori inuadere eum possent, ante se & milites suos præmittens triginta millia sagittariorum. Francus autem præmisit x millia sagittariorum, & gentem innumerabilem c c c millium peditum, ac paneria fratris sui Comitis, item Comitis Flandriæ, ducis Lotaringiæ, & aliorum, post illos ponens Bohemos & Alemannos. Nolebat enim honorem progrediendi dare Alemannis. Ita se Franci crediderunt securos: manens ipse Francus cum exercitu suo circa x v i millium equitum.
units.tr: When King John of Bohemia and his son Charles came to Trier, news immediately arrived of the English king's crossing into the land of France, and that the French were begging the Bohemians for help. These men at once set out for France. The Englishman, entering the part of France called Normandy, with some distinguished cities conquered and others quite small ones destroyed, sent the plunder to England, and laid waste that land for sixty miles around with the fire of burning. After this he advanced to within one mile of the city of Paris, and there, for many days, he boasted and laid waste much; Philip, not daring to come out of Paris against him with a far larger force, at last withdrew for lack of provisions and came down toward the city of Amiens. Philip set out after him with an innumerable host of horse and foot, four days' journey behind; and on the night after the Englishman had lain at a certain place, the Frenchman camped there the following night. The Englishman, sensing that they were following him, marched through a certain wood one day more swiftly, and early in the morning, withdrawn as it were beside the wood, prepared himself for battle. The Frenchman, crossing with his army, had believed the Englishman to have gone a single day's journey on, but behold, he found him ready for battle. For the Englishman had placed all his horses, with their grooms, beside him near the wood, and committed himself to the foot-soldiers, surrounding himself with carts, so that the French horsemen could attack him only at the front wing and nowhere else. He sent ahead of himself and his soldiers thirty thousand archers. The Frenchman sent ahead ten thousand archers and an innumerable host of 300,000 foot-soldiers, and the pavises of his brother the count, likewise of the Count of Flanders, the Duke of Lorraine and others, placing behind them the Bohemians and Germans; for he did not wish to give the Germans the honour of advancing. So the French believed themselves secure, while the Frenchman himself remained with his army with about sixteen thousand horsemen.

units.la: Congredientibus autem primis ad conflictum, circa meridiem, sabbato post Bartholomei apostoli, anno Domini M. CCC. XLVI, diuq; certatibus, sagittarijsq; Franci terga vertentibus, ac cum populo fugientibus: tota Franci acies fugam dedit, eo reclamante, diuq; cum paucis manente. Diu autē in certamine remanserant Alemanni, ita quòd multa millia hominū sunt occisa. Ceciderunt inter alios Ioannes rex Bohemiæ, qui cœcus fuerat, & se ad conflictū per Henricum Monachi de Basilea, & H. de Clingenberg milites, fecit adduci: Rudolfus dux Lotaringiæ, comes Flandriæ, co-mes mes de Blefs nepos Franci, Comes de Salmis, dictus de Rotbach, H. de Ratsamhusen, Henricus monachi de Basilea, H.de Clingenberg, & alij plures electi.
units.tr: When the first troops joined battle, about noon on the Saturday after the feast of the apostle Bartholomew, in the year of the Lord 1346, and after a long fight, the French archers turned their backs and fled with the common people, and the whole French line took flight, though he protested and remained a while with a few men. The Germans, however, had stayed long in the fight, so that many thousands of men were killed. Among others fell John, king of Bohemia, who was blind; he had himself led into the battle by Henry the monk of Basel and the knights H. of Clingenberg. Also fell Rudolf, duke of Lorraine, the Count of Flanders, the Count of Blois, the nephew of the Frenchman, the Count of Salm, called of Rothbach, H. of Ratsamhausen, Henry the monk of Basel, H. of Clingenberg, and many other chosen men.

units.la: Anglus autem post recessum inimicorum, videns Ioannem regem Bohemię occisum, dolens super eum dixit: Alter lectus regem Bohemiæ deceret, quàm sic iacere in terra: celebratisq; solennissimè exequijs eius, ipsum in Lubelburg cum xii dextrarijs, habentib. arma Bohemiæ deorsum versa, transmisit. Doluit autè Anglus de Alemannis dicens: Et bene hi in morte cum Franco pergunt, qui eos odio prosequitur, nec eis quicq; largitur: & ego eos diligens, largitus sum eisdem. Carolus autem cum armis Imperialibus fugiens de conflictu cū alijs, cùm à Franco aliquid peteret, saltem pro 10 Alemannorū expensis, qui sibi in adiutorium venissent, nihil dedit eidem. Dicebatur autē, q. Francus magnam pecuniā dederit Ioanni Bohemo regi pro stipendio Alemannorum quos adduxerat: quā ille eis non assignans, sed eam sibi retinuit, & Coloniensi archiepiscopo pro coronatione Caroli filij sui destinauit. Filius autem Franci, ac dux Burgundiæ, existentes in Vasconia cū viginti millibus, in obsidione cuiusdā munitionis, optimè per Comite de Herbe, capitaneũ Angli victæ treugas fecerunt cū Comite animo subueniendi Franco: sed anteq; eò venerunt, Francus victus est, vt pfertur.
units.tr: The Englishman, after the withdrawal of the enemy, seeing that King John of Bohemia had been killed, grieved over him and said: "Another bed would have befitted the king of Bohemia than to lie thus on the ground." After celebrating his funeral most solemnly, he sent him to Luxembourg with twelve horses, bearing the arms of Bohemia reversed. The Englishman also grieved over the Germans, saying: "Well do these men go to death with the Frenchman, who persecutes them with hatred and gives them nothing; while I, loving them, have given them gifts." Charles, fleeing from the battle with the imperial arms, along with others, asked the Frenchman for something, at least to cover the expenses of ten Germans who had come to help him, but he gave him nothing. It was said, moreover, that the Frenchman had given King John of Bohemia a large sum of money for the pay of the Germans he had brought; but John did not hand it over to them, keeping it for himself, and sent it to the Archbishop of Cologne for the coronation of his son Charles. The son of the Frenchman and the Duke of Burgundy, who were in Gascony with twenty thousand men, having besieged a certain fortress which was very well defended by the Count of Herbe, captain of the English, made a truce with the Count with the intention of helping the Frenchman; but before they came there, the Frenchman had been defeated, as is reported.

units.la: Eiecerat autem Francus Robertum comitem Attrebatensem, fororiũ & consanguineum suum de Comitatu, pro eo quod dixerat, se scire iuuenem, quem secum tenuit, Anglus, fuisse filium quondam Caroli regis Francię, & ob quæda alia: conferens comitatum duci Burgundiæ, cuius sororem habet Francus. Qui Robertus Anglo feruenter adhæsit. Anglus autem post victoriam rediens ad mare, obuiam inuenit Reginam, quæ cum victualibus transfretârat, & cum gente.
units.tr: The Frenchman had also expelled from his county Robert, Count of Artois, his nephew and kinsman, because he had said that he knew the young man whom the Englishman held with him to be the son of the late King Charles of France, and for certain other reasons; and he granted the county to the Duke of Burgundy, whose sister the Frenchman had as wife. This Robert clung fervently to the Englishman. The Englishman, returning to the sea after his victory, met the Queen, who had crossed the channel with provisions and with troops.

units.la: Obsedit autem Anglus ciuitatem Kalis maritimam, habentem portum propinquiorem versus Angliam, ex qua damna plurima est perpessus, quæ est de Comitatu Attrebatensi prædicto, & duci Burgundiæ est subiecta.
units.tr: The Englishman besieged the maritime city of Calais, which has a harbour nearer to England. He suffered many losses there. The city belongs to the aforementioned county of Artois and is subject to the Duke of Burgundy.

units.la: Licet autem ab antiquo inter Anglos & Francos super terra Vasconiæ lis fuerit immortalis, causam tamen speciale discordiæ horum Philippi & Eduardi super regno Franciæ, digrediens à materia, duxi breuiter exprimendam.
units.tr: Although there has been an ancient and unending dispute between the English and the French over the land of Gascony, I have decided, digressing from my subject, to set out briefly the particular cause of the quarrel between Philip and Edward over the kingdom of France.

units.la: Olim Philippus Pulcher, rex Franciæ, qui regnauit tempore Clementis Papæ quinti & Heinrici Imperatoris, quiq; omnes Iudæos à terra sua expulit, eorū thesauris retentis: ordinem quoq; Templariorum, propter eorum potentiam & diuitias, pro quibus aspirauit, confictis in eos quibusdā turpibus, ab ipso Papa destrui procurauit, quorum domus & bona Hospitalarijs Hierosolymitanis sunt vnita, fecitq; idem Papa quosdam fratres eiusdem ordinis Templariorum, ad instinctum Franci igne cremari, per quod tamen fratres Hierosolymitani modicũ profecerunt. Qui Philippus habuit fratrem Carolum, huius Philippi de Valesio regis patrem. Item habuit tres filios, Ludouicum, Philippũ & Carolum: quorum primus & tertius de Burgundia sorores duas habuerunt vxores. Habuit etiam ipse Rex filiam reginam Angliæ, matrem prædicti Eduardi. Hæc post natiuitatem Eduardi veniens ad Philippum patrem, Eduardum maritum suum de Sodomia deferens, ipsum de patris auxilio captiuauit, & vsq; ad mortem tenuit captiuatum. Quo defuncto, hic Eduardus præclarus regnans, matrem captiuauit, & detinuit captiuam: multosq; qui in necem patris conspirasse propter adulteram Reginam dicebantur, occidit. Hæc Angla antequam discederet à curia patris, nedũ maritum de Sodomia, sed & tres vxores fratrum suorum de trium militum adulterio accusauit, nec cessauit, nisi decollatis vxoribus, militibus excoriatione extinctis. Ludouici quoq; vxore extincta, idem Clementiam filiam Caroli tertij regis Siciliæ neptem quondā Rudolphi Romanorum regis, duxit vxorem. Quibus Ludouico & Philippo, post mortem patris successiuè regnantibus, & sine prole defunctis, cùm iam Carolus frater eorum regnaret: venit ad eum ducissa Burgundiæ, mater vxoris eius captæ, timens huic similiter mortis periculũ imminere, dicens eis: Peccaui domine, iungens vobis matrimonio filiam meam, quâ pater vester de sacro fonte leuauit. Et adducens Ducissa quosdam testes repertos ad Clementem Papā quintum, gaudente rege, diuortiũ per Papam fieri procurauit. Regiq; Carolo, filia quondam Heinrici Imperatoris, soror prædicti regis Bohemiæ, ex tunc data est in vxorem, quæ formosa valde, omnes alias virtutibus & moribus mulieres antecessit. Transiens autem quadam vice Rex, & Robertus Atrebatensis Comes, causa venationis iuxta castrum, in quo prior vxor morabatur captiua, missa familia sua in syluam, ipse Rex & Comes sunt castrum ingressi. Illa autem existens in lotione capitis, fugiente familia, viso Rege, se in modum crucifixi ad pedes Regis prostrauit: timuit enim ex aliqua delatione clam Regem iratu venisse. Erat autem pulchra & amabilis valde. Rex autem leuans ipsam, egresso Comite, eam repente cognoscens, recessit: ex quo illa impraegnata, soli nunciauit Comiti, rogans, vt ipse virtute sua vitae mulieris & partus insidias praecaueret: quae pariens masculum, clam eo subtracto, alienum submisit. Verus autem filius ex ordinatione Comitis, ad amitam suam, praedictam reginam Angliae est transmissus, quem cum clam delicatè nutriuit: putatiuus autem filius breuiter expirauit. Debebatur enim, Carolum patruum, praedictorum trium filiorum curam, quasi regni, gerentem, ad regnum aspirasse, & ob hoc filiorum regis mortem petisse. Mortuo autem eodem Carolo, & post eum Carolo rege ex vxore sua de Lüzelnburg nulla prole relicta, ecce hic Philippus, antiqui Caroli filius, sibi regnum vsurpat; qui omnes reges Franciae à tempore Caroli Magni diuitijs & potentia antecessit.
units.tr: Long ago Philip the Fair, king of France, who reigned in the time of Pope Clement V and Emperor Henry, expelled all the Jews from his land and kept their treasures. Because of the power and riches of the Order of the Templars, which he coveted, he also had the Order destroyed by the Pope himself, having brought certain shameful charges against its members. Their houses and goods were united with those of the Hospitallers of Jerusalem. At the Frenchman's instigation the same Pope had some brothers of that Templar order burned with fire, though the Jerusalem brothers gained little by this. This Philip had a brother Charles, the father of Philip of Valois, the king. He also had three sons, Louis, Philip and Charles. The first and third of these had wives who were two sisters from Burgundy. The king himself had a daughter, who became queen of England and mother of the Edward mentioned above. After Edward's birth this daughter came to her father Philip and accused her husband Edward of sodomy. With her father's help she had him imprisoned, and kept him captive until his death. After his death, this Edward, who reigned as a famous king, imprisoned his mother and kept her captive. He also killed many men who were said to have conspired to murder his father on account of the adulterous queen. Before she left her father's court, this Englishwoman accused not only her husband of sodomy but also the wives of her brothers of adultery with three knights. She did not stop until the wives were beheaded and the knights were put to death by flaying. When the wife of Louis also died, Louis married Clemence, daughter of Charles III, king of Sicily, and granddaughter of the former Rudolf, king of the Romans. Louis and Philip reigned one after the other after their father's death, and both died without issue. When their brother Charles was already reigning, the duchess of Burgundy, mother of his captive wife, came to him. Fearing that a similar danger of death hung over her, she said to them: "Lord, I have sinned, joining my daughter to you in marriage, whom your father lifted from the holy font." The duchess then brought some witnesses found against the marriage to Pope Clement V, and with the king rejoicing, she arranged for the Pope to grant a divorce. Then the daughter of the late Emperor Henry, sister of the aforesaid king of Bohemia, was given to King Charles as his wife. She was very beautiful and surpassed all other women in virtues and manners. Once the king and Robert, count of Artois, were passing by a castle where the first wife was kept captive, for the purpose of hunting. The king's retinue had been sent into the wood, and the king and the count entered the castle. The woman was washing her head, and when her attendants fled and she saw the king, she threw herself face down at his feet like a crucified person, for she feared that the king had come in anger, having been secretly informed against her. She was very beautiful and most lovable. The king raised her up, and when the count had left, he suddenly recognised her and withdrew. From this she became pregnant, and she told only the count, begging him to use his power to guard the life of the woman and against plots over the birth. When she bore a son, it was secretly taken from her and a substitute was put in its place. The true son, by the count's arrangement, was sent to his aunt, the aforesaid queen of England, and she secretly raised him delicately, while the supposed son soon died. For it is said that Charles, the uncle who was acting as guardian of the three sons, as though of the kingdom, aspired to the throne, and for this reason sought the death of the king's sons. After this same Charles died, and after King Charles had died leaving no offspring by his wife of Luxembourg, behold, this Philip, son of the former Charles, seized the kingdom for himself. He surpassed all the kings of France since the time of Charlemagne in wealth and power.

units.la: Mortuo autem Eduardo Anglo in captiuitate, eiq; Eduardo succedente praeclaro, filiumq; Caroli auunculi sui secum habente, victoq; per eum rege Scotorum: idem Anglus cum praedicto Philippo litem pro regno viriliter est ingressus, non praetendes tam auunculi filium propter sententiam Papae: quam se praedicto vltimo regi Carolo proximiorem haeredem: cum Francia à nullo haberi dicatur in feodum, quamuis e contra nullus per foemininam lineam in regnum successisse dicatur.
units.tr: When Edward of England died in captivity, Edward his successor, a famous king who had with him the son of his uncle Charles, and who through him had defeated the king of the Scots, entered the struggle for the kingdom with the aforesaid Philip with great spirit. He did not put forward the son of his uncle so much on account of the Pope's sentence, as himself being the nearer heir to the last king, Charles. For France is said to be held in fief by no one, although conversely no one is said to have succeeded to the kingdom through the female line.

units.la: Praedicto anno XLVI, Albertus dux Austriae emens à Ioanne de Stauffen oppidum Münster Brisgaugiae S. Ruperti, castrum Scharffenstein, quod à duce tenebatur in feudum, sub Friburg, castrum cum oppido confregerat, asserens sibi obligata, nec tempore statuto redempta.
units.tr: In the aforementioned year 1346, Duke Albert of Austria bought the town of Münster of St Ruprecht in Breisgau from John of Stauffen. He broke into the castle of Scharffenstein, which was held in fief from the duke, below Freiburg, and the castle with the town. He claimed that these had been pledged to him and had not been redeemed at the agreed time.

units.la: Anglo illis temporibus in obsidione occupato, rex Scotorum ex instructione Franci, latenter, vt creditur, Angliam est ingressus. Anglus munitus scripsit Anglis: qui ingrediente rege Scotorum, occisa omni sua gente, ipsum ceperunt.
units.tr: While the Englishman was occupied with the siege at that time, the king of the Scots, at the instigation of the Frenchman, secretly entered England, as is believed. The Englishman, forewarned, wrote to the English, who, when the king of the Scots entered, killed his whole army and captured him.

units.la: Eisdem temporibus, scilicet anno Domini M. CCC. XLVI, Dominica ante festum Martini, Papa in Consistorio publico praedictu Carolum in Romanorum regem solenniter approbauit: quem cum Aquenses & Colonienses non recepissent, in Bunna ab archiepiscopo Coloniensi, dominica ante Andreae, extitit coronatus, & ab ipso Coloniensis, Treuerensis, Gerlacus de Naslaw prouisus Moguntinus, archiepiscopi: item Monasteriensis, Metensis, Leodiensis & Virdunensis episcopi, de suis regalibus sunt investiti. Propter quod Papa sciens sibi aduersari Ludouicum principe & Vngarum, cum Mediolanensi, antiquo hoste sedis apostolicae, amicitiae ligam firmauit.
units.tr: At the same time, namely in the year of the Lord 1346, on the Sunday before the feast of St Martin, the Pope in public consistory solemnly approved Charles as king of the Romans. When the people of Aachen and Cologne did not receive him, he was crowned at Bonn by the archbishop of Cologne on the Sunday before St Andrew's. By the same archbishop of Cologne, by the archbishop of Trier, and by Gerlach of Nassau, provided archbishop of Mainz, and likewise by the bishops of Münster, Metz, Liège and Verdun, he was invested with the royal regalia. Because of this the Pope, knowing that Louis, prince and Hungarian, together with Milan, an ancient enemy of the apostolic see, was opposed to him, firmed up a league of friendship.

units.la: Praedicto anno XLVI, mense Iulio, Carolus rex Hungariae de iugulatione fratris dolens, cum magno exercitu, sc. LXX millium equitum, Aquileiam est ingressus, Patriarcham coercens, ingrediendi Apuliam via quaerens. Intromisit autem se defensioni Rhodis ciuitatis maritimę, quâ olim Veneti obsederant, cupiens ibi portum maris habere. Et cum diu rex in terra, Veneti vero circa ipsarum ciuitatę iacuissent in mari: Venetorum exercitus latenter de montanis egrediens, magnam occidit multitudinem Hungarorum (triumphauerant enim Veneti cum domino Mediolanesi & Veronensibus, ita quòd potentes fuerunt) sic quòd Hungarus iuuenis & inexpertus litium, fructratus proposito suo & negocio, Vngariam est ingressus: Veneti autem ciuitatem vicerunt. Papa enim sciens sibi aduersari Ludouicum principem Vngarum, cum Mediolanensi antiquo hoste foedus amicitiae ligauit.
units.tr: In the aforesaid year 1346, in July, King Charles of Hungary, grieving over the murder of his brother, entered Aquileia with a great army, namely 70,000 horsemen, restraining the patriarch and seeking a way into Apulia. He involved himself in the defence of the maritime city of Rhodes, which the Venetians had once besieged, desiring to have a harbour there. The king stayed on land for a long time, while the Venetians lay at sea around the city. Then the Venetian army, coming secretly out of the mountains, killed a great multitude of Hungarians. For the Venetians had triumphed with the lord of Milan and the people of Verona, and so they were powerful. Thus the young Hungarian, inexperienced in wars, frustrated in his purpose and undertaking, entered Hungary, and the Venetians conquered the city. For the Pope, knowing that Louis, prince of Hungary, was opposed to him, bound a league of friendship with the Milanese, an ancient enemy.

units.la: Eodem Iulij mense Ludouicus princeps cum Ludouico & Stephano filijs suis, Comitatum Tirolis ingressus, in Trideto, quod sibi & filio ratione ipsius Comitatus subesse credidit, sicut ante cum Vngaro & Mastino Veronensi habere colloquium nitebatur. Episcopus autem Tridentinus ad preces regis Bohemiae sedis prouisus, assumpta sibi gente Mediolanensi, Tridentinos à praedicti Ludouici Marchionis deuotione retraxit, & custoditis montanis, ne illi conuenire possent, impediuit.
units.tr: In the same month of July, Prince Louis, together with his sons Louis and Stephen, entered the county of Tyrol and went into Trent. He believed that Trent and his son were subject to him by reason of that county, just as before he had striven to hold a conference with the Hungarian and with Mastino of Verona. The bishop of Trent, provided to the see at the request of the king of Bohemia, took Milanese troops with him and drew the Trentines away from the allegiance of the aforesaid Marquis Louis. Having guarded the mountains so that they could not meet, he prevented it.

units.la: Licet autem scriberetur Principi, de praedictis principibus Electoribus, quòd ad eligendum regem terminum statuissent, credere hoc noluit, de archiepiscopo Treuerensi & duce Saxoniæ, quia ipsum elegerant, quoufq; veritatem percepit. Et veniēs in Suevia, sibi Comites & Barones quos potuit, attraxit, Marchioniq; Missensi filiastro suo, (cuius vxor relictis pluribus liberis, code anno obijt, qui filiaster in lite, quā cum Moguntino habuit, de Principe conquerebatur) magnam, vt contra eum non esset, pecuniā assignauit. Conuocatis quoq; ciuitatibus Spiræ, ipsas concorditer reperit in sua devotioneferuentes: ita quòd nec vna earū, Rheni, Sueuiæ, vel Franconiæ, electionem Caroli aut processus Papæ curauit, nec quisq; illarum partiū, aliquos contra Principe publicare processus audebat. Basileenses tantū, licet ratione episcopi sui, & pgeniei Monachorū inibi præualentiū & Caroloni fauentiū, ipsum receptare crederetur: videtes tñ tantam aliarū ciuitatum concordiā, se adhæsuros Principi firmius alijs decreuerunt.
units.tr: Although it was written to the Prince that the aforesaid electors had set a date for electing a king, he would not believe this of the archbishop of Trier and the duke of Saxony, because they had elected him, until he learned the truth. Coming into Swabia, he drew to himself as many counts and barons as he could. He also assigned a large sum of money to the Margrave of Meissen, his stepson, so that he would not be against him. (This stepson's wife died this year, leaving several children. In the lawsuit he had with the archbishop of Mainz, the stepson complained about the Prince.) He also summoned the cities of Speyer, and found them all in agreement and fervent in his devotion. So none of them, whether of the Rhine, Swabia or Franconia, cared about Charles's election or the Pope's proceedings, and none of those parties dared to publish proceedings against the Prince. Only the people of Basel, although it was believed they would harbour Charles on account of their bishop and the monks who prevailed there and favoured Charles, saw such concord among the other cities. They decided to adhere more firmly to the Prince than the others.

units.la: Reuersa autem Imperatrix de Holandia in mense Nouembri, anno prædicto, relicto inibi Wilhelmo filio, à Principe cū gaudio in Franckfort est recepta, q simul trāsiere Monacū. Venerunt aūt cum ipsa solenes nuncij Angli in Francfurt, Principe & Anglum colligare quærentes, cum quibus Princeps cum pleno colligandi mandato, Robertum ducem Bauariæ, filium fratris sui, Wolframum de Nellenburg, magistrum ordinis Teutonicorū per Alemaniam, & Lud. Comitē de Otingen, destinauit.
units.tr: The Empress returned from Holland in November of the aforesaid year, leaving her son Wilhelm there. She was received with joy by the Prince at Frankfurt, and they then went together to Munich. Solemn English envoys also came to Frankfurt with her, seeking to form an alliance with the Prince. The Prince sent Duke Robert of Bavaria, his brother's son, Wolfram of Nellenburg, master of the Teutonic Order in Germany, and Count Ludwig of Oettingen to conclude the alliance, giving them full authority to bind it.

units.la: Carolus autem electus latenter per Elsatiam & Sueuiam transiuit, & ad terram Bohemiæ properauit, vbi honorificè est receptus. Postea de mense Februarij anno Domini x lvii, ipse Carolus electus, cum Carolo rege Hungariæ genero suo, & cū Alberto Australi colloquium habuerunt in Vienna. Quibus simul euntibus in Presburg eiusdem Vngari, Ludouicus princeps statim in Vienna colloquium secretissimum habuit cum Australi prædicto. Bohemus autem veniens Tridentum, pro reliabendo Comitatu Tirolis, de auxilio Mediolanensium instituit. Iuerat autē marchio Brandenburgensis Prussiam contra gentiles, cuius vxor castrum Tirolis omnibus necessarijs muniuit ad annū. Engelmarus autem miles, potens in comitatu, qui & ipsum tradidit Marchioni, tractatus habuit hinc inde. Marchio autem intelligens hoc, illico est reuersus. Bohemus autem cum oppidum Meron, & alia plurima vicisset, veniente Principe cum magno exercitu, victa per se comburens, reuersus est Tridentum. Princeps quoq; similiter est reuersus, quia maxima fuit caristia vtrobiq;. Ludouicus autem Marchio, ipseq; Bohemus, in ipso Comitatu multis mensibus se inuicem infestarunt. Bohemus quoq;, cui etiam adhæsit episcopus Curiensis, aliquas munitiones per se victas, Mediolanensi pro multa pecunia obligauit.
units.tr: Meanwhile Charles, the elected rival, slipped secretly through Alsace and Swabia and hurried to the land of Bohemia, where he was honourably received. Afterwards, in February of the year of the Lord 1357, Charles the elected king and Charles, king of Hungary, his son-in-law, held a conference with Albert of Austria at Vienna. While they were travelling together to Pressburg in Hungary, Duke Ludwig at once held a most secret conference at Vienna with the aforesaid Albert. The Bohemian, however, coming to Trent, resolved to recover the county of Tyrol with the help of the Milanese. The margrave of Brandenburg had gone to Prussia against the heathens, but his wife garrisoned the castle of Tyrol with every necessity for a year. Engelmar, a knight powerful in the county, who had also handed the castle over to the margrave, held negotiations on both sides. When the margrave learned of this, he at once returned. The Bohemian, having taken the town of Meran and many other places, burned the captured places and returned to Trent when the Prince approached with a large army. The Prince too withdrew similarly, because there was the greatest scarcity of food on both sides. Duke Ludwig, the margrave, and the Bohemian himself harassed each other for many months in that county. The Bohemian, to whom the bishop of Chur also adhered, pledged some fortifications which he had taken to the Milanese for a large sum of money.

units.la: Temporibus prædictis, de mense Aprili, domini de Westerburg & de Isenburg, habitantes in terra ex opposito ciuitati Confluentiæ, vltra Rhenum, archiepiscopum Treuirensem & suos, in fauorem Principis, diffidarunt, pro eo quòd elegerant Carolonem, contra electionem Principis, literam huiusmodi diffidationis ad Bopardiam mittentes. Confluentini autem Treuirensi attinentes, cum exercitu Rhenum transeuntes, quoddam castrū, quod erat commune, tam Treuerensi, quàm domino de Westerburg pro domino suo solo apprehendere voluerunt. Illi autem Domini habentes latenter multitudinē armatorū, irruentes in illos, ducentos occiderūt & captiuarunt. Receperat autē Treuerēsis in Treueri ciuitate de Carolone electo, nuntios cū literis, qualiter plures munitiones comitatus Tirolis vicerit, de quib. cum fidelibus suis gratulans, est gaudisus. Et ecce venerūt sibi noua de strage prædicta, ob quæ se abscondēs, collapsus animo est perplexus. Eo tempore de consilio Principis & voluntate H. de Virnenberg archiepiscopi Moguntini, assignatis, eidem redditibus mille marcatum, commissa est administratio Moguntinensis tribus Canonicis de Capitulo, quibus & Princeps auxilium iuramento promisit, & ortum est schisma magnū: iudicibus Gerlaci prouisi archiepiscopi constitutis in ciuitate Moguntina absoluentibus ligata per iudices H. depositi in Altauilla constitutis: processusque apostolici pro Gerlaco prouisio directi, per aliquos Moguntinos ostijs ecclesiæ Moguntinæ affigebantur, affixos semper aliqui tollebant. Clerus quoq; diuisus, qui H. adhærebat & obediebat, cœpit paulatim adhærere Gerlaco. Marchio quoq; Misnensis & Lantgrauius Hassiæ in partibus Thuringiæ multum infestauerant archiepiscopum, Principe non eū defendente, alijs occupato. Erfordenses verò Gerlaco adhæserunt verbo, sed non facto. Marchio quoq; Misnensis oppidū Saltzach, ipse verò & comes de Hennenberg castrū Mulburg, Lantgrauius vero Haffiæ oppidum Nüwstat, munitiones Maguntinæ ecclesiæ, pro se habendi animo, occupauerunt: prædicti enim Marchio & Comes, quilibet sc. eorum filiũ & filiam, alterius filio & filiæ, matrimonialiter copulârunt.
units.tr: At the time mentioned, in April, the lords of Westerburg and Isenburg, living in the land opposite the city of Koblenz beyond the Rhine, renounced their allegiance (diffidarunt) to the archbishop of Trier and his followers, in favour of the Prince, because they had elected Charles against the Prince's election; they sent a letter of this renunciation to Boppard. The men of Koblenz, who were allied to Trier, crossed the Rhine with an army and wished to seize a certain castle which was held in common by the Trier men and by the lord of Westerburg, as if it belonged to their lord alone. But those lords, who had secretly gathered a crowd of armed men, rushed upon them, killing two hundred and taking others prisoner. The archbishop of Trier, meanwhile, had received in the city of Trier messengers from Charles the elected king, with letters saying that he had conquered several fortifications of the county of Tyrol; rejoicing over these with his loyal followers, he was glad. And behold, news of the aforesaid slaughter came to him, and hiding himself because of it, he collapsed in spirit and was perplexed. At that time, with the counsel and consent of the Prince and of Heinrich of Virneburg, archbishop of Mainz, an annual income of a thousand marks was assigned to him, and the administration of Mainz was entrusted to three canons of the chapter, to whom the Prince also promised aid under oath. A great schism arose: at Mainz, judges appointed by the provisional archbishop Gerlach absolved those who had been bound by the judges of Heinrich, who had been deposed and were sitting at Altavilla; and the apostolic processes issued for the provisional Gerlach were fixed by some Mainz men to the doors of the church of Mainz, and whoever had fixed them were always taking them down again. The clergy, too, was divided: those who adhered to and obeyed Heinrich gradually began to adhere to Gerlach. The margrave of Meissen and the landgrave of Hesse also greatly harassed the archbishop in the parts of Thuringia, the Prince not defending him, being occupied with other matters. The people of Erfurt adhered to Gerlach in word, but not in deed. The margrave of Meissen seized the town of Salzach, he himself and the count of Henneberg the castle of Mühlberg, and the landgrave of Hesse the town of Neustadt, fortifications of the church of Mainz, intending to hold them for themselves; for the aforesaid margrave and count had each joined in marriage their son and daughter to the other's daughter and son.

units.la: Eodem tempore, de mense Septembri, Conradus de Kirckel, præpositus ecclesiæ Spirensis, & Canonicus Maguntinus **** à Principe, & H. Moguntino, se solus, volentibus alijs duob. sibi coelectis, de administratione ecclesiæ Mogūtinensis intromisit, cui munitiones & gentes obedway-erunt. Hic statim omnes redditus præposituræ maioris ecclesiæ Moguntinensis abstulit Ioanni de Columna Cardinali, qui vt prepositus eam tenuit, redditusq; omnium prælatorum, Henrico non obedientium, occupauit. Hic treugas inter Principem & suos, specialiter de Westerburg & Isenburg, & inter Treuerenses, vsq; ad festum natiuitatis Ioannis Baptistæ ordinauit, omnia gerens strenuè & prudenter.
units.tr: At the same time, in September, Konrad of Kirchheim, provost of the church of Speyer and a canon of Mainz, was installed in the administration of the church of Mainz by the Prince and by Heinrich of Mainz alone, the other two co-elected men being unwilling; the fortifications and the people obeyed him. He at once took away all the revenues of the greater provostship of the church of Mainz from Cardinal Giovanni Colonna, who had held it as provost, and he seized the revenues of all the prelates who did not obey Heinrich. He arranged truces between the Prince and his followers, especially the lords of Westerburg and Isenburg, and between the men of Trier, until the feast of the Nativity of John the Baptist, conducting everything vigorously and prudently.

units.la: Eodem anno Domini M. CCC. XLVII, in principio mensis Iulij, gens Caroli Bohemi ingrediēs Bauariam inferiorem, cum duobus millibus galeatorum, multas ibidem villas combussit, multis barbarica feritate occisis, & pluribus captiuatis contra quos Princeps pro custodia terræ multos ibi destinauit armatos.
units.tr: In the same year of the Lord 1347, at the beginning of July, the army of Charles the Bohemian entered Lower Bavaria with two thousand men-at-arms, burned many villages there, killed many with barbarous savagery and took many captive; against them the Prince sent many armed men there to guard the land.

units.la: Eodem mense congregante archiepiscopo Treuerensi exercitum animo inuadēdi dominos de Westerburg & de Isenburg: ecce populus Leodiensis expugnās quoddam castrū episcopi Leodiensis, custodes castri eius decapitauit, nobiles & plebeios. Propter quod episcopus Leodiensis de adiutorio Treuerensis, ducis Brabantiæ, & aliorum terræ magnatum, volens obsidere Leodium, populis illius & aliarum plurium ciuitatum, quæ illis in adiutorium aduenerant, egredientibus ciuitatem contra eos, confligens, eis terga vertentibus x millia occidit ex illis: Dominus enim de Valckenberg, frater priori anno ibidem occisi, & Comes Montium, nemini pepercerunt, sicq; episcopus Leodiensis de populo Leodiensi disposuit vt volebat.
units.tr: In the same month, while the archbishop of Trier was gathering an army intending to attack the lords of Westerburg and Isenburg, behold, the people of Liège stormed a certain castle of the bishop of Liège and beheaded its guards, nobles and commoners alike. On account of this, the bishop of Liège, with the aid of the Trier man, the duke of Brabant and other magnates of the land, wished to besiege Liège. When the people of Liège and of several other cities who had come to their aid sallied out of the city against them and fought, and turned their backs, he killed ten thousand of them; for the lord of Valkenburg, brother of the man killed there the previous year, and the count of Mons spared no one. And so the bishop of Liège disposed of the people of Liège as he wished.

units.la: Eodem tempore quidam Iacobus Laurentij, notarius prudens & facundus, plebeius, Romæ in tribunum electus, scelera vindicans, ac omnem iurisdictionem vrbis exercens, vnum de Vrsinis decapitauit, Columnenses ab vrbe exterminans. Papa de his turbato arguente Romanos, idē tribunus Clementi Papæ scripsit, q; nisi infra annum rediret ad vrbem, & ibidem resideret, se cum Romanis aliū Papam creaturum.
units.tr: At the same time a certain Jacob Laurentius, a prudent and eloquent notary of plebeian birth, was elected tribune at Rome; avenging crimes and exercising full jurisdiction in the city, he beheaded one of the Orsini and drove the Colonna out of the city. When the Pope, troubled by these events, rebuked the Romans, this same tribune wrote to Pope Clement that unless he returned to the city within a year and resided there, he would create another pope with the Romans.

units.la: Occiso autem priori anno Comite Flandriæ in conflictu, Flandrenses filium eius honorificè receperunt, sibiq; filiam regis Angliæ desponsantes. Ille autem opportunitate capta, ad Francum redijt, dicens: Se nolle ducere illius filiam, qui sibi patrem occidisset. Flandrenses autem marchionē Iuliacensem in fauorem Angli, & filiæ, in Capitaneum receperunt. Misit autē Anglus pro duce Geldriæ, filio sororis suæ, qui filiā ducis Brabantiæ, pmisit ducere in vxorē, sibi iuueni non audenti contradicere, filiam eiusdem marchionis Iuliacensis desponsans. Verum ipse dux Gelriæ & comes Flandriæ cum filiabus ducis Brabātiæ matrimonium contraxerunt. Idem q; dux Brabantiæ duobus filijs suis, primogenito scilicet, filiam Ioannis ducis Normanniæ, primogeniti Franci: secundo verò, filiam ducis de Bourbon, sororem relictæ Bohemi, in matrimonium copulauit. Direxit autem Anglus gentem in Scotiam pro disponendis rebus regis capti, sororij ipsius Angli, quibus se quibusdam terrigenis opponentibus de instinctu Franci, multi iterum capti sunt & occisi.
units.tr: When the Count of Flanders had been killed in battle the previous year, the Flemings honourably received his son and betrothed to him the daughter of the king of England. He, however, seizing the opportunity, returned to the French king, saying that he was unwilling to marry the daughter of the man who had killed his father. The Flemings then received the margrave of Jülich as their captain, in favour of the Englishman and his daughter. The Englishman sent for the duke of Guelders, his sister's son, who was permitted by the duke of Brabant to marry his daughter; the young man did not dare to refuse, and he betrothed himself to the daughter of the same margrave of Jülich. But in fact the duke of Guelders and the count of Flanders contracted marriages with the daughters of the duke of Brabant. The same duke of Brabant also joined in marriage two of his sons: the eldest to the daughter of John, duke of Normandy, the eldest son of the French king, and the second to the daughter of the duke of Bourbon, sister of the late Bohemian. The Englishman, moreover, sent troops into Scotland to arrange the affairs of the captured king, the brother-in-law of the Englishman; some of the native people opposed them at the instigation of the French king, and many were again taken and killed.

units.la: Perseuerante autem Anglo in obsidione Kales ferè per annum & nolente eam recipere ad gratiam quoquo modo: strinxerat enim eam in tantum, quòd nec introitus nec exitus patebat. Ad eam tandem Francus (qui interdum per se, interdum per Ioannem filium suum pluries congregauit exercitus, sed Angli exercitum non accessit) in principio Augusti appropinquauit exercitus Angli & Flandrensium ad vnam leucam. Quapropter etiam nolente Anglo, Flandrenses Cales ad gratiam receperunt, & forenses & intrinsecos Angli gratiæ commiserunt. Quod cernens Francus per tres leucas illico retrocessit. Anglus autem eiectis incolis & occupatis thesauris, ciuitatem Cales rexit per Anglos. Data sunt autem ei tam per Sedem Apostolicam, quàm per Franci terram LXXX millia marcarum argenti, quòd inducias vsq; ad festum natiuitatis beati Ioannis Baptistæ ex tunc concessit, ita quòd in statu, quo nunc fuerunt, quilibet remaneret.
units.tr: While the Englishman persisted in the siege of Calais for almost a year, unwilling to receive it back to favour in any way (for he had so pressed it that neither entry nor exit was open), the Frenchman (who at times gathered armies himself and at times through his son John, but did not bring his army to the Englishman's) approached Calais at the beginning of August with an army of the English and Flemings, to within one league. Therefore, although the Englishman was unwilling, the Flemings received Calais back into favour, and the English committed both the outsiders and the insiders to grace. Seeing this, the Frenchman at once withdrew three leagues. The Englishman, however, expelled the inhabitants, seized the treasures, and ruled the city of Calais through Englishmen. Eighty thousand marks of silver were given to him, both by the Apostolic See and from the land of France, on condition that from then on he would grant a truce until the feast of the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, so that each would remain in the state in which they now were.

units.la: Eodem anno M. CCC. XLVII, de mense Septembri, cùm ingressi fuissent Stephanus, filius Ludouici Principis, & omnes ciuitates Sueuiæ cum eo iuxta Zolre, animo Inuadêdi Barones, quorū octodecim priori anno in Oberendorff ducis de Decke coiurauerant, & qui Carolum electum dicebantur fouere: oppidum Hechingen comitis de Zolre vacuum inuenerunt, quod quibusdam pactis initis nõ fregerunt. Volentibus autê eis obsidere oppidum Sulz, Waltheri de Geroltsecke, seruitoris & consanguinei Comitum de Wirtenberg, ijdem comites quamuis essent præsides Principis, asserentes hæc sine eorum consilio inchoata, restituerunt, quibus & eidem Waltehro tanta affluxit nobilium multitudo in auxilium, quòd ciuitates Sueuiæ recesserunt de campo.
units.tr: In the same year, 1347, in September, Stephen, son of Prince Louis, entered the territory near Zollern with all the cities of Swabia, intending to attack the barons. Eighteen of these barons had conspired the year before at Oberndorf with the Duke of Teck, and they were said to favour Charles the elected king. They found the town of Hechingen, belonging to the Count of Zollern, empty, and did not break into it because of certain agreements made. When they wished to besiege the town of Sulz, Walter of Geroldseck, servant and kinsman of the Counts of Württemberg, was restored to them by those same counts, who, though they were the Prince's protectors, declared that these things had been begun without their counsel. So great a crowd of nobles flowed to the aid of Walter that the cities of Swabia withdrew from the field.

units.la: Erant autê duo fratres habentes munitionem iuxta syluam Bohemiæ, principis seruitores, nominati Rammerouwer, quorū iunior dicens, sibi principem nil dare, Caroloni Bohemiæ se obstrinxit. Princeps verò seniorem innocentem capiens, decollauit.
units.tr: There were two brothers, named Rammerouwer, who held a fortress near the Bohemian forest and were servants of the Prince. The younger of them, saying that the Prince gave him nothing, bound himself to Charles of Bohemia. The Prince seized the elder, who was innocent, and had him beheaded.

units.la: Eo tempore Ioanna ducissa Austriæ veniens Alsatiam, se Argentinensi, Basiliensi & Constantiensi episcopis, item Thuricensibus & Bernensibus colligauit, & cū Ottone de Ochsenstein, quòd resignauit Thanne & Sennheim, de quibus Berchtoldus episcopus Argentinensis ipsam inuestiuit, amicabiliter comportauit: quæ in reditu ad Austriam Ludouicum principem visitans, ab eo honorificè est recepta.
units.tr: At that time Joanna, Duchess of Austria, came into Alsace and allied herself with the bishops of Strasbourg, Basel and Constance, and likewise with the people of Zurich and Bern. She also came to a friendly arrangement with Otto of Ochsenstein, who resigned Thann and Sennheim, which Berthold, bishop of Strasbourg, had conferred on her. On her return to Austria she visited Prince Louis, and he received her with honour.

units.la: Eo tempore Humbertus Delphini, qui per annum steterat inter Curtos, defuncta sibi vxore, nepte quondam Ruperti regis ex sorore, infecto negotio est reuersus. Papa enim iuxta promissum suum, nec thesaurū nec gentem misit eodem. Rex enim Curtorum, cùm venisset Delphinus in terram suam, in quandam ciuitatē fortem per Christianos obtentam, ex quo nomine ecclesiæ venerat, suspicatus eum magnam habituram sequelā, treugas fecit cum eo, animo visitandi personam: & intelligens q; absq; Alemannis venerit, nec ex facto imperij cernebat mulieb̃re personam, ipsumq; paruipendens recessit, & magis ex aduentu eius animosus factus est.
units.tr: At that time Humbert, the Dauphin, who had stayed for a year among the Curti, returned without accomplishing his business, his wife having died. She was a niece, through her sister, of the former King Rupert. The Pope, despite his promise, sent neither money nor men. When the Dauphin came into the king's land, into a certain strong city held by Christians, from which he had come in the name of the Church, the king of the Curti, suspecting that he would have a large following, made a truce with him, intending to visit his person. Understanding that he had come without Germans, and seeing nothing of the imperial power in a woman's person, the king made light of him and withdrew, and became the more bold because of his arrival.

units.la: Eodem anno princeps Ludouicus in venatione vrsi, in syluis iuxta Monacum, paralysi percussus de equo corruens, expirauit, anno Domini M. CCC. XLVII, quinto Idus Octobris, anno regni sui XXXIII finito minus octo diebus, Imperij verò XIX.
units.tr: In the same year, Prince Louis, while hunting bear in the woods near Munich, was struck by paralysis, fell from his horse and died on 11 October 1347, in the thirty-third year of his reign less eight days, and the nineteenth of his imperial rule.

units.la: Egressus est itaq; de Bohemia, cum magno equitatu, in Bauariam, animo inuadê di terram Ludouici Principis, Carolus rex Bohemiæ, electus in regem Romanorum, filius quondam Ioannis regis Bohemiæ, nepos quondam Henrici de Luxelburg Romanorum Imperatoris: itē pronepos ex filia & nepte Rudolfi de Habspurg, Romanorum regis: itē nepos ex filia quondam Wenceslai Bohemorū regis, proneposq; Ioannis ducis Brabatiæ, sororius Philippi regis Franciæ: cuiusq; Philippi primogenitus Ioanes dux Normandiæ ipsius Caroli est sororius: ipse Carolus socer Caroli regis Hungariæ, socerq; Rudolfi ducis Austriæ: & veniens in terrā ipsius Ludouici Bauariā, intellecta morte Principis, Ratisponam perrexit, vbi tanquam rex Romanorum illico est receptus. Deinde veniens Nurnberg, ac grauibus factis promissionibus Burggrauio ibidem, quem euadere non potuit, in Nurnberg est receptus.
units.tr: Thereupon Charles, king of Bohemia, elected king of the Romans, set out from Bohemia with a great cavalry force and entered Bavaria, intending to attack the lands of Prince Louis. He was the son of the late John, king of Bohemia, and grandson of the late Henry of Luxembourg, Roman emperor. He was also great-grandson, through a daughter and granddaughter, of Rudolf of Habsburg, king of the Romans; grandson through a daughter of the late Wenceslas, king of the Bohemians; and great-grandson of John, duke of Brabant, brother-in-law of Philip, king of France. Philip's firstborn, John, duke of Normandy, is Charles's brother-in-law. Charles himself is father-in-law of Charles, king of Hungary, and father-in-law of Rudolf, duke of Austria. On entering the land of Louis in Bavaria and learning of the Prince's death, he went on to Regensburg, where he was at once received as king of the Romans. Then he came to Nuremberg, and after making heavy promises to the burgrave there, whom he could not evade, he was received in Nuremberg.

units.la: Miserunt autem Eberhardus & Vlricus fratres, comites de Wirtenberg, secretarios suos singulos ad regem, & ad Ludouicum marchionem in Brandenburg, quærentes, cuius eorum se seruitio obligarent: & reuertentibus secretarijs priùs ad regem missis, ipsi comites cautione recepta de LXX millibus florenorū, eius se seruitio astrinxerunt. De quo alij secretarij à Marchione venientes, & pactum de centum millibus florenorum afferentes, comites plurimùm sunt commoti. Duoq; fratres de Hohenlohe, vnus Bambergensis episcopus, alter Herbipolensem tenens episcopatum contra Albertum de Hohenberg, Sedis apostolicæ prouisum, similiter se regis seruitio astrinxerunt.
units.tr: The brothers Eberhard and Ulrich, counts of Württemberg, sent their secretaries, one each, to the king and to Louis, margrave of Brandenburg, asking to which of them they should bind their service. When the secretaries first sent to the king returned, the counts, having received security for 70,000 florins, bound themselves to his service. Other secretaries then came from the margrave, bringing an agreement for 100,000 florins, and the counts were much disturbed by this. The two brothers of Hohenlohe, one the bishop of Bamberg and the other holding the bishopric of Würzburg against Albert of Hohenberg, who had been provided by the Apostolic See, likewise bound themselves to the king's service.

units.la: Interea Berchtoldus episcopus Argentinensis, conuenientibus Argentinæ Ciuitatibus & Baronibus ligæ Alsatiæ, ipsius regis commendationi insistens, ac se eum mantenturum affirmans, cùm & omnes de Liechtenberg sibi fauerent, ciuitates Alsatiæ, timentes infringi ligam pacis, quasi inuitos ad eius obedientiam inclinauit, sicque Argentinæ etiam honorificè est receptus, ipsum episcopum in gradibus ecclesiæ, indutus regalibus insignibus, habens coronam auream in capite, & pomum & sceptrum in manibus, de suis regalibus, præstito sibi homagio, solenniter inuestiuit. Deinde per ciuitates imperij Elsatię, quæ & singulę eum receperant, Basileam ascendit. Spopondit enim ciuitatibus, se relaxationem processuum Papalium curaturum.
units.tr: Meanwhile Berthold, bishop of Strasbourg, met with the cities of Alsace and the barons of the Alsatian league. Insisting on the king's recommendation, and affirming that he would maintain him, since all of Liechtenberg favoured him, he inclined the cities of Alsace, who feared that the league of peace would be broken, towards obedience to the king, as though they were unwilling. So the king was honourably received at Strasbourg too. The bishop, clothed in royal insignia, with a golden crown on his head and an orb and sceptre in his hands, was solemnly invested with his regalia, and homage was rendered to him. Then he went up to Basel through the imperial cities of Alsace, each of which had received him. For he promised the cities that he would take care to have the Papal processes revoked.

units.la: Interea Conradus de <bl>Kirckel</bl> minister Maguntinę sedis ac Treuerensis omnimodam concordiā tractauerunt, inter H. archiepiscopū Moguntinum ac Regē, & Treuerensem archiepiscopum, oppidaq; Imperialia in Wederaugia, Gerlacūq; de <bl>Wassove</bl>, prouisum sedis Apostolicæ cōpetenter prouiderant in vita: H. destituto post eius morte ipsam sedem habituru quiete. Verum ipse Gerlacus de potētia & adiutorio Caroli confidēs, negotio infecto ascendit Argentinam. Quod videntes H. Moguntinus, Conradus minister eius & prædicta oppida, se liberis defuncti Principis colligarunt, quod totum, si de Argentina descendisset Carolus rex, celeriter expeditū fuisset.
units.tr: Meanwhile Conrad Kirckel, minister of the sees of Mainz and Trier, negotiated complete concord between H., archbishop of Mainz, the king, and the archbishop of Trier, and the imperial towns in the Wetterau. Gerlach of Wassove, who had been provided by the Apostolic See, had been suitably provided for during his life, and H. was to have the see in peace after his death. But Gerlach himself, trusting in the power and help of Charles, went up to Strasbourg without concluding the business. Seeing this, H. of Mainz, his minister Conrad, and the aforesaid towns allied themselves with the children of the deceased Prince. The whole matter would have been quickly settled had King Charles come down from Strasbourg.

units.la: Venit autem Rex Basileam, in vigilia Thomæ, anno Domini M. CCC. XLVIII, vbi interdictum Papale diu seruatum fuit, nec Basilienses eum recipere intenderant, nisi diuina rehaberent. Et ecce in sero venit Marquardus de Randecke prępositus Babenbergensis de Curia Auinionensi, ferens commissionem factam Babenbergensi episcopo, & absolutionibus & relaxationibus impendendis, & vnam clausam bullam regi directam: & gauisus rex misit illico & Argentinensi, Basiliensi, Babenbergensi Herbipolensi episcopis, præsentibus.
units.tr: The king came to Basel on the eve of St Thomas in the year of the Lord 1348, where the papal interdict had long been observed. The Baslers had intended not to receive him unless they recovered divine services. And behold, in the evening Marquard of Randeck, provost of Bamberg, came from the Avignon court, bringing a commission made to the bishop of Bamberg for granting absolutions and relaxations, and one sealed bull addressed to the king. The king rejoiced and at once sent for the bishops of Strasbourg, Basel, Bamberg and Würzburg to be present.

units.la: In clausa autem Bulla hortabatur Papa regem, vt auerteret Carolum regem Vngariæ generum suum, ne se colligaret prophano Nicolao Laurentij, vrbis Romæ tribuno. Exosus enim erat Papæ Tribunus, quia eum vocauerat ad residendum in vrbe. In clausis etiam literis misit copiam literę per Tribunum Papæ directæ, in qua Tribunus eum per Papam de plurib. fuisset argutus, respondit inter alia: Se terram S Petri, animo defendēdi à tyrannis, tenere, seq; quasi inuitum ad tribunatum assumptū, nec oportere Papam procedere contra ipsum, vt officium ipsum dimittat, quod dimittere quantum in eo est, asseruit se paratum. Cūm autē antiquitus Romani habuerint Patricios, Senatores præfectos, tribunos, & multos officiatos, quis eis inhibuerit, tales hodie habere? quæsiuit. Cūm & honore dignos olim varijs coronis insigniuerint: quis eos arguet, quòd ipsum Tribunum Laurea & quibusdam coronis aliis coronauerint? Nec mirum, quòd in concha marmorea Constantini Imperatoris se lauari permisit, in qua Paganus extitit baptizatus, cūm in ipsius Tribuni lauacro plura fuerint signa facta, quàm in Constantini baptismo: prosequendo mirabilia de pace & tranquillitate vrbis & patriæ, quæ breui tempore suo asseruit diuino intuitu esse facta, cum tempore promotionis suæ, tā de dote vxoris, quàm de calamo suo vix habuit quinquaginta florenos, & in persona sua plura operatus fit, quàm Bonifacius Papa cum thesauro suo, vel Carolus Magnus cum sua potentia, procurârint. Argutus etiam quòd in citatione qua coram se & Romanis citauit Ludouicum ducem Bauariæ, & Carolum regem Bohemię, se intromittentes de regno Romano, Bauarum ducē nominauit, cūm per Papam Ducatu fuerit priuatus: Bohemum verò Romanorum regem non nominauerit, quamuis fuerit in regem Romanorum per sedem Apostolicam approbatus; respondit: Se non magnam de huiusmodi titulis vim fecisse, cūm & olim Romani sibi colligarint principes & amicos: cur & hodie regi Vngariæ & alijs se colligare non deberent, non videret: pluraq; alia seriosa rescripsit.
units.tr: In the sealed bull the Pope urged the king to turn away Charles, king of Hungary, his son-in-law, from allying himself with the profane Nicholas, son of Laurence, tribune of the city of Rome. The tribune was hateful to the Pope, because the Pope had summoned him to reside in the city. With the sealed letters the Pope also sent a copy of a letter addressed to him by the tribune. In it, the tribune, who had been much accused by the Pope on many points, answered among other things that he held the land of St Peter in order to defend it from tyrants, that he had been raised to the tribunate against his will, and that the Pope ought not to proceed against him in order to make him give up the office; he declared himself ready to give it up, so far as lay in him. But since in antiquity the Romans had patricians, senators, prefects, tribunes and many officials, he asked, who forbade them to have such men today? Since they had also honoured worthy men with various crowns, who would accuse them of having crowned this tribune with a laurel and certain other crowns? Nor was it strange that he allowed himself to be washed in the marble basin of Emperor Constantine, in which the pagan had been baptized, since more signs had been wrought in this tribune's bath than at Constantine's baptism. He went on to speak of marvels concerning the peace and tranquillity of the city and country, which he asserted had been done in his short time by divine providence, although at the time of his elevation he scarcely had fifty florins, from his wife's dowry and from his own pen. More had been achieved through his person than Pope Boniface had brought about with his treasure, or Charles the Great with his power. He also objected that in the summons he issued before himself and the Romans against Louis, duke of Bavaria, and Charles, king of Bohemia, who meddled in the Roman kingdom, he named the Bavarian duke, though the Pope had deprived him of the duchy, but did not name the Bohemian as king of the Romans, although he had been approved as king of the Romans by the Apostolic See. He answered that he had not made much of such titles, since the Romans had formerly allied themselves with princes and friends. He did not see why they should not now ally themselves with the king of Hungary and others. He wrote back many other serious things.

units.la: Summa autem Commissionis, Babenbergensi episcopo factæ, talis erat:
units.tr: The substance of the commission given to the bishop of Bamberg was as follows:

units.la: Cūm multi, qui sententias, processus & pœnas Ioannis Papæ, influēti as adhærentibus quon-dam Ludouico de Bauaria hæretico, & de hæresi damnato, redire cupiant ad ecclesia vnitatem: committimus tibi, vt qui confessi fuerint errores suos, confessatos & non confessatos, & pœnas quas inciderunt explicitè vel implicitè, & iurauerint, deinceps fidem catholicam habe-re, & fideles fore sedi Apostolicæ: & nulli deinceps hæretico vel schismatico fauere, & credere quod non spectat ad Imperatorem, Papam deponere, & alium creare, sed hoc hæresim esse da-mnatam: & quòd nullum pro Imperatore habebunt, nisi per sedem Apostolicam probatum, nec relicta & liberis ipsius Ludouici fauebunt, nisi cum ecclesia reformentur, & Carolo Ro-manorum regi per sedem approbato parebunt, ab huiusmodi sententijs & pœnis absoluas, &c. ita quòd si in aliquo contrauenerint in sententias & pœnas pristinas relabantur: & quòd pro-curatoriorum & gestorum formam ipse Bambergensis Papæ rescriberet, sub publicis instru-mentis.
units.tr: Since many who wish to return to the unity of the Church, having been affected by the sentences, processes and penalties of Pope John against the adherents of the former heretic Ludwig of Bavaria, who was condemned for heresy, we commit to you that those who have confessed their errors, both those confessed and those not confessed, and the penalties they have incurred, explicitly or implicitly, and who have sworn that henceforth they will hold the Catholic faith and be faithful to the Apostolic See, and that they will favour no heretic or schismatic from now on, and will believe that it is not the business of the Emperor to depose the Pope and create another, but that this is a condemned heresy; and that they will acknowledge no one as Emperor unless he has been approved by the Apostolic See, nor will they favour the widow and children of Ludwig himself unless they are reformed by the Church, and that they will obey Charles, King of the Romans, approved by the See: you are to absolve from such sentences and penalties, etc., on the condition that if they act against any of these, they fall back into their former sentences and penalties; and that the Bishop of Bamberg himself is to write back to the Pope the form of the proxies and acts, under public instruments.

units.la: Visa autem forma huiusmodi dura, omnibus displicente, aliqui consuluerunt eam non acceptandam esse per Regem, sed occultandam, & pro alia forma Papæ scribendum. Sed quia timor erat Basilienses non iuraturos Regi, nisi reformarentur diuina, reticriptū oportuit exhiberi. Cùm autem ciues nec errores vellent fateri, nec secundū formam iurare, clerus autem quasi poenitens quòd cessault, etsi non tam occasione quæreret celebrandi, animo nunq; mandata similia receptandi: ecce comparuerunt Magistri & Consules Basilienses coram Rege, & prædictis Episcopis & multis de Capitulo Basiliensi: coram quibus Chunradus de Berenuels magister ciuitatis, nomine vniuersitatis vulgariter coram tabellione proposuit in hæc verba: Domine Bambergensis, sciatis, quòd nec fateri nec credere volumus, quòd quondam dominus noster Ludouicus Romanorum Imperator vnquâ fuerit hæreticus. Quemcunq; etiam nobis dederint Principes Electores, vel maior pars ex eis, pro Romanorum rege vel Imperatore, illum pro tali habebimus, etiamsi nunquam Papam requireret: nec quicq; aliud faciemus, quod sit contra iura Imperij quouis modo. Sed si habetis potestatem à do-mino Papa, quòd vultis nobis remittere omnia peccata nostra, placet. Et conuertens se ad populum, dixit: Datis mihi & Chunrado Monacho potestatem petendi, vt absoluamini à peccatis vestris? Qui dicebant: Placet nobis: nec aliud procuratorium habuerunt. Qui duo milites seorsum coram Secretario Papæ, Ioanne de pistorio præsente, iurauerunt secundum mandati formam: licq; relaxatis processibus diuina publicè sunt reassumpta, ciuesq; regi solitum præstiterunt iuramentum, sc. quòd ius suæ aduocatiæ seruarent. Basiliensis quoq; episcopus Ioannes Sennæ, & Abbas Morbacensis de re-galibus suis solenniter inuestiti sunt. Ciuitates autem, præsertim Argentina, exasperatæ fuerunt propter formā huiusmodi. Rex quoq; cum mulieribus Basiliensib. in choreis satis fatuos gestus habebat. In die quoq; sancto natiuitatis Domini, rex cōmunicatus fuit, legitq; in Missa galli cantu alta voce, habēs in manu euaginatū gladiū, euangeliū: Exiit edictum à Cæsare Augusto. In die Stephani aut à Basilea recedens, cùm crederetur cum sua gente iturus, clam ingressus nauiculam, cū paucis in Rheno descen-dens, in castro Burdtheim pernoctans, crastino transiens versus Ehenheim quasi la-tenter. Cùm autē gens sua descenderet per terram, eisq; in Alsatia & in Basilea multa fuissent abstracta: quidam valentes Bohemi se postremo ponentes in insidijs, præmiserunt duos, quorum vnus spadonem duxit ad manum. Ipsi verò transfuerunt per syluam, in loco qui dicitur Satellose. Et venerunt quidā nobiles Basilienses, ascendētes econtrà, q credebant, ducentē spadonem alicui abstulisse, ipsum abstulerunt eidem. Altera verò fugiens, dixit Bohemis: qui insequentes, alios captiuârunt, & Wernhe-rum de Eptingen Hospitalarium eis resistentem grauiter vulnerauerunt. A quo recepta cautione, de præsentando se regi, alios Mülhusen oppidum imperiale secū duxerunt. Amici autem captorum, cū noctu se circa Mülhusen posuissent, ac genti Regis transitus non esset securus, dimissi sunt captiui ad gratiam regis: Bohemiq; rege celeriter versus Hagenowe sunt secuti. Dedit autē & obligauit rex seruitorib. suis omnes vtilitates Alsatiæ, ita quòd inibi per diem non haberet expensas. Descendit etiam per Wizenberg versus Spiram, vbi sub quibusdam pactis extitit intromissus. Lectis autē ibi quibusdam processibus ex parte Gerlaci prouisi Moguntini, cōtra H. archiepiscopum & suos fautores, quorum aliqui domicilium Spirę habebant, de hoc populus ibi-dem est commotus. Postea rege veniente Wormatiam circa vesperas, conuenerunt clerus & consules ciuitatis, & quæsitum est à clero, num vellent absoluì? quid sentirēt de processibus? Qui cùm econtra quærerent à consulibus, quid ipsi sentirent: illisq; dicentibus, Se de illis nihil sentire, clerusq; diceret idipsum, animo nihil faciendi ab inuicem recesserunt. In crepusculo verò Collegia constituentes procuratores, singulares verò curati & clerici per se ipsos, & religiosi per procuratores, iuramentis præstitis, per Bambergensem absoluti fuerunt. Et cùm mane populus more solito vellet audire diuina, clerusq; nollet coram populo celebrare, factus est tumultus: clausisq; portis omnibus, populus ad hospitiū regis, ad quod Bambergensis confugerat, armatus accessit: Ipseq; Bambergensis mandante rege territo, omnem clerum & populum Wormatiensem sine omni conditione & iuramento absoluit: & statim omnis clerus, religiosus & se-cularis, contra iuramentum serò præstitum, publicè diuina resumpsit. Post hæc rex iuit Moguntiam, vbi sub pacto ne introduceret Gerlacum prouisum Papæ, vel aliquas legi-literas permitteret, honorifice est receptus. Vbi ad eum venerunt Balduinus Treuerensis, quasi latenter, cum paucis, vbi & noua receperant, quòd feria quinta præcedenti, sc. proxima post Epiphaniam Domini, anno M. CCC. XLVIII, procuratores & secretarij Ludouici Marchionis in Brandenburg, item ducum Palatinorum Rheni, Erici ducis Saxoniæ, & H. archiepiscopi Maguntini per Papam, tanquam electores principes maiorem partem facientes, in Eduardum regem Angliæ, habentem cum eis procuratorem & secretarium suum, in Romanum regē, ex opposito villæ Rens super Rhenum, sub castro Lonstein, concordauerunt eligendū, de hoc quoq; confecte sub sigillis eorundem principum literæ, in præsentia omniū inibi conuenientium, publicè legebātur, & quòd ipse Anglus se vellet intromittere, dicebatur, de quo & literæ à principibus ciuitatibus sunt directæ: ex quo in Germania turbatio magna est suborta. Nuncij autem Francofurtensium, à rege, inquirente eos super sui receptione, infecto negotio recesserunt: Sicq; rex cum timore Wormatiam à Moguntia est reuersus. Maneq; volens recedere, expectante omni gente sua armata ante hospitium suum, non pagatis hospitibus Curiæ & coquinæ suę: & diu expectante tota gente, iterum ad querelam vnius carnificis, regem arrestantis, ne discederet, factus est in populo tumultus. Promittentibus autem pluribus ne discederent hospitibus non pagatis, rex Spiram perrexit. Proscripto autem carnifice à Wormatia, ipse Spirę ad gratiam regis veniens, ad preces regias est resumptus.
units.tr: When this harsh form was seen, it displeased everyone, and some advised that it should not be accepted by the king but concealed, and that another form should be written for the Pope. But since there was fear that the people of Basel would not swear to the king unless divine services were restored, the rescript had to be shown. Since, however, the citizens would neither confess their errors nor swear according to the form, and the clergy, as if repentant that they had given way, though not seeking an occasion to celebrate and never intending in their hearts to accept such mandates, the masters and consuls of Basel came before the king, and before the aforesaid bishops and many from the chapter of Basel. There Conrad Berenfels, master of the city, speaking on behalf of the whole community, put forward in the vernacular, before a notary, these words: "Lord of Bamberg, you should know that we neither wish to confess nor to believe that our late lord Ludwig, Roman Emperor, was ever a heretic. Whomever the electoral princes, or the greater part of them, give us as Roman king or emperor, we will hold as such, even if he never asked the Pope; nor will we do anything contrary to the laws of the Empire in any way. But if you have power from the lord Pope to remit all our sins, we are pleased." And turning to the people, he said: "Have you given me and Conrad the monk the power to seek that you be absolved of your sins?" They said: "We are pleased," and they had no other proxy. These two knights swore separately before the Pope's secretary, John of Pistoia being present, according to the form of the mandate. The processes were then relaxed, divine services were publicly resumed, and the citizens gave the king the customary oath, namely that they would keep the rights of his advocacy. The bishop of Basel, John of Senn, and the abbot of Murbach were solemnly invested with their regalia. The cities, especially Strasbourg, were exasperated because of this form. The king also made rather foolish gestures in dances with the women of Basel. On the holy day of the Lord's Nativity, the king received communion, and while the cock was crowing he read the Gospel aloud at Mass, holding a drawn sword in his hand: There went out a decree from Caesar Augustus. On St Stephen's day, leaving Basel, while it was believed he would go with his people, he secretly boarded a small boat, and descending the Rhine with a few men, he spent the night in the castle of Burdtheim and the next day went on towards Ehenheim as if in secret. When his people came down by land, many things had been carried off from them in Alsace and in Basel. Some strong Bohemians, placing themselves last in an ambush, sent two ahead, one of whom led a eunuch by the hand. They themselves crossed through the forest at a place called Satellose. And some noble citizens of Basel came up to meet them, supposing that the eunuch leading someone had taken him away from him; they took him from the man. The other, fleeing, told the Bohemians; they pursued and took others captive, and they severely wounded Werner of Eptingen, the Hospitaller, who resisted them. From him, having taken a pledge that they would present themselves to the king, they led the others with them to the imperial town of Mulhausen. But when the friends of the captives had camped at night near Mulhausen, and the passage for the king's people was not safe, the captives were released into the king's favour; and the Bohemians quickly followed the king towards Hagenau. The king gave and pledged to his servants all the revenues of Alsace, so that they would have no expenses there for a day. He also descended through Wizenberg towards Speyer, where under certain agreements he was admitted. Then, certain processes from the side of Gerlach, provost of Mainz, against Archbishop H. and his supporters, some of whom had their homes in Speyer, were read there, and the people there were stirred up by this. Afterwards, when the king came to Worms about vespers, the clergy and the consuls of the city gathered, and the clergy were asked whether they wished to be absolved, and what they thought of the processes. When they in turn asked the consuls what they themselves thought, and the consuls replied that they thought nothing of them, and the clergy said the same, they withdrew from one another with no intention of doing anything. At twilight, however, the colleges appointed proxies, while individual parish priests and clerics acted for themselves, and the religious through proxies; after the oaths were sworn, they were absolved by the Bishop of Bamberg. And when in the morning the people, as usual, wished to hear divine services, and the clergy would not celebrate before the people, a tumult arose; all the gates were closed, and the armed people approached the king's lodging, to which the Bishop of Bamberg had fled. The Bishop of Bamberg, at the king's command and in fear, absolved all the clergy and people of Worms without any condition or oath; and at once all the clergy, religious and secular, contrary to the oath belatedly sworn, publicly resumed divine services. After this the king went to Mainz, where, under an agreement that he would not admit Gerlach, provost appointed by the Pope, nor permit any letters to be read, he was honourably received. There Baldwin of Trier came to him, secretly, with a few men, and there they received news that on the Thursday before, that is, the day after the Epiphany of the Lord, in the year 1348, the proxies and secretaries of Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg, likewise of the Palatine dukes of the Rhine, of Eric, Duke of Saxony, and of H., Archbishop of Mainz, appointed by the Pope, acting as the electoral princes forming the greater part, had agreed to elect Edward, King of England, who had his own proxy and secretary with them, as Roman king, opposite the village of Rhens on the Rhine, below the castle of Lahneck; a letter confirmed under the seals of the same princes was publicly read in the presence of all gathered there, and it was said that this Englishman wished to intrude himself; letters were also sent from the princes to the cities concerning this, and from this a great disturbance arose in Germany. The envoys of the Frankfurters, when asked by the king about their reception of him, withdrew with the business undone; and so the king, with fear, returned from Mainz to Worms. In the morning, wishing to leave, while all his armed people waited before his lodging, the king's court and kitchen had not been paid by their hosts, and while the whole company waited for a long time, a tumult again arose among the people over the complaint of a single executioner, who arrested the king so that he could not depart. But when many promised that the unpaid hosts would not be left unpaid, the king went on to Speyer. The executioner was banished from Worms, and he himself came to Speyer into the king's favour and was readmitted at the king's request.

units.la: Ascendente autem episcopo Argentinensi & baronibus Alsatiæ, qui descendebant, rex Sueuiam perrexit, animo fidelitatem à ciuitatibus Sueuiæ recipiendi, in quadragesima. Pergens autem Rotenburg comitum de Hohenberg, vbi hastiludiorū curia est indicta, & latenter sub armis Schilhardi de Rechberg haltiludens, per N. de lapide militem fuit in terram prostratus. Intelligens autem miles regem esse, equū sibi adraxit: quem rex LX marcis redemit. Mane autē volentib. illis diuidere per galeas torneamentū, & reperta cassidę sine signo, intellectoq; quòd regis esset, consilio inito per milites, à torneamento cessarunt. Dicebant enim, si periclitaretur nobiscū, posset dici in futurū, regem traditū fuisse per Sueuos. Veniens autem Vlmam ibidē à XXIIII Sueuiæ oppidis, sub quibusdā pactis iuramentis per ea pisitiis, est receptus. Volens autē ire Norēberg, & deinde Bohemiā, positis sibi insidijs per marchionē de Brandēburg, reuersus est Vlmā, & deinde per aliā viam veniens Norenberg, Bohemiā est reuersus.
units.tr: When the bishop of Strasbourg and the barons of Alsace, who were coming down, had gone up, the king set out for Swabia, intending to receive the allegiance of the Swabian cities, in Lent. Going to Rottenburg, of the counts of Hohenberg, where a tournament had been proclaimed, and jousting secretly under the arms of Schilhard of Rechberg, he was thrown to the ground by a knight, N. de Lapide. The knight, realizing that he was the king, took back his horse, which the king redeemed for sixty marks.
